tree.label: The bank balance sheet under Basel III
tree.desc: Every branch is a part of the book; every leaf carries the rules that govern it.

children.label: Assets and exposures
children.desc: What the bank owns or is owed. These drive risk-weighted assets, and therefore the capital requirement.

children.label: Credit risk — standardised approach
children.desc: The default method for measuring credit risk. Exposures are sorted into classes and each class carries a prescribed risk weight.

children.label: Sovereign exposures
children.desc: Central governments and central banks. Weights follow external ratings, with national discretion for domestic-currency exposures.

children.label: Public sector entities
children.desc: Non-central-government PSEs, weighted by reference to their sovereign or as banks.

children.label: Multilateral development banks
children.desc: MDBs meeting the eligibility criteria attract a 0% weight.

children.label: Bank exposures
children.desc: Claims on other banks, graded by the External Credit Risk Assessment Approach or the Standardised Credit Risk Assessment Approach.

children.label: Covered bonds
children.desc: Bonds secured on a ring-fenced cover pool, attracting preferential weights.

children.label: Securities firms and other financial institutions
children.desc: Treated as banks where subject to equivalent prudential standards, otherwise as corporates.

children.label: Corporate exposures
children.desc: Claims on companies.

children.label: General corporate
children.desc: Rated and unrated corporates.

children.label: Small and medium enterprises
children.desc: SMEs below the revenue threshold take a preferential weight; those meeting the retail criteria move to regulatory retail instead.

children.label: Specialised lending
children.desc: Project, object and commodities finance, where repayment depends on the asset financed.

children.label: Subordinated debt, equity and other capital instruments
children.desc: Weighted at 150% for subordinated debt and capital instruments other than equities.

children.label: Retail exposures
children.desc: Exposures to individuals and small businesses. Credit cards live here.
children.note: Basel's product criterion names credit cards, charge cards and overdrafts explicitly (CRE20.65(1)).

children.label: Regulatory retail criteria
children.desc: Three tests: the product criterion, a EUR 1m cap on aggregated exposure to one counterparty, and a 0.2% granularity limit.

children.label: Regulatory retail — transactors · 45%
children.desc: Cards repaid in full at every scheduled date for twelve months. The lowest retail weight in the framework.
children.note: No US regulatory report discloses the transactor split, so this weight cannot be evidenced from public filings.

children.label: Regulatory retail — revolvers · 75%
children.desc: Regulatory retail that is not transactor business. The default where transactor status cannot be shown.

children.label: Other retail · 100%
children.desc: Retail exposures failing the regulatory retail criteria.

children.label: Real estate exposures
children.desc: Exposures secured by immovable property, split by property type and by whether repayment depends materially on cash flows the property generates.

children.label: Regulatory residential real estate
children.desc: Owner-occupied and buy-to-let housing meeting the regulatory criteria; weight varies by loan-to-value.

children.label: Regulatory commercial real estate
children.desc: Commercial property meeting the regulatory criteria.

children.label: Other real estate
children.desc: Exposures secured by property that fail the regulatory criteria.

children.label: Land acquisition, development and construction
children.desc: ADC lending, weighted at 150% unless the residential carve-out applies.

children.label: Currency mismatch multiplier
children.desc: A 1.5x multiplier on unhedged retail and residential exposures where the borrower's income is in a different currency from the loan.

children.label: Defaulted exposures
children.desc: Exposures past due more than 90 days or otherwise in default, weighted at 100% or 150% depending on provisioning.

children.label: Other assets
children.desc: The residual bucket. Note that the US rule places credit-card loans here rather than in a retail class.

children.label: Counterparty credit risk and credit derivatives
children.desc: Exposures whose value depends on a counterparty's performance.

children.label: Due diligence requirements
children.desc: Banks must perform their own assessment rather than relying mechanically on external ratings.

children.label: Credit risk — internal ratings-based approach
children.desc: Banks with supervisory approval estimate their own risk parameters. Requires PD, LGD and EAD estimates that public filings do not contain.

children.label: Categorisation of exposures
children.desc: The IRB asset classes: corporate, sovereign, bank, retail, equity and purchased receivables.

children.label: Qualifying revolving retail exposures
children.desc: The IRB home of credit cards, split into transactors and revolvers, with its own asset correlation.

children.label: Retail risk components and functions
children.desc: PD, LGD and EAD estimation for retail, including drawdown behaviour on undrawn card lines.

children.label: Corporate, sovereign and bank exposures
children.desc: Foundation and advanced approaches for wholesale exposures.

children.label: Minimum requirements for IRB use
children.desc: Rating system design, validation, governance and the data history required for approval.

children.label: Credit risk mitigation
children.desc: What a bank may recognise to reduce an exposure: collateral, guarantees, credit derivatives and netting. These are the levers that cut RWA without shrinking the book.

children.label: Eligible collateral and haircuts
children.desc: The simple and comprehensive approaches, and the haircuts applied to collateral value.

children.label: Guarantees and credit derivatives
children.desc: Substitution of the protection provider's risk weight for the obligor's.

children.label: On-balance sheet netting
children.desc: Netting of loans against deposits with the same counterparty.

children.label: Maturity mismatch and currency mismatch
children.desc: Adjustments where protection matures before the exposure or is denominated differently.

children.label: Securitisation exposures
children.desc: Positions in securitised pools, whether retained as originator or bought as investor. Credit-card receivables are a common underlying.

children.label: Definitions and scope
children.desc: Traditional and synthetic securitisation, tranching, and what counts as a securitisation exposure.

children.label: Revolving securitisations and early amortisation
children.desc: Structures backed by revolving credit — credit cards above all — and the provisions that accelerate repayment when performance deteriorates.
children.note: The natural route for a card issuer to move receivables off balance sheet.

children.label: Significant risk transfer and operational requirements
children.desc: What an originator must demonstrate before it may stop holding capital against the underlying pool.

children.label: Implicit support
children.desc: Support beyond contractual obligation, which forces the bank back into holding capital against the whole pool.

children.label: Simple, transparent and comparable criteria
children.desc: The STC criteria that unlock preferential capital treatment.

children.label: Capital calculation hierarchy
children.desc: SEC-IRBA, SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA and the 1250% fallback.

children.label: High-quality liquid assets
children.desc: The unencumbered assets a bank holds to survive a thirty-day stress. The numerator of the Liquidity Coverage Ratio.

children.label: Characteristics and operational requirements
children.desc: What makes an asset liquid in stress, and the operational control the bank must demonstrate over it.

children.label: Level 1 assets
children.desc: Cash, central bank reserves and qualifying sovereign debt. No haircut, no cap.

children.label: Level 2A assets
children.desc: Certain sovereign, corporate and covered bonds. 15% haircut; Level 2 capped at 40% of the stock.

children.label: Level 2B assets
children.desc: Lower-rated corporates, some equities and RMBS. Heavier haircuts and a 15% cap.

children.label: Trading book and market risk
children.desc: Positions held with trading intent. Deliberately outside the scope of a credit-card study; the branch is here so the tree is structurally complete.

children.label: Operational risk
children.desc: Loss from failed processes, people, systems or external events. Measured from a business indicator plus an internal loss multiplier.

children.label: Liabilities and funding
children.desc: How the book is paid for. Funding stability determines both the liquidity requirement and how safely the asset side can be grown.

children.label: Deposits
children.desc: Retail and wholesale deposit funding, graded by how likely it is to run.

children.label: Retail deposits — stable · 3–5% run-off
children.desc: Insured deposits in a transactional relationship. The stickiest funding a bank has.

children.label: Retail deposits — less stable · 10%+
children.desc: Uninsured, high-value, rate-driven or internet-sourced retail deposits.

children.label: Small business customer deposits
children.desc: Treated as retail where aggregate funding from one customer is below EUR 1 million.

children.label: Wholesale — operational deposits · 25%
children.desc: Balances held for clearing, custody or cash management.

children.label: Wholesale — non-operational · 40% / 100%
children.desc: Corporate and sovereign funding without an operational relationship.

children.label: Funding from financial institutions · 100%
children.desc: Assumed to run in full within thirty days.

children.label: Secured funding and repo
children.desc: Repo and other collateralised borrowing, with run-off driven by the collateral's quality.

children.label: Net stable funding ratio
children.desc: A one-year constraint requiring stable funding against illiquid assets. Where the LCR governs a thirty-day shock, the NSFR governs the shape of the book.

children.label: Available stable funding
children.desc: Capital and liabilities weighted by how reliably they stay for a year.

children.label: Required stable funding
children.desc: Assets and off-balance-sheet exposures weighted by how hard they are to monetise. Undrawn commitments carry an RSF charge.

children.label: Interdependent assets and liabilities
children.desc: The narrow case where a matched pair may be excluded from both sides.

children.label: Off-balance sheet
children.desc: Promises to lend that have not been drawn. For a card issuer this is the largest exposure the bank has, and the one most easily overlooked.
children.note: Across the 50 small card banks in this study, undrawn commitments are several times the drawn book.

children.label: Credit conversion factors
children.desc: How an undrawn promise becomes a credit-equivalent exposure.

children.label: Unconditionally cancellable commitments · 10% CCF
children.desc: Commitments the bank may cancel at any time without notice. Credit-card lines are the archetype.
children.note: Basel applies 10%; the US rule in force applies 0% (12 CFR 217.33(b)(1)). This single divergence is the largest in the study.

children.label: Other commitments · 40% CCF
children.desc: Commitments that cannot be cancelled at will, regardless of maturity.

children.label: Direct credit substitutes · 100% CCF
children.desc: Guarantees, standby letters of credit and acceptances that stand in for direct lending.

children.label: Transaction-related contingents · 50% CCF
children.desc: Performance bonds, bid bonds and warranties.

children.label: Trade-related contingents · 20% CCF
children.desc: Short-term self-liquidating letters of credit arising from the movement of goods.

children.label: Undrawn facilities under the liquidity standard
children.desc: The thirty-day drawdown assumed on committed lines. Unconditionally cancellable facilities are excluded from this section and left to national discretion.
children.note: LCR40.59 excludes unconditionally cancellable facilities, routing them to LCR40.67. The property that earns a card line a low conversion factor also removes it from the 5% drawdown.

children.label: Off-balance sheet in the leverage exposure measure
children.desc: The leverage ratio converts the same commitments, but with its own floor, so it can bind where the risk-based ratio does not.

children.label: Capital
children.desc: What absorbs loss. The constraint every asset-side decision ultimately runs into.

children.label: Common Equity Tier 1
children.desc: Common shares, retained earnings and disclosed reserves. The highest-quality capital and the binding constraint in practice.
headings: Common shares issued by the bank

children.label: Additional Tier 1
children.desc: Perpetual instruments subordinated to depositors, with fully discretionary coupons.

children.label: Tier 2
children.desc: Gone-concern capital: subordinated debt with a minimum original maturity of five years.

children.label: Regulatory adjustments and deductions
children.desc: Goodwill, deferred tax assets, holdings in other financial institutions and the threshold deductions.

children.label: Minimum capital ratios
children.desc: CET1 at least 4.5% of RWA, Tier 1 at least 6%, total capital at least 8%, at all times.

children.label: Buffers above the minimum
children.desc: The capital conservation buffer, the countercyclical buffer and the G-SIB surcharge. Eroding them constrains distributions rather than breaching a minimum.

children.label: Capital conservation buffer · 2.5%
children.desc: CET1 held above the minimum; falling into the range caps dividends, buybacks and bonuses.

children.label: Countercyclical buffer · 0–2.5%
children.desc: Raised by national authorities when credit growth runs ahead of the economy.

children.label: Systemic surcharges
children.desc: Additional CET1 for global and domestic systemically important banks.

children.label: Transitional arrangements
children.desc: Phase-in and grandfathering of instruments that no longer qualify.

children.label: Constraints that cut across the book
children.desc: Requirements that do not attach to one asset class but bind the balance sheet as a whole.

children.label: Leverage ratio
children.desc: Tier 1 capital over a non-risk-weighted exposure measure, at least 3%. A backstop that bites hardest on banks whose assets carry low risk weights.

children.label: Liquidity coverage ratio
children.desc: HQLA over net thirty-day stressed outflows, at least 100%. The requirement itself; its inputs sit under Assets and Liabilities.

children.label: Large exposures and concentration
children.desc: A cap of 25% of Tier 1 capital on exposure to a single counterparty or group of connected clients.

children.label: Supervisory review — Pillar 2
children.desc: Where the supervisor judges risks the formulas miss.

children.label: Credit risk management and provisioning
children.desc: Underwriting standards, expected credit loss practice and the adequacy of allowances.

children.label: Concentration risk
children.desc: Risk from correlated exposures that individually sit inside every limit.

children.label: Interest rate risk in the banking book
children.desc: Economic value and earnings sensitivity to rate moves.

children.label: Liquidity monitoring metrics
children.desc: Contractual maturity mismatch, funding concentration and available unencumbered assets.

children.label: Stress testing and ICAAP
children.desc: The bank's own assessment of capital adequacy under adverse conditions.

children.label: Disclosure — Pillar 3
children.desc: What must be published. This determines what an outside analyst can see at all.

children.label: Scope and proportionality
children.desc: Which banks the framework binds, how groups are consolidated, and how requirements scale with size and systemic importance.

R-LEV20.7-minimum-3pct.title: 3% minimum leverage ratio at all times
R-LEV20.7-minimum-3pct.statement: A bank must maintain a leverage ratio (Tier 1 capital / total leverage ratio exposure measure) of at least 3% at all times.
R-LEV20.7-minimum-3pct.quote: Banks must meet a 3% leverage ratio minimum requirement at all times.

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks. In the US the 3% supplementary leverage ratio (12 CFR 217 subpart B) applies only to advanced-approaches/Category I-III firms; small banks instead face a 4% generic tier 1 leverage ratio and, if opted in, the 9% community bank leverage ratio. The 3% figure is therefore the Basel benchmark, not the binding US number for a small bank.

R-LEV20.7-minimum-3pct.portfolio_relevance: This is the non-risk-based backstop: because the denominator is unweighted, shifting the book toward low-risk-weight assets (agency MBS, cash, sovereigns) relieves RWA-based ratios but not this one, so it becomes the binding constraint exactly when a bank de-risks. Conversely, a shift into credit cards raises RWA sharply while adding the same denominator per dollar of on-balance-sheet balance.

R-LEV20.3-ratio-definition.title: Definition of the leverage ratio
R-LEV20.3-ratio-definition.statement: The leverage ratio equals the capital measure (numerator) divided by the exposure measure (denominator), expressed as a percentage.
R-LEV20.3-ratio-definition.quote: The leverage ratio is defined as the capital measure (the numerator) divided by the exposure measure (the denominator), with this ratio expressed as a percentage:

applies_to.note: Structural definition; no proportionality gate.

R-LEV20.3-ratio-definition.portfolio_relevance: Fixes the computable form of the constraint: any portfolio change is evaluated as a change in the unweighted denominator versus Tier 1 capital, so asset growth of any risk quality dilutes the ratio one-for-one.

R-LEV20.4-capital-measure-tier1.title: Numerator is Tier 1 capital
R-LEV20.4-capital-measure-tier1.statement: The capital measure for the leverage ratio is Tier 1 capital (CET1 and/or Additional Tier 1) as defined in CAP10, measured on the same basis as under the risk-based framework.
R-LEV20.4-capital-measure-tier1.quote: The capital measure for the leverage ratio is Tier 1 capital – comprising Common Equity Tier 1 and/or Additional Tier 1 instruments – as defined in CAP10.

applies_to.note: Tier 2 capital does not count; a small bank that funds growth with subordinated debt qualifying only as Tier 2 gets no leverage-ratio relief.

R-LEV20.4-capital-measure-tier1.portfolio_relevance: Constrains the funding side of any portfolio expansion: only CET1 and AT1 raise the numerator, so retained earnings on a credit card book (high margin) directly buy leverage headroom while Tier 2 issuance does not.

R-LEV20.5-exposure-measure-components.title: Four components of the leverage ratio exposure measure
R-LEV20.5-exposure-measure-components.statement: The total leverage ratio exposure measure is the sum of on-balance sheet exposures (excluding on-balance sheet derivative and SFT exposures), derivative exposures, SFT exposures and off-balance sheet items.
R-LEV20.5-exposure-measure-components.quote: A bank's total leverage ratio exposure measure is the sum of the following exposures, as defined in LEV30: (1) on-balance sheet exposures (excluding on-balance sheet derivative and securities financing transaction exposures); (2) derivative exposures; (3) securities financing transaction exposures; and (4) off-balance sheet items.

applies_to.note: For a typical small North American bank components (2) and (3) are near zero, so the measure collapses to total assets plus CCF-weighted off-balance sheet items.

R-LEV20.5-exposure-measure-components.portfolio_relevance: Identifies the four addends a portfolio optimiser must model; for a card-heavy small bank the decisive term is component (4), the undrawn credit card lines converted at a CCF, which does not appear on the balance sheet at all.

R-LEV20.6-quarter-end-calculation.title: Quarter-end calculation of both measures
R-LEV20.6-quarter-end-calculation.statement: Both the capital measure and the exposure measure must be calculated on a quarter-end basis.
R-LEV20.6-quarter-end-calculation.quote: Both the capital measure and the exposure measure are to be calculated on a quarter-end basis.

applies_to.note: Quarter-end point-in-time measurement is what makes the rule checkable against published quarterly Call Report / FR Y-9C data.

R-LEV20.6-quarter-end-calculation.portfolio_relevance: A point-in-time quarter-end denominator means window-dressing is possible: drawing down or letting card balances run off before quarter end mechanically improves the ratio, which is precisely the behaviour LEV30.6 warns against.

R-LEV20.6-more-frequent-calculation.title: Optional more frequent (daily/monthly average) calculation subject to supervisory approval
R-LEV20.6-more-frequent-calculation.statement: A bank may, with supervisory approval, calculate the leverage ratio more frequently (e.g. daily or monthly averaging) provided it does so consistently.
R-LEV20.6-more-frequent-calculation.quote: However, banks may, subject to supervisory approval, use more frequent calculations (eg daily or monthly averaging) as long as they do so consistently.

applies_to.note: Explicit supervisory-approval gate. US small banks in practice use average total consolidated assets for the generic leverage ratio, which is the averaging variant.

R-LEV20.6-more-frequent-calculation.portfolio_relevance: Averaging removes the quarter-end window-dressing lever, so a bank on an averaging basis cannot temporarily shrink card balances or undrawn lines at period end to relieve the leverage constraint.

R-LEV20.1-backstop-purpose.title: Leverage ratio as non-risk-based backstop
R-LEV20.1-backstop-purpose.statement: The leverage ratio exists to restrict the build-up of leverage and to reinforce risk-based capital requirements with a simple, non-risk-based backstop measure.
R-LEV20.1-backstop-purpose.quote: reinforce the risk-based capital requirements with a simple, non-risk-based “backstop” measure.

applies_to.note: Statement of purpose; no proportionality gate.

R-LEV20.1-backstop-purpose.portfolio_relevance: Establishes the analytic premise of the whole domain: the leverage ratio is deliberately insensitive to risk weight, so it caps the total balance sheet a given Tier 1 base can support regardless of how the credit portfolio is composed.

R-LEV20.2-capture-on-and-off-bs.title: Leverage must capture both on- and off-balance sheet sources
R-LEV20.2-capture-on-and-off-bs.statement: The leverage measure is intended to capture both on-balance sheet and off-balance sheet sources of a bank's leverage.
R-LEV20.2-capture-on-and-off-bs.quote: the leverage should adequately capture both the on- and off-balance sheet sources of banks’ leverage.

applies_to.note: Rationale paragraph underpinning the OBS/CCF rules in LEV30.45-30.56.

R-LEV20.2-capture-on-and-off-bs.portfolio_relevance: Justifies charging undrawn credit card lines in the denominator: moving credit exposure off balance sheet (unfunded lines rather than funded balances) does not fully escape the leverage constraint.

R-LEV30.1-gross-accounting-values.title: Exposure measure follows gross accounting values
R-LEV30.1-gross-accounting-values.statement: The leverage ratio exposure measure generally follows gross accounting values.
R-LEV30.1-gross-accounting-values.quote: The leverage ratio exposure measure generally follows gross accounting values.

applies_to.note: Anchors the measure to reported accounting balances, which is what makes it computable from published quarterly financials.

R-LEV30.1-gross-accounting-values.portfolio_relevance: Means the denominator can be proxied from reported gross balance sheet totals, so any portfolio simulation can map dollar-for-dollar changes in loan balances into the leverage denominator without a risk-weight model.

R-LEV30.2-no-crm-no-netting.title: No credit risk mitigation or asset/liability netting in the exposure measure
R-LEV30.2-no-crm-no-netting.statement: Unless a specific provision says otherwise, a bank must not use physical or financial collateral, guarantees or other credit risk mitigation to reduce the leverage ratio exposure measure, and must not net assets against liabilities.
R-LEV30.2-no-crm-no-netting.quote: banks must not take account of physical or financial collateral, guarantees or other credit risk mitigation techniques to reduce the leverage ratio exposure measure, nor may banks net assets and liabilities.

applies_to.note: General prohibition; the derivative/SFT sections carve out narrow exceptions.

R-LEV30.2-no-crm-no-netting.portfolio_relevance: Removes every CRM lever that works under the risk-based framework: collateralising or guaranteeing a card or SME book cuts RWA but leaves the leverage denominator untouched, so a de-risking strategy built on collateral does nothing for this constraint.

R-LEV30.3-tier1-deduction-symmetry.title: Items deducted from Tier 1 may also be deducted from the exposure measure
R-LEV30.3-tier1-deduction-symmetry.statement: Any item (other than liability-related adjustments) that is deducted from Tier 1 capital under Basel III may also be deducted from the leverage ratio exposure measure.
R-LEV30.3-tier1-deduction-symmetry.quote: any item deducted from Tier 1 capital according to the Basel III framework and regulatory adjustments other than those related to liabilities may be deducted from the leverage ratio exposure measure.

applies_to.note: Prevents double-counting: an asset removed from the numerator may also leave the denominator.

R-LEV30.3-tier1-deduction-symmetry.portfolio_relevance: Makes goodwill, intangibles and deducted capital investments neutral to the ratio, so acquisitions financed by intangibles neither help nor hurt leverage headroom, unlike loan growth which fully consumes it.

R-LEV30.3-irb-provision-shortfall.title: IRB provision shortfall deducted from Tier 1 may be deducted from the exposure measure
R-LEV30.3-irb-provision-shortfall.statement: For IRB banks, the shortfall of eligible provisions relative to expected loss that CAP10.19 requires to be deducted from CET1 may also be deducted from the leverage ratio exposure measure.
R-LEV30.3-irb-provision-shortfall.quote: (2) for banks using the internal ratings-based (IRB) approach to determining capital requirements for credit risk, CAP10.19 requires any shortfall in the stock of eligible provisions relative to expected loss amounts to be deducted from CET1 capital. The same amount may be deducted from the leverage ratio exposure measure

applies_to.note: Approach-gated: only banks on IRB for credit risk. Effectively irrelevant to small North American banks, which are all on the standardised approach.

R-LEV30.3-irb-provision-shortfall.portfolio_relevance: An IRB card portfolio with expected loss above provisions is penalised twice in the numerator, and this rule restores symmetry in the denominator; a standardised small bank gets no equivalent relief.

R-LEV30.4-no-liability-deduction.title: Liability items must not be deducted from the exposure measure
R-LEV30.4-no-liability-deduction.statement: Liability items, including gains/losses on fair-valued liabilities and DVA-type adjustments from changes in the bank's own credit risk, must not be deducted from the leverage ratio exposure measure.
R-LEV30.4-no-liability-deduction.quote: Liability items must not be deducted from the leverage ratio exposure measure.

applies_to.note: No proportionality gate.

R-LEV30.4-no-liability-deduction.portfolio_relevance: Blocks the funding-side lever: a bank cannot shrink the leverage denominator by revaluing its own debt, so the only ways to create headroom are shrinking assets/commitments or raising Tier 1.

R-LEV30.5-securitisation-exclusion.title: Securitised exposures may be excluded only if risk transference is recognised
R-LEV30.5-securitisation-exclusion.statement: An originating bank may exclude securitised exposures from the leverage ratio exposure measure only if the traditional securitisation meets the CRE40.24 operational requirements for recognition of risk transference; retained securitisation exposures must still be included.
R-LEV30.5-securitisation-exclusion.quote: an originating bank may exclude securitised exposures from its leverage ratio exposure measure if the securitisation meets the operational requirements for the recognition of risk transference according to CRE40.24. Banks meeting these conditions must include any retained securitisation exposures in their leverage ratio exposure measure.

applies_to.note: Conditional on meeting CRE40.24 operational requirements; retained tranches and seller's interest never leave the measure.

R-LEV30.5-securitisation-exclusion.portfolio_relevance: This is the principal legitimate route for a card issuer to shrink the leverage denominator: securitising receivables removes them only if genuine risk transfer is achieved, and the retained seller's interest and credit-enhancing tranches stay in, capping the relief obtainable.

R-LEV30.5-non-qualifying-securitisation-.title: Non-qualifying and synthetic securitisations stay in the exposure measure
R-LEV30.5-non-qualifying-securitisation-.statement: Where a traditional securitisation fails the risk-transference operational requirements, or where the securitisation is synthetic, the securitised exposures must be included in the leverage ratio exposure measure.
R-LEV30.5-non-qualifying-securitisation-.quote: eg traditional securitisations that do not meet the operational requirements for the recognition of risk transference or synthetic securitisations, the securitised exposures must be included in the leverage ratio exposure measure.

applies_to.note: No proportionality gate.

R-LEV30.5-non-qualifying-securitisation-.portfolio_relevance: Closes the synthetic-securitisation escape: buying credit protection on a card book cuts RWA but leaves the full securitised balance in the leverage denominator, so a synthetic de-risking trade does nothing for the backstop.

R-LEV30.6-anti-avoidance-vigilance.title: Vigilance against exposure-measure-minimising structures
R-LEV30.6-anti-avoidance-vigilance.statement: Banks and supervisors should be particularly vigilant to transactions and structures whose effect is to inadequately capture the bank's sources of leverage, including moving assets off the balance sheet.
R-LEV30.6-anti-avoidance-vigilance.quote: Banks and supervisors should be particularly vigilant to transactions and structures that have the result of inadequately capturing banks’ sources of leverage.

applies_to.note: Qualitative anti-avoidance standard; enforced through Pillar 2 rather than a formula.

R-LEV30.6-anti-avoidance-vigilance.portfolio_relevance: This is the qualitative constraint on portfolio restructuring: any re-engineering whose primary effect is to shrink the leverage denominator without transferring risk (off-balance-sheet vehicles, agency-model transformations, collateral swaps) is explicitly flagged for supervisory challenge.

R-LEV30.6-pillar2-charge-for-avoidance.title: Supervisors may impose a Pillar 2 charge on leverage-minimising structures
R-LEV30.6-pillar2-charge-for-avoidance.statement: Where supervisors are concerned that transactions are not adequately captured in the exposure measure, they may require enhanced leverage management, additional reporting, and/or that the exposure be adequately capitalised through a Pillar 2 capital charge.
R-LEV30.6-pillar2-charge-for-avoidance.quote: Supervisory actions may include requiring enhancements in banks’ management of leverage, imposing operational requirements (eg additional reporting to supervisors) and/or requiring that the relevant exposure is adequately capitalised through a Pillar 2 capital charge.

applies_to.note: Discretionary supervisory action, not a computable formula; the list of actions is explicitly non-exhaustive.

R-LEV30.6-pillar2-charge-for-avoidance.portfolio_relevance: Adds a contingent capital cost to aggressive denominator management, so an optimiser should treat leverage-minimising restructurings as carrying an expected Pillar 2 add-on rather than as free headroom.

R-LEV30.7-central-bank-reserve-exemption.title: National discretion to exempt central bank reserves, with offsetting recalibration
R-LEV30.7-central-bank-reserve-exemption.statement: A jurisdiction may temporarily exempt central bank reserves from the exposure measure in exceptional macroeconomic circumstances, but must then increase the calibration of the minimum leverage ratio commensurately to offset the exemption.
R-LEV30.7-central-bank-reserve-exemption.quote: a jurisdiction may temporarily exempt central bank reserves from the leverage ratio exposure measure in exceptional macroeconomic circumstances. To maintain the same level of resilience provided by the leverage ratio, a jurisdiction applying this discretion must also increase the calibration of the minimum leverage ratio requirement commensurately to offset the impact of exempting central bank reserves.

applies_to.note: Explicit national-discretion gate, time-limited and conditional on recalibrating the minimum upward. The US applied a comparable temporary SLR reserve/Treasury exclusion in 2020-2021.

numeric_values: temporary exemption of central bank reserves
commensurate increase in the minimum leverage ratio calibration
R-LEV30.7-central-bank-reserve-exemption.portfolio_relevance: Directly changes the leverage cost of holding cash at the central bank: when active, parking liquidity in reserves stops consuming leverage capacity, which can flip the optimal mix between reserves and loan growth in a single quarter.

R-LEV30.8-all-balance-sheet-assets.title: All balance sheet assets included in the exposure measure
R-LEV30.8-all-balance-sheet-assets.statement: A bank must include all balance sheet assets in the leverage ratio exposure measure, including on-balance sheet derivatives collateral and SFT collateral, except on-balance sheet derivative and SFT assets covered by LEV30.13 to LEV30.44.
R-LEV30.8-all-balance-sheet-assets.quote: Banks must include all balance sheet assets in their leverage ratio exposure measure, including on-balance sheet derivatives collateral and collateral for SFTs, with the exception of on-balance sheet derivative and SFT assets that are covered in LEV30.13 to LEV30.44.

applies_to.note: For a small bank with negligible derivatives and SFTs this rule makes the denominator essentially equal to total assets plus off-balance sheet equivalents.

R-LEV30.8-all-balance-sheet-assets.portfolio_relevance: Sets the on-balance-sheet term of the denominator at total assets, so every incremental dollar of drawn credit card balance, mortgage or Treasury security consumes the same leverage capacity irrespective of risk weight.

R-LEV30.8-fiduciary-assets-excluded.title: Fiduciary assets excludable if derecognition criteria are met
R-LEV30.8-fiduciary-assets-excluded.statement: Fiduciary assets recognised on the balance sheet under the operative accounting framework may be excluded from the exposure measure if they meet the IFRS 9 derecognition criteria and, where applicable, IFRS 10 deconsolidation.
R-LEV30.8-fiduciary-assets-excluded.quote: Where a bank according to its operative accounting framework recognises fiduciary assets on the balance sheet, these assets can be excluded from the leverage ratio exposure measure provided that the assets meet the IFRS 9 criteria for derecognition

applies_to.note: Conditional on IFRS 9/IFRS 10 tests; US GAAP filers generally do not gross up fiduciary assets, so the relief is largely moot for US community banks.

R-LEV30.8-fiduciary-assets-excluded.portfolio_relevance: Lets a trust-heavy bank keep custodial balances out of the denominator, making fee-based fiduciary business a leverage-cheap way to grow revenue relative to expanding the loan book.

R-LEV30.9-accounting-value-less-specific.title: On-balance sheet non-derivative assets at accounting value less specific provisions
R-LEV30.9-accounting-value-less-specific.statement: On-balance sheet, non-derivative assets are included in the exposure measure at their accounting values less deductions for associated specific provisions.
R-LEV30.9-accounting-value-less-specific.quote: On-balance sheet, non-derivative assets are included in the leverage ratio exposure measure at their accounting values less deductions for associated specific provisions.

applies_to.note: Directly computable from net loans and leases in a Call Report.

R-LEV30.9-accounting-value-less-specific.portfolio_relevance: Means the leverage denominator uses net rather than gross carrying values, so building specific reserves on a deteriorating card book mechanically shrinks the denominator even as it reduces Tier 1 through earnings.

R-LEV30.9-general-provisions-deduction.title: General provisions that reduced Tier 1 may be deducted from the exposure measure
R-LEV30.9-general-provisions-deduction.statement: General provisions or general loan-loss reserves as defined in CAP10.18 which have reduced Tier 1 capital may be deducted from the leverage ratio exposure measure.
R-LEV30.9-general-provisions-deduction.quote: In addition, general provisions or general loan-loss reserves as defined in CAP10.18 which have reduced Tier 1 capital may be deducted from the leverage ratio exposure measure.

applies_to.note: Only the portion of general reserves that actually reduced Tier 1 (i.e. not the part re-included in Tier 2) qualifies.

R-LEV30.9-general-provisions-deduction.portfolio_relevance: Makes the leverage ratio approximately provision-neutral: a CECL build on a credit card portfolio cuts both numerator and denominator, so the ratio degrades far less than a naive Tier-1-only calculation would suggest.

R-LEV30.9-gp-definition-applies-to-all-b.title: CAP10.18 general-provision definition applies to SA and IRB banks alike for leverage
R-LEV30.9-gp-definition-applies-to-all-b.statement: For leverage ratio purposes, the CAP10.18 definition of general provisions/general loan-loss reserves applies to all banks regardless of whether they use the standardised or IRB approach for credit risk.
R-LEV30.9-gp-definition-applies-to-all-b.quote: for the purposes of the leverage ratio exposure measure the definition of general provisions/general loan-loss reserves specified in CAP10.18 applies to all banks regardless of whether they use the standardised approach or the IRB approach for credit risk for their risk- based capital calculations.

applies_to.note: Explicitly approach-agnostic: this is one of the few places the Framework says a definition binds SA and IRB banks identically.

R-LEV30.9-gp-definition-applies-to-all-b.portfolio_relevance: Guarantees that the provision-offset lever in the leverage denominator is available to a standardised small bank on exactly the same terms as to a large IRB bank, so provisioning policy is a size-neutral leverage lever.

R-LEV30.11-settlement-date-accounting-to.title: Settlement date accounting routed to the off-balance sheet treatment
R-LEV30.11-settlement-date-accounting-to.statement: Banks using settlement date accounting are subject to the off-balance sheet item treatment set out in LEV30.45 onwards rather than the on-balance sheet treatment.
R-LEV30.11-settlement-date-accounting-to.quote: Banks using settlement date accounting will be subject to the treatment set out in LEV30.45 to

applies_to.note: Accounting-election dependent; determines whether unsettled purchases enter as balance sheet assets or as 100% CCF commitments (LEV30.49(3)).

R-LEV30.11-settlement-date-accounting-to.portfolio_relevance: Shows the accounting election is not leverage-neutral: a settlement-date-accounting bank carries unsettled securities purchases as a 100% CCF off-balance sheet commitment, so a securities-buying programme consumes leverage capacity before it appears on the balance sheet.

R-LEV30.12-cash-pooling-daily-transfer.title: Daily-transfer cash pooling measured on the single net account balance
R-LEV30.12-cash-pooling-daily-transfer.statement: Where a cash pooling arrangement transfers participating customer balances into a single account at least daily and the bank is not liable for individual balances after transfer, the individual accounts are deemed extinguished and the single account balance is the basis of the exposure measure.
R-LEV30.12-cash-pooling-daily-transfer.quote: where a cash pooling arrangement entails a transfer at least on a daily basis of the credit and /or debit balances of the individual participating customer accounts into a single account balance, the individual participating customer accounts are deemed to be extinguished and transformed into a single account balance upon the transfer provided the bank is not liable for the balances on an individual basis upon the transfer.

applies_to.note: Conditional on a daily transfer frequency and on legal non-liability for individual balances. Materially relevant only to banks running commercial treasury/cash-management products; rare at small US community banks.

numeric_values: transfer at least on a daily basis
R-LEV30.12-cash-pooling-daily-transfer.portfolio_relevance: Rewards a commercial deposit franchise structured as a true daily-sweep pool: only the net pooled balance enters the denominator, so an SME treasury-services business can be grown with far less leverage consumption than the gross client balances imply.

R-LEV30.12-cash-pooling-failure-gross-up.title: Failed cash pooling conditions force gross inclusion of individual balances
R-LEV30.12-cash-pooling-failure-gross-up.statement: If the conditions for non-daily cash pooling are not met, the individual balances of the participating customer accounts must be reflected separately (gross) in the leverage ratio exposure measure.
R-LEV30.12-cash-pooling-failure-gross-up.quote: In the event the conditions below are not met, the individual balances of the participating customer accounts must be reflected separately in the leverage ratio exposure measure.

applies_to.note: Includes a supervisory judgement gate: the bank's supervisor must not deem the transfer frequency inadequate.

R-LEV30.12-cash-pooling-failure-gross-up.portfolio_relevance: Creates a cliff-edge in the denominator for cash-management products: losing the legal-enforceability or maturity-matching conditions converts a small net balance into a large gross one, potentially breaching the leverage constraint without any change in economic risk.

R-LEV30.13-derivative-two-components.title: Derivative exposure = replacement cost plus potential future exposure
R-LEV30.13-derivative-two-components.statement: For leverage ratio purposes, derivative exposures are included through two components: replacement cost (RC) and potential future exposure (PFE).
R-LEV30.13-derivative-two-components.quote: exposures to derivatives are included by means of two components: (1) replacement cost (RC); and (2) potential future exposure (PFE).

applies_to.note: Counterparty-credit component of the denominator; near-zero for a small North American bank with only customer interest-rate swaps.

R-LEV30.13-derivative-two-components.portfolio_relevance: Defines the derivative addend of the denominator; for a small bank this term is negligible, so leverage headroom is governed almost entirely by loans plus off-balance sheet commitments.

R-LEV30.14-alpha-1-4.title: Alpha multiplier of 1.4 on derivative RC plus PFE
R-LEV30.14-alpha-1-4.statement: A bank must calculate its derivative exposures as a scalar multiplier alpha of 1.4 times the sum of replacement cost and potential future exposure.
R-LEV30.14-alpha-1-4.quote: Banks must calculate their exposures associated with all derivative transactions, including where a bank sells protection using a credit derivative, as a scalar multiplier alpha set at 1.4 times the sum of the RC and the PFE

applies_to.note: No proportionality gate, but immaterial for banks with negligible derivative books.

R-LEV30.14-alpha-1-4.portfolio_relevance: Prices derivative activity at a 40% premium in the leverage denominator, making hedging via derivatives more leverage-expensive than the notional economics suggest and biasing small banks toward cash hedges.

R-LEV30.16-pfe-multiplier-one.title: PFE multiplier fixed at one for leverage purposes
R-LEV30.16-pfe-multiplier-one.statement: For the leverage ratio framework the PFE multiplier is fixed at one, removing the recognition of over-collateralisation and negative mark-to-market that the risk-based framework allows.
R-LEV30.16-pfe-multiplier-one.quote: For the purposes of the leverage ratio framework, the multiplier is fixed at one.

applies_to.note: Deliberate divergence from the risk-based SA-CCR treatment.

R-LEV30.16-pfe-multiplier-one.portfolio_relevance: Denies collateral-driven PFE relief in the denominator, so over-collateralising derivative positions improves risk-based ratios but not the leverage backstop.

R-LEV30.22-collateral-received-not-nette.title: Collateral received cannot reduce the derivative exposure measure
R-LEV30.22-collateral-received-not-nette.statement: A bank must not reduce its leverage ratio exposure measure by any collateral received from a derivative counterparty, whether or not netting is permitted under accounting or the risk-based framework.
R-LEV30.22-collateral-received-not-nette.quote: a bank must not reduce the leverage ratio exposure measure amount by any collateral received from the counterparty.

applies_to.note: Narrow exception only for qualifying cash variation margin under LEV30.24-30.25.

R-LEV30.22-collateral-received-not-nette.portfolio_relevance: Confirms that collateralisation is not a leverage-management tool; a bank cannot create headroom for loan growth by demanding more collateral on its derivative book.

R-LEV30.23-gross-up-collateral-provided.title: Gross-up for derivatives collateral provided
R-LEV30.23-gross-up-collateral-provided.statement: A bank must gross up its leverage ratio exposure measure by the amount of any derivatives collateral it has provided where posting that collateral reduced its balance sheet assets under the operative accounting framework.
R-LEV30.23-gross-up-collateral-provided.quote: banks must gross up their leverage ratio exposure measure by the amount of any derivatives collateral provided where the provision of that collateral has reduced the value of their balance sheet assets under their operative accounting framework.

applies_to.note: No proportionality gate.

R-LEV30.23-gross-up-collateral-provided.portfolio_relevance: Prevents shrinking the denominator by posting assets away as margin, so a bank cannot free leverage capacity for lending growth by pledging securities.

R-LEV30.31-written-credit-derivative-not.title: Written credit derivatives included at effective notional amount
R-LEV30.31-written-credit-derivative-not.statement: The effective notional amount referenced by a written credit derivative must be included in the leverage ratio exposure measure (subject to narrow client-clearing exclusions and defined offsets against purchased protection).
R-LEV30.31-written-credit-derivative-not.quote: the effective notional amount referenced by a written credit derivative is to be included in the leverage ratio exposure measure

applies_to.note: Offsets against purchased protection require same reference name, equal-or-longer maturity, same-or-more-conservative material terms and no wrong-way correlation.

R-LEV30.31-written-credit-derivative-not.portfolio_relevance: Treats sold credit protection as if it were a funded loan, so a bank cannot synthesise credit exposure (including to card or consumer reference pools) off balance sheet without consuming full leverage capacity.

R-LEV30.37-sft-principal-gross-plus-ccr.title: SFT exposure as principal: gross SFT assets plus a counterparty credit measure
R-LEV30.37-sft-principal-gross-plus-ccr.statement: A bank acting as principal must include in the exposure measure the sum of gross SFT assets recognised for accounting purposes (with no accounting netting) and a measure of counterparty credit risk calculated as current exposure without a PFE add-on.
R-LEV30.37-sft-principal-gross-plus-ccr.quote: General treatment (bank acting as principal): the sum of the amounts in LEV30.37 (1) and LEV30.37 (2) is to be included in the leverage ratio exposure measure

applies_to.note: Materially relevant only to banks with repo/securities lending books; typically near zero for small North American banks.

R-LEV30.37-sft-principal-gross-plus-ccr.portfolio_relevance: Repo funding is charged gross in the denominator, so financing a securities portfolio through repo consumes leverage capacity twice over (asset plus counterparty measure) relative to deposit funding.

R-LEV30.37-sft-cash-netting-conditions.title: SFT cash payable/receivable netting only under three strict conditions
R-LEV30.37-sft-cash-netting-conditions.statement: Cash payables and cash receivables in SFTs with the same counterparty may be measured net only if the transactions have the same explicit final settlement date, the set-off right is legally enforceable including in default, and the parties intend or are subject to net or functionally equivalent settlement.
R-LEV30.37-sft-cash-netting-conditions.quote: cash payables and cash receivables in SFTs with the same counterparty may be measured net if all the following criteria are met

applies_to.note: Open-ended transactions that can be unwound at any time are expressly ineligible, which excludes most evergreen repo.

R-LEV30.37-sft-cash-netting-conditions.portfolio_relevance: Restricts the only netting relief available in the SFT denominator to matched, same-date, legally enforceable positions, so a matched book strategy delivers leverage relief only when documented to this standard.

R-LEV30.40-sft-reverse-sale-accounting.title: Reverse sale accounting for SFTs achieving derecognition
R-LEV30.40-sft-reverse-sale-accounting.statement: Where sale accounting is achieved for an SFT, the bank must reverse all sales-related accounting entries and calculate the exposure as if the SFT had been a financing transaction.
R-LEV30.40-sft-reverse-sale-accounting.quote: where sale accounting is achieved for an SFT under the bank's operative accounting framework, the bank must reverse all sales-related accounting entries

applies_to.note: Anti-avoidance: accounting derecognition of an SFT does not achieve leverage derecognition.

R-LEV30.40-sft-reverse-sale-accounting.portfolio_relevance: Blocks the use of sale-accounting repo structures to move securities off the leverage denominator at quarter end, a classic window-dressing route.

R-LEV30.42-sft-agent-indemnity-treatment.title: Agent SFT with indemnity: only the counterparty credit measure applies
R-LEV30.42-sft-agent-indemnity-treatment.statement: A bank acting as agent in an SFT that indemnifies a customer only for the difference between the value lent and the collateral received, and that does not own or control the underlying cash or securities, calculates its exposure measure by applying only the LEV30.37(2) counterparty credit component.
R-LEV30.42-sft-agent-indemnity-treatment.quote: Where a bank acting as agent in an SFT provides an indemnity or guarantee to a customer or counterparty for any difference between the value of the security or cash the customer has lent and the value of collateral the borrower has provided and the bank does not own or control the underlying cash or security resource, then the bank will be required to calculate its leverage ratio exposure measure by applying only LEV30.37 (2).

applies_to.note: Conditional relief; if the bank provides no indemnity at all the SFT need not be recognised in the measure.

R-LEV30.42-sft-agent-indemnity-treatment.portfolio_relevance: Makes agency securities lending far cheaper in leverage terms than principal repo, which is why LEV30.6 flags principal-to-agency model conversion as a structure supervisors should scrutinise.

R-LEV30.43-sft-agent-further-exposure.title: Agent economically exposed beyond the guarantee must include the full amount
R-LEV30.43-sft-agent-further-exposure.statement: Where an agent bank is economically exposed beyond the guaranteed difference to the underlying security or cash, a further exposure equal to the full amount of that security or cash must be included in the leverage ratio exposure measure.
R-LEV30.43-sft-agent-further-exposure.quote: In situations where the bank is further economically exposed (ie beyond the guarantee for the difference) to the underlying security or cash in the transaction, a further exposure equal to the full amount of the security or cash must be included in the leverage ratio exposure measure.

applies_to.note: Carve-out for client omnibus accounts where collateral is segregated and exposure is computed client-by-client.

R-LEV30.43-sft-agent-further-exposure.portfolio_relevance: Caps the agency-model arbitrage: reinvesting or on-lending client collateral converts the cheap agency treatment into a full gross inclusion, eliminating the leverage advantage.

R-LEV30.45-obs-scope-definition.title: Scope of off-balance sheet items, including unconditionally cancellable commitments
R-LEV30.45-obs-scope-definition.statement: Off-balance sheet items for the leverage ratio include commitments (including liquidity facilities) whether or not unconditionally cancellable, direct credit substitutes, acceptances, standby letters of credit and trade letters of credit.
R-LEV30.45-obs-scope-definition.quote: OBS items include commitments (including liquidity facilities), whether or not unconditionally cancellable, direct credit substitutes, acceptances, standby letters of credit and trade letters of credit.

applies_to.note: Critical scope point: unconditionally cancellable commitments are inside the leverage exposure measure even though the US community bank leverage ratio denominator (average total consolidated assets) excludes off-balance sheet items entirely.

R-LEV30.45-obs-scope-definition.portfolio_relevance: This is the single most important scope rule for a card issuer: the entire undrawn credit card line book is an off-balance sheet item for leverage purposes even though card lines are contractually cancellable at will, so unused line growth consumes leverage capacity.

R-LEV30.45-obs-derivative-carve-out.title: OBS items accounted for as derivatives take the derivative treatment
R-LEV30.45-obs-derivative-carve-out.statement: If an off-balance sheet item is treated as a derivative exposure under the bank's accounting standard, it must be measured as a derivative exposure and the OBS/CCF treatment does not apply.
R-LEV30.45-obs-derivative-carve-out.quote: If the OBS item is treated as a derivative exposure per the bank's relevant accounting standard, then the item must be measured as a derivative exposure for the purpose of the leverage ratio exposure measure.

applies_to.note: Accounting-classification driven; prevents double counting between the OBS and derivative components.

R-LEV30.45-obs-derivative-carve-out.portfolio_relevance: Determines whether an unfunded facility is charged at a CCF or at 1.4 x (RC+PFE); mortgage rate-lock commitments accounted for as derivatives migrate out of the CCF grid entirely.

R-LEV30.46-ccf-applied-to-notional.title: CCFs applied to the notional amount of OBS items
R-LEV30.46-ccf-applied-to-notional.statement: For the leverage ratio, the CCFs set out in LEV30.49 to LEV30.56 must be applied to the notional amount of off-balance sheet items to determine their exposure amount.
R-LEV30.46-ccf-applied-to-notional.quote: For the purpose of determining the exposure amount of OBS items for the leverage ratio, the CCFs set out in LEV30.49 to LEV30.56 must be applied to the notional amount.

applies_to.note: The leverage CCF grid mirrors but is not identical to the CRE20 standardised grid; the leverage framework has no zero-CCF category.

R-LEV30.46-ccf-applied-to-notional.portfolio_relevance: Gives the exact conversion mechanism a model needs: OBS contribution to the denominator = notional x CCF, so the reported unused-commitment notional in a Call Report schedule maps directly into leverage consumption.

R-LEV30.47-undrawn-times-ccf.title: OBS conversion formula: committed but undrawn amount times CCF
R-LEV30.47-undrawn-times-ccf.statement: Off-balance sheet items are converted into credit exposures by multiplying the committed but undrawn amount by the applicable credit conversion factor.
R-LEV30.47-undrawn-times-ccf.quote: For the purposes of the leverage ratio, OBS items will be converted into credit exposures by multiplying the committed but undrawn amount by a CCF.

applies_to.note: The base is the undrawn amount only, so drawn balances are captured once through the on-balance sheet term.

numeric_values: exposure = committed but undrawn amount x CCF
R-LEV30.47-undrawn-times-ccf.portfolio_relevance: Defines the computable lever for a card book: leverage denominator from cards = drawn balances (100%) + undrawn lines x CCF, so line management (cutting unused limits) is a direct, immediate way to create leverage headroom without shedding earning assets.

R-LEV30.47-commitment-definition.title: Definition of commitment for leverage purposes
R-LEV30.47-commitment-definition.statement: A commitment is any contractual arrangement offered by the bank and accepted by the client to extend credit, purchase assets or issue credit substitutes.
R-LEV30.47-commitment-definition.quote: commitment means any contractual arrangement that has been offered by the bank and accepted by the client to extend credit, purchase assets or issue credit substitutes.

applies_to.note: Requires both offer by the bank and acceptance by the client; a pre-approved solicitation not yet accepted is outside the definition.

R-LEV30.47-commitment-definition.portfolio_relevance: Sets the boundary of what must be counted: an accepted credit card account with an assigned limit is a commitment from acceptance onward, so growth in accounts (not just balances) consumes leverage capacity.

R-LEV30.47-uncancellable-inclusion.title: Unconditionally cancellable arrangements are commitments
R-LEV30.47-uncancellable-inclusion.statement: The definition of commitment expressly includes any arrangement that the bank can unconditionally cancel at any time without prior notice to the obligor.
R-LEV30.47-uncancellable-inclusion.quote: It includes any such arrangement that can be unconditionally cancelled by the bank at any time without prior notice to the obligor.

applies_to.note: This is the specific hook that pulls US credit card lines (which are unconditionally cancellable by contract) into the leverage exposure measure, notwithstanding a 0% CCF in some risk-based regimes.

R-LEV30.47-uncancellable-inclusion.portfolio_relevance: The decisive rule for credit card portfolios: contractual cancellability, which removes the line from many risk-based calculations, does not remove it from the leverage denominator, so a card book with a low utilisation rate carries hidden leverage cost that the RWA view never shows.

R-LEV30.47-conditional-cancellation-incl.title: Conditionally cancellable arrangements are also commitments
R-LEV30.47-conditional-cancellation-incl.statement: The definition of commitment also includes arrangements the bank can cancel if the obligor fails to meet conditions in the facility document, including conditions precedent to initial or subsequent drawdown.
R-LEV30.47-conditional-cancellation-incl.quote: It also includes any such arrangement that can be cancelled by the bank if the obligor fails to meet conditions set out in the facility document, including conditions that must be met by the obligor prior to any initial or subsequent drawdown arrangement.

applies_to.note: Covenant-conditioned and material-adverse-change facilities are commitments; drafting cancellation triggers into the facility does not remove the exposure.

R-LEV30.47-conditional-cancellation-incl.portfolio_relevance: Closes the documentation route to shrinking the denominator: adding covenants or drawdown conditions to SME revolvers does not convert them out of commitment status, so contractual restructuring cannot avoid the CCF charge.

R-LEV30.47-national-discretion-exemption.title: National discretion to exempt certain arrangements from the commitment definition
R-LEV30.47-national-discretion-exemption.statement: A jurisdiction may exempt certain arrangements from the commitment definition only where the bank receives no fees or commissions, the client must apply for each drawdown, the bank has full authority over each drawdown, and the bank assesses creditworthiness immediately prior to each drawdown.
R-LEV30.47-national-discretion-exemption.quote: At national discretion, a jurisdiction may exempt certain arrangements from the definition of commitments provided that the following conditions are met: (i) the bank receives no fees or commissions to establish or maintain the arrangements; (ii) the client is required to apply to the bank for the initial and each subsequent drawdown;

applies_to.note: Explicit national-discretion gate with four cumulative conditions; not adopted uniformly, and a fee-earning arrangement can never qualify.

R-LEV30.47-national-discretion-exemption.portfolio_relevance: Defines the only structure that escapes the commitment charge entirely: an unfeed, application-by-application, freshly underwritten facility. Credit card lines fail conditions (i) and (ii) outright, so they can never qualify.

R-LEV30.47-exemption-confined-corporates.title: Exempted arrangements confined to closely monitored corporate and SME counterparties
R-LEV30.47-exemption-confined-corporates.statement: Arrangements exempted from the commitment definition are confined to certain arrangements for corporates and small or medium-sized entities where counterparties are closely monitored on an ongoing basis.
R-LEV30.47-exemption-confined-corporates.quote: Exempted arrangements that met the above criteria are confined to certain arrangements for corporates and small or medium-sized entities, where counterparties are closely monitored on an ongoing basis.

applies_to.note: Product-scope restriction inside the national discretion: retail and revolving retail arrangements are outside the exemption by construction.

R-LEV30.47-exemption-confined-corporates.portfolio_relevance: Confirms retail and credit card commitments can never obtain the exemption, so a bank seeking OBS leverage relief must shift toward closely monitored corporate/SME uncommitted lines rather than restructuring its consumer book.

R-LEV30.48-provisions-deducted-post-ccf.title: Provisions against OBS exposures deducted after the CCF is applied
R-LEV30.48-provisions-deducted-post-ccf.statement: Specific and general provisions set aside against off-balance sheet exposures that have decreased Tier 1 capital may be deducted from the credit exposure equivalent amount, i.e. from the post-CCF amount.
R-LEV30.48-provisions-deducted-post-ccf.quote: specific and general provisions set aside against OBS exposures that have decreased Tier 1 capital may be deducted from the credit exposure equivalent amount of those exposures (ie the exposure amount after the application of the relevant CCF).

applies_to.note: Only provisions that actually reduced Tier 1 qualify; deduction is applied post-CCF, not to the notional.

R-LEV30.48-provisions-deducted-post-ccf.portfolio_relevance: Under CECL a US bank reserves for expected losses on unfunded card commitments; this rule lets that reserve be netted against the post-CCF exposure, partially offsetting the leverage cost of a large undrawn line book.

R-LEV30.48-obs-floor-zero.title: Total OBS equivalent amount floored at zero
R-LEV30.48-obs-floor-zero.statement: After deducting provisions, the resulting total off-balance sheet equivalent amount for OBS exposures cannot be less than zero.
R-LEV30.48-obs-floor-zero.quote: However, the resulting total off-balance sheet equivalent amount for OBS exposures cannot be less than zero.

applies_to.note: Floor applies to the total, not item by item.

numeric_values: floor of zero on total OBS equivalent amount
R-LEV30.48-obs-floor-zero.portfolio_relevance: Caps the provisioning offset: heavy reserving against unfunded card lines can reduce the OBS contribution to zero but can never create negative denominator credit that would subsidise on-balance-sheet growth.

R-LEV30.49-100pct-direct-credit-substitu.title: 100% CCF for direct credit substitutes
R-LEV30.49-100pct-direct-credit-substitu.statement: A 100% CCF applies to direct credit substitutes, including general guarantees of indebtedness, standby letters of credit serving as financial guarantees for loans and securities, and acceptances.
R-LEV30.49-100pct-direct-credit-substitu.quote: A 100% CCF will be applied to the following items: (1) Direct credit substitutes, eg general guarantees of indebtedness (including standby letters of credit serving as financial guarantees for loans and securities) and acceptances (including endorsements with the character of acceptances).

applies_to.note: Highest CCF band; no maturity distinction.

R-LEV30.49-100pct-direct-credit-substitu.portfolio_relevance: Financial standby letters of credit consume leverage capacity dollar-for-dollar exactly like a funded loan, so a fee-driven guarantee business is the most leverage-expensive off-balance sheet product a small bank can grow.

R-LEV30.49-100pct-forward-purchases.title: 100% CCF for forward asset purchases and commitments with certain drawdown
R-LEV30.49-100pct-forward-purchases.statement: A 100% CCF applies to forward asset purchases, forward forward deposits and partly paid shares and securities, which represent commitments with certain drawdown.
R-LEV30.49-100pct-forward-purchases.quote: (2) Forward asset purchases, forward forward deposits and partly paid shares and securities, which represent commitments with certain drawdown.

applies_to.note: Rationale is certainty of drawdown, which is why no maturity or cancellability discount is available.

R-LEV30.49-100pct-forward-purchases.portfolio_relevance: Forward commitments to purchase loan pools or securities consume full leverage capacity from trade date, so a bank cannot pre-commit to portfolio expansion without immediately booking the denominator effect.

R-LEV30.49-100pct-unsettled-purchases.title: 100% CCF for unsettled financial asset purchases under settlement date accounting
R-LEV30.49-100pct-unsettled-purchases.statement: A 100% CCF applies to the exposure amount associated with unsettled financial asset purchases (the commitment to pay) where regular-way unsettled trades are accounted for at settlement date.
R-LEV30.49-100pct-unsettled-purchases.quote: (3) The exposure amount associated with unsettled financial asset purchases (ie the commitment to pay) where regular-way unsettled trades are accounted for at settlement date.

applies_to.note: Offsetting against unsettled sales is permitted only for trading book assets fair valued through income and settled DvP.

R-LEV30.49-100pct-unsettled-purchases.portfolio_relevance: Ties back to LEV30.11: settlement-date-accounting banks pay the full leverage charge on pending securities purchases, so quarter-end portfolio reallocation is charged before it settles.

R-LEV30.49-100pct-other-credit-substitut.title: 100% CCF catch-all for uncategorised credit substitutes
R-LEV30.49-100pct-other-credit-substitut.statement: A 100% CCF applies to off-balance sheet items that are credit substitutes not explicitly included in any other category.
R-LEV30.49-100pct-other-credit-substitut.quote: (4) Off-balance sheet items that are credit substitutes not explicitly included in any other category.

applies_to.note: Residual catch-all; the default for any novel credit-substitute structure is the maximum CCF.

R-LEV30.49-100pct-other-credit-substitut.portfolio_relevance: Sets the default penalty for financial engineering: a novel off-balance sheet credit structure is charged at 100% unless it clearly fits a lower-CCF category, removing the incentive to invent unclassified products.

R-LEV30.50-50pct-nif-ruf.title: 50% CCF for note issuance and revolving underwriting facilities
R-LEV30.50-50pct-nif-ruf.statement: A 50% CCF applies to note issuance facilities and revolving underwriting facilities, regardless of the maturity of the underlying facility.
R-LEV30.50-50pct-nif-ruf.quote: A 50% CCF will be applied to note issuance facilities and revolving underwriting facilities regardless of the maturity of the underlying facility.

applies_to.note: Maturity-blind, unlike the older Basel II standardised treatment. Rare at small North American banks.

R-LEV30.50-50pct-nif-ruf.portfolio_relevance: Removes the maturity-shortening lever for underwriting facilities: a bank cannot reduce the leverage charge by writing shorter NIFs/RUFs, so this business carries a fixed half-notional denominator cost.

R-LEV30.51-50pct-transaction-contingent.title: 50% CCF for transaction-related contingent items
R-LEV30.51-50pct-transaction-contingent.statement: A 50% CCF applies to certain transaction-related contingent items such as performance bonds, bid bonds, warranties and standby letters of credit related to particular transactions.
R-LEV30.51-50pct-transaction-contingent.quote: A 50% CCF will be applied to certain transaction-related contingent items (eg performance bonds, bid bonds, warranties and standby letters of credit related to particular transactions).

applies_to.note: Distinguished from financial standbys, which take 100% under LEV30.49(1).

R-LEV30.51-50pct-transaction-contingent.portfolio_relevance: Creates a 2:1 leverage advantage for performance standbys over financial standbys, so a small bank can halve the denominator cost of its letter-of-credit book by shifting its mix toward performance-related instruments.

R-LEV30.52-40pct-commitments.title: 40% CCF for commitments generally
R-LEV30.52-40pct-commitments.statement: A 40% CCF applies to commitments, regardless of the maturity of the underlying facility, unless they qualify for a lower CCF.
R-LEV30.52-40pct-commitments.quote: A 40% CCF will be applied to commitments, regardless of the maturity of the underlying facility, unless they qualify for a lower CCF.

applies_to.note: Maturity-blind: the old 20%/50% split by original maturity under or over one year does not apply in the leverage framework.

R-LEV30.52-40pct-commitments.portfolio_relevance: This is the default charge on undrawn SME and commercial revolvers: every dollar of unused committed line adds 40 cents to the leverage denominator, so a bank close to its leverage floor can free capacity fastest by reducing committed but unused facilities.

R-LEV30.53-20pct-trade-lc.title: 20% CCF for short-term self-liquidating trade letters of credit
R-LEV30.53-20pct-trade-lc.statement: A 20% CCF applies, for both issuing and confirming banks, to short-term self-liquidating trade letters of credit arising from the movement of goods.
R-LEV30.53-20pct-trade-lc.quote: A 20% CCF will be applied to both the issuing and confirming banks of short- term self-liquidating trade letters of credit arising from the movement of goods

applies_to.note: Requires the instrument to be short-term, self-liquidating and goods-movement related; applies symmetrically to issuing and confirming banks.

R-LEV30.53-20pct-trade-lc.portfolio_relevance: Trade finance is the cheapest committed off-balance sheet product in the leverage framework at one fifth of notional, so a bank optimising against the backstop is rewarded for tilting contingent business toward documentary trade credit.

R-LEV30.54-10pct-unconditionally-cancell.title: 10% CCF for unconditionally cancellable commitments
R-LEV30.54-10pct-unconditionally-cancell.statement: A 10% CCF applies to commitments that are unconditionally cancellable at any time by the bank without prior notice, or that effectively provide for automatic cancellation on deterioration in the borrower's creditworthiness.
R-LEV30.54-10pct-unconditionally-cancell.quote: A 10% CCF will be applied to commitments that are unconditionally cancellable at any time by the bank without prior notice, or that effectively provide for automatic cancellation due to deterioration in a borrower's creditworthiness.

applies_to.note: This is the operative CCF for US credit card lines, which are contractually unconditionally cancellable. Note the divergence: the US community bank leverage ratio denominator excludes off-balance sheet items entirely, so a CBLR bank does not pick up this 10% charge even though a Basel-consistent computation would.

R-LEV30.54-10pct-unconditionally-cancell.portfolio_relevance: The single most computable credit card rule in this domain: each dollar of unused card line adds 10 cents to the leverage denominator, so at a 3% minimum every $100 of unused card line requires roughly $0.30 of Tier 1 even though it carries no balance and no interest income.

R-LEV30.54-supervisor-may-raise-ccf.title: Supervisors should consider a higher CCF where cancellation is constrained in practice
R-LEV30.54-supervisor-may-raise-ccf.statement: National supervisors should evaluate jurisdiction-specific factors that may constrain a bank's ability to cancel a commitment in practice and consider applying a higher CCF to certain commitments as appropriate.
R-LEV30.54-supervisor-may-raise-ccf.quote: National supervisors should evaluate various factors in the jurisdiction, which may constrain banks' ability to cancel the commitment in practice, and consider applying a higher CCF to certain commitments as appropriate.

applies_to.note: Explicit national-discretion uplift. In the US, consumer protection rules (CARD Act notice requirements for rate and line changes) are exactly the kind of practical constraint contemplated here.

numeric_values: higher CCF than 10% at supervisory discretion
R-LEV30.54-supervisor-may-raise-ccf.portfolio_relevance: Makes the 10% card CCF a floor rather than a certainty: where consumer-protection law slows line cuts, a supervisor may charge more, so a card-concentrated bank should stress its leverage ratio at CCFs above 10%.

R-LEV30.55-lower-of-two-ccfs.title: Lower of two applicable CCFs for an undertaking to provide a commitment
R-LEV30.55-lower-of-two-ccfs.statement: Where there is an undertaking to provide a commitment on an off-balance sheet item, the bank applies the lower of the two applicable CCFs.
R-LEV30.55-lower-of-two-ccfs.quote: Where there is an undertaking to provide a commitment on an off-balance sheet item, banks are to apply the lower of the two applicable CCFs.

applies_to.note: Avoids compounding CCFs on nested commitments.

R-LEV30.55-lower-of-two-ccfs.portfolio_relevance: Prevents double-charging nested facilities, so structuring a commitment-to-commit does not multiply the leverage cost; the cheapest applicable band governs.

R-LEV30.55-lower-ccf-examples.title: Worked CCF outcomes for nested commitments: 10% instead of 100%, 20% instead of 40%
R-LEV30.55-lower-ccf-examples.statement: An unconditionally cancellable commitment to issue direct credit substitutes takes a 10% CCF instead of 100%, and a commitment to open short-term self-liquidating trade letters of credit takes a 20% CCF instead of 40%.
R-LEV30.55-lower-ccf-examples.quote: if a bank has an unconditionally cancellable commitment described in CRE20.100 to issue direct credit substitutes, a 10% CCF will be applied (instead of a 100% CCF).

applies_to.note: Illustrative footnote fixing the arithmetic of the lower-of rule.

R-LEV30.55-lower-ccf-examples.portfolio_relevance: Quantifies a tenfold leverage saving available purely from making a guarantee facility unconditionally cancellable, which is a concrete and legally simple portfolio restructuring lever for a leverage-constrained bank.

R-LEV30.56-obs-securitisation.title: OBS securitisation exposures follow CRE40.20(2)
R-LEV30.56-obs-securitisation.statement: Off-balance sheet securitisation exposures must be treated as per CRE40.20(2) for the purposes of the leverage ratio exposure measure.
R-LEV30.56-obs-securitisation.quote: OBS securitisation exposures must be treated as per CRE40.20 (2).

applies_to.note: Cross-reference into the securitisation framework rather than the LEV CCF grid.

R-LEV30.56-obs-securitisation.portfolio_relevance: Governs the leverage cost of liquidity facilities and servicer advances supporting a card master trust, so a securitising issuer must count its off-balance sheet support commitments even after the receivables themselves leave the measure.

R-LEV40.1-gsib-buffer-tier1.title: G-SIB leverage ratio buffer met with Tier 1 capital
R-LEV40.1-gsib-buffer-tier1.statement: Banks identified as G-SIBs under SCO40 must meet a leverage ratio buffer requirement in addition to the minimum, and must meet it with Tier 1 capital.
R-LEV40.1-gsib-buffer-tier1.quote: banks identified as global systemically important banks (G-SIBs) according to SCO40 must also meet a leverage ratio buffer requirement. Consistent with the capital measure required to meet the leverage ratio minimum described in LEV20.4, G-SIBs must meet the leverage ratio buffer with Tier 1 capital.

applies_to.note: Size-gated: applies only to banks designated G-SIBs under SCO40. Explicitly not applicable to small or medium North American banks.

R-LEV40.1-gsib-buffer-tier1.portfolio_relevance: Defines the size threshold above which the leverage constraint tightens; useful as the boundary condition in a size-conditional model, and as the reason small banks face a flat 3% while the largest face 3% plus a buffer.

R-LEV40.2-buffer-50pct-of-hla.title: G-SIB leverage buffer set at 50% of the higher loss-absorbency requirement
R-LEV40.2-buffer-50pct-of-hla.statement: The leverage ratio buffer is set at 50% of a G-SIB's higher loss-absorbency risk-based requirement, so a 2% HLA requirement produces a 1% leverage ratio buffer.
R-LEV40.2-buffer-50pct-of-hla.quote: The leverage ratio buffer will be set at 50% of a G-SIB’s higher loss-absorbency risk-based requirements. For example, a G-SIB subject to a 2% higher loss- absorbency requirement would be subject to a 1% leverage ratio buffer requirement.

applies_to.note: G-SIB only; the buffer scales with the SCO40 bucket.

R-LEV40.2-buffer-50pct-of-hla.portfolio_relevance: Links the leverage floor to systemic-importance scoring, so for the largest banks growing the balance sheet raises both the denominator and, via the G-SIB score, the required ratio itself; small banks face no such feedback.

R-LEV40.4-distribution-constraints.title: Capital distribution constraints tied to a 3% leverage minimum plus buffer
R-LEV40.4-distribution-constraints.statement: A G-SIB is free of minimum capital conservation standards only if it meets both its CET1 risk-based requirements (4.5% minimum plus 2.5% conservation buffer plus HLA and any countercyclical buffer) and its Tier 1 leverage ratio requirement, defined as the 3% minimum plus the G-SIB leverage ratio buffer.
R-LEV40.4-distribution-constraints.quote: its Tier 1 leverage ratio requirement (defined as a 3% leverage ratio minimum requirement and the G-SIB leverage ratio buffer) will not be subject to minimum capital conservation standards.
