applies_to.note: G-SIB only; the binding constraint is the more severe of the risk-based and leverage conservation standards.

R-LEV40.4-distribution-constraints.portfolio_relevance: Converts a leverage shortfall into a dividend and buyback restriction, which means the leverage backstop constrains capital return before it constrains lending, and the worse of the two ratios governs.

R-LEV40.5-conservation-table.title: Leverage ratio conservation bands from 3% to 3.50%
R-LEV40.5-conservation-table.statement: For a G-SIB in the first HLA bucket, minimum capital conservation ratios step down across leverage ratio bands: 100% of earnings retained between 3% and 3.125%, 80% above 3.125% to 3.25%, 60% above 3.25% to 3.375%, 40% above 3.375% to 3.50%, and 0% above 3.50%.

applies_to.note: Illustrative table for a G-SIB in the first (1%) HLA bucket; bands scale with the bucket. Not applicable to small or medium banks, but it is the only place the framework gives an explicit leverage-ratio-to-payout mapping.

R-LEV40.5-conservation-table.portfolio_relevance: Gives a fully computable step function from leverage ratio to permitted payout, which is directly reusable as the template for modelling how a leverage shortfall throttles earnings retention and therefore future portfolio growth capacity.

R-NSF20.2-nsfr-min-100.title: NSFR minimum of 100% on an ongoing basis
R-NSF20.2-nsfr-min-100.statement: A bank's available stable funding divided by its required stable funding must be at least 100% at all times.
R-NSF20.2-nsfr-min-100.quote: The NSFR is defined as the amount of available stable funding relative to the amount of required stable funding. This ratio should be equal to at least 100% on an ongoing basis.

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks. The US implementation (12 CFR 249 subpart K) applies the full NSFR only to Category I-III firms with a reduced 85%/70% requirement for Category IV; small North American banks are exempt, so for this project the ratio is a shadow/analytical constraint.

R-NSF20.2-nsfr-min-100.portfolio_relevance: This is the binding denominator constraint: any growth in credit-card receivables raises RSF, so the bank must simultaneously raise ASF (stable deposits or term funding) or shrink other assets to keep the ratio at 100%.

R-NSF20.2-asf-definition.title: Definition of available stable funding
R-NSF20.2-asf-definition.statement: Available stable funding is the portion of capital and liabilities expected to be reliable over a one-year horizon.
R-NSF20.2-asf-definition.quote: Available stable funding” is defined as the portion of capital and liabilities expected to be reliable over the one-year time horizon considered by the NSFR.

applies_to.note: Definitional; no proportionality gate.

R-NSF20.2-asf-definition.portfolio_relevance: Defines the numerator that a credit-card book must be funded from, making core retail deposits the cheapest way to support card growth.

R-NSF20.2-rsf-definition.title: Definition of required stable funding
R-NSF20.2-rsf-definition.statement: Required stable funding is a function of the liquidity characteristics and residual maturities of a bank's assets and its off-balance sheet exposures.
R-NSF20.2-rsf-definition.quote: The amount of stable funding required ("required stable funding") of an institution is a function of the liquidity characteristics and residual maturities of the various assets held by that institution as well as those of its off- balance sheet exposures.

applies_to.note: Definitional; no proportionality gate.

R-NSF20.2-rsf-definition.portfolio_relevance: Establishes that undrawn credit-card lines (off-balance sheet) as well as drawn balances both create a stable-funding requirement.

R-NSF20.3-quarterly-reporting.title: NSFR must be reported at least quarterly
R-NSF20.3-quarterly-reporting.statement: Banks must report the NSFR at least quarterly, with a reporting lag no longer than that allowed under the Basel capital standards.
R-NSF20.3-quarterly-reporting.quote: The NSFR must be reported at least quarterly. The time lag in reporting should not surpass the allowable time lag under the Basel capital standards.

applies_to.note: Reporting frequency matches the quarterly Call Report / Consolidated Financial Statements cadence, which is what makes the NSFR checkable against published small-bank filings.

R-NSF20.3-quarterly-reporting.portfolio_relevance: Fixes the observation frequency at which a portfolio's funding mix is tested, so quarter-end card balances and undrawn lines are the measured quantity.

R-NSF30.2-funding-tenor-calibration.title: Longer-term liabilities assumed more stable than short-term
R-NSF30.2-funding-tenor-calibration.statement: The NSFR is calibrated so that liabilities of longer contractual tenor are assumed to be more stable than short-term liabilities.
R-NSF30.2-funding-tenor-calibration.quote: Funding tenor: the net stable funding ratio (NSFR) is generally calibrated such that longer-term liabilities are assumed to be more stable than short- term liabilities.

applies_to.note: Calibration principle underlying the ASF factor ladder.

R-NSF30.2-funding-tenor-calibration.portfolio_relevance: Explains why lengthening CD/term-deposit maturity beyond one year is the highest-yielding lever for a card-heavy bank short of stable funding.

R-NSF30.2-retail-sme-stability.title: Retail and small business funding assumed more stable than wholesale
R-NSF30.2-retail-sme-stability.statement: Short-term deposits from retail customers and funding from small business customers are assumed to be behaviourally more stable than wholesale funding of the same maturity.
R-NSF30.2-retail-sme-stability.quote: Funding type and counterparty: the NSFR is calibrated under the assumption that short-term (maturing in less than one year) deposits provided by retail customers and funding provided by small business customers are behaviourally more stable than wholesale funding of the same maturity from other counterparties.

applies_to.note: Calibration principle; the counterparty split drives the 95%/90% vs 50%/0% ASF gap.

numeric_values: maturing in less than one year
R-NSF30.2-retail-sme-stability.portfolio_relevance: A monoline card bank funded by brokered or wholesale money is structurally penalised relative to one funded by core retail deposits, even at identical maturity.

R-NSF30.3-resilient-credit-creation.title: Stable funding required for a proportion of real-economy lending
R-NSF30.3-resilient-credit-creation.statement: The NSFR requires stable funding for some proportion of lending to the real economy so that this intermediation continues.
R-NSF30.3-resilient-credit-creation.quote: Resilient credit creation: the NSFR requires stable funding for some proportion of lending to the real economy in order to ensure the continuity of this type of intermediation.

applies_to.note: Calibration criterion for RSF factors.

R-NSF30.3-resilient-credit-creation.portfolio_relevance: Justifies why consumer and card lending carries a positive RSF factor rather than being treated as self-liquidating.

R-NSF30.3-rollover-assumption.title: Banks assumed to roll over a significant proportion of maturing loans
R-NSF30.3-rollover-assumption.statement: RSF factors are calibrated assuming banks will roll over a significant proportion of maturing loans in order to preserve customer relationships.
R-NSF30.3-rollover-assumption.quote: Bank behaviour: the NSFR is calibrated under the assumption that banks may seek to roll over a significant proportion of maturing loans to preserve customer relationships.

applies_to.note: Calibration criterion; explains why contractually short revolving exposures still attract RSF.

R-NSF30.3-rollover-assumption.portfolio_relevance: A bank cannot argue that revolving card balances run off within a year; the framework assumes they are re-lent, so they must be funded.

R-NSF30.3-asset-tenor.title: Short-dated assets require a smaller proportion of stable funding
R-NSF30.3-asset-tenor.statement: Assets maturing in less than one year are assumed to require a smaller proportion of stable funding because the bank could let them mature instead of rolling them over.
R-NSF30.3-asset-tenor.quote: Asset tenor: the NSFR assumes that some short-dated assets (maturing in less than one year) require a smaller proportion of stable funding because banks would be able to allow some proportion of those assets to mature instead of rolling them over.

applies_to.note: Calibration criterion behind the sub-one-year 50% RSF bucket.

numeric_values: maturing in less than one year
R-NSF30.3-asset-tenor.portfolio_relevance: Creates the incentive to keep retail loans contractually under one year (50% RSF) rather than one year or more (65%/85% RSF).

R-NSF30.4-obs-stable-funding.title: Off-balance sheet commitments require additional stable funding
R-NSF30.4-obs-stable-funding.statement: Additional stable funding must support at least a small portion of the potential liquidity calls from off-balance sheet commitments and contingent funding obligations.
R-NSF30.4-obs-stable-funding.quote: Additional stable funding sources are also required to support at least a small portion of the potential calls on liquidity arising from off-balance sheet commitments and contingent funding obligations.

applies_to.note: Concrete factors are set in NSF30.34, including national discretion for unconditionally revocable facilities.

R-NSF30.4-obs-stable-funding.portfolio_relevance: Undrawn credit-card lines are not free under the NSFR: granting large open-to-buy capacity itself consumes stable funding.

R-NSF30.5-asf-measurement-basis.title: ASF measured on contractual maturity and withdrawal propensity
R-NSF30.5-asf-measurement-basis.statement: ASF is measured from the relative stability of funding sources, including contractual maturity of liabilities and differences in funding providers' propensity to withdraw.
R-NSF30.5-asf-measurement-basis.quote: The amount of ASF is measured based on the broad characteristics of the relative stability of an institution’s funding sources, including the contractual maturity of its liabilities and the differences in the propensity of different types of funding providers to withdraw their funding.

applies_to.note: Definitional basis for the five ASF buckets.

R-NSF30.5-asf-measurement-basis.portfolio_relevance: Sets counterparty type and contractual maturity as the only two ASF levers a bank can pull on the liability side.

R-NSF30.6-asf-calculation.title: ASF computed as carrying value assigned to five categories times ASF factor
R-NSF30.6-asf-calculation.statement: ASF must be computed by assigning the carrying value of capital and liabilities to one of five categories, multiplying each by its ASF factor and summing the weighted amounts.
R-NSF30.6-asf-calculation.quote: The amount of ASF must be calculated by first assigning the carrying value of an institution’s capital and liabilities to one of five categories as presented below. The amount assigned to each category is then multiplied by an ASF factor, and the total ASF is the sum of the weighted amounts.

applies_to.note: Mechanical calculation rule; the five categories are 100%, 95%, 90%, 50% and 0%.

R-NSF30.6-asf-calculation.portfolio_relevance: Gives the exact linear form ASF = sum(factor_i x liability_i), which is directly computable from a Call Report deposit breakdown.

R-NSF30.6-carrying-value-def.title: Definition of carrying value for ASF
R-NSF30.6-carrying-value-def.statement: Carrying value is the amount at which a liability or equity instrument is recorded before any regulatory deductions, filters or other adjustments.
R-NSF30.6-carrying-value-def.quote: Carrying value represents the amount at which a liability or equity instrument is recorded before the application of any regulatory deductions, filters or other adjustments.

applies_to.note: Definitional; makes ASF inputs read directly off the balance sheet.

R-NSF30.6-carrying-value-def.portfolio_relevance: Means ASF inputs are gross book values from published financials, so no regulatory adjustment layer is needed to compute the numerator.

R-NSF30.7-call-option-earliest.title: Assume investors redeem call options at the earliest possible date
R-NSF30.7-call-option-earliest.statement: When determining the maturity of an equity or liability instrument, the bank must assume investors exercise call options at the earliest possible date.
R-NSF30.7-call-option-earliest.quote: When determining the maturity of an equity or liability instrument, the bank must assume investors redeem call options at the earliest possible date.

applies_to.note: Supervisors additionally consider reputational factors for bank-discretion options.

R-NSF30.7-call-option-earliest.portfolio_relevance: Callable term funding cannot be counted at its legal maturity, so a card bank cannot manufacture 100% ASF from investor-callable notes.

R-NSF30.7-long-dated-cashflows.title: Only cash flows at or beyond six-month and one-year horizons count as long-dated
R-NSF30.7-long-dated-cashflows.statement: For long-dated liabilities, only the portion of cash flows falling at or beyond the six-month and one-year horizons is treated as having that effective residual maturity.
R-NSF30.7-long-dated-cashflows.quote: For long-dated liabilities, only the portion of cash flows falling at or beyond the six-month and one-year time horizons should be treated as having an effective residual maturity of six months or more and one year or more, respectively.

applies_to.note: Applies to amortising or staged liabilities.

R-NSF30.7-long-dated-cashflows.portfolio_relevance: Amortising wholesale funding decays out of the 100% ASF bucket as it seasons, so a card book funded that way faces a rolling ASF shortfall.

R-NSF30.10-asf100-regulatory-capital.title: 100% ASF for regulatory capital excluding short-dated Tier 2
R-NSF30.10-asf100-regulatory-capital.statement: Total regulatory capital before capital deductions receives a 100% ASF factor, excluding the proportion of Tier 2 instruments with residual maturity of less than one year.
R-NSF30.10-asf100-regulatory-capital.quote: Liabilities and capital instruments receiving a 100% ASF factor comprise: (1) the total amount of regulatory capital, before the application of capital deductions, as defined in CAP10, excluding the proportion of Tier 2 instruments with residual maturity of less than one year;

applies_to.note: Capital amounts are post-transition (fully implemented Basel III) per the NSF30.10 footnote.

numeric_values: residual maturity of less than one year (Tier 2 exclusion)
R-NSF30.10-asf100-regulatory-capital.portfolio_relevance: Equity is the only funding source that is simultaneously loss-absorbing and 100% stable, so raising capital relaxes both the RWA and NSFR constraints on card growth.

R-NSF30.10-asf100-term-liabilities.title: 100% ASF for borrowings and term deposits with residual maturity of one year or more
R-NSF30.10-asf100-term-liabilities.statement: Secured and unsecured borrowings and liabilities including term deposits with effective residual maturities of one year or more receive a 100% ASF factor; cash flows falling below one year from such liabilities do not qualify.
R-NSF30.10-asf100-term-liabilities.quote: the total amount of secured and unsecured borrowings and liabilities (including term deposits) with effective residual maturities of one year or more. Cash flows falling below the one-year horizon but arising from liabilities with a final maturity greater than one year do not qualify for the 100% ASF factor;

applies_to.note: Effective, not legal, residual maturity, per NSF30.7.

numeric_values: residual maturity of one year or more
R-NSF30.10-asf100-term-liabilities.portfolio_relevance: Terming out CDs or FHLB advances past one year is the direct offset to the 85% RSF a long-dated card book imposes.

R-NSF30.10-asf100-retail-term-deposits.title: 100% ASF for retail term deposits over one year with significant early-withdrawal penalty
R-NSF30.10-asf100-retail-term-deposits.statement: Retail term deposits maturing over one year that cannot be withdrawn early without significant penalty receive a 100% ASF factor.
R-NSF30.10-asf100-retail-term-deposits.quote: retail term deposits maturing over one year that cannot be withdrawn early without significant penalty.

applies_to.note: The penalty test is the discriminator against NSF30.11/NSF30.12, which give 95%/90% to over-one-year retail deposits withdrawable without significant penalty.

R-NSF30.10-asf100-retail-term-deposits.portfolio_relevance: A small bank can lift ASF by 5-10 points on the same deposit balance simply by adding a meaningful early-withdrawal penalty to its long-dated retail CDs.

R-NSF30.11-asf95-stable-retail.title: 95% ASF for stable retail and small business deposits
R-NSF30.11-asf95-stable-retail.statement: Stable non-maturity (demand) deposits, term deposits with residual maturity of less than one year, and term deposits over one year withdrawable early without significant penalty, provided by retail and small business customers, receive a 95% ASF factor.
R-NSF30.11-asf95-stable-retail.quote: Liabilities receiving a 95% ASF factor comprise “stable” (as defined in LCR40.7 to LCR40.12) non-maturity (demand) deposits and/or term deposits with residual maturities of less than one year,and/or term deposits with residual maturities greater than one year that can be withdrawn early without a significant penalty, provided by retail and small business customers.

applies_to.note: 'Stable' takes the LCR40.7-LCR40.12 meaning (fully insured deposits in an established relationship or transactional account); small business customers per LCR40.23-LCR40.24.

numeric_values: residual maturities of less than one year
residual maturities greater than one year
R-NSF30.11-asf95-stable-retail.portfolio_relevance: Insured core retail deposits are the cheapest NSFR funding available to a small bank, so a card portfolio funded from an insured branch deposit base is far less NSFR-constrained than one funded by brokered or online money.

R-NSF30.11-retail-sme-definitions.title: Retail deposits and small business customers take their LCR definitions
R-NSF30.11-retail-sme-definitions.statement: For NSFR purposes, retail deposits are defined in LCR40.5 and small business customers are defined in LCR40.23 and LCR40.24.
R-NSF30.11-retail-sme-definitions.quote: Retail deposits are defined in LCR40.5. Small business customers are defined in LCR40.23 and. LCR40.24

applies_to.note: Cross-chapter definitional dependency: the ASF factor cannot be evaluated without the LCR40 retail/SME tests (LCR40.24 sets the aggregate funding threshold below which an SME is treated as retail).

R-NSF30.11-retail-sme-definitions.portfolio_relevance: Determines which deposit lines in a Call Report can be treated as 95%/90% ASF rather than 50% wholesale, which is the single largest swing factor in a small bank's NSFR.

R-NSF30.12-asf90-less-stable-retail.title: 90% ASF for less stable retail and small business deposits
R-NSF30.12-asf90-less-stable-retail.statement: Less stable non-maturity deposits, term deposits under one year, and term deposits over one year withdrawable early without significant penalty, provided by retail and small business customers, receive a 90% ASF factor.
R-NSF30.12-asf90-less-stable-retail.quote: Liabilities receiving a 90% ASF factor comprise “less stable” (as defined in LCR40. 13 to LCR40.15) non-maturity (demand) deposits and/or term deposits with residual maturities of less than one year, and/or term deposits with residual maturities greater than one year that can be withdrawn early without a significant penalty, provided by retail and small business customers.

applies_to.note: 'Less stable' per LCR40.13-LCR40.15, which national supervisors may further sub-divide; typically uninsured or non-relationship retail balances.

numeric_values: residual maturities of less than one year
residual maturities greater than one year
R-NSF30.12-asf90-less-stable-retail.portfolio_relevance: Uninsured retail deposits fund a card book 5 percentage points less efficiently than insured ones, so deposit insurance coverage is a measurable NSFR lever.

R-NSF30.12-lcr-definitions-not-runoff.title: ASF follows LCR stable/less-stable definitions, not jurisdictional run-off rates
R-NSF30.12-lcr-definitions-not-runoff.statement: Retail and small business deposits are classified using the LCR definitions rather than the run-off rates applied locally, so deposits subject to outflow assumptions higher than 5% and 10% may still be treated as stable or less stable unless the jurisdiction chooses a more conservative (lower ASF) treatment.
R-NSF30.12-lcr-definitions-not-runoff.quote: The treatment of retail and small business deposits follows the definitions provided in the LCR standard and not the run-off rates applied to them in a particular jurisdiction. Thus, retail and small business deposits that are subject to higher (than 5% and 10%) outflow assumptions than those for stable and less stable deposits in the LCR could be treated as stable and less stable, unless a given jurisdiction chooses to apply a more conservative treatment (lower ASF).

applies_to.note: Explicit national discretion to apply a lower ASF than the Basel default; a jurisdictional overlay must be checked before the 95%/90% factors are applied.

R-NSF30.12-lcr-definitions-not-runoff.portfolio_relevance: Prevents a national high-outflow classification (e.g. rate-sensitive or brokered retail money) from automatically stripping ASF credit, but flags that a jurisdiction may do so, which would tighten funding for a deposit-funded card book.

R-NSF30.13-asf50-nonfin-corporate.title: 50% ASF for sub-one-year funding from non-financial corporates
R-NSF30.13-asf50-nonfin-corporate.statement: Secured and unsecured funding with residual maturity of less than one year provided by non-financial corporate customers receives a 50% ASF factor.
R-NSF30.13-asf50-nonfin-corporate.quote: Liabilities receiving a 50% ASF factor comprise: (1) funding (secured and unsecured) with a residual maturity of less than one year provided by non-financial corporate customers;

applies_to.note: Applies where the depositor exceeds the LCR small-business threshold.

numeric_values: residual maturity of less than one year
R-NSF30.13-asf50-nonfin-corporate.portfolio_relevance: Corporate deposits fund a card book at roughly half the efficiency of retail deposits, so a shift in the deposit base toward business accounts mechanically tightens the NSFR.

R-NSF30.13-asf50-operational-deposits.title: 50% ASF for operational deposits
R-NSF30.13-asf50-operational-deposits.statement: Operational deposits as defined in LCR40.26 to LCR40.36 receive a 50% ASF factor.
R-NSF30.13-asf50-operational-deposits.quote: operational deposits (as defined in LCR40.26 to); LCR40.36

applies_to.note: Operational deposit status depends on the LCR40.26-LCR40.36 clearing, custody and cash-management tests; the corresponding asset side receives a 50% RSF under NSF30.29(4).

R-NSF30.13-asf50-operational-deposits.portfolio_relevance: Correspondent and cash-management balances give only half ASF credit, so a small bank relying on them to fund consumer credit is structurally disadvantaged.

R-NSF30.13-asf50-sovereign-pse.title: 50% ASF for sub-one-year funding from sovereigns, PSEs and development banks
R-NSF30.13-asf50-sovereign-pse.statement: Funding with residual maturity of less than one year from sovereigns, public sector entities, and multilateral and national development banks receives a 50% ASF factor.
R-NSF30.13-asf50-sovereign-pse.quote: funding with residual maturity of less than one year from sovereigns, public sector entities (PSEs), and multilateral and national development banks;

applies_to.note: Whether a national development bank qualifies is subject to supervisory guidance per the NSF30.13 footnote.

numeric_values: residual maturity of less than one year
R-NSF30.13-asf50-sovereign-pse.portfolio_relevance: Public-sector and municipal deposits, common in small US banks, carry only 50% ASF, so a large municipal deposit book weakens support for a card portfolio.

R-NSF30.13-asf50-other-6m-1y.title: 50% ASF for other funding with residual maturity between six months and one year
R-NSF30.13-asf50-other-6m-1y.statement: Other secured and unsecured funding with residual maturity between six months and less than one year, including funding from central banks and financial institutions, receives a 50% ASF factor.
R-NSF30.13-asf50-other-6m-1y.quote: other funding (secured and unsecured) not included in the categories above with residual maturity between six months to less than one year, including funding from central banks and financial institutions.

applies_to.note: Below six months the same funding drops to 0% ASF under NSF30.14(1).

numeric_values: between six months to less than one year
R-NSF30.13-asf50-other-6m-1y.portfolio_relevance: Creates a hard six-month cliff: FHLB advances or interbank funding rolled at under six months contribute nothing, so pushing them past six months is a cheap NSFR repair.

R-NSF30.14-asf0-residual.title: 0% ASF for all other liabilities including sub-six-month bank and central bank funding
R-NSF30.14-asf0-residual.statement: All other liabilities and equity not in a higher category, including funding with residual maturity of less than six months from central banks and financial institutions, receive a 0% ASF factor.
R-NSF30.14-asf0-residual.quote: Liabilities receiving a 0% ASF factor comprise: (1) all other liabilities and equity categories not included in the above categories, including other funding with residual maturity of less than six months from central banks and financial institutions;

applies_to.note: Residual catch-all category; a national-discretion carve-out exists for cooperative network deposits.

numeric_values: residual maturity of less than six months
R-NSF30.14-asf0-residual.portfolio_relevance: Short-term wholesale borrowing gives zero credit, so a card book funded by sub-six-month fed funds purchased or repo is entirely unsupported under the NSFR.

R-NSF30.14-asf0-no-stated-maturity.title: 0% ASF for liabilities without a stated maturity, with 100%/50% exceptions
R-NSF30.14-asf0-no-stated-maturity.statement: Liabilities without a stated maturity, including short and open maturity positions, receive a 0% ASF factor, except deferred tax liabilities and minority interest, which may receive 100% ASF if effective maturity is one year or more or 50% if between six months and less than one year.
R-NSF30.14-asf0-no-stated-maturity.quote: other liabilities without a stated maturity. This category must include short positions and open maturity positions that are not otherwise captured under NSF30.10 to NSF30.13. Two exceptions may be recognised for liabilities without a stated maturity, which would then be assigned either a 100% ASF factor if the effective maturity is one year or greater, or 50%, if the effective maturity is between six months and less than one year: (a) first, deferred tax liabilities, which should be treated according to the nearest possible date on which such liabilities could be realised; and (b) second, minority interest, which should be treated according to the term of the instrument, usually in perpetuity.

applies_to.note: The two exceptions are permissive ('may be recognised').

numeric_values: effective maturity one year or greater
between six months and less than one year
R-NSF30.14-asf0-no-stated-maturity.portfolio_relevance: Ensures that open-ended balance-sheet liabilities cannot be counted as stable funding for a revolving card book, closing the symmetry gap with NSF30.32(3).

R-NSF30.14-coop-network-85-cap.title: National discretion for cooperative network deposits, ASF capped at 85%
R-NSF30.14-coop-network-85-cap.statement: At national discretion, deposits between banks within the same cooperative network may be excluded from the 0% ASF category and assigned an ASF up to the RSF factor applied to the depositing bank, not to exceed 85%.
R-NSF30.14-coop-network-85-cap.quote: At the discretion of national supervisors, deposits between banks within the same cooperative network maybe excluded from liabilities receiving a 0% ASF provided they are either (a) required by law in some jurisdictions to be placed at the central organisation and are legally constrained within the cooperative bank network as minimum deposit requirements, or (b) in the context of common task sharing and legal, statutory or contractual arrangements, so long as the bank that has received the monies and the bank that has deposited participate in the same institutional network’s mutual protection scheme against illiquidity and insolvency of its members. Such deposits maybe assigned an ASF up to the RSF factor assigned by regulation for the same deposits to the depositing bank, not to exceed 85%.

applies_to.note: Explicit national discretion, conditional on statutory placement or a mutual protection scheme. Materially relevant to small mutual/cooperative institutions; the US has no equivalent carve-out, so Canadian credit-union centrals are the closest North American analogue.

R-NSF30.14-coop-network-85-cap.portfolio_relevance: Lets small network-member banks count central-organisation deposits as stable funding, materially changing how much consumer credit a cooperative institution can carry.

R-NSF30.15-rsf-calculation.title: RSF computed as carrying value times RSF factor plus weighted off-balance sheet exposures
R-NSF30.15-rsf-calculation.statement: RSF is calculated by assigning the carrying value of assets to categories, multiplying each by its RSF factor and summing, then adding off-balance sheet activity multiplied by its RSF factor.
R-NSF30.15-rsf-calculation.quote: The amount of RSF is calculated by first assigning the carrying value of an institution’s assets to the categories listed below. The carrying value of an asset item should generally be recorded by following its accounting value, ie net of specific provisions, in line with CRE20.1 and the requirements for on-balance sheet, non-derivative assets in LEV30. The amount assigned to each category is then multiplied by its associated RSF factor, and the total RSF is the sum of the weighted amounts added to the amount of off-balance-sheet activity (or potential liquidity exposure) multiplied by its associated RSF factor.

applies_to.note: Applies identically under SA and IRB; NSF30.15 requires SA risk weights in all cases.

R-NSF30.15-rsf-calculation.portfolio_relevance: Gives the exact linear form RSF = sum(factor_i x asset_i) + sum(factor_j x undrawn_j), which is the objective function a portfolio optimiser constrains.

R-NSF30.15-carrying-value-net-provisions.title: Asset carrying value is accounting value net of specific provisions
R-NSF30.15-carrying-value-net-provisions.statement: The carrying value of an asset should be its accounting value, net of specific provisions, consistent with CRE20.1 and the LEV30 requirements for on-balance sheet non-derivative assets.
R-NSF30.15-carrying-value-net-provisions.quote: The carrying value of an asset item should generally be recorded by following its accounting value, ie net of specific provisions, in line with CRE20.1 and the requirements for on-balance sheet, non-derivative assets in LEV30.

applies_to.note: Ties the NSFR asset measure to the same net-of-provision basis used in CRE20 and the leverage ratio.

R-NSF30.15-carrying-value-net-provisions.portfolio_relevance: Building card-loss allowances reduces RSF one-for-one with the net receivable, so provisioning mechanically eases the NSFR even as it hits capital.

R-NSF30.15-sa-risk-weights-mandatory.title: Standardised approach risk weights must be used for NSFR regardless of IRB status
R-NSF30.15-sa-risk-weights-mandatory.statement: A bank must use the standardised approach risk weights in CRE20 to determine its NSFR treatment even if it uses the internal ratings-based approach.
R-NSF30.15-sa-risk-weights-mandatory.quote: Regardless of whether a bank uses the internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the standardised approach risk weights in CRE20 must be used to determine the NSFR treatment.

applies_to.note: This is the approach-mapping rule: IRB banks cannot use modelled risk weights to place assets into the 65%/85% RSF buckets. It makes the NSFR computable for small SA-only banks on the same basis as large IRB banks.

R-NSF30.15-sa-risk-weights-mandatory.portfolio_relevance: Means the 35%-risk-weight test that separates 65% RSF from 85% RSF is always the CRE20 standardised test, so credit-card receivables (75%+ SA retail risk weight) can never reach the 65% bucket.

R-NSF30.15-hqla-definition.title: HQLA for NSFR purposes ignores LCR operational requirements and Level 2 caps
R-NSF30.15-hqla-definition.statement: For NSFR purposes HQLA means all HQLA without regard to the LCR operational requirements or the LCR caps on Level 2 and Level 2B assets.
R-NSF30.15-hqla-definition.quote: For the purposes of calculating the NSFR, high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) are defined as all HQLA without regard to Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) operational requirements and LCR caps on Level 2 and Level 2B assets that may otherwise limit the ability of some HQLA to be included as eligible HQLA in calculation of the LCR.

applies_to.note: HQLA defined in LCR30; operational requirements at LCR30.13-LCR30.28 are disapplied for the NSFR.

R-NSF30.15-hqla-definition.portfolio_relevance: A securities book that is capped out of LCR HQLA still gets the low 5%/15%/50% RSF factors, so substituting securities for card receivables relieves the NSFR more than the LCR would suggest.

R-NSF30.16-contractual-residual-maturity.title: Assets allocated to maturity buckets by contractual residual maturity
R-NSF30.16-contractual-residual-maturity.statement: Unless the NSFR standard states otherwise, assets must be allocated to maturity buckets according to their contractual residual maturity.
R-NSF30.16-contractual-residual-maturity.quote: Unless explicitly stated otherwise in the NSFR standard, assets must be allocated to maturity buckets according to their contractual residual maturity.

applies_to.note: Subject to embedded optionality per NSF30.7 and NSF30.17.

R-NSF30.16-contractual-residual-maturity.portfolio_relevance: Behavioural runoff models cannot be used to shorten the assumed life of a card book; only contractual terms and the NSF30.17 overrides count.

R-NSF30.16-rsf-factor-meaning.title: RSF factors approximate the amount of an asset that must be funded over one year
R-NSF30.16-rsf-factor-meaning.statement: RSF factors approximate the portion of an asset that would have to be funded because it will be rolled over or could not be monetised over one year without significant expense, and that amount must be supported by stable funding.
R-NSF30.16-rsf-factor-meaning.quote: The RSF factors assigned to various types of assets are intended to approximate the amount of a particular asset that would have to be funded, either because it will be rolled over, or because it could not be monetised through sale or used as collateral in a secured borrowing transaction over the course of one year without significant expense. Under the standard, such amounts must be supported by stable funding.

applies_to.note: Interpretive principle for the RSF ladder.

numeric_values: over the course of one year
R-NSF30.16-rsf-factor-meaning.portfolio_relevance: Explains why securitisable card receivables are still funded at 85%: sale capacity, not just maturity, drives the factor, so a bank with a proven ABS channel is still charged as if it had none.

R-NSF30.17-extension-option.title: Assume investors exercise any option to extend asset maturity
R-NSF30.17-extension-option.statement: When determining an asset's maturity, the bank must assume investors exercise any option to extend maturity.
R-NSF30.17-extension-option.quote: When determining the maturity of an instrument, the bank must assume investors exercise any option to extend maturity.

applies_to.note: For bank-discretion extension options, supervisors weigh reputational factors that may prevent non-exercise.

R-NSF30.17-extension-option.portfolio_relevance: Borrower-extendable consumer loans must be assumed to run long, pushing them from the 50% into the 65%/85% RSF bucket.

R-NSF30.17-amortising-loans.title: Amortising loans may split the portion due within one year into the short bucket
R-NSF30.17-amortising-loans.statement: For amortising loans, the portion coming due within the one-year horizon may be treated in the less-than-one-year residual maturity category.
R-NSF30.17-amortising-loans.quote: For amortising loans (or other principal repayment claims), the portion that comes due within the one-year horizon may be treated in the less-than-one- year residual maturity category.

applies_to.note: Permissive; requires the bank to be able to split contractual amortisation schedules, which small banks may not report publicly.

R-NSF30.17-amortising-loans.portfolio_relevance: Amortising instalment loans get partial 50% RSF treatment that revolving card balances cannot claim, so converting card debt into instalment plans lowers RSF for the near-term amortising slice.

R-NSF30.17-no-stated-maturity-65-85.title: Unencumbered loans without a stated final maturity deemed over one year and given 65% or 85% RSF
R-NSF30.17-no-stated-maturity-65-85.statement: Unencumbered loans with no stated final maturity, even where the borrower may repay in full without penalty at the next rate reset, are deemed to have an effective residual maturity of more than one year and must receive either a 65% or an 85% RSF factor depending on their standardised-approach risk weight.
R-NSF30.17-no-stated-maturity-65-85.quote: Unencumbered loans without a stated final maturity, even where the borrower may repay the loan in full and without penalty charges at the next rate reset date, are deemed to have an effective residual maturity period of more than one year and must be given either a 65% or 85% RSF factor depending on their risk weights under the standardised approach for credit risk.

applies_to.note: The 65% vs 85% split turns on the CRE20 standardised risk weight (35% or lower gets 65%), and NSF30.15 forces SA risk weights even for IRB banks.

numeric_values: effective residual maturity of more than one year
R-NSF30.17-no-stated-maturity-65-85.portfolio_relevance: This is the decisive credit-card rule: revolving card receivables have no stated final maturity, so they are forced into the long bucket at 85% RSF (SA retail risk weight exceeds 35%), meaning roughly 85 cents of stable funding per dollar of drawn card balance.

R-NSF30.17-review-date-discretion.title: Supervisors may allow the next review date to be used as maturity date
R-NSF30.17-review-date-discretion.statement: Where a facility or loan has a contractual review date at which the bank may decide whether to renew, supervisors may authorise on a case-by-case basis the use of the next review date as the maturity date.
R-NSF30.17-review-date-discretion.quote: If there is a contractual provision with a review date at which the bank may determine whether a given facility or loan is renewed or not, supervisors may authorise, on a case by case basis, banks to use the next review date as the maturity date.

applies_to.note: Explicit case-by-case supervisory approval gate; supervisors must weigh incentives and the actual likelihood of non-renewal, and reputational constraints mean non-renewal options are generally assumed not exercised.

R-NSF30.17-review-date-discretion.portfolio_relevance: The only available escape from the 85% RSF on revolving credit: restructuring card lines with hard contractual review dates could move balances to the 50% sub-one-year bucket, but only with prior supervisory sign-off.

R-NSF30.18-central-bank-rsf-floor-5.title: Reduced RSF for exceptional central bank operations floored at 5%
R-NSF30.18-central-bank-rsf-floor-5.statement: For exceptional central bank liquidity absorbing operations with residual maturity of six months or more, the RSF factor applied to claims on the central bank must not be lower than 5%.
R-NSF30.18-central-bank-rsf-floor-5.quote: For those operations with a residual maturity equal to or greater than six months, the RSF factor must not be lower than 5%.

applies_to.note: Requires supervisors to agree the factor with the relevant central bank and to monitor the ongoing impact; only applies to operations designated exceptional.

numeric_values: residual maturity equal to or greater than six months
R-NSF30.18-central-bank-rsf-floor-5.portfolio_relevance: Caps the relief a bank can obtain from parking liquidity at the central bank during stress, so it cannot be used to offset a card book's RSF beyond the 5% floor.

R-NSF30.20-encumbered-assets.title: RSF for encumbered assets: 100% at one year, 50% floor between six months and one year
R-NSF30.20-encumbered-assets.statement: Assets encumbered for one year or more must receive a 100% RSF factor; assets encumbered for between six months and less than one year must receive at least a 50% RSF factor, retaining any higher unencumbered factor.
R-NSF30.20-encumbered-assets.quote: Assets on the balance sheet that are encumbered for one year or more must receive a 100% RSF factor. Assets encumbered for a period of between six months and less than one year that would, if unencumbered, receive an RSF factor lower than or equal to 50% must receive a 50% RSF factor. Assets encumbered for between six months and less than one year that would, if unencumbered, receive an RSF factor higher than 50% must retain that higher RSF factor.

applies_to.note: Encumbered assets include assets backing securities or covered bonds and assets pledged in securities financing transactions; 'unencumbered' takes its LCR30.16 meaning.

numeric_values: encumbered for one year or more
between six months and less than one year
R-NSF30.20-encumbered-assets.portfolio_relevance: Pledging card receivables into a term securitisation or FHLB collateral pool for a year or more pushes them to 100% RSF, so on-balance-sheet secured funding of a card book worsens the NSFR asset side even as it improves the liability side.

R-NSF30.20-encumbrance-under-6m.title: Assets with under six months of encumbrance remaining may be treated as unencumbered
R-NSF30.20-encumbrance-under-6m.statement: Where assets have less than six months remaining in the encumbrance period, they may receive the same RSF factor as an equivalent unencumbered asset.
R-NSF30.20-encumbrance-under-6m.quote: Where assets have less than six months remaining in the encumbrance period, those assets may receive the same RSF factor as an equivalent asset that is unencumbered.

applies_to.note: Permissive; the remaining encumbrance period, not the original term, is what counts.

numeric_values: less than six months remaining encumbrance
R-NSF30.20-encumbrance-under-6m.portfolio_relevance: Short-dated pledges of card collateral avoid the encumbrance penalty entirely, favouring rolling short secured facilities over term ABS on the RSF side.

R-NSF30.22-sft-gross-reporting.title: Securities financing transactions reported gross unless LEV30 netting conditions are met
R-NSF30.22-sft-gross-reporting.statement: Amounts receivable and payable under securities financing transactions should be reported gross on the RSF and ASF sides respectively, except that transactions with a single counterparty may be netted where the LEV30 netting conditions are satisfied.
R-NSF30.22-sft-gross-reporting.quote: Amounts receivable and payable under these securities financing transactions should generally be reported on a gross basis, meaning that the gross amount of such receivables and payables should be reported on the RSF side and ASF side, respectively. The only exception is that securities financing transactions with a single counterparty may be measured on a net basis when calculating the NSFR, provided that the netting conditions for securities financing transactions set out in LEV30 are met.

applies_to.note: Materially relevant only where a bank runs repo/reverse repo books; most small North American banks have negligible SFT activity.

R-NSF30.22-sft-gross-reporting.portfolio_relevance: Prevents a bank from shrinking measured RSF by netting repo books, so balance-sheet gross-up from funding a card portfolio through repo is fully captured.

R-NSF30.25-rsf0-cash-and-reserves.title: 0% RSF for cash, central bank reserves and short-dated central bank claims
R-NSF30.25-rsf0-cash-and-reserves.statement: Coins and banknotes immediately available, all central bank reserves including required and excess reserves, and all claims on central banks with residual maturities of less than six months receive a 0% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.25-rsf0-cash-and-reserves.quote: Assets assigned a 0% RSF factor comprise: (1) coins and banknotes immediately available to meet obligations; (2) all central bank reserves (including required reserves and excess reserves); (3) all claims on central banks with residual maturities of less than six months;

applies_to.note: Supervisors may agree a different factor for required reserves with the relevant central bank; 'claims' is broader than loans and includes central bank bills.

numeric_values: residual maturities of less than six months
R-NSF30.25-rsf0-cash-and-reserves.portfolio_relevance: Reserves at the Fed are RSF-free, so a bank can restore its NSFR by shifting from card receivables (85% RSF) into central bank balances at a cost of the full yield spread.

R-NSF30.26-rsf5-level1.title: 5% RSF for unencumbered Level 1 assets
R-NSF30.26-rsf5-level1.statement: Unencumbered Level 1 assets as defined in LCR30.41, other than those receiving a 0% RSF, receive a 5% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.26-rsf5-level1.quote: Assets assigned a 5% RSF factor comprise unencumbered Level 1 assets as defined in LCR30.41, excluding assets receiving a 0% RSF as specified above, and including:

applies_to.note: Includes marketable securities claims on sovereigns, central banks, PSEs, BIS, IMF, ECB or MDBs assigned a 0% risk weight under CRE20.

R-NSF30.26-rsf5-level1.portfolio_relevance: Treasuries and agency-guaranteed paper cost 5 cents of stable funding per dollar versus 85 cents for card receivables, quantifying the NSFR cost of every dollar shifted from securities into cards.

R-NSF30.27-rsf10-secured-fi-loans.title: 10% RSF for sub-six-month loans to financial institutions secured by Level 1 assets
R-NSF30.27-rsf10-secured-fi-loans.statement: Unencumbered loans to financial institutions with residual maturities of less than six months, secured against Level 1 assets and where the bank may freely rehypothecate the collateral for the life of the loan, receive a 10% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.27-rsf10-secured-fi-loans.quote: Assets assigned a 10% RSF factor comprise unencumbered loans to financial institutions with residual maturities of less than six months, where the loan is secured against Level 1 assets as defined in LCR30.41, and where the bank has the ability to freely rehypothecate the received collateral for the life of the loan.

applies_to.note: Requires both Level 1 collateral and an unrestricted rehypothecation right; failing either test drops the exposure to 15% under NSF30.28(2).

numeric_values: residual maturities of less than six months
R-NSF30.27-rsf10-secured-fi-loans.portfolio_relevance: Sets the cheapest available lending use of balance sheet, giving the lower bound against which the funding cost of a card portfolio should be benchmarked.

R-NSF30.28-rsf15-level2a.title: 15% RSF for unencumbered Level 2A assets
R-NSF30.28-rsf15-level2a.statement: Unencumbered Level 2A assets as defined in LCR30.43, including securities of sovereigns, central banks, PSEs and MDBs with a 20% risk weight under CRE20, receive a 15% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.28-rsf15-level2a.quote: Assets assigned a 15% RSF factor comprise: (1) unencumbered Level 2A assets as defined in LCR30.43, including: (a) marketable securities representing claims on or guaranteed by sovereigns, central banks, PSEs or multilateral development banks that are assigned a 20% risk weight under CRE20;

applies_to.note: Also covers corporate debt securities and covered bonds rated at least AA-; the 20% risk weight is the CRE20 standardised weight in all cases per NSF30.15.

numeric_values: credit rating equal or equivalent to at least AA–
R-NSF30.28-rsf15-level2a.portfolio_relevance: Municipal and agency holdings typical of small US banks cost 15% RSF, one sixth of the funding burden of an equivalent card balance.

R-NSF30.28-rsf15-other-fi-loans.title: 15% RSF for other sub-six-month loans to financial institutions
R-NSF30.28-rsf15-other-fi-loans.statement: All other unencumbered loans to financial institutions with residual maturities of less than six months that do not qualify for the 10% factor receive a 15% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.28-rsf15-other-fi-loans.quote: all other unencumbered loans to financial institutions with residual maturities of less than six months not included in NSF30.27.

applies_to.note: Residual category for unsecured or inadequately secured short interbank placements.

numeric_values: residual maturities of less than six months
R-NSF30.28-rsf15-other-fi-loans.portfolio_relevance: Fed funds sold and short interbank placements consume only 15% stable funding, making them the natural parking place when a card book pushes the NSFR toward the limit.

R-NSF30.29-rsf50-level2b.title: 50% RSF for unencumbered Level 2B assets
R-NSF30.29-rsf50-level2b.statement: Unencumbered Level 2B assets as defined in LCR30.45, including RMBS rated at least AA, corporate debt rated A+ to BBB- and exchange-traded common equity not issued by financial institutions, receive a 50% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.29-rsf50-level2b.quote: unencumbered Level 2B assets as defined and subject to the conditions set forth in LCR30.45, including: (a) residential mortgage-backed securities with a credit rating of at least AA; (b) corporate debt securities (including commercial paper) with a credit rating of between A+ and BBB–; and (c) exchange-traded common equity shares not issued by financial institutions or their affiliates;

applies_to.note: Subject to the LCR30.45 Level 2B conditions; the NSFR ignores the LCR Level 2B cap per the NSF30.15 footnote.

numeric_values: credit rating of at least AA (RMBS)
credit rating of between A+ and BBB–
R-NSF30.29-rsf50-level2b.portfolio_relevance: Retained senior tranches of a card or mortgage securitisation rated in these bands sit at 50% RSF, so securitising and holding a senior tranche cuts RSF by 35 points versus holding the whole-loan card book at 85%.

R-NSF30.29-rsf50-fi-6m-1y.title: 50% RSF for loans to financial institutions and central banks maturing in six to twelve months
R-NSF30.29-rsf50-fi-6m-1y.statement: All loans to financial institutions and central banks with residual maturity between six months and less than one year receive a 50% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.29-rsf50-fi-6m-1y.quote: all loans to financial institutions and central banks with residual maturity of between six months and less than one year;

applies_to.note: Beyond one year, loans to financial institutions jump to 100% RSF under NSF30.32(4).

numeric_values: between six months and less than one year
R-NSF30.29-rsf50-fi-6m-1y.portfolio_relevance: Marks the six-month cliff on interbank assets: extending a placement past six months triples its RSF from 15% to 50%.

R-NSF30.29-rsf50-retail-under-1y.title: 50% RSF for non-HQLA with residual maturity under one year, including retail and small business loans
R-NSF30.29-rsf50-retail-under-1y.statement: All other non-HQLA assets with a residual maturity of less than one year, for example loans to non-financial corporate clients, loans to retail customers (natural persons) and small business customers, and loans to sovereigns, national development banks and PSEs, receive a 50% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.29-rsf50-retail-under-1y.quote: all other non-HQLA not included in the above categories that have a residual maturity of less than one year, for example, loans to non-financial corporate clients, loans to retail customers (ie natural persons) and small business customers, and loans to sovereigns, national development banks and PSEs.

applies_to.note: Only reachable where the loan has a contractual residual maturity under one year; NSF30.17 forces loans with no stated final maturity out of this bucket into 65%/85% regardless of repricing frequency.

numeric_values: residual maturity of less than one year
R-NSF30.29-rsf50-retail-under-1y.portfolio_relevance: The target bucket for consumer credit: a short-dated instalment loan funds at 50% while an identical-yield revolving card balance funds at 85%, a 35-point stable-funding saving from restructuring revolving debt into sub-one-year term loans.

R-NSF30.30-rsf65-residential-mortgage.title: 65% RSF for residential mortgages of one year or more with 35% or lower risk weight
R-NSF30.30-rsf65-residential-mortgage.statement: Unencumbered residential mortgages with residual maturity of one year or more that would qualify for a 35% or lower risk weight under CRE20 receive a 65% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.30-rsf65-residential-mortgage.quote: Assets assigned a 65% RSF factor comprise: (1) unencumbered residential mortgages with a residual maturity of one year or more that would qualify for a 35% or lower risk weight under CRE20; and

applies_to.note: The 35% test uses the CRE20 standardised risk weight even for IRB banks (NSF30.15), so it turns on LTV and the loan's qualifying-mortgage status.

numeric_values: residual maturity of one year or more
R-NSF30.30-rsf65-residential-mortgage.portfolio_relevance: Low-LTV residential mortgages fund at 65% versus 85% for card receivables, so shifting a small bank's consumer book toward qualifying mortgages relieves 20 points of RSF per dollar.

R-NSF30.30-rsf65-other-low-rw-loans.title: 65% RSF for other long-dated loans qualifying for a 35% or lower risk weight
R-NSF30.30-rsf65-other-low-rw-loans.statement: Other unencumbered loans not otherwise categorised, including loans to sovereigns, MDBs, PSEs and national development banks but excluding loans to financial institutions, with residual maturity of one year or more and a 35% or lower CRE20 risk weight, receive a 65% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.30-rsf65-other-low-rw-loans.quote: other unencumbered loans, including loans to sovereigns, multilateral development banks, PSEs and national development banks, not included in the above categories, excluding loans to financial institutions, with a residual maturity of one year or more that would qualify for a 35% or lower risk weight under CRE20.

applies_to.note: Standardised risk weights apply regardless of IRB status; loans to financial institutions are expressly excluded from this bucket.

numeric_values: residual maturity of one year or more
R-NSF30.30-rsf65-other-low-rw-loans.portfolio_relevance: Confirms that no unsecured retail or card exposure can reach 65% RSF, because CRE20 gives regulatory retail and other retail exposures risk weights well above 35%.

R-NSF30.31-rsf85-performing-loans.title: 85% RSF for long-dated performing loans not qualifying for a 35% or lower risk weight
R-NSF30.31-rsf85-performing-loans.statement: Other unencumbered performing loans that do not qualify for the 35% or lower risk weight under CRE20 and have residual maturities of one year or more, excluding loans to financial institutions, receive an 85% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.31-rsf85-performing-loans.quote: other unencumbered performing loans that do not qualify for the 35% or lower risk weight under CRE20 and have residual maturities of one year or more, excluding loans to financial institutions;

applies_to.note: Read with NSF30.17: revolving credit with no stated final maturity is deemed to be one year or more, so drawn credit-card balances fall here. 'Performing' means not past due more than 90 days and not defaulted under CRE20.

numeric_values: residual maturities of one year or more
R-NSF30.31-rsf85-performing-loans.portfolio_relevance: The core credit-card RSF factor: each dollar of drawn, performing card receivable requires 85 cents of available stable funding, so a card-heavy small bank needs roughly 0.85 of stable funding per dollar of book plus the off-balance sheet charge on undrawn lines.

R-NSF30.31-rsf85-securities.title: 85% RSF for long-dated non-HQLA securities and exchange-traded equities
R-NSF30.31-rsf85-securities.statement: Unencumbered securities with remaining maturity of one year or more and exchange-traded equities that are not in default and do not qualify as HQLA receive an 85% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.31-rsf85-securities.quote: unencumbered securities with a remaining maturity of one year or more and exchange-traded equities, that are not in default and do not qualify as HQLA according to the LCR standard;

applies_to.note: Non-HQLA test uses the LCR definitions read without the LCR caps (NSF30.15 footnote).

numeric_values: remaining maturity of one year or more
R-NSF30.31-rsf85-securities.portfolio_relevance: Non-HQLA retained securitisation tranches of a card book carry the same 85% RSF as the underlying receivables, so securitising without achieving HQLA-eligible or Level 2B-rated tranches produces no NSFR benefit.

R-NSF30.31-performing-loan-definition.title: Definition of performing loans for RSF purposes
R-NSF30.31-performing-loan-definition.statement: Performing loans are those not past due for more than 90 days and not otherwise classified as a defaulted exposure under CRE20.
R-NSF30.31-performing-loan-definition.quote: Performing loans are considered to be those that are not past due for more than 90 days or otherwise classified as a defaulted exposure under CRE20.

applies_to.note: Cross-references the CRE20 default definition; the 90-day past-due test maps directly onto the delinquency buckets small banks report.

R-NSF30.31-performing-loan-definition.portfolio_relevance: Sets the 90-day boundary at which a card receivable jumps from 85% to 100% RSF, so rising card delinquency directly increases required stable funding on top of provisions and RWA.

R-NSF30.32-rsf100-encumbered-1y.title: 100% RSF for assets encumbered for one year or more
R-NSF30.32-rsf100-encumbered-1y.statement: All assets encumbered for a period of one year or more receive a 100% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.32-rsf100-encumbered-1y.quote: Assets assigned a 100% RSF factor comprise: (1) all assets that are encumbered for a period of one year or more;

applies_to.note: Consistent with NSF30.20; encumbrance is measured by remaining period, not original term.

numeric_values: encumbered for a period of one year or more
R-NSF30.32-rsf100-encumbered-1y.portfolio_relevance: Term ABS or covered-bond structures collateralised by card receivables push the pledged pool from 85% to 100% RSF, so the funding benefit must exceed a 15-point RSF penalty on the collateral.

R-NSF30.32-rsf100-no-stated-maturity.title: 100% RSF for assets without a stated maturity
R-NSF30.32-rsf100-no-stated-maturity.statement: Assets without a stated maturity that are not encumbered for a year or more and are not net derivative assets, including non-maturity reverse repos unless the bank can demonstrate they would effectively mature within one year, receive a 100% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.32-rsf100-no-stated-maturity.quote: assets without a stated maturity not included in NSF30.32 (1) and NSF30.32 (2) (including non-maturity reverse repos unless banks can demonstrate to supervisors that the non-maturity reverse repo would effectively mature in less than one year);

applies_to.note: The demonstration to supervisors is an explicit evidentiary gate. Note the carve-out in NSF30.17: unencumbered loans without a stated final maturity go to 65%/85%, not here.

numeric_values: effectively mature in less than one year
R-NSF30.32-rsf100-no-stated-maturity.portfolio_relevance: Any open-ended asset other than a loan is fully funded, so only the NSF30.17 loan carve-out keeps revolving card receivables at 85% rather than 100%.

R-NSF30.32-rsf100-npl-and-other.title: 100% RSF for non-performing loans and other residual assets
R-NSF30.32-rsf100-npl-and-other.statement: All other assets not otherwise categorised, including non-performing loans, loans to financial institutions with residual maturity of one year or more, non-exchange-traded equities, fixed assets, items deducted from regulatory capital, retained interest, insurance assets, subsidiary interests and defaulted securities, receive a 100% RSF factor.
R-NSF30.32-rsf100-npl-and-other.quote: all other assets not included in the above categories, including non- performing loans, loans to financial institutions with a residual maturity of one year or more, non-exchange-traded equities, fixed assets, items deducted from regulatory capital, retained interest, insurance assets, subsidiary interests and defaulted securities;

applies_to.note: 'Retained interest' explicitly captures seller's interests and retained residuals in securitisations, which is the standard structure for credit-card master trusts.

numeric_values: residual maturity of one year or more (loans to financial institutions)
R-NSF30.32-rsf100-npl-and-other.portfolio_relevance: A card book's delinquent balances and its retained securitisation interest both attract 100% RSF, so credit deterioration and off-balance-sheet card funding structures each raise required stable funding above the 85% base rate.

R-NSF30.33-obs-rationale.title: RSF assigned to off-balance sheet activities for exposures likely to be funded within one year
R-NSF30.33-obs-rationale.statement: The NSFR assigns an RSF factor to off-balance sheet activities so that institutions hold stable funding for the portion of such exposures expected to require funding within one year.
R-NSF30.33-obs-rationale.quote: The NSFR assigns an RSF factor to various off-balance sheet activities in order to ensure that institutions hold stable funding for the portion of off- balance sheet exposures that may be expected to require funding within a one- year horizon.

applies_to.note: Principle; the operative factors are in the NSF30.34 table.

R-NSF30.33-obs-rationale.portfolio_relevance: Establishes that unused credit-card lines create an RSF charge measured on expected drawdown within a year, making open-to-buy a balance-sheet cost rather than a free option.

R-NSF30.34-obs-categories.title: Off-balance sheet exposures categorised by facility type consistent with the LCR
R-NSF30.34-obs-categories.statement: Off-balance sheet exposure categories are identified based broadly on whether the commitment is a credit or liquidity facility or some other contingent funding obligation, with the specific types and RSF factors set out in Table 1.
R-NSF30.34-obs-categories.quote: Consistent with the LCR, the NSFR identifies off-balance-sheet exposure categories based broadly on whether the commitment is a credit or liquidity facility or some other contingent funding obligation. Table 1 identifies the specific types of off-balance-sheet exposures to be assigned to each off-balance sheet category and their associated RSF factor.

applies_to.note: Category definitions mirror the LCR facility taxonomy, so revocability of the commitment is the classifying variable.

R-NSF30.34-obs-categories.portfolio_relevance: Makes the revocability of card lines the switch that determines whether they attract the fixed 5% factor or a nationally set factor.

R-NSF30.34-obs-5pct-undrawn.title: 5% RSF on the undrawn portion of irrevocable and conditionally revocable credit and liquidity facilities
R-NSF30.34-obs-5pct-undrawn.statement: Irrevocable and conditionally revocable credit and liquidity facilities to any client attract a 5% RSF factor applied to the currently undrawn portion.
R-NSF30.34-obs-5pct-undrawn.quote: 5% of the currently Irrevocable and conditionally revocable credit and liquidity undrawn portion facilities to any client

applies_to.note: The Table 1 text is column-interleaved in the source: the RSF factor column reads '5% of the currently undrawn portion' and the category column reads 'Irrevocable and conditionally revocable credit and liquidity facilities to any client'. Applies 'to any client', so no counterparty distinction.

R-NSF30.34-obs-5pct-undrawn.portfolio_relevance: Where card lines are irrevocable or only conditionally revocable, every dollar of unused credit line costs 5 cents of stable funding; since undrawn card lines typically run 3-5x drawn balances at small issuers, this can rival the 85% charge on drawn balances in absolute size.

R-NSF30.34-obs-national-discretion.title: National supervisors set RSF factors for other contingent funding obligations including unconditionally revocable facilities
R-NSF30.34-obs-national-discretion.statement: National supervisors may specify the RSF factors, based on their national circumstances, for other contingent funding obligations including unconditionally revocable credit and liquidity facilities, trade finance-related obligations, guarantees and letters of credit, and non-contractual obligations.
R-NSF30.34-obs-national-discretion.quote: National supervisors may Other contingent funding obligations, including products specify the RSF factors and instruments such as unconditionally revocable credit based on their national and liquidity facilities; trade finance-related obligations circumstances (including guarantees and letters of credit);

applies_to.note: Explicit national discretion with no Basel-specified number. The Table 1 text is column-interleaved: the factor column reads 'National supervisors may specify the RSF factors based on their national circumstances'. Decisive for North America because US and Canadian credit-card lines are typically unconditionally cancellable, so the applicable factor is set nationally (the US NSFR rule assigns 0% to unconditionally cancellable commitments).

R-NSF30.34-obs-national-discretion.portfolio_relevance: The single largest jurisdictional swing for a card issuer: if undrawn card lines are unconditionally revocable they escape the 5% Basel charge and take a nationally set (in the US, zero) factor, so the NSFR cost of a card portfolio is dominated by drawn balances rather than open-to-buy.

R-NSF30.35-interdependent-definition.title: Definition of interdependent assets and liabilities
R-NSF30.35-interdependent-definition.statement: Supervisors may determine in limited circumstances that asset and liability items are interdependent where the liability cannot fall due while the asset remains on the balance sheet, the asset's principal flows can only repay that liability, and the liability cannot fund other assets.
R-NSF30.35-interdependent-definition.quote: National supervisors have discretion in limited circumstances to determine whether certain asset and liability items, on the basis of contractual arrangements, are interdependent such that the liability cannot fall due while the asset remains on the balance sheet, the principal payment flows from the asset cannot be used for something other than repaying the liability, and the liability cannot be used to fund other assets.

applies_to.note: National discretion, exercisable only in limited circumstances and not applicable to derivatives per the NSF30.35 FAQ.

R-NSF30.35-interdependent-definition.portfolio_relevance: Defines the only route by which a matched-funded lending programme (e.g. a pass-through card or mortgage funding vehicle) can be removed from both sides of the NSFR.

R-NSF30.35-interdependent-criteria.title: Interdependent items may be assigned 0% RSF and 0% ASF subject to four criteria
R-NSF30.35-interdependent-criteria.statement: For interdependent items, supervisors may set both the RSF and ASF factors to 0%, subject to criteria including that the items are clearly identifiable and that the maturity and principal amount of the liability and its interdependent asset are the same.
R-NSF30.35-interdependent-criteria.quote: For interdependent items, supervisors may adjust RSF and ASF factors so that they are both 0%, subject to the following criteria: (1) The individual interdependent asset and liability items must be clearly identifiable. (2) The maturity and principal amount of both the liability and its interdependent asset must be the same.

applies_to.note: Requires supervisory approval; two further criteria apply (the bank acts solely as a pass-through unit, and the counterparties for each pair must not be the same).

R-NSF30.35-interdependent-criteria.portfolio_relevance: A pass-through funding programme exactly matched in maturity and principal drops out of the NSFR entirely, giving a restructuring route for a portfolio that would otherwise consume 85% stable funding.

R-NSF30.37-interdependent-transparency.title: Interdependent treatment must be transparently set out in national regulation
R-NSF30.37-interdependent-transparency.statement: The instances in which supervisors exercise the interdependent-item discretion should be transparent, explicit and clearly outlined in each jurisdiction's regulations.
R-NSF30.37-interdependent-transparency.quote: The instances where supervisors will exercise the discretion to apply this exceptional treatment should be transparent, explicit and clearly outlined in the regulations of each jurisdiction,

applies_to.note: Directed at supervisors rather than banks; makes the national list of interdependent treatments a checkable input to any cross-jurisdiction NSFR comparison.

R-NSF30.37-interdependent-transparency.portfolio_relevance: Means a jurisdiction's published list of interdependent treatments can be read off directly when calibrating whether a bank's matched funding programme escapes the NSFR.

R-LEX10.2-granularity-assumption.title: Pillar 1 capital assumes infinitely granular portfolios and ignores concentration risk
R-LEX10.2-granularity-assumption.statement: The minimum risk-based capital requirements implicitly assume an infinitely granular portfolio and therefore do not capture concentration risk, which is why a separate large exposures framework is needed.
R-LEX10.2-granularity-assumption.quote: the minimum capital requirements (Pillar 1) of the Basel risk-based capital framework implicitly assume that a bank holds infinitely granular portfolios, ie no form of concentration risk is considered in calculating capital requirements

applies_to.note: Design rationale, not an operative obligation; explains why RWA-based metrics alone under-measure single-name risk.

R-LEX10.2-granularity-assumption.portfolio_relevance: Establishes the analytical premise that a highly granular credit card book generates essentially no measurable large-exposure charge, so shifting from lumpy commercial credit into granular card receivables relaxes the concentration constraint even though RWA density rises.

R-LEX10.4-level-of-application.title: Large exposures framework applies at every tier of the banking group
R-LEX10.4-level-of-application.statement: The large exposures framework must be applied at the same level of consolidation as the risk-based capital requirements, ie at every tier within a banking group.
R-LEX10.4-level-of-application.quote: it must apply at the same level as the risk-based capital requirements are required to be applied following SCO10, ie at every tier within a banking group.

applies_to.note: Level of application follows SCO10; for a single-bank US holding company the consolidated and bank levels typically coincide.

R-LEX10.4-level-of-application.portfolio_relevance: Means a concentration test must be run against consolidated Tier 1 as reported in the quarterly filing, so a card portfolio booked in a subsidiary still consumes the parent's single-name headroom.

R-LEX10.5-scope-internationally-active.title: Framework binds all internationally active banks; jurisdictions may be stricter
R-LEX10.5-scope-internationally-active.statement: The large exposures framework applies to all internationally active banks, and member jurisdictions may impose more stringent standards.
R-LEX10.5-scope-internationally-active.quote: The large exposures framework is applicable to all internationally active banks. As with all other standards issued by the Committee, member jurisdictions have the option to set more stringent standards.

applies_to.note: Baseline Basel scope is internationally active banks only; small North American banks fall in scope only where the national authority extends it (see LEX10.5 second limb). In the US the single-counterparty credit limit applies to large holding companies, so for small banks this is a benchmark rather than a binding rule.

R-LEX10.5-scope-internationally-active.portfolio_relevance: Determines whether the 25% limit is a binding constraint or a voluntary diagnostic for a given small bank; drives whether concentration headroom enters the optimiser as a hard or soft bound.

R-LEX10.5-national-extension.title: National discretion to extend the framework to smaller banks with a different approach
R-LEX10.5-national-extension.statement: Jurisdictions may extend the large exposures framework to a wider range of banks and may develop a different approach for banks that fall outside the scope of the Basel framework.
R-LEX10.5-national-extension.quote: They also have the option to extend the application to a wider range of banks, with the possibility – if they deem it necessary – to develop a different approach for banks that usually fall outside the scope of the Basel framework.

applies_to.note: Explicit national-discretion gate; the accompanying footnote notes such banks might be allowed to recognise physical collateral, which the Basel large exposures framework otherwise refuses.

R-LEX10.5-national-extension.portfolio_relevance: Flags that any large-exposure constraint imposed on a small North American bank is a national overlay whose calibration (and collateral eligibility) may differ, so modelled headroom for small banks should be treated as jurisdiction-dependent.

R-LEX10.6-consolidated-aggregation.title: Aggregate all third-party exposures across the consolidation group against group Tier 1
R-LEX10.6-consolidated-aggregation.statement: At the consolidated level a bank must aggregate all exposures to third parties across the regulatory consolidation group and compare that aggregate with the group's Tier 1 capital.
R-LEX10.6-consolidated-aggregation.quote: a bank must consider all exposures to third parties across the relevant regulatory consolidation group and compare the aggregate of those exposures with the group’s Tier 1 capital.

applies_to.note: Denominator is consolidated group Tier 1 capital, directly observable in quarterly regulatory filings.

R-LEX10.6-consolidated-aggregation.portfolio_relevance: Sets the denominator for every concentration ratio: growing Tier 1 capital, not shrinking exposures, is an equally valid way to create headroom for a concentrated commercial or card-partner exposure.

R-LEX10.7-all-counterparties-in-scope.title: All counterparties are in scope; only sovereigns are exempt
R-LEX10.7-all-counterparties-in-scope.statement: A bank must consider exposures to any counterparty; the only counterparties exempted from the framework are sovereigns as defined in LEX30.31.
R-LEX10.7-all-counterparties-in-scope.quote: A bank must consider exposures to any counterparty. The only counterparties that are exempted from the framework are sovereigns as defined in LEX30.31.

applies_to.note: Specific treatments and further exemptions are enumerated in LEX30.31 to LEX30.59.

R-LEX10.7-all-counterparties-in-scope.portfolio_relevance: Only sovereign exposures give unlimited concentration capacity, so a bank near its limit can only park balance sheet in sovereigns/central banks without consuming single-name headroom.

R-LEX10.7-residual-subject-to-limit.title: Any exposure type not explicitly exempted is fully subject to the limit
R-LEX10.7-residual-subject-to-limit.statement: Any exposure type not included in the specific-treatment provisions of LEX30.31 to LEX30.59 is subject in all respects to the large exposure limit.
R-LEX10.7-residual-subject-to-limit.quote: Any exposure type not included in LEX30.31 to LEX30.59 is subject in all respects to the large exposure limit.

applies_to.note: Closed-list exemption logic: no residual carve-out for retail or consumer exposures exists in the large exposures framework.

R-LEX10.7-residual-subject-to-limit.portfolio_relevance: Confirms there is no retail or credit-card exemption in the large exposures framework; card exposures escape the limit only through obligor-level granularity, not through an asset-class carve-out.

R-LEX10.8-large-exposure-10pct-t1.title: Definition of a large exposure: 10% or more of Tier 1 capital
R-LEX10.8-large-exposure-10pct-t1.statement: The sum of all exposure values to a single counterparty or group of connected counterparties is a large exposure when it equals or exceeds 10% of the bank's Tier 1 capital as defined in CAP10.2.
R-LEX10.8-large-exposure-10pct-t1.quote: must be defined as a large exposure if it is equal to or above 10% of the bank’s Tier 1 capital (as defined in CAP10.2). The exposure values must be measured as specified in LEX30.

applies_to.note: Reporting trigger, distinct from the 25% hard limit in LEX20.1.

R-LEX10.8-large-exposure-10pct-t1.portfolio_relevance: Defines the reporting threshold: exposures above 10% of Tier 1 attract supervisory scrutiny well before the 25% breach point, creating a soft ceiling that discourages single-name commercial or card-partner concentrations above one tenth of capital.

R-LEX10.9-gcc-single-counterparty.title: A group of connected counterparties is treated as a single counterparty
R-LEX10.9-gcc-single-counterparty.statement: Where counterparties have relationships or dependencies such that the failure of one would very likely cause the others to fail, they form a group of connected counterparties that must be treated as a single counterparty for the limit and for reporting.
R-LEX10.9-gcc-single-counterparty.quote: A group of this sort, referred to in this framework as a group of connected counterparties, must be treated as a single counterparty.

applies_to.note: Aggregation rule; drives both the 25% limit and the LEX20.1 to LEX20.4 reporting requirements.

R-LEX10.9-gcc-single-counterparty.portfolio_relevance: Prevents a bank from splitting a concentrated relationship across affiliated borrowers; a card programme run through several affiliated retail partners aggregates into one counterparty line.

R-LEX10.10-gcc-control-criterion.title: Connectedness criterion 1: control relationship
R-LEX10.10-gcc-control-criterion.statement: Two or more natural or legal persons are deemed a group of connected counterparties if one of them, directly or indirectly, has control over the other(s).
R-LEX10.10-gcc-control-criterion.quote: Two or more natural or legal persons shall be deemed a group of connected counterparties if at least one of the following criteria is satisfied. (1) Control relationship: one of the counterparties, directly or indirectly, has control over the other(s).

applies_to.note: Either criterion alone is sufficient; control is the objective limb, elaborated in LEX10.12 to LEX10.15.

R-LEX10.10-gcc-control-criterion.portfolio_relevance: Forces roll-up of exposures across corporate families, so an apparently diversified SME or commercial-card book concentrated in one ownership group is measured as a single obligor.
