R-LEX10.10-gcc-economic-interdependence.title: Connectedness criterion 2: economic interdependence
R-LEX10.10-gcc-economic-interdependence.statement: Counterparties are also a group of connected counterparties where financial problems, in particular funding or repayment difficulties, at one would likely cause funding or repayment difficulties at the other(s).
R-LEX10.10-gcc-economic-interdependence.quote: (2) Economic interdependence: if one of the counterparties were to experience financial problems, in particular funding or repayment difficulties, the other (s), as a result, would also be likely to encounter funding or repayment difficulties.

applies_to.note: Subject to the 5% of Tier 1 screening threshold in LEX10.18 and the rebuttal in LEX10.17.

R-LEX10.10-gcc-economic-interdependence.portfolio_relevance: Captures contagion between legally unrelated borrowers (eg a card programme partner and its funding provider), so apparent diversification across separate legal entities does not always create concentration headroom.

R-LEX10.11-assess-relationships.title: Banks must actively assess counterparty relationships against both criteria
R-LEX10.11-assess-relationships.statement: Banks must assess the relationship amongst counterparties against both the control and the economic-interdependence criteria in order to establish the existence of a group of connected counterparties.
R-LEX10.11-assess-relationships.quote: Banks must assess the relationship amongst counterparties with reference to LEX10.10 (1) and LEX10.10 (2) above in order to establish the existence of a group of connected counterparties.

applies_to.note: Operational obligation; the depth of the economic-interdependence assessment is proportionate per LEX10.18.

R-LEX10.11-assess-relationships.portfolio_relevance: Imposes a data and process cost on holding concentrated commercial relationships, which a granular retail card book largely avoids because obligor-level exposures fall below the screening thresholds.

R-LEX10.12-control-50pct-voting.title: Automatic control presumption at more than 50% of voting rights
R-LEX10.12-control-50pct-voting.statement: Banks must automatically treat the control criterion as satisfied where one entity owns more than 50% of the voting rights of the other entity.
R-LEX10.12-control-50pct-voting.quote: banks must automatically consider that criterion LEX10.10 (1) is satisfied if one entity owns more than 50% of the voting rights of the other entity.

applies_to.note: Bright-line test; rebuttable only in exceptional cases with supervisory agreement under LEX10.15.

R-LEX10.12-control-50pct-voting.portfolio_relevance: A hard, computable grouping trigger: exposures to entities more than 50% commonly owned must be summed before testing the 25% limit, which mechanically reduces apparent diversification in commercial and SME books.

R-LEX10.13-control-additional-criteria.title: Additional control indicators beyond majority voting rights
R-LEX10.13-control-additional-criteria.statement: Banks must additionally assess connectedness based on control using voting agreements, significant influence over the appointment or dismissal of the management or supervisory body, and significant influence over senior management.
R-LEX10.13-control-additional-criteria.quote: In addition, banks must assess connectedness between counterparties based on control using the following criteria: (1) Voting agreements (eg control of a majority of voting rights pursuant to an agreement with other shareholders);

applies_to.note: Judgement-based extension of the LEX10.12 bright line; not mechanically computable from public filings.

R-LEX10.13-control-additional-criteria.portfolio_relevance: Widens the grouping perimeter beyond legal ownership, meaning a portfolio restructuring that merely re-papers exposures across nominally independent entities under common effective control does not create headroom.

R-LEX10.14-accounting-guidance.title: Refer to internationally recognised accounting standards when determining control
R-LEX10.14-accounting-guidance.statement: Banks are expected to refer to criteria in appropriate internationally recognised accounting standards for further qualitative guidance in determining control.
R-LEX10.14-accounting-guidance.quote: Banks are also expected to refer to criteria specified in appropriate internationally recognised accounting standards for further qualitative guidance when determining control.

applies_to.note: Expectation rather than hard rule; ties the regulatory grouping perimeter to the consolidation concepts already used in the financial statements.

R-LEX10.14-accounting-guidance.portfolio_relevance: Allows the connected-group perimeter to be approximated from accounting consolidation disclosures, which is the only practicable data source when testing a small bank's public filings.

R-LEX10.15-control-rebuttal.title: Rebuttal of a control-based grouping in exceptional cases
R-LEX10.15-control-rebuttal.statement: Where control has been established, a bank may still demonstrate to its supervisor in exceptional cases that the control does not result in the entities forming a group of connected counterparties.
R-LEX10.15-control-rebuttal.quote: a bank may still demonstrate to its supervisor in exceptional cases, eg due to the existence of specific circumstances and corporate governance safeguards, that such control does not necessarily result in the entities concerned constituting a group of connected counterparties.

applies_to.note: Explicit supervisory-approval gate; available only in exceptional cases and requires demonstration to the supervisor.

R-LEX10.15-control-rebuttal.portfolio_relevance: Provides a supervisory escape valve that can restore concentration headroom without any change in portfolio composition, but only with regulator sign-off and corporate-governance ring-fencing.

R-LEX10.16-econ-50pct-receipts.title: Economic interdependence indicator: 50% or more of gross receipts or expenditures
R-LEX10.16-econ-50pct-receipts.statement: Banks must treat as an indicator of economic interdependence the case where 50% or more of one counterparty's annual gross receipts or gross expenditures derives from transactions with the other counterparty.
R-LEX10.16-econ-50pct-receipts.quote: (1) Where 50% or more of one counterparty's gross receipts or gross expenditures (on an annual basis) is derived from transactions with the other counterparty

applies_to.note: Minimum qualitative criterion; assessment only mandatory above the 5% of Tier 1 screen in LEX10.18.

numeric_values: 50% of gross receipts or gross expenditures (annual)
R-LEX10.16-econ-50pct-receipts.portfolio_relevance: A computable grouping trigger for commercial books: single-customer-dependent SME borrowers must be aggregated with their dominant counterparty, penalising supply-chain-concentrated lending relative to a granular card book.

R-LEX10.16-econ-guarantee-link.title: Economic interdependence indicator: significant guarantee or other liability
R-LEX10.16-econ-guarantee-link.statement: Economic interdependence must be considered where one counterparty has fully or partly guaranteed the other's exposure, or is otherwise liable, and the exposure is so significant that the guarantor is likely to default if a claim occurs.
R-LEX10.16-econ-guarantee-link.quote: (2) Where one counterparty has fully or partly guaranteed the exposure of the other counterparty, or is liable by other means, and the exposure is so significant that the guarantor is likely to default if a claim occurs;

applies_to.note: Interacts with LEX30.14: a guarantee both shifts exposure to the guarantor and can connect guarantor and obligor into one group.

R-LEX10.16-econ-guarantee-link.portfolio_relevance: Means guarantee-based credit risk mitigation can backfire for concentration purposes, since a substantial guarantee may connect guarantor and borrower into a single counterparty rather than diversifying the exposure.

R-LEX10.16-econ-common-repayment-source.title: Economic interdependence indicator: same expected source of repayment
R-LEX10.16-econ-common-repayment-source.statement: Economic interdependence must be considered where the expected source of funds to repay the loans of both counterparties is the same and neither has an independent income source from which the loan may be serviced and fully repaid.
R-LEX10.16-econ-common-repayment-source.quote: (4) When the expected source of funds to repay the loans of both counterparties is the same and neither counterparty has another independent source of income from which the loan may be serviced and fully repaid;

applies_to.note: Minimum qualitative criterion; most likely to bite on owner-operator SME and personal-guarantee lending at community banks.

R-LEX10.16-econ-common-repayment-source.portfolio_relevance: Aggregates borrower and guarantor-owner exposures that share a single cash-flow source, which is the typical failure mode of small-bank commercial books and a reason to prefer independently-funded retail obligors.

R-LEX10.16-econ-common-funding-source.title: Economic interdependence indicator: shared majority funding source
R-LEX10.16-econ-common-funding-source.statement: Economic interdependence must be considered where two or more counterparties rely on the same source for the majority of their funding and no alternative provider could be found if that common provider defaulted.
R-LEX10.16-econ-common-funding-source.quote: (7) When two or more counterparties rely on the same source for the majority of their funding and, in the event of the common provider’s default, an alternative provider cannot be found

applies_to.note: Minimum qualitative criterion; captures one-way and two-way funding dependence.

numeric_values: majority of funding from a common provider
R-LEX10.16-econ-common-funding-source.portfolio_relevance: Connects warehouse-funded or single-lender-dependent originators (including non-bank card and consumer lenders a small bank may lend to) into one counterparty group, capping aggregate exposure to a funding-dependent origination channel.

R-LEX10.17-econ-interdependence-rebuttal.title: Rebuttal of economic interdependence where alternatives exist
R-LEX10.17-econ-interdependence-rebuttal.statement: A bank need not combine economically related counterparties into a group if it can demonstrate to its supervisor that one could overcome financial difficulties, or even the other's default, by finding alternative business partners or funding sources within an appropriate time period.
R-LEX10.17-econ-interdependence-rebuttal.quote: Provided that the bank can demonstrate to its supervisor that a counterparty which is economically closely related to another counterparty may overcome financial difficulties, or even the second counterparty’ s default, by finding alternative business partners or funding sources within an appropriate time period, the bank does not need to combine these counterparties to form a group of connected counterparties.

applies_to.note: Supervisory-demonstration gate; the criteria in LEX10.16 do not automatically imply grouping.

R-LEX10.17-econ-interdependence-rebuttal.portfolio_relevance: Gives a documented route to de-group economically related borrowers and recover headroom without disposing of exposures, but the relief is discretionary and evidence-dependent.

R-LEX10.18-econ-interdependence-5pct-scr.title: Economic interdependence must be investigated above 5% of Tier 1 capital
R-LEX10.18-econ-interdependence-5pct-scr.statement: Banks are expected to identify possible connected counterparties on the basis of economic interdependence in all cases where the sum of all exposures to one individual counterparty exceeds 5% of Tier 1 capital.
R-LEX10.18-econ-interdependence-5pct-scr.quote: banks are expected to identify possible connected counterparties on the basis of economic interdependence in all cases where the sum of all exposures to one individual counterparty exceeds 5% of Tier 1 capital.

applies_to.note: This is the framework's de minimis screen: below 5% of Tier 1 per individual counterparty, no economic-interdependence investigation is expected.

R-LEX10.18-econ-interdependence-5pct-scr.portfolio_relevance: This is the key small-exposure carve-out for a granular card book: because individual cardholder exposures are orders of magnitude below 5% of Tier 1, no connectedness analysis is triggered, so growing card receivables adds capital charge but essentially zero large-exposure compliance burden or headroom consumption.

R-LEX10.18-proportionality-carveout.title: Proportionality: interdependence investigation need not exceed exposure size
R-LEX10.18-proportionality-carveout.statement: Investigation of economic interdependencies is not required where it would not be proportionate to the size of the exposures.
R-LEX10.18-proportionality-carveout.quote: There are cases where a thorough investigation of economic interdependencies will not be proportionate to the size of the exposures.

applies_to.note: Explicit proportionality principle underpinning the 5% of Tier 1 screening threshold.

R-LEX10.18-proportionality-carveout.portfolio_relevance: Codifies that granular, small-ticket portfolios such as credit cards are exempt from the operational cost of connectedness analysis, making them cheap to hold on the concentration dimension relative to commercial exposures.

R-LEX20.1-large-exposure-limit-25pct.title: Large exposure limit: 25% of Tier 1 capital at all times
R-LEX20.1-large-exposure-limit-25pct.statement: The sum of all exposure values to a single counterparty or to a group of connected counterparties must not exceed 25% of the bank's Tier 1 capital at all times.
R-LEX20.1-large-exposure-limit-25pct.quote: The sum of all the exposure values of a bank to a single counterparty or to a group of connected counterparties must not be higher than 25% of the bank’s Tier 1 capital at all times.

applies_to.note: The core hard limit of the framework. Binding continuously ('at all times'), not just at quarter-end reporting dates. Denominator is Tier 1 capital per CAP10.2, not total capital.

R-LEX20.1-large-exposure-limit-25pct.portfolio_relevance: The central computable concentration constraint: max single-counterparty exposure = 0.25 x Tier 1. It caps how much a bank can lend to any one card programme partner, correspondent bank, or corporate borrower, and rewards migration toward granular retail card balances that consume essentially no single-name headroom.

R-LEX20.1-gsib-to-gsib-15pct.title: Tighter 15% limit for G-SIB exposures to another G-SIB
R-LEX20.1-gsib-to-gsib-15pct.statement: For a global systemically important bank's exposures to another G-SIB the large exposure limit is set at 15% of Tier 1 capital rather than 25%.
R-LEX20.1-gsib-to-gsib-15pct.quote: this figure is set at 15% for a global systemically important bank’s (G-SIB’s) exposures to another GSIB.

applies_to.note: Applies only where both the bank and the counterparty are G-SIBs; detailed in LEX40. Not materially relevant to small North American banks except as a constraint on their large counterparties.

R-LEX20.1-gsib-to-gsib-15pct.portfolio_relevance: Restricts interbank concentration between the largest banks; for a small bank it matters indirectly, as it limits how much balance sheet the largest counterparties can extend to each other and shapes the correspondent-banking market.

R-LEX20.2-tier1-capital-base.title: Capital base for the limit is Tier 1 capital as defined in CAP10.2
R-LEX20.2-tier1-capital-base.statement: Exposures must be measured as specified in LEX30 and the capital base for the large exposures framework is Tier 1 capital as defined in CAP10.2.
R-LEX20.2-tier1-capital-base.quote: The exposures must be measured as specified in LEX30. Tier 1 capital for the purpose of the large exposures framework is the Tier 1 capital defined in CAP10.2.

applies_to.note: Tier 1 (CET1 plus Additional Tier 1), excluding Tier 2; directly reported in quarterly regulatory capital schedules.

R-LEX20.2-tier1-capital-base.portfolio_relevance: Fixes the denominator as Tier 1 rather than total capital, so subordinated-debt issuance does not create concentration headroom while common-equity or AT1 issuance does.

R-LEX20.3-breach-notification.title: Limit breaches must be exceptional, immediately reported and rapidly rectified
R-LEX20.3-breach-notification.statement: Breaches of the large exposure limit must remain the exception, must be communicated immediately to the supervisor and must be rapidly rectified.
R-LEX20.3-breach-notification.quote: Breaches of the limit, which must remain the exception, must be communicated immediately to the supervisor and must be rapidly rectified.

applies_to.note: No cure period is quantified; 'immediately' and 'rapidly' are left to supervisory interpretation.

R-LEX20.3-breach-notification.portfolio_relevance: Makes the 25% limit effectively a hard rather than soft bound in optimisation: passive breaches caused by a fall in Tier 1 capital must be cured by forced exposure reduction, so portfolios should be run with a buffer below 25%.

R-LEX20.4-report-pre-and-post-crm.title: Report exposure values both before and after credit risk mitigation
R-LEX20.4-report-pre-and-post-crm.statement: Banks must report to the supervisor the exposure values both before and after application of credit risk mitigation techniques.
R-LEX20.4-report-pre-and-post-crm.quote: Banks must report to the supervisor the exposure values before and after application of the credit risk mitigation techniques.

applies_to.note: Gross and net reporting; supervisory reporting rather than public disclosure, so not observable in published financials.

R-LEX20.4-report-pre-and-post-crm.portfolio_relevance: Means CRM cannot hide a gross concentration from the supervisor, so relying on collateral or guarantees to stay under the limit still exposes the underlying concentration to supervisory challenge.

R-LEX20.4-report-le-10pct.title: Report all exposures at or above 10% of Tier 1 capital
R-LEX20.4-report-le-10pct.statement: Banks must report all exposures whose values measured under LEX30 equal or exceed 10% of Tier 1 capital, ie all exposures meeting the definition of a large exposure.
R-LEX20.4-report-le-10pct.quote: (1) all exposures with values measured as specified in LEX30 equal to or above 10% of the bank's Tier 1 capital (ie meeting the definition of a large exposure in LEX10.8);

applies_to.note: Post-CRM measurement basis; complements the gross-of-CRM limb in the same paragraph.

R-LEX20.4-report-le-10pct.portfolio_relevance: Sets the concentration reporting trigger at 10% of Tier 1, which functions as a de facto soft limit because banks generally manage below it to avoid recurring supervisory reporting and challenge.

R-LEX20.4-report-gross-of-crm-10pct.title: Report exposures at or above 10% of Tier 1 measured gross of CRM
R-LEX20.4-report-gross-of-crm-10pct.statement: Banks must also report all other exposures whose values, measured without the effect of credit risk mitigation, equal or exceed 10% of Tier 1 capital.
R-LEX20.4-report-gross-of-crm-10pct.quote: (2) all other exposures with values measured as specified in LEX30 without the effect of credit risk mitigation being taken into account equal to or above 10% of the bank's Tier 1 capital;

applies_to.note: Catches exposures that only fall below 10% because of CRM substitution.

R-LEX20.4-report-gross-of-crm-10pct.portfolio_relevance: Removes the incentive to use collateral or guarantees purely to duck the reporting threshold, since gross concentrations above 10% of Tier 1 remain reportable regardless of mitigation.

R-LEX20.4-report-exempted-10pct.title: Report exempted exposures at or above 10% of Tier 1 capital
R-LEX20.4-report-exempted-10pct.statement: Banks must report all exempted exposures whose values equal or exceed 10% of the bank's Tier 1 capital.
R-LEX20.4-report-exempted-10pct.quote: (3) all the exempted exposures with values equal to or above 10% of the bank's Tier 1 capital; and

applies_to.note: Applies to sovereign, QCCP-clearing and other exempt exposures; exemption from the limit does not exempt from reporting.

R-LEX20.4-report-exempted-10pct.portfolio_relevance: Large sovereign or exempt positions used as a parking place for balance sheet remain visible to the supervisor, so shifting concentration into exempt assets reduces the measured limit usage but not supervisory attention.

R-LEX20.4-report-largest-20.title: Report the 20 largest counterparty exposures irrespective of size
R-LEX20.4-report-largest-20.statement: Banks must report their largest 20 exposures to counterparties measured under LEX30 and included in the scope of application, irrespective of the size of those exposures relative to Tier 1 capital.
R-LEX20.4-report-largest-20.quote: (4) their largest 20 exposures to counterparties measured as specified in LEX30 and included in the scope of application, irrespective of the values of these exposures relative to the bank's Tier 1 capital.

applies_to.note: Unconditional top-20 reporting; the only large exposures requirement that bites even for a bank with no exposure above 10% of Tier 1.

R-LEX20.4-report-largest-20.portfolio_relevance: Guarantees a permanent concentration data feed regardless of portfolio granularity; for a card-heavy small bank the top 20 will be dominated by correspondent banks, securities issuers and programme partners rather than cardholders.

R-LEX30.1-scope-on-and-off-balance-sheet.title: Exposure scope covers on- and off-balance sheet, banking and trading book
R-LEX30.1-scope-on-and-off-balance-sheet.statement: A bank must consider both on- and off-balance sheet exposures in either the banking or trading book, and instruments with counterparty credit risk, as defined under the risk-based capital framework.
R-LEX30.1-scope-on-and-off-balance-sheet.quote: It must consider both on- and off-balance sheet exposures included in either the banking or trading book and instruments with counterparty credit risk under the risk-based capital framework.

applies_to.note: Exposure universe is aligned with the risk-based capital framework definitions.

R-LEX30.1-scope-on-and-off-balance-sheet.portfolio_relevance: Brings undrawn commitments and card lines into the concentration measure, so a large committed but undrawn facility to a single obligor consumes limit headroom even before it is drawn.

R-LEX30.2-capital-deducted-excluded.title: Exposures deducted from capital are excluded from the limit
R-LEX30.2-capital-deducted-excluded.statement: An exposure amount to a counterparty that is deducted from capital must not be added to other exposures to that counterparty for the purpose of the large exposure limit.
R-LEX30.2-capital-deducted-excluded.quote: An exposure amount to a counterparty that is deducted from capital must not be added to other exposures to that counterparty for the purpose of the large exposure limit.

applies_to.note: Avoids double-counting: an amount already removed from Tier 1 does not also consume the limit measured against Tier 1.

R-LEX30.2-capital-deducted-excluded.portfolio_relevance: Holdings already deducted from capital (eg reciprocal financial-sector investments) do not consume concentration headroom, so the deduction and the limit are mutually exclusive penalties rather than cumulative.

R-LEX30.2-1250pct-rw-included.title: 1,250% risk-weighted exposures remain subject to the limit
R-LEX30.2-1250pct-rw-included.statement: Where an exposure is 1,250% risk-weighted rather than deducted, it must be added to other exposures to the same counterparty and the sum is subject to the large exposure limit.
R-LEX30.2-1250pct-rw-included.quote: This general approach does not apply where an exposure is 1,250% risk-weighted. When this is the case, this exposure must be added to any other exposures to the same counterparty and the sum is subject to the large exposure limit

applies_to.note: Footnote to LEX30.2; carve-out from the deduction exclusion, unless the exposure is separately exempted.

R-LEX30.2-1250pct-rw-included.portfolio_relevance: Retained first-loss tranches of a securitised card portfolio carry both a 1,250% risk weight and full large-exposure consumption, so securitising a card book to release RWA does not release single-name concentration capacity on the retained piece.

R-LEX30.3-exposure-value-accounting-valu.title: Exposure value is the accounting value, or optionally gross of provisions
R-LEX30.3-exposure-value-accounting-valu.statement: The exposure value must be the accounting value of the exposure, net of specific provisions and value adjustments; alternatively a bank may use the exposure value gross of specific provisions and value adjustments.
R-LEX30.3-exposure-value-accounting-valu.quote: The exposure value must be defined as the accounting value of the exposure. As an alternative, a bank may consider the exposure value gross of specific provisions and value adjustments

applies_to.note: The accompanying footnote clarifies that the accounting value is net of specific provisions and value adjustments; the gross basis is an optional conservative alternative.

R-LEX30.3-exposure-value-accounting-valu.portfolio_relevance: Links concentration measurement directly to book carrying values available in published financials, and means specific provisioning on a distressed single-name exposure mechanically reduces measured limit usage.

R-LEX30.4-ccr-exposure-sa-ccr.title: Counterparty credit risk exposures measured using SA-CCR
R-LEX30.4-ccr-exposure-sa-ccr.statement: For instruments giving rise to counterparty credit risk other than securities financing transactions, the exposure value must be the exposure at default under the standardised approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR).
R-LEX30.4-ccr-exposure-sa-ccr.quote: The exposure value for instruments that give rise to counterparty credit risk and are not securities financing transactions must be the exposure at default according to the standardised approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR).

applies_to.note: Internal model methods are not permitted for large exposures purposes; SA-CCR is mandatory. Materially relevant only to banks with derivatives books.

R-LEX30.4-ccr-exposure-sa-ccr.portfolio_relevance: Forces a standardised, non-modelled derivative exposure measure into the concentration test, so hedging concentrations with derivatives creates measurable new counterparty exposure at SA-CCR values.

R-LEX30.5-sft-comprehensive-approach.title: SFT exposures measured under the comprehensive approach with supervisory haircuts
R-LEX30.5-sft-comprehensive-approach.statement: Banks should calculate the exposure value for securities financing transactions using the comprehensive approach with supervisory haircuts.
R-LEX30.5-sft-comprehensive-approach.quote: Banks should calculate the exposure value for their securities financing transaction (SFT) exposures applying the comprehensive approach with supervisory haircuts described in CRE22.

applies_to.note: Supervisory haircuts only; own-estimate and modelled haircuts are excluded (see LEX30.13).

R-LEX30.5-sft-comprehensive-approach.portfolio_relevance: Repo and securities-lending concentration must be measured with prescribed haircuts, removing any modelling benefit and making collateralised interbank funding consume more headroom than a modelled measure would suggest.

R-LEX30.6-off-balance-ccf-floor-10pct.title: Off-balance sheet items converted at standardised CCFs with a 10% floor
R-LEX30.6-off-balance-ccf-floor-10pct.statement: For large exposures purposes off-balance sheet items are converted into credit exposure equivalents using the credit conversion factors of the standardised approach for credit risk, subject to a floor of 10%.
R-LEX30.6-off-balance-ccf-floor-10pct.quote: off-balance sheet items will be converted into credit exposure equivalents through the use of credit conversion factors (CCFs) by applying the CCFs set out for the standardised approach for credit risk for risk-based capital requirements, with a floor of 10%.

applies_to.note: Standardised CCFs are used even by IRB banks; the 10% floor overrides any lower SA CCF, including the 0% CCF available for unconditionally cancellable commitments under the standardised approach.

R-LEX30.6-off-balance-ccf-floor-10pct.portfolio_relevance: Directly hits undrawn credit card lines: a commitment that attracts a 0% or low CCF for RWA purposes is still converted at no less than 10% for concentration purposes, so a card programme with very large undrawn lines to one connected obligor group consumes real headroom that RWA measurement would show as nil.

R-LEX30.7-eligible-crm-sa-only.title: Only standardised-approach eligible CRM counts for large exposures
R-LEX30.7-eligible-crm-sa-only.statement: Eligible credit risk mitigation techniques for large exposures purposes are limited to unfunded credit protection and financial collateral meeting the minimum requirements and eligibility criteria of the standardised approach for risk-based capital purposes.
R-LEX30.7-eligible-crm-sa-only.quote: Eligible credit risk mitigation (CRM) techniques for large exposures purposes are those that meet the minimum requirements and eligibility criteria for the recognition of unfunded credit protection and financial collateral that qualify as eligible financial collateral under the standardised approach for risk-based capital requirement purposes.

applies_to.note: Applies to all banks including IRB banks; unfunded credit protection means guarantees and credit derivatives per CRE22.

R-LEX30.7-eligible-crm-sa-only.portfolio_relevance: Narrows the mitigants that can create concentration headroom to financial collateral and guarantees, so physical or receivables collateral behind a concentrated commercial exposure gives no relief against the 25% limit.

R-LEX30.8-irb-collateral-ineligible.title: IRB-only collateral cannot reduce large exposure values
R-LEX30.8-irb-collateral-ineligible.statement: Collateral that is eligible only under the internal ratings-based approach, namely receivables, commercial and residential real estate and other collateral, is not eligible to reduce exposure values for large exposures purposes.
R-LEX30.8-irb-collateral-ineligible.quote: Other forms of collateral that are only eligible under the internal-ratings based approach in accordance with CRE32.8 (receivables, commercial and residential real estate and other collateral) are not eligible to reduce exposure values for large exposures purposes.

applies_to.note: Removes the IRB collateral advantage for concentration purposes; IRB banks must fall back to the standardised collateral list.

R-LEX30.8-irb-collateral-ineligible.portfolio_relevance: Real-estate-secured concentrations get no large-exposure relief from their collateral, so a bank with a lumpy CRE book faces full gross concentration measurement while a granular unsecured card book faces essentially none.

R-LEX30.9-mandatory-crm-recognition.title: CRM used for capital purposes must also be recognised for large exposures
R-LEX30.9-mandatory-crm-recognition.statement: A bank must recognise an eligible CRM technique in its exposure calculation whenever it has used that technique to calculate risk-based capital requirements, provided the large exposures recognition conditions are met.
R-LEX30.9-mandatory-crm-recognition.quote: A bank must recognise an eligible CRM technique in the calculation of an exposure whenever it has used this technique to calculate the risk-based capital requirements, and provided it meets the conditions for recognition under the large exposures framework.

applies_to.note: Consistency requirement: recognition is mandatory, not elective, once used for capital.

R-LEX30.9-mandatory-crm-recognition.portfolio_relevance: Prevents cherry-picking of mitigation between the capital and concentration calculations, and mechanically transfers exposure to the protection provider whenever CRM is claimed for RWA relief.

R-LEX30.10-maturity-mismatch-thresholds.title: Maturity mismatch hedges: one-year original and three-month residual thresholds
R-LEX30.10-maturity-mismatch-thresholds.statement: Hedges with maturity mismatches are recognised only where their original maturity is at least one year and the residual maturity of the hedge is not less than three months.
R-LEX30.10-maturity-mismatch-thresholds.quote: hedges with maturity mismatches are recognised only when their original maturities are equal to or greater than one year and the residual maturity of a hedge is not less than three months.

applies_to.note: Mirrors the risk-based capital treatment in CRE22.10 to CRE22.14.

R-LEX30.10-maturity-mismatch-thresholds.portfolio_relevance: Short-dated protection cannot be used to manufacture concentration headroom near a limit breach, forcing genuine exposure reduction rather than a short-tenor hedge as the remedy.

R-LEX30.11-maturity-mismatch-adjustment.title: Maturity mismatch adjustment mirrors the risk-based capital calculation
R-LEX30.11-maturity-mismatch-adjustment.statement: Where a recognised credit risk mitigant has a maturity mismatch, the adjustment of the credit protection for large exposures purposes uses the same approach as in the risk-based capital requirement.
R-LEX30.11-maturity-mismatch-adjustment.quote: the adjustment of the credit protection for the purpose of calculating large exposures is determined using the same approach as in the risk-based capital requirement.

applies_to.note: Applies to collateral, on-balance sheet netting, guarantees and credit derivatives.

R-LEX30.11-maturity-mismatch-adjustment.portfolio_relevance: Ensures the haircut applied to mismatched protection is identical in the capital and concentration engines, so a single CRM parameter set drives both constraints in a portfolio model.

R-LEX30.12-loan-deposit-netting.title: On-balance sheet loan-deposit netting may be used for large exposures
R-LEX30.12-loan-deposit-netting.statement: Where a bank has legally enforceable netting arrangements for loans and deposits, it may calculate large exposure values on a net credit exposure basis consistent with its capital requirements calculation.
R-LEX30.12-loan-deposit-netting.quote: Where a bank has in place legally enforceable netting arrangements for loans and deposits, it may calculate the exposure values for large exposures purposes according to the calculation it uses for capital requirements purposes

applies_to.note: Conditional on the on-balance sheet netting conditions in CRE22.68 and CRE22.69, notably legal enforceability.

R-LEX30.12-loan-deposit-netting.portfolio_relevance: Lets a bank net a concentrated borrower's deposits against its loans to create headroom, favouring lending to counterparties that are also material depositors.

R-LEX30.13-crm-reduction-amount.title: Amount by which the original counterparty exposure is reduced
R-LEX30.13-crm-reduction-amount.statement: A bank must reduce the exposure to the original counterparty by the amount of eligible CRM recognised for capital purposes, being the protected portion for unfunded protection, the collateralised portion under the simple approach, the recognised collateral value for counterparty credit risk instruments, or haircut-adjusted collateral under the comprehensive approach.
R-LEX30.13-crm-reduction-amount.quote: A bank must reduce the value of the exposure to the original counterparty by the amount of the eligible CRM technique recognised for risk-based capital requirements purposes. This recognised amount is: (1) the value of the protected portion in the case of unfunded credit protection;

applies_to.note: Four recognition bases depending on whether the simple or comprehensive approach, or a counterparty credit risk measure, is used.

R-LEX30.13-crm-reduction-amount.portfolio_relevance: Defines exactly how much single-name headroom a guarantee or collateral pledge frees up, which is the computable lever for restructuring a near-limit exposure without selling it.

R-LEX30.13-supervisory-haircuts-only.title: Supervisory haircuts mandatory; internally modelled haircuts prohibited
R-LEX30.13-supervisory-haircuts-only.statement: Collateral amounts must be reduced using the supervisory haircuts of the comprehensive approach and internally modelled haircuts must not be used.
R-LEX30.13-supervisory-haircuts-only.quote: The haircuts used to reduce the collateral amount are the supervisory haircuts under the comprehensive approach. Internally modelled haircuts must not be used.

applies_to.note: Explicit prohibition on internal models in the large exposures framework, binding equally on IRB banks; supervisory haircuts are set out in CRE22.49 and CRE22.50.

R-LEX30.13-supervisory-haircuts-only.portfolio_relevance: Removes model-driven optimisation of collateral values, so the concentration constraint is fully reproducible from public data using prescribed haircuts and cannot be softened by internal estimates.

R-LEX30.14-substitution-to-crm-provider.title: Substitution: a new exposure to the CRM provider must be recognised
R-LEX30.14-substitution-to-crm-provider.statement: Whenever a bank recognises a reduction of exposure to the original counterparty due to eligible CRM, it must recognise an exposure to the CRM provider equal to the amount by which the original exposure was reduced.
R-LEX30.14-substitution-to-crm-provider.quote: Whenever a bank is required to recognise a reduction of the exposure to the original counterparty due to an eligible CRM technique, it must also recognise an exposure to the CRM provider. The amount assigned to the CRM provider is the amount by which the exposure to the original counterparty is reduced

applies_to.note: Substitution approach; the exception in LEX30.28 applies to certain non-financial CDS arrangements.

R-LEX30.14-substitution-to-crm-provider.portfolio_relevance: CRM relocates rather than removes concentration, so using one insurer or guarantor across many exposures builds a new single-name concentration in the protection provider that can itself breach the 25% limit.

R-LEX30.15-aggregate-banking-and-trading.title: Trading book and banking book exposures to the same counterparty must be summed
R-LEX30.15-aggregate-banking-and-trading.statement: A bank must add exposures to a single counterparty arising in the trading book to its banking book exposures to that counterparty when calculating total exposure.
R-LEX30.15-aggregate-banking-and-trading.quote: A bank must add any exposures to a single counterparty arising in the trading book to any other exposures to that counterparty that lie in the banking book to calculate its total exposure to that counterparty.

applies_to.note: Aggregation rule rather than a market risk rule; for small banks with immaterial trading books total exposure is effectively the banking book amount.

R-LEX30.15-aggregate-banking-and-trading.portfolio_relevance: Blocks book-shifting as a headroom strategy: moving a bond position on an existing borrower into the trading book does not reduce measured concentration.

R-LEX30.29-no-cross-book-netting.title: Netting across banking and trading books is prohibited
R-LEX30.29-no-cross-book-netting.statement: Netting across the banking and trading books is not permitted for large exposures purposes.
R-LEX30.29-no-cross-book-netting.quote: Netting across the banking and trading books is not permitted.

applies_to.note: Complements LEX30.15: exposures aggregate across books but offsets do not.

R-LEX30.29-no-cross-book-netting.portfolio_relevance: An asymmetric rule that makes concentration measurement strictly additive across books, so short trading positions cannot offset a banking book loan concentration to the same name.

R-LEX30.31-sovereign-exemption.title: Sovereign and central bank exposures are exempt from the framework
R-LEX30.31-sovereign-exemption.statement: Banks' exposures to sovereigns and their central banks are exempted from the large exposures framework, and the exemption extends to public sector entities treated as sovereigns.
R-LEX30.31-sovereign-exemption.quote: banks' exposures to sovereigns and their central banks as set out in CRE20.7 to CRE20.10 are exempted. This exemption also applies to public sector entities treated as sovereigns according to CRE20.

applies_to.note: The only counterparty-class exemption from the limit itself; reporting under LEX20.4 still applies per LEX30.33.

R-LEX30.31-sovereign-exemption.portfolio_relevance: Treasuries, agency and qualifying PSE holdings consume no single-name headroom, making the securities portfolio the natural sink when a bank must shrink a concentrated loan relationship.

R-LEX30.31-sovereign-guaranteed-portion.title: Sovereign-guaranteed or sovereign-collateralised portions are excluded
R-LEX30.31-sovereign-guaranteed-portion.statement: Any portion of an exposure guaranteed by, or secured by financial instruments issued by, sovereigns is excluded from the scope of the framework to the extent the CRM eligibility criteria are met.
R-LEX30.31-sovereign-guaranteed-portion.quote: Any portion of an exposure guaranteed by, or secured by financial instruments issued by, sovereigns would be similarly excluded from the scope of this framework to the extent that the eligibility criteria for recognition of the credit risk mitigation are met.

applies_to.note: Conditional on the CRM eligibility criteria being satisfied for the guarantee or the sovereign collateral.

R-LEX30.31-sovereign-guaranteed-portion.portfolio_relevance: Government-guaranteed lending programmes (eg SBA-type guarantees) and Treasury-collateralised exposures drop out of the concentration test entirely, giving a concrete restructuring lever for a concentrated commercial book.

R-LEX30.32-sovereign-linked-not-connecte.title: Entities linked only through an exempt sovereign need not be grouped
R-LEX30.32-sovereign-linked-not-connecte.statement: Entities outside the sovereign exemption that are controlled by, or economically dependent on, an entity within the sovereign exemption and are otherwise unconnected need not be deemed a group of connected counterparties.
R-LEX30.32-sovereign-linked-not-connecte.quote: Where two (or more) entities that are outside the scope of the sovereign exemption are controlled by or economically dependent on an entity that falls within the scope of the sovereign exemption defined in LEX30.31, and are otherwise not connected, those entities need not be deemed to constitute a group of connected counterparties

applies_to.note: Prevents all state-controlled entities in a jurisdiction from collapsing into one counterparty group.

R-LEX30.32-sovereign-linked-not-connecte.portfolio_relevance: Preserves concentration capacity for lending to multiple government-linked entities, which matters for municipal and public-sector-adjacent lending at community banks.

R-LEX30.33-report-exempt-sovereign.title: Exempt sovereign exposures must still be reported when large
R-LEX30.33-report-exempt-sovereign.statement: A bank must report exposures subject to the sovereign exemption where those exposures meet the criteria for definition as a large exposure.
R-LEX30.33-report-exempt-sovereign.quote: a bank must report exposures subject to the sovereign exemption if these exposures meet the criteria for definition as a large exposure

applies_to.note: Threshold is the LEX10.8 definition, ie 10% or more of Tier 1 capital.

R-LEX30.33-report-exempt-sovereign.portfolio_relevance: Large sovereign positions remain visible in supervisory reporting, so shifting a concentrated exposure into government securities is transparent to the supervisor even though it relieves the limit.

R-LEX30.34-hedged-exempt-exposure.title: Hedging an exempt exposure creates a live exposure to the protection provider
R-LEX30.34-hedged-exempt-exposure.statement: If an exposure to an exempted entity is hedged by a credit derivative, the bank must recognise an exposure to the credit protection provider even though the original exposure is exempt.
R-LEX30.34-hedged-exempt-exposure.quote: if a bank has an exposure to an exempted entity which is hedged by a credit derivative, the bank will have to recognise an exposure to the counterparty providing the credit protection as prescribed in LEX30.14 and LEX30.28, notwithstanding the fact that the original exposure is exempted.

applies_to.note: Substitution applies asymmetrically: the exempt leg stays exempt but the protection leg is live.

R-LEX30.34-hedged-exempt-exposure.portfolio_relevance: Hedging a sovereign position converts an unconstrained exposure into a constrained one against the protection seller, so hedging activity can consume concentration headroom that the underlying asset did not.

R-LEX30.35-intraday-interbank-exempt.title: Intraday interbank exposures are outside the framework
R-LEX30.35-intraday-interbank-exempt.statement: Intraday interbank exposures are not subject to the large exposures framework, either for reporting purposes or for application of the large exposure limit.
R-LEX30.35-intraday-interbank-exempt.quote: intraday interbank exposures are not subject to the large exposures framework, either for reporting purposes or for application of the large exposure limit.

applies_to.note: Carve-out motivated by payment and settlement continuity; end-of-day interbank exposures remain fully in scope.

R-LEX30.35-intraday-interbank-exempt.portfolio_relevance: Card settlement and correspondent payment flows that peak intraday do not consume limit headroom, so a card issuer's settlement concentration with its correspondent bank is measured only on the overnight balance.

R-LEX30.36-interbank-breach-tolerance.title: Supervisors may accept an ex post breach of an interbank limit in stress
R-LEX30.36-interbank-breach-tolerance.statement: In stressed circumstances supervisors may have to accept an ex post breach of an interbank limit in order to help ensure stability in the interbank market.
R-LEX30.36-interbank-breach-tolerance.quote: In stressed circumstances, supervisors may have to accept a breach of an interbank limit ex post, in order to help ensure stability in the interbank market.

applies_to.note: Supervisory discretion, exercised ex post and only in stressed conditions; not a planning assumption.

R-LEX30.36-interbank-breach-tolerance.portfolio_relevance: Introduces state-contingent softness in the interbank leg of the constraint, meaning a stress-scenario model should not force interbank deleveraging at the 25% boundary the way it must for corporate exposures.

R-LEX30.37-covered-bond-definition.title: Definition of a covered bond
R-LEX30.37-covered-bond-definition.statement: Covered bonds are bonds issued by a bank or mortgage institution that are subject by law to special public supervision protecting bond holders, with proceeds invested in assets capable of covering the claims attached to the bonds and available on a priority basis on issuer failure.
R-LEX30.37-covered-bond-definition.quote: Covered bonds are bonds issued by a bank or mortgage institution and are subject by law to special public supervision designed to protect bond holders.

applies_to.note: Gateway definition for the preferential exposure value in LEX30.38; requires a statutory covered bond regime.

R-LEX30.37-covered-bond-definition.portfolio_relevance: Defines the only debt instrument class that receives a discounted exposure value for concentration purposes, relevant to securities-portfolio composition choices.

R-LEX30.38-covered-bond-20pct-value.title: Qualifying covered bonds may be valued at 20% of nominal; others at 100%
R-LEX30.38-covered-bond-20pct-value.statement: A covered bond satisfying the definition may be assigned an exposure value of no less than 20% of the nominal value of the holding, other covered bonds must be assigned 100% of nominal, and the counterparty is the issuing bank.
R-LEX30.38-covered-bond-20pct-value.quote: A covered bond satisfying the conditions set out in LEX30.37 may be assigned an exposure value of no less than 20% of the nominal value of the bank's covered bond holding. Other covered bonds must be assigned an exposure value equal to 100% of the nominal value of the bank's covered bond holding. The counterparty to which the exposure value is assigned is the issuing bank.

applies_to.note: The 20% is a floor, not a fixed value; the preferential treatment is conditional on the LEX30.39 pool eligibility conditions. Covered bonds are rare in US small-bank securities portfolios.

R-LEX30.38-covered-bond-20pct-value.portfolio_relevance: A five-fold reduction in measured exposure for qualifying covered bonds means bank-issuer concentration can be built up in covered bond form rather than senior unsecured, a direct securities-portfolio restructuring lever.

R-LEX30.39-covered-bond-pool-eligibility.title: Covered bond cover pool eligibility: RW and LTV thresholds
R-LEX30.39-covered-bond-pool-eligibility.statement: To qualify for an exposure value below 100%, the cover pool must consist exclusively of qualifying claims, including residential real estate claims qualifying for a 35% or lower risk weight with LTV of 80% or lower, and commercial real estate claims qualifying for a 100% or lower risk weight with LTV of 60% or lower.
R-LEX30.39-covered-bond-pool-eligibility.quote: (b) claims secured by mortgages on residential real estate that would qualify for a 35% or lower risk weight under CRE20 for credit risk and have a loan-to-value ratio of 80% or lower; and/or (c) claims secured by commercial real estate that would qualify for the 100% or lower risk-weight under CRE20 and with a loan-to-value ratio of 60% or lower;

applies_to.note: Risk weight tests reference CRE20 standardised weights; LTV measurement follows the operational requirements of CRE36.131 per LEX30.40.

R-LEX30.39-covered-bond-pool-eligibility.portfolio_relevance: Sets hard collateral quality gates on the preferential 20% exposure value, so the concentration benefit of covered bonds is only available against conservative mortgage pools and cannot be extended to consumer or card collateral.

R-LEX30.39-covered-bond-overcollateralis.title: Covered bond pool must be overcollateralised by at least 10%
R-LEX30.39-covered-bond-overcollateralis.statement: The nominal value of the asset pool assigned to the covered bond instruments should exceed their nominal outstanding value by at least 10%, and where the legislative framework does not require this the issuer must publicly disclose on a regular basis that the pool meets the 10% requirement in practice.
R-LEX30.39-covered-bond-overcollateralis.quote: The nominal value of the pool of assets assigned to the covered bond instrument(s) by its issuer should exceed its nominal outstanding value by at least 10%.

applies_to.note: Where the legislative framework does not stipulate at least 10%, the issuing bank must publicly disclose on a regular basis that the cover pool meets the 10% requirement in practice.

R-LEX30.39-covered-bond-overcollateralis.portfolio_relevance: An investor-side eligibility test that is checkable from issuer disclosure, and on the issuance side an encumbrance cost that reduces the assets available to unsecured creditors.

R-LEX30.40-covered-bond-ltv-operational.title: Covered bond conditions must hold at inception and throughout maturity
R-LEX30.40-covered-bond-ltv-operational.statement: The covered bond eligibility conditions must be satisfied at the inception of the bond and throughout its remaining maturity, using the CRE36.131 operational requirements for objective market value and frequent revaluation of collateral.
R-LEX30.40-covered-bond-ltv-operational.quote: The conditions set out in LEX30.39 must be satisfied at the inception of the covered bond and throughout its remaining maturity.

applies_to.note: Ongoing rather than point-in-time test; requires collateral revaluation capability.

R-LEX30.40-covered-bond-ltv-operational.portfolio_relevance: The 20% exposure value can be lost mid-life if the pool deteriorates, so a covered-bond-based concentration strategy carries a cliff risk of the exposure value jumping back to 100% of nominal.

R-LEX30.41-structures-in-scope.title: Exposures through funds, securitisations and other structures must be assigned to counterparties
R-LEX30.41-structures-in-scope.statement: Banks must consider exposures even where a structure lies between the bank and the underlying assets, and must assign the amount invested in the structure to specific counterparties; such structures include funds, securitisations and other structures with underlying assets.
R-LEX30.41-structures-in-scope.quote: Banks must assign the exposure amount, ie the amount invested in a particular structure, to specific counterparties following the approach described below. Such structures include funds, securitisations and other structures with underlying assets.

applies_to.note: Applies to money market funds, mutual funds, ABS and CLO holdings common in small-bank securities portfolios.

R-LEX30.41-structures-in-scope.portfolio_relevance: Prevents indirect concentration via funds or ABS, so a bank cannot rebuild a single-name exposure through a wrapper; card ABS holdings must be traced to their obligors or to the structure under the granularity test.

R-LEX30.42-granularity-025pct-no-lookthr.title: No look-through required where each underlying is below 0.25% of Tier 1
R-LEX30.42-granularity-025pct-no-lookthr.statement: A bank may assign the exposure amount to the structure itself as a distinct counterparty if it can demonstrate that its exposure to each underlying asset of the structure is smaller than 0.25% of Tier 1 capital, in which case look-through is not required.
R-LEX30.42-granularity-025pct-no-lookthr.quote: A bank may assign the exposure amount to the structure itself, defined as a distinct counterparty, if it can demonstrate that the bank's exposure amount to each underlying asset of the structure is smaller than 0.25% of its Tier 1 capital

applies_to.note: Considers only exposures to underlying assets arising from the investment in the structure, valued per LEX30.48 and LEX30.49.

R-LEX30.42-granularity-025pct-no-lookthr.portfolio_relevance: This is the granularity carve-out that makes credit card ABS cheap on the concentration dimension: because no individual cardholder in a card master trust comes near 0.25% of Tier 1, the whole holding can be treated as a single exposure to the structure with no look-through cost.

R-LEX30.42-whole-investment-below-025pct.title: Test is automatically passed if the whole investment is below 0.25% of Tier 1
R-LEX30.42-whole-investment-below-025pct.statement: The granularity test is by definition passed if the bank's whole investment in a structure is below 0.25% of its Tier 1 capital.
R-LEX30.42-whole-investment-below-025pct.quote: By definition, this required test will be passed if the bank’s whole investment in a structure is below 0.25% of its Tier 1 capital.

applies_to.note: Footnote to LEX30.42; the simplest computable form of the granularity carve-out, requiring only the position size and Tier 1 capital.

R-LEX30.42-whole-investment-below-025pct.portfolio_relevance: Gives a directly computable de minimis rule for structured holdings from public data: any fund or ABS position under 0.25% of Tier 1 needs no look-through at all, so a diversified small-ticket ABS book carries no concentration analysis burden.

R-LEX30.43-mandatory-lookthrough-025pct.title: Mandatory look-through for underlying assets at or above 0.25% of Tier 1
R-LEX30.43-mandatory-lookthrough-025pct.statement: A bank must look through the structure to identify underlying assets whose exposure value equals or exceeds 0.25% of Tier 1 capital, and add those underlying exposures to any other direct or indirect exposure to the same counterparty.
R-LEX30.43-mandatory-lookthrough-025pct.quote: A bank must look through the structure to identify those underlying assets for which the underlying exposure value is equal to or above 0.25% of its Tier 1 capital.

applies_to.note: Requires obligor-level data on the structure's underlying pool, which is often unavailable for a small bank's fund holdings.

R-LEX30.43-mandatory-lookthrough-025pct.portfolio_relevance: Concentrated structures (eg a CLO with chunky corporate names) drag their underlying obligors into the bank's limit calculation, penalising concentrated wrappers relative to granular consumer ABS.

R-LEX30.43-partial-lookthrough.title: Partial look-through is permitted for sub-threshold underlyings
R-LEX30.43-partial-lookthrough.statement: The bank's exposure amounts to underlying assets that are below 0.25% of Tier 1 capital may be assigned to the structure itself, so partial look-through is permitted.
R-LEX30.43-partial-lookthrough.quote: The bank's exposure amount to the underlying assets that are below 0.25% of the bank's Tier 1 capital may be assigned to the structure itself (ie partial look-through is permitted).

applies_to.note: Mixed treatment within one structure; the residual granular tail is treated as a single exposure to the structure.

R-LEX30.43-partial-lookthrough.portfolio_relevance: Lets a bank look through only the lumpy names in a structure and treat the granular retail tail as a single exposure, which is exactly the treatment a credit card securitisation attracts.

R-LEX30.44-unknown-client-assignment.title: Unidentifiable underlyings: structure or unknown client depending on 0.25% test
R-LEX30.44-unknown-client-assignment.statement: If a bank cannot identify the underlying assets of a structure, it must assign the total exposure to the structure where the total does not exceed 0.25% of Tier 1 capital, and otherwise must assign the total exposure amount to the unknown client.
R-LEX30.44-unknown-client-assignment.quote: If a bank is unable to identify the underlying assets of a structure: (1) where the total amount of its exposure does not exceed 0.25% of its Tier 1 capital, the bank must assign the total exposure amount of its investment to the structure; (2) otherwise, it must assign this total exposure amount to the unknown client.

applies_to.note: The default treatment when pool-level transparency is absent, which is the common case for small-bank fund and ABS holdings.

R-LEX30.44-unknown-client-assignment.portfolio_relevance: Opaque structured holdings above 0.25% of Tier 1 all collapse into one 'unknown client' bucket, so accumulating several non-transparent fund positions can breach the 25% limit even though the positions are economically unrelated.

R-LEX30.45-unknown-client-aggregation.title: All unknown exposures aggregate into a single counterparty subject to the limit
R-LEX30.45-unknown-client-aggregation.statement: A bank must aggregate all unknown exposures as if they related to a single counterparty, the unknown client, to which the large exposure limit applies.
R-LEX30.45-unknown-client-aggregation.quote: The bank must aggregate all unknown exposures as if they related to a single counterparty (the unknown client), to which the large exposure limit would apply.

applies_to.note: The unknown client bucket is itself capped at 25% of Tier 1 under LEX20.1.

R-LEX30.45-unknown-client-aggregation.portfolio_relevance: Creates a hard cap on aggregate opaque exposure at 25% of Tier 1, which is a computable constraint on how much of a securities portfolio can be held in structures without pool transparency.

R-LEX30.46-no-regulatory-arbitrage.title: Look-through decision must not be driven by regulatory arbitrage
R-LEX30.46-no-regulatory-arbitrage.statement: Where the look-through approach is not required, a bank must nevertheless demonstrate that regulatory arbitrage considerations did not influence the decision, for example that it has not circumvented the limit by investing in several individually immaterial transactions with identical underlying assets.
R-LEX30.46-no-regulatory-arbitrage.quote: a bank must nevertheless be able to demonstrate that regulatory arbitrage considerations have not influenced the decision whether to look through or not

applies_to.note: Anti-avoidance overlay on the 0.25% granularity carve-out.

R-LEX30.46-no-regulatory-arbitrage.portfolio_relevance: Blocks the obvious gaming strategy of splitting a concentrated exposure across many small structures with identical underlyings, so granularity relief must reflect genuine diversification.

R-LEX30.47-nominal-amount-if-no-lta.title: Exposure to a structure without look-through is the nominal amount invested
R-LEX30.47-nominal-amount-if-no-lta.statement: If the look-through approach need not be applied, a bank's exposure to the structure must be the nominal amount it invests in the structure.
R-LEX30.47-nominal-amount-if-no-lta.quote: If the LTA need not be applied, a bank's exposure to the structure must be the nominal amount it invests in the structure.

applies_to.note: Nominal, not fair value or risk-weighted amount.

R-LEX30.47-nominal-amount-if-no-lta.portfolio_relevance: Makes the concentration cost of a structured holding equal to its full nominal size against a single 'structure' counterparty, so several tranches of the same securitisation aggregate at par against the 25% limit.

R-LEX30.48-pro-rata-lookthrough.title: Look-through exposure value is the pro rata share of each underlying asset
R-LEX30.48-pro-rata-lookthrough.statement: Where look-through is required, the exposure value assigned to a counterparty equals the pro rata share the bank holds in the structure multiplied by the value of the underlying asset, and must be added to any other direct or indirect exposure to that counterparty.
R-LEX30.48-pro-rata-lookthrough.quote: the exposure value assigned to a counterparty is equal to the pro rata share that the bank holds in the structure multiplied by the value of the underlying asset in the structure.

applies_to.note: Worked example in the paragraph: a 1% share of a structure holding 20 assets of value 5 each gives an exposure of 0.05 per counterparty.

numeric_values: 1% share x asset value 5 = 0.05 exposure (worked example)
R-LEX30.48-pro-rata-lookthrough.portfolio_relevance: Gives the exact arithmetic for allocating fund and ABS holdings to obligors, which is the computable bridge between a securities portfolio and single-name concentration usage.

R-LEX30.49-tranche-exposure-value.title: Tranched structures: lower of tranche value and underlying nominal, then pro rata
R-LEX30.49-tranche-exposure-value.statement: For tranched structures the exposure value to an underlying asset is computed by first taking the lower of the value of the tranche invested in and the nominal value of each underlying asset, then applying the pro rata share of the bank's investment in the tranche, assuming pro rata loss distribution within the tranche.
R-LEX30.49-tranche-exposure-value.quote: (1) first, consider the lower of the value of the tranche in which the bank invests and the nominal value of each underlying asset included in the underlying portfolio of assets (2) second, apply the pro rata share of the bank's investment in the tranche to the value determined in the first step above.

applies_to.note: Assumes pro rata distribution of losses amongst investors in a single tranche; ignores tranche subordination.

R-LEX30.49-tranche-exposure-value.portfolio_relevance: Concentration measurement for a securitisation tranche ignores credit enhancement, so a senior card ABS tranche is measured on the same underlying-asset basis as a junior one; relief comes only from pool granularity, not from seniority.

R-LEX30.50-third-party-risk-factor.title: Third parties may be an additional risk factor inherent in a structure
R-LEX30.50-third-party-risk-factor.statement: Banks must identify third parties, such as originators, fund managers, liquidity providers and credit protection providers, that may constitute an additional risk factor inherent in a structure itself rather than in its underlying assets.
R-LEX30.50-third-party-risk-factor.quote: Banks must identify third parties that may constitute an additional risk factor inherent in a structure itself rather than in the underlying assets.

applies_to.note: Such a third party can be a common risk factor across several structures the bank invests in.

R-LEX30.50-third-party-risk-factor.portfolio_relevance: Identifies servicer, sponsor and liquidity-provider risk in card securitisations as a concentration factor, so investing across several card ABS programmes from the same sponsor does not diversify the concentration.

R-LEX30.51-common-risk-factor-gcc.title: Investments sharing a common risk factor form a group of connected counterparties
R-LEX30.51-common-risk-factor-gcc.statement: Banks must connect their investments in structures that share a common risk factor to form a group of connected counterparties, so that the sum of investments associated with that third party is subject to the large exposure limit.
R-LEX30.51-common-risk-factor-gcc.quote: The first implication is that banks must connect their investments in those structures with a common risk factor to form a group of connected counterparties.

applies_to.note: Not automatic: the paragraph notes the manager may not be an additional risk factor where legal separation of management and custody is mandated.

numeric_values: 25% of Tier 1 capital (aggregate across structures with a common manager)
R-LEX30.51-common-risk-factor-gcc.portfolio_relevance: Caps aggregate exposure to a single fund manager, ABCP sponsor or protection seller at the 25% limit, constraining how much of a securities book can be sourced from one sponsor even when the underlying pools are unrelated.

R-LEX30.52-multiple-third-parties.title: Exposure assigned to each of multiple third-party risk drivers
R-LEX30.52-multiple-third-parties.statement: Where a bank considers multiple third parties to be potential drivers of additional risk, it must assign the exposure resulting from the investment in the relevant structures to each of those third parties.
R-LEX30.52-multiple-third-parties.quote: the bank must assign the exposure resulting from the investment in the relevant structures to each of the third parties.

applies_to.note: Deliberate multiple counting: the same investment consumes headroom against every identified third-party risk driver.

R-LEX30.52-multiple-third-parties.portfolio_relevance: A single structured position can consume limit headroom several times over against different sponsors and protection providers, making complex multi-party structures disproportionately expensive on the concentration dimension relative to whole-loan card receivables held directly.

R-CRE30.1-irb-supervisory-approval.title: IRB approach is available only with supervisory approval
R-CRE30.1-irb-supervisory-approval.statement: A bank may rely on its own internal estimates of PD, LGD, EAD and M only if it has received supervisory approval to use the IRB approach and meets the minimum conditions and disclosure requirements.
R-CRE30.1-irb-supervisory-approval.quote: banks that have received supervisory approval to use the IRB approach may rely on their own internal estimates of risk components in determining the capital requirement for a given exposure

applies_to.note: Explicit supervisory-approval gate. In the US, the advanced approaches (12 CFR 217 subpart E) are mandatory only for Category I/II organisations (roughly >=USD 250bn assets or >=USD 75bn cross-jurisdictional activity); a small North American bank cannot use IRB, so every CRE30-CRE35 rule is a counterfactual benchmark for it rather than a live constraint.

R-CRE30.1-irb-supervisory-approval.portfolio_relevance: Gates the entire IRB toolkit: a small bank cannot obtain the lower QRRE risk weights on its credit-card book at all, so any credit-card growth is capitalised at standardised-approach weights regardless of measured loss experience.

R-CRE30.3-residual-100pct-rw.title: Residual 100% risk weight where no IRB treatment is specified
R-CRE30.3-residual-100pct-rw.statement: Where an IRB treatment is not specified for an exposure, it receives a 100% risk weight (except where a 0% risk weight applies under the standardised approach), and the resulting RWA is treated as representing unexpected loss only.
R-CRE30.3-residual-100pct-rw.quote: In cases where an IRB treatment is not specified, the risk weight for those other exposures is 100%, except when a 0% risk weight applies under the standardised approach, and the resulting risk-weighted assets are assumed to represent UL only.

applies_to.note: Applies to IRB banks only; the 0% carve-out follows the standardised approach.

R-CRE30.3-residual-100pct-rw.portfolio_relevance: Sets a punitive default weight on any residual/unclassified banking-book asset, discouraging accumulation of miscellaneous non-classified exposures relative to well-defined retail or corporate buckets.

R-CRE30.4-asset-class-categorisation.title: Mandatory categorisation of banking-book exposures into five IRB asset classes
R-CRE30.4-asset-class-categorisation.statement: Under the IRB approach a bank must categorise all banking-book exposures into the corporate, sovereign, bank, retail and equity asset classes according to the definitions in CRE30.
R-CRE30.4-asset-class-categorisation.quote: Under the IRB approach, banks must categorise banking-book exposures into broad classes of assets with different underlying risk characteristics, subject to the definitions set out below. The classes of assets are (a) corporate, (b) sovereign, (c) bank, (d) retail, and (e) equity.

applies_to.note: Structural requirement for all IRB banks.

R-CRE30.4-asset-class-categorisation.portfolio_relevance: Defines the buckets over which any portfolio-composition optimisation must be expressed; a shift of balances between corporate and retail classes changes which risk-weight function applies.

R-CRE30.4-retail-three-subclasses.title: Retail asset class contains three separately identified sub-classes
R-CRE30.4-retail-three-subclasses.statement: The retail asset class is subdivided into three separately identified sub-classes.
R-CRE30.4-retail-three-subclasses.quote: Within the retail asset class, three sub-classes are separately identified.

applies_to.note: Definitional; the three sub-classes are enumerated in CRE30.23.

R-CRE30.4-retail-three-subclasses.portfolio_relevance: Establishes that credit-card balances must be reported and capitalised separately from mortgages and other retail, so the mix across these three sub-classes is itself a capital lever.

R-CRE30.19-retail-definition.title: Two-part test for classifying an exposure as retail
R-CRE30.19-retail-definition.statement: An exposure qualifies as retail only if it satisfies all borrower/size criteria in CRE30.20 and all pool-size criteria in CRE30.22.
R-CRE30.19-retail-definition.quote: An exposure is categorised as a retail exposure if it meets all of the criteria set out in CRE30.20 (which relate to the nature of the borrower and value of individual exposures) and all of the criteria set out in CRE30.22 (which relate to the size of the pool of exposures).

applies_to.note: Conjunctive test: failing either limb pushes the exposure into the corporate class.

R-CRE30.19-retail-definition.portfolio_relevance: Failing the pooled-management limb reclassifies a card or small-business line into the corporate class, where the maturity-adjusted risk-weight function generally produces materially higher RWA.

R-CRE30.20-individuals-revolving-retail.title: Credit cards and other revolving credit to individuals are retail regardless of size
R-CRE30.20-individuals-revolving-retail.statement: Exposures to individuals, including revolving credits and lines of credit such as credit cards and overdrafts as well as personal term loans and leases, are generally eligible for retail treatment regardless of exposure size, though supervisors may set thresholds separating retail from corporate.
R-CRE30.20-individuals-revolving-retail.quote: Exposures to individuals – such as revolving credits and lines of credit (eg credit cards, overdrafts, or retail facilities secured by financial instruments) as well as personal term loans and leases (eg instalment loans, auto loans and leases, student and educational loans, personal finance, or other exposures with similar characteristics) – are generally eligible for retail treatment regardless of exposure size, although supervisors may wish to establish exposure thresholds to distinguish between retail and corporate exposures.

applies_to.note: National discretion: supervisors may impose exposure thresholds distinguishing retail from corporate.

R-CRE30.20-individuals-revolving-retail.portfolio_relevance: Confirms that the whole credit-card book of an individual-obligor issuer qualifies for retail treatment without a size cap, so card growth does not risk falling out of the retail class on size grounds alone.

R-CRE30.20-sme-retail-1m-threshold.title: EUR 1 million group exposure threshold for small-business retail treatment
R-CRE30.20-sme-retail-1m-threshold.statement: Loans to small businesses that are managed as retail are eligible for retail treatment only if the banking group's total exposure to that borrower, on a consolidated basis, is less than EUR 1 million; loans extended through or guaranteed by an individual face the same threshold.
R-CRE30.20-sme-retail-1m-threshold.quote: (3) Where loans are extended to small businesses and managed as retail exposures they are eligible for retail treatment provided the total exposure of the banking group to a small business borrower (on a consolidated basis where applicable) is less than €1 million. Small business loans extended through or guaranteed by an individual are subject to the same exposure threshold.

applies_to.note: Hard EUR 1m threshold measured at consolidated banking-group level; CRE30.21 asks supervisors to apply it flexibly.

R-CRE30.20-sme-retail-1m-threshold.portfolio_relevance: Caps how large an individual SME relationship can grow before it must leave the retail pool and be capitalised on the corporate risk-weight function, penalising relationship concentration in a small-business book.

R-CRE30.22-large-pool-criterion.title: Retail exposures must sit in a large, pooled-managed portfolio
R-CRE30.22-large-pool-criterion.statement: To be treated as retail, an exposure must be one of a large pool of exposures that the bank manages on a pooled basis.
R-CRE30.22-large-pool-criterion.quote: (1) The exposure must be one of a large pool of exposures, which are managed by the bank on a pooled basis.

applies_to.note: 'Large pool' is not numerically defined in the Framework; supervisory judgement applies.

R-CRE30.22-large-pool-criterion.portfolio_relevance: A bank that shrinks a retail segment below a credibly 'large' pool, or begins to underwrite it case-by-case, loses retail treatment for the whole segment — a real constraint on running down a card portfolio.

R-CRE30.22-sme-pooled-management.title: Sub-EUR 1 million small-business exposures may be pooled as retail if managed consistently
R-CRE30.22-sme-pooled-management.statement: A small-business exposure below EUR 1 million may be treated as retail if the bank treats it consistently over time and in the same manner as other retail exposures in its internal risk management systems, originates it similarly, and manages it as part of a pool rather than individually.
R-CRE30.22-sme-pooled-management.quote: (2) Where a loan gives rise to a small business exposure below €1 million, it may be treated as retail exposures if the bank treats such exposures in its internal risk management systems consistently over time and in the same manner as other retail exposures.

applies_to.note: Optional treatment conditional on demonstrable consistency of internal risk management.

R-CRE30.22-sme-pooled-management.portfolio_relevance: Rewards banks that industrialise small-business underwriting into a pooled retail process, since pooled SME balances attract the retail rather than corporate risk-weight function.

R-CRE30.23-identify-three-retail-subclas.title: Banks must separately identify residential mortgage, QRRE and other retail
R-CRE30.23-identify-three-retail-subclas.statement: Within the retail asset class banks are required to identify separately residential mortgage loans, qualifying revolving retail exposures, and all other retail exposures.
R-CRE30.23-identify-three-retail-subclas.quote: Within the retail asset class category, banks are required to identify separately three sub-classes of exposures: (1) residential mortgage loans, as defined above; (2) qualifying revolving retail exposures, as defined in the following paragraph; and (3) all other retail exposures.

applies_to.note: Mandatory segmentation for all IRB retail portfolios.

R-CRE30.23-identify-three-retail-subclas.portfolio_relevance: Forces the credit-card book to be carved out as QRRE (if it qualifies) or fall into 'other retail', which is the single largest driver of the effective retail risk weight.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-all-criteria.title: QRRE status must be established at sub-portfolio level and all criteria met
R-CRE30.24-qrre-all-criteria.statement: All of the QRRE criteria must be satisfied for a sub-portfolio to be treated as qualifying revolving retail, applied at a sub-portfolio level consistent with the bank's general retail segmentation, with segmentation at national or country level (or below) as the general rule.
R-CRE30.24-qrre-all-criteria.quote: All of the following criteria must be satisfied for a sub-portfolio to be treated as a qualifying revolving retail exposure (QRRE). These criteria must be applied at a sub-portfolio level consistent with the bank’s segmentation of its retail activities generally. Segmentation at the national or country level (or below) should be the general rule.

applies_to.note: Test is conjunctive and applied per sub-portfolio, not per exposure; segmentation is expected at national level or below.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-all-criteria.portfolio_relevance: Means QRRE benefits cannot be claimed for a mixed card book: the bank must be able to carve out a clean, homogeneous sub-portfolio that satisfies every criterion, otherwise the whole segment reverts to 'other retail' weights.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-revolving-unsecured-unco.title: QRRE criterion 1: revolving, unsecured and uncommitted exposures
R-CRE30.24-qrre-revolving-unsecured-unco.statement: To qualify as QRRE the exposures must be revolving, unsecured and uncommitted both contractually and in practice, where revolving means customers' outstanding balances may fluctuate based on their own borrow/repay decisions up to a bank-established limit.
R-CRE30.24-qrre-revolving-unsecured-unco.quote: (1) The exposures are revolving, unsecured, and uncommitted (both contractually and in practice). In this context, revolving exposures are defined as those where customers’ outstanding balances are permitted to fluctuate based on their decisions to borrow and repay, up to a limit established by the bank.

applies_to.note: The 'uncommitted in practice' limb is a behavioural test, not merely a contractual one.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-revolving-unsecured-unco.portfolio_relevance: Secured or contractually committed card-like products (eg secured cards, committed lines) are excluded from QRRE, so a shift toward secured card products moves balances into the higher-correlation 'other retail' function.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-individuals.title: QRRE criteria 2 and 3: individual obligors and EUR 100,000 exposure cap
