R-CRE30.24-qrre-individuals.statement: QRRE exposures must be to individuals and the maximum exposure to a single individual in the sub-portfolio must be EUR 100,000 or less.
R-CRE30.24-qrre-individuals.quote: (2) The exposures are to individuals. (3) The maximum exposure to a single individual in the sub-portfolio is €100,000 or less.

applies_to.note: Business-card and commercial-card balances to non-individual obligors fall outside QRRE.

numeric_values: €100,000 maximum exposure to a single individual
R-CRE30.24-qrre-individuals.portfolio_relevance: Excludes commercial/business card programmes from QRRE and caps individual card lines, so a card issuer pushing high-limit or small-business cards forfeits the QRRE correlation benefit on that sub-portfolio.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-100k-limit.title: QRRE single-obligor limit of EUR 100,000
R-CRE30.24-qrre-100k-limit.statement: No single individual's exposure within a QRRE sub-portfolio may exceed EUR 100,000.
R-CRE30.24-qrre-100k-limit.quote: (3) The maximum exposure to a single individual in the sub-portfolio is €100,000 or less.

applies_to.note: Directly computable ceiling on per-obligor QRRE exposure; measured on the sub-portfolio.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-100k-limit.portfolio_relevance: A hard, checkable ceiling: raising credit limits on premium card customers above roughly EUR 100k breaks QRRE eligibility for the sub-portfolio containing them.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-low-loss-volatility.title: QRRE criterion 4: demonstrated low volatility of loss rates
R-CRE30.24-qrre-low-loss-volatility.statement: Because QRRE asset correlation assumptions are markedly below those of the other retail risk-weight function at low PD, a bank must demonstrate that its use of the QRRE function is confined to portfolios showing low volatility of loss rates relative to their average level, especially in low PD bands.
R-CRE30.24-qrre-low-loss-volatility.quote: (4) Because the asset correlation assumptions for the QRRE risk-weight function are markedly below those for the other retail risk-weight function at low PD values, banks must demonstrate that the use of the QRRE risk-weight function is constrained to portfolios that have exhibited low volatility of loss rates, relative to their average level of loss rates, especially within the low PD bands.

applies_to.note: Evidential burden falls on the bank; the QRRE correlation constant itself is set in the CRE31.15 formula, which is rendered as an image and is not present in the parsed paragraph text.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-low-loss-volatility.portfolio_relevance: Ties the lower QRRE capital charge to demonstrated loss-rate stability, so a card book whose charge-off rate becomes volatile can lose the favourable correlation and see RWA jump without any change in balances.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-loss-rate-data.title: QRRE criterion 5: retention of sub-portfolio loss-rate data
R-CRE30.24-qrre-loss-rate-data.statement: Loss-rate data for the QRRE sub-portfolio must be retained so that the volatility of loss rates can be analysed.
R-CRE30.24-qrre-loss-rate-data.quote: (5) Data on loss rates for the sub-portfolio must be retained in order to allow analysis of the volatility of loss rates.

applies_to.note: Data-retention obligation supporting criterion 4.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-loss-rate-data.portfolio_relevance: An operational prerequisite: a bank without a clean multi-year card loss-rate history at sub-portfolio level cannot claim QRRE treatment even if its economics would qualify.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-supervisor-concurrence.title: QRRE criterion 6: supervisor must concur with the classification
R-CRE30.24-qrre-supervisor-concurrence.statement: The supervisor must agree that QRRE treatment is consistent with the underlying risk characteristics of the sub-portfolio.
R-CRE30.24-qrre-supervisor-concurrence.quote: (6) The supervisor must concur that treatment as a qualifying revolving retail exposure is consistent with the underlying risk characteristics of the sub- portfolio.

applies_to.note: Explicit supervisory-concurrence gate on top of the objective criteria.

R-CRE30.24-qrre-supervisor-concurrence.portfolio_relevance: QRRE treatment is revocable by the supervisor, so the capital benefit assumed in any card-portfolio plan is contingent rather than mechanical.

R-CRE30.25-qrre-transactor-definition.title: Definition of a QRRE transactor (12-month full-repayment test)
R-CRE30.25-qrre-transactor-definition.statement: The QRRE sub-class splits into transactors and revolvers; a transactor is an obligor on a credit card or charge card facility whose balance has been repaid in full at each scheduled repayment date for the previous 12 months, or an overdraft facility with no drawdowns over the previous 12 months.
R-CRE30.25-qrre-transactor-definition.quote: The QRRE sub-class is split into exposures to transactors and revolvers. A QRRE transactor is an exposure to an obligor that meets the definition set out in CRE20. 64 of the standardised approach. That is, the exposure is to an obligor in relation to a facility such as credit card or charge card where the balance has been repaid in full at each scheduled repayment date for the previous 12 months, or the exposure is in relation to an overdraft facility if there have been no drawdowns over the previous 12 months.

applies_to.note: The transactor definition is imported from the standardised approach (CRE20.64), so it is materially relevant to small standardised-approach banks too, even though CRE30.25 itself sits in the IRB chapter.

numeric_values: 12 months of full repayment at each scheduled repayment date
R-CRE30.25-qrre-transactor-definition.portfolio_relevance: The single most important credit-card segmentation in Basel III: transactor balances attract materially lower capital than revolver balances, so shifting the card mix toward full-payers reduces RWA. Note that US Call Report/FDIC data do not report the transactor/revolver split, so this must be proxied.

R-CRE30.25-qrre-revolver-residual.title: All non-transactor QRRE, including thin-file accounts, are revolvers
R-CRE30.25-qrre-revolver-residual.statement: Every QRRE exposure that is not a transactor is a revolver, including QRRE exposures with less than 12 months of repayment history.
R-CRE30.25-qrre-revolver-residual.quote: All exposures that are not QRRE transactors are QRRE revolvers, including QRRE exposures with less than 12 months of repayment history.

applies_to.note: Residual classification; newly originated accounts default to the more capital-intensive revolver bucket for their first 12 months.

numeric_values: less than 12 months of repayment history
R-CRE30.25-qrre-revolver-residual.portfolio_relevance: Newly booked card accounts are treated as revolvers for a full year regardless of behaviour, so rapid card-account growth mechanically raises RWA and the higher QRRE revolver PD floor before any seasoning benefit appears.

R-CRE30.28-purchased-retail-topdown.title: Purchased retail receivables eligible for top-down IRB treatment
R-CRE30.28-purchased-retail-topdown.statement: Purchased retail receivables are eligible for the top-down approach, provided the purchasing bank complies with the IRB rules for retail exposures and the minimum operational requirements of CRE34 and CRE36.
R-CRE30.28-purchased-retail-topdown.quote: Purchased retail receivables, provided the purchasing bank complies with the IRB rules for retail exposures, are eligible for the top-down approach as permitted within the existing standards for retail exposures.

applies_to.note: Conditional on full compliance with retail IRB rules plus CRE34/CRE36 operational minimums.

R-CRE30.28-purchased-retail-topdown.portfolio_relevance: Allows a bank to buy whole card or personal-loan receivable pools and capitalise them pool-wise rather than obligor-wise, making portfolio acquisition a viable alternative to organic origination.

R-CRE30.30-purchased-receivables-conc-li.title: Supervisors must set concentration limits for top-down purchased corporate receivables
R-CRE30.30-purchased-receivables-conc-li.statement: National supervisors must establish concentration limits above which capital must be calculated using the bottom-up minimum requirements for corporate exposures; the limits may reference single-exposure size relative to the pool, pool size as a percentage of regulatory capital, or maximum individual exposure size.
R-CRE30.30-purchased-receivables-conc-li.quote: (4) National supervisors must also establish concentration limits above which capital charges must be calculated using the minimum requirements for the bottom-up approach for corporate exposures.

applies_to.note: The numeric limits are set at national discretion, not in the Basel text.

R-CRE30.30-purchased-receivables-conc-li.portfolio_relevance: Puts a jurisdiction-set ceiling on how concentrated a purchased receivable pool may be before the capital-efficient top-down treatment is withdrawn.

R-CRE30.34-airb-500m-revenue-cap.title: A-IRB prohibited for large corporates (revenue > EUR 500m) and for bank/financial exposures
R-CRE30.34-airb-500m-revenue-cap.statement: The advanced IRB approach cannot be used for exposures to general corporates in groups with total consolidated annual revenues greater than EUR 500 million, nor for bank asset class exposures or other securities firms and financial institutions.
R-CRE30.34-airb-500m-revenue-cap.quote: the A-IRB approach cannot be used for the following: (1) Exposures to general corporates (ie exposures to corporates that are not classified as specialised lending) belonging to a group with total consolidated annual revenues greater than €500m.

applies_to.note: Basel III output-floor-era restriction; measurement of the revenue threshold is governed by CRE30.35.

R-CRE30.34-airb-500m-revenue-cap.portfolio_relevance: Removes own-LGD/own-EAD modelling benefits from large-corporate and financial-institution lending, tilting the relative capital attractiveness of the book toward retail and small-corporate exposures where A-IRB remains available.

R-CRE30.35-revenue-threshold-measurement.title: Measurement basis for the EUR 500m corporate revenue threshold
R-CRE30.35-revenue-threshold-measurement.statement: The revenue threshold must be measured from audited financial statements (consolidated where applicable) using the average amounts calculated over the prior three years, or the latest amounts updated every three years.
R-CRE30.35-revenue-threshold-measurement.quote: The figures must be based on the average amounts calculated over the prior three years, or on the latest amounts updated every three years by the bank.

applies_to.note: Prescribes the averaging window for a scope test, making the test resistant to single-year revenue swings.

R-CRE30.35-revenue-threshold-measurement.portfolio_relevance: Prevents a borrower from oscillating in and out of A-IRB eligibility year to year, stabilising the capital treatment of a corporate relationship over a three-year horizon.

R-CRE30.42-retail-own-estimates-only.title: Retail is A-IRB only: own PD, LGD and EAD estimates are mandatory
R-CRE30.42-retail-own-estimates-only.statement: For retail exposures banks must provide their own estimates of PD, LGD and EAD; there is no foundation approach for the retail asset class.
R-CRE30.42-retail-own-estimates-only.quote: For retail exposures, banks must provide their own estimates of PD, LGD and EAD. There is no foundation approach for this asset class.

applies_to.note: Materially raises the modelling bar for any bank seeking IRB treatment of a card book: there is no supervisory-parameter fallback.

R-CRE30.42-retail-own-estimates-only.portfolio_relevance: A bank cannot obtain IRB treatment of its credit-card portfolio by using supervisory LGD/EAD; it must build and validate own-estimate PD, LGD and EAD models, which is why small North American card issuers stay on the standardised approach.

R-CRE30.45-irb-rollout-whole-asset-class.title: IRB adoption must be extended across an entire asset class
R-CRE30.45-irb-rollout-whole-asset-class.statement: Once a bank adopts an IRB approach for part of its holdings within an asset class, it is expected to extend that approach across all holdings within that asset class.
R-CRE30.45-irb-rollout-whole-asset-class.quote: Once a bank adopts an IRB approach for part of its holdings within an asset class, it is expected to extend it across all holdings within that asset class.

applies_to.note: Anti-cherry-picking rule; phased roll-out is permitted under CRE30.47 subject to supervisory agreement.

R-CRE30.45-irb-rollout-whole-asset-class.portfolio_relevance: Blocks cherry-picking: a bank cannot IRB-model only its best-performing card segment and leave the rest on the standardised approach to arbitrage the difference.

R-CRE30.45-qrre-separate-asset-class.title: QRRE is a distinct asset class for IRB roll-out purposes
R-CRE30.45-qrre-separate-asset-class.statement: For roll-out purposes the relevant asset classes are enumerated as sovereigns, banks, corporates, specialised lending, corporate purchased receivables, QRRE, retail residential mortgages, other retail, and retail purchased receivables.
R-CRE30.45-qrre-separate-asset-class.quote: In this context, the relevant assets classes are as follows: (1) Sovereigns (2) Banks (3) Corporates (excluding specialised lending and purchased receivables) (4) Specialised lending (5) Corporate purchased receivables (6) QRRE (7) Retail residential mortgages (8) Other retail (excluding purchased receivables) (9) Retail purchased receivables

applies_to.note: Nine roll-out asset classes; QRRE is item (6) and is therefore a roll-out unit in its own right.

R-CRE30.45-qrre-separate-asset-class.portfolio_relevance: Because QRRE is its own roll-out class, a bank can adopt IRB for its whole card book without simultaneously modelling mortgages or other retail — but it must then cover the entire QRRE book.

R-CRE30.47-rollout-business-unit-complet.title: IRB adoption within a business unit must cover the whole asset class in that unit
R-CRE30.47-rollout-business-unit-complet.statement: When a bank adopts an IRB approach for an asset class within a particular business unit, it must apply the IRB approach to all exposures within that asset class in that unit.
R-CRE30.47-rollout-business-unit-complet.quote: However, when a bank adopts an IRB approach for an asset class within a particular business unit, it must apply the IRB approach to all exposures within that asset class in that unit.

applies_to.note: Phased roll-out is allowed across units and from F-IRB to A-IRB, but never partially within a unit's asset class.

R-CRE30.47-rollout-business-unit-complet.portfolio_relevance: Prevents intra-unit segmentation games; a card-issuing unit must run its entire QRRE book on the same approach, so partial optimisation within one unit is not available.

R-CRE30.48-no-capital-relief-intragroup.title: No capital relief for intra-group transfers designed to reduce group capital during roll-out
R-CRE30.48-no-capital-relief-intragroup.statement: During the IRB roll-out period supervisors will ensure no capital relief is granted for intra-group transactions designed to reduce a banking group's aggregate capital charge by transferring credit risk among entities on the standardised, foundation and advanced IRB approaches, including asset sales and cross guarantees.
R-CRE30.48-no-capital-relief-intragroup.quote: During the roll-out period, supervisors will ensure that no capital relief is granted for intra-group transactions which are designed to reduce a banking group’s aggregate capital charge by transferring credit risk among entities on the standardised approach, foundation and advanced IRB approaches. This includes, but is not limited to, asset sales or cross guarantees.

applies_to.note: Anti-arbitrage rule specific to the roll-out period; enforcement is supervisory.

R-CRE30.48-no-capital-relief-intragroup.portfolio_relevance: Directly constrains portfolio restructuring: moving a card portfolio to a group affiliate on a different approach, or covering it with a cross guarantee, yields no capital benefit during roll-out.

R-CRE30.49-immaterial-exposure-exemption.title: Immaterial exposures may be exempted from IRB and left on the standardised approach
R-CRE30.49-immaterial-exposure-exemption.statement: Exposures that are immaterial in size and perceived risk profile within their asset class may, with supervisory approval, be exempt from the roll-out requirements and capitalised under the standardised approach, with the supervisor able to require more capital under the SRP.
R-CRE30.49-immaterial-exposure-exemption.quote: Some exposures that are immaterial in terms of size and perceived risk profile within their asset class may be exempt from the requirements in the previous two paragraphs, subject to supervisory approval.

applies_to.note: Explicit proportionality/materiality carve-out, but gated on supervisory approval and no numeric materiality threshold is given in the Basel text.

R-CRE30.49-immaterial-exposure-exemption.portfolio_relevance: Gives a bank a legitimate route to keep a small residual card or niche retail book on standardised weights instead of building a model for it, at the cost of possible SRP add-ons.

R-CRE30.50-no-voluntary-return-to-sa.title: Voluntary reversion from IRB to the standardised approach is severely restricted
R-CRE30.50-no-voluntary-return-to-sa.statement: Banks adopting IRB for an asset class are expected to continue using it; a voluntary return to the standardised or foundation approach is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, such as divestiture of a large fraction of the bank's credit business in that asset class, and must be approved by the supervisor.
R-CRE30.50-no-voluntary-return-to-sa.quote: A voluntary return to the standardised or foundation approach is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, such as divestiture of a large fraction of the bank’s credit-related business in that asset class, and must be approved by the supervisor.

applies_to.note: One-way ratchet with a supervisory-approval gate; divestiture of a large fraction of the business is the named exception.

R-CRE30.50-no-voluntary-return-to-sa.portfolio_relevance: Makes the choice to IRB-model a card book effectively irreversible, so a bank cannot switch back to standardised weights when its modelled QRRE parameters deteriorate.

R-CRE31.3-defaulted-exposure-rwa.title: RWA for defaulted exposures: K x 12.5 x EAD
R-CRE31.3-defaulted-exposure-rwa.statement: For a defaulted exposure the capital requirement K equals the greater of zero and the difference between its LGD and the bank's best estimate of expected loss, and the risk-weighted asset amount is the product of K, 12.5 and EAD.
R-CRE31.3-defaulted-exposure-rwa.quote: The capital requirement (K) for a defaulted exposure is equal to the greater of zero and the difference between its LGD (described in CRE36.83) and the bank’s best estimate of expected loss (described in CRE36.86). The risk-weighted asset amount for the defaulted exposure is the product of K, 12.5, and the EAD.

applies_to.note: Applies across all IRB asset classes including QRRE; 12.5 is the reciprocal of the 8% minimum capital ratio.

R-CRE31.3-defaulted-exposure-rwa.portfolio_relevance: Defaulted card balances carry RWA only to the extent LGD exceeds the bank's best estimate of expected loss, so aggressive provisioning on delinquent card accounts reduces the RWA those accounts carry.

R-CRE31.7-financial-institution-correlat.title: 1.25x asset-correlation multiplier for large and unregulated financial institutions
R-CRE31.7-financial-institution-correlat.statement: A multiplier of 1.25 is applied to the correlation parameter for exposures to regulated financial institutions with total assets of USD 100 billion or more, and to unregulated financial institutions regardless of size.
R-CRE31.7-financial-institution-correlat.quote: A multiplier of 1.25 is applied to the correlation parameter of all exposures to financial institutions meeting the following criteria: (1) Regulated financial institutions whose total assets are greater than or equal to USD100 billion.

applies_to.note: Size test is applied to the counterparty (>= USD 100bn total assets), measured from the most recent audited consolidated financial statements of the parent.

R-CRE31.7-financial-institution-correlat.portfolio_relevance: Penalises interbank and non-bank-financial exposure to very large or unregulated financial counterparties, making it capital-cheaper to redeploy the same balance sheet into retail or non-financial corporate lending.

R-CRE31.8-sme-firm-size-adjustment.title: SME firm-size adjustment to the corporate correlation (0.04 x (1 - (S - 5)/45))
R-CRE31.8-sme-firm-size-adjustment.statement: Banks may separately distinguish SME borrowers, defined as corporate exposures where reported consolidated group sales are less than EUR 50 million, and apply a firm-size adjustment of 0.04 x (1 - (S - 5)/45) to the corporate risk-weight formula, where S is annual sales in EUR millions.
R-CRE31.8-sme-firm-size-adjustment.quote: banks will be permitted to separately distinguish exposures to SME borrowers (defined as corporate exposures where the reported sales for the consolidated group of which the firm is a part is less than €50 million) from those to large firms. A firm-size adjustment (ie 0.04 x (1 – (S – 5) / 45)) is made to the corporate risk weight formula for exposures to SME borrowers.

applies_to.note: S is bounded between EUR 5m and EUR 50m; CRE31.9 allows total assets to be substituted for sales at national discretion where sales are not meaningful.

R-CRE31.8-sme-firm-size-adjustment.portfolio_relevance: Directly computable RWA discount for lending to smaller firms: shifting corporate balances toward sub-EUR 50m borrowers lowers the asset correlation by up to 0.04 and therefore lowers RWA.

R-CRE31.8-sme-5m-floor.title: Sales below EUR 5 million floored at EUR 5 million for the SME adjustment
R-CRE31.8-sme-5m-floor.statement: For the purposes of the SME firm-size adjustment, reported sales of less than EUR 5 million are treated as if they were equal to EUR 5 million.
R-CRE31.8-sme-5m-floor.quote: Reported sales of less than €5 million will be treated as if they were equivalent to €5 million for the purposes of the firm-size adjustment for SME borrowers.

applies_to.note: Caps the maximum benefit of the firm-size adjustment at the S = 5 point.

R-CRE31.8-sme-5m-floor.portfolio_relevance: Caps the SME capital discount, so moving further down-market below EUR 5m of borrower sales yields no additional correlation benefit while adding credit risk.

R-CRE31.13-three-retail-rw-functions.title: Three retail risk-weight functions with no maturity adjustment
R-CRE31.13-three-retail-rw-functions.statement: There are three separate retail risk-weight functions, driven by separate assessments of PD and LGD, and none of them contains the full maturity adjustment component present in the bank, sovereign and corporate function.
R-CRE31.13-three-retail-rw-functions.quote: There are three separate risk-weight functions for retail exposures, as defined in CRE31.14 to CRE31.16. Risk weights for retail exposures are based on separate assessments of PD and LGD as inputs to the risk-weight functions. None of the three retail risk-weight functions contain the full maturity adjustment component that is present in the risk-weight function for exposures to banks, sovereigns and corporates.

applies_to.note: Retail RWA depends only on PD, LGD and EAD; effective maturity M is not an input.

numeric_values: no maturity adjustment (M not an input)
R-CRE31.13-three-retail-rw-functions.portfolio_relevance: Because retail RWA carries no maturity adjustment, lengthening or shortening the contractual tenor of a card or personal-loan product does not change its capital charge — only PD, LGD and EAD do.

R-CRE31.14-mortgage-rw-function.title: Residential mortgage retail risk-weight function
R-CRE31.14-mortgage-rw-function.statement: Retail exposures that are not in default and are secured or partly secured by residential mortgages are risk-weighted using the residential mortgage retail formula, which also applies to the unsecured portion of such mortgages.
R-CRE31.14-mortgage-rw-function.quote: For exposures defined in CRE30.19 that are not in default and are secured or partly secured by residential mortgages, risk weights will be assigned based on the following formula:

applies_to.note: The formula itself (including the fixed 0.15 asset correlation) is rendered as an image in the source PDF and is not present in the parsed paragraph text, so the constant cannot be quoted from this corpus.

R-CRE31.14-mortgage-rw-function.portfolio_relevance: Assigns the highest fixed retail asset correlation to mortgages, so a mortgage-heavy retail mix carries more systematic-risk capital per unit of PD than a QRRE-heavy mix at low PD levels.

R-CRE31.15-qrre-rw-function.title: QRRE risk-weight function applies to non-defaulted qualifying revolving retail
R-CRE31.15-qrre-rw-function.statement: Qualifying revolving retail exposures as defined in CRE30.23 and CRE30.24 that are not in default are risk-weighted using the dedicated QRRE risk-weight formula.
R-CRE31.15-qrre-rw-function.quote: For qualifying revolving retail exposures as defined in CRE30.23 and CRE30.24 that are not in default, risk weights are defined based on the following formula:

applies_to.note: Available only where the CRE30.24 QRRE criteria are met and the supervisor concurs. The QRRE asset-correlation constant (0.04) sits inside a formula image and is not present in the parsed paragraph text, so it cannot be quoted from this corpus.

R-CRE31.15-qrre-rw-function.portfolio_relevance: This is the capital reward for a clean, low-volatility credit-card book: the QRRE function carries the lowest fixed asset correlation in the retail suite, so qualifying card balances consume less capital than identical balances in 'other retail'.

R-CRE31.16-other-retail-rw-function.title: Other retail risk-weight function with PD-varying correlation
R-CRE31.16-other-retail-rw-function.statement: All other retail exposures that are not in default are risk-weighted using a function whose asset correlation varies with PD.
R-CRE31.16-other-retail-rw-function.quote: For all other retail exposures that are not in default, risk weights are assigned based on the following function, which allows correlation to vary with PD:

applies_to.note: The correlation interpolation (0.03 to 0.16 in PD) is in the formula image, not in the parsed text.

R-CRE31.16-other-retail-rw-function.portfolio_relevance: This is the fallback function a credit-card book falls into if it fails the QRRE criteria; its PD-varying correlation is markedly higher than QRRE's at low PD, so losing QRRE status raises card RWA most for the highest-quality accounts.

R-CRE32.4-pd-floor-005.title: 0.05% PD floor for corporate and bank exposures
R-CRE32.4-pd-floor-005.statement: Except for sovereign asset class exposures, the PD used as input into the risk-weight formula and the expected loss calculation must not be less than 0.05%.
R-CRE32.4-pd-floor-005.quote: With the exception of exposures in the sovereign asset class, the PD for each exposure that is used as input into the risk weight formula and the calculation of expected loss must not be less than 0.05%.

applies_to.note: Sovereign exposures are exempt; the parallel retail floors are in CRE32.58.

R-CRE32.4-pd-floor-005.portfolio_relevance: Caps the RWA benefit of moving to very high-quality corporate borrowers: below 5bp of modelled PD, further credit-quality improvement yields no capital saving.

R-CRE32.6-firb-lgd-45-40.title: F-IRB supervisory LGD of 45% for financials and 40% for other corporates
R-CRE32.6-firb-lgd-45-40.statement: Under the foundation approach, unsecured senior claims on sovereigns, banks, securities firms and other financial institutions are assigned a 45% LGD, while unsecured senior claims on other corporates are assigned a 40% LGD.
R-CRE32.6-firb-lgd-45-40.quote: Under the foundation approach, senior claims on sovereigns, banks, securities firms and other financial institutions (including insurance companies and any financial institutions in the corporate asset class) that are not secured by recognised collateral will be assigned a 45% LGD. Senior claims on other corporates that are not secured by recognised collateral will be assigned a 40% LGD.

applies_to.note: F-IRB only; no foundation approach exists for retail (CRE30.42).

R-CRE32.6-firb-lgd-45-40.portfolio_relevance: Makes unsecured lending to financial counterparties 12.5% more LGD-expensive than to non-financial corporates on identical PD, favouring non-financial corporate credit in an F-IRB book.

R-CRE32.7-subordinated-lgd-75.title: 75% LGD for all subordinated claims
R-CRE32.7-subordinated-lgd-75.statement: All subordinated claims on corporates, sovereigns and banks are assigned a 75% LGD under the foundation approach; supervisors may at national discretion apply a wider definition of subordination including economic subordination.
R-CRE32.7-subordinated-lgd-75.quote: All subordinated claims on corporates, sovereigns and banks will be assigned a 75% LGD.

applies_to.note: National discretion to extend the subordination definition to economically subordinated unsecured facilities.

R-CRE32.7-subordinated-lgd-75.portfolio_relevance: Subordinated positions carry roughly 1.7x-1.9x the LGD of senior claims, so moving up the capital structure of the same borrower is a direct RWA reduction lever.

R-CRE32.9-simple-approach-unavailable.title: The simple collateral approach is not available under IRB
R-CRE32.9-simple-approach-unavailable.statement: The simple approach to collateral available in the standardised approach cannot be used by banks applying the IRB approach.
R-CRE32.9-simple-approach-unavailable.quote: The simple approach to collateral presented in the standardised approach is not available to banks applying the IRB approach.

applies_to.note: IRB banks must use the comprehensive approach / LGD* mechanics of CRE32.10-CRE32.14.

R-CRE32.9-simple-approach-unavailable.portfolio_relevance: Removes the substitution-style collateral shortcut, forcing IRB banks to compute haircut-adjusted LGD*, which typically gives less collateral credit than the simple approach for volatile collateral.

R-CRE32.11-firb-collateral-lgd-table.title: F-IRB LGD and haircut schedule by eligible collateral type
R-CRE32.11-firb-collateral-lgd-table.statement: Under the foundation approach eligible receivables and eligible residential/commercial real estate attract a 20% LGD with a 40% haircut, other eligible physical collateral a 25% LGD with a 40% haircut, eligible financial collateral a 0% LGD, and ineligible collateral a 100% haircut.
R-CRE32.11-firb-collateral-lgd-table.quote: Eligible receivables 20% 40% Eligible residential real 20% 40% estate / commercial real estate Other eligible physical 25% 40% collateral Ineligible collateral Not 100% applicable

applies_to.note: F-IRB parameters; the table is flattened from a source table in the parse.

numeric_values: 20% LGD / 40% haircut (residential or commercial real estate)
R-CRE32.11-firb-collateral-lgd-table.portfolio_relevance: Quantifies exactly how much capital relief each collateral type buys, so securing an SME or corporate book with real estate or receivables cuts LGD from 40-45% to 20% subject to a 40% haircut.

R-CRE32.16-corporate-lgd-floors.title: LGD parameter floors for corporate exposures under A-IRB
R-CRE32.16-corporate-lgd-floors.statement: Own-estimate LGDs for corporate exposures must not fall below 25% unsecured, or below 0% for financial collateral, 10% for receivables, 10% for commercial or residential real estate and 15% for other physical collateral; the floors do not apply to sovereign exposures.
R-CRE32.16-corporate-lgd-floors.quote: LGD parameter floors for corporate exposures Unsecured Secured 25% Varying by collateral type: 0% financial 10% receivables 10% commercial or residential real estate 15% other physical

applies_to.note: A-IRB floors introduced by the December 2017 Basel III finalisation; sovereign asset class exempt. Partial security is floored on a weighted-average basis per CRE32.17.

numeric_values: 10% commercial or residential real estate LGD floor
R-CRE32.16-corporate-lgd-floors.portfolio_relevance: Caps the RWA benefit a bank can obtain from optimistic internal LGD modelling on corporate lending, limiting the payoff from collateral-heavy restructuring of a corporate book.

R-CRE32.31-securitised-drawn-balances.title: Capital must still be held on undrawn balances when only drawn revolving balances are securitised
R-CRE32.31-securitised-drawn-balances.statement: Where only the drawn balances of revolving facilities have been securitised, banks must continue to hold required capital against the undrawn balances associated with the securitised exposures.
R-CRE32.31-securitised-drawn-balances.quote: When only the drawn balances of revolving facilities have been securitised, banks must ensure that they continue to hold required capital against the undrawn balances associated with the securitised exposures.

applies_to.note: Anti-arbitrage rule for revolving securitisations; parallel retail-specific version at CRE32.66.

R-CRE32.31-securitised-drawn-balances.portfolio_relevance: Blocks the classic credit-card master-trust arbitrage: selling drawn card receivables into a securitisation does not relieve the bank of capital on the undrawn lines that remain.

R-CRE32.32-ead-ccf-undrawn.title: EAD for undrawn commitments: CCF method or direct A-IRB estimate
R-CRE32.32-ead-ccf-undrawn.statement: In the foundation approach EAD is the committed but undrawn amount multiplied by a credit conversion factor; in the advanced approach EAD for undrawn commitments may be either the undrawn amount times a CCF or derived from direct estimates of total facility EAD.
R-CRE32.32-ead-ccf-undrawn.quote: In the foundation approach, EAD is calculated as the committed but undrawn amount multiplied by a credit conversion factor (CCF). In the advanced approach, EAD for undrawn commitments may be calculated as the committed but undrawn amount multiplied by a CCF or derived from direct estimates of total facility EAD.

applies_to.note: Two permitted EAD construction methods under A-IRB; the CCF route is the only one available under F-IRB.

R-CRE32.32-ead-ccf-undrawn.portfolio_relevance: Defines the mechanical link between undrawn credit-card lines and EAD, which is the quantity a card issuer can most directly influence through line-management policy.

R-CRE32.32-commitment-definition.title: IRB definition of commitment is identical to the standardised approach
R-CRE32.32-commitment-definition.statement: In both the foundation and advanced approaches, the definition of commitments is the same as in the standardised approach as set out in CRE20.94.
R-CRE32.32-commitment-definition.quote: In both the foundation approach and advanced approaches, the definition of commitments is the same as in the standardised approach, as set out in CRE20. 94.

applies_to.note: Cross-reference: the operative definition lives at CRE20.94 in the standardised approach chapter, so it binds standardised-approach banks identically.

R-CRE32.32-commitment-definition.portfolio_relevance: Ensures the 'undrawn commitment' base used for card EAD is the same object under both approaches, so a standardised-to-IRB comparison of a card book can use a single reported undrawn-lines figure.

R-CRE32.33-firb-ccfs-equal-sa.title: F-IRB uses the standardised approach CCFs
R-CRE32.33-firb-ccfs-equal-sa.statement: The types of instruments and the credit conversion factors applied to them under the foundation IRB approach are the same as those in the standardised approach as set out in CRE20.94 to CRE20.101.
R-CRE32.33-firb-ccfs-equal-sa.quote: The types of instruments and the CCFs applied to them under the F-IRB approach are the same as those in the standardised approach, as set out in CRE20.94 to CRE20.101.

applies_to.note: F-IRB inherits the SA CCF grid wholesale; only A-IRB banks may model CCFs.

R-CRE32.33-firb-ccfs-equal-sa.portfolio_relevance: A foundation-approach bank gains no EAD modelling benefit on undrawn card lines: its off-balance-sheet conversion is fixed at the standardised grid, so only line size, not observed drawdown behaviour, moves EAD.

R-CRE32.34-ccf-base-lower-of.title: CCF is applied to the lower of unused committed line and any constrained availability
R-CRE32.34-ccf-base-lower-of.statement: The amount to which the CCF is applied is the lower of the unused committed credit line and the value reflecting any constraint on the facility's availability, such as a ceiling on lending tied to the borrower's reported cash flow, provided the bank has sufficient line monitoring and management procedures to support the constraint.
R-CRE32.34-ccf-base-lower-of.quote: The amount to which the CCF is applied is the lower of the value of the unused committed credit line, and the value that reflects any possible constraining of the availability of the facility, such as the existence of a ceiling on the potential lending amount which is related to a borrower’s reported cash flow.

applies_to.note: Recognition of the lower constrained amount is conditional on demonstrable line-monitoring and management procedures.

R-CRE32.34-ccf-base-lower-of.portfolio_relevance: Rewards active line management: a bank that operationally constrains available credit below the nominal limit and can evidence the controls applies the CCF to the smaller base, reducing EAD on undrawn card and revolving lines.

R-CRE32.36-own-ead-undrawn-revolving.title: A-IRB own EAD estimates permitted for undrawn revolving commitments below 100% CCF
R-CRE32.36-own-ead-undrawn-revolving.statement: Banks meeting the minimum requirements for own EAD estimates may use internal EAD estimates for undrawn revolving commitments to extend credit, purchase assets or issue credit substitutes, provided the exposure is not subject to a 100% CCF in the foundation approach; standardised CCFs must be used for all other off-balance-sheet items and where the minimum requirements are not met.
R-CRE32.36-own-ead-undrawn-revolving.quote: to use their own internal estimates of EAD for undrawn revolving commitments to extend credit, purchase assets or issue credit substitutes provided the exposure is not subject to a CCF of 100% in the foundation approach

applies_to.note: Conditional on meeting the CRE36.89-CRE36.98 minimum requirements for own EAD estimates; exposures already at a 100% CCF are excluded.

R-CRE32.36-own-ead-undrawn-revolving.portfolio_relevance: This is the provision that lets a card issuer estimate its own CCF from observed drawdown-to-default history on undrawn card lines, converting good line-management data directly into lower EAD and RWA.

R-CRE32.36-ead-floor-50pct.title: EAD floor: on-balance-sheet amount plus 50% of off-balance-sheet at the SA CCF
R-CRE32.36-ead-floor-50pct.statement: For every non-sovereign exposure, the EAD used as input into the risk-weight formula and expected loss calculation is floored at the sum of the on-balance-sheet amount and 50% of the off-balance-sheet exposure computed with the applicable standardised approach CCF.
R-CRE32.36-ead-floor-50pct.quote: The EAD for each exposure that is not in the sovereign asset class that is used as input into the risk weight formula and the calculation of expected loss is subject to a floor that is the sum of: (i) the on balance sheet amount; and (ii) 50% of the off balance sheet exposure using the applicable CCF in the standardised approach.

applies_to.note: Basel III finalisation floor; sovereign asset class exempt. Parallel retail version at CRE32.64.

numeric_values: 50% of off-balance-sheet exposure at the SA CCF
EAD floor = on-BS amount + 50% x SA CCF x off-BS amount
R-CRE32.36-ead-floor-50pct.portfolio_relevance: Caps how far a bank can model down EAD on undrawn commitments: no matter how low its observed drawdown rate, EAD cannot fall below on-balance-sheet plus half the standardised conversion, bounding the capital benefit of a large undrawn card line book.

R-CRE32.36-revolving-facility-definition.title: Definition of a revolving loan facility
R-CRE32.36-revolving-facility-definition.statement: A revolving loan facility lets the borrower decide how often and at what intervals to withdraw, and allows drawdown, repayment and re-drawing; facilities permitting prepayment and subsequent redraw of prepayments count as revolving.
R-CRE32.36-revolving-facility-definition.quote: A revolving loan facility is one that lets a borrower obtain a loan where the borrower has the flexibility to decide how often to withdraw from the loan and at what time intervals. A revolving facility allows the borrower to drawdown, repay and re-draw loans advanced to it. Facilities that allow prepayments and subsequent redraws of those prepayments are considered as revolving.

applies_to.note: Footnote definition determining which facilities qualify for own EAD estimates.

R-CRE32.36-revolving-facility-definition.portfolio_relevance: Determines the boundary of the own-EAD-estimate privilege: home-equity lines and prepay-and-redraw products count as revolving and so may use modelled CCFs, while term instalment loans may not.

R-CRE32.44-firb-maturity-25y.title: F-IRB effective maturity fixed at 2.5 years (6 months for repo-style)
R-CRE32.44-firb-maturity-25y.statement: Effective maturity is 2.5 years for exposures under the foundation approach, except repo-style transactions where it is 6 months (M = 0.5); national supervisors may require all banks in their jurisdiction to measure M facility by facility.
R-CRE32.44-firb-maturity-25y.quote: Effective maturity (M) will be 2.5 years for exposures to which the bank applies the foundation approach, except for repo-style transactions where the effective maturity is 6 months (ie M=0.5).

applies_to.note: National discretion for supervisors to require explicit M measurement by all banks in the jurisdiction.

R-CRE32.44-firb-maturity-25y.portfolio_relevance: Under F-IRB, shortening the contractual tenor of corporate lending yields no capital benefit because M is fixed at 2.5 years regardless of actual maturity.

R-CRE32.45-fixed-maturity-500m.title: National discretion to fix M at 2.5 years for small domestic corporates
R-CRE32.45-fixed-maturity-500m.statement: Banks using any element of A-IRB must measure effective maturity for each facility, but national supervisors may allow M to be fixed at 2.5 years for facilities to domestic corporate borrowers whose consolidated group sales and total assets are both less than EUR 500 million, applied to all A-IRB banks in that country rather than bank by bank.
R-CRE32.45-fixed-maturity-500m.quote: national supervisors may allow the effective maturity to be fixed at 2.5 years (the “fixed maturity treatment”) for facilities to certain smaller domestic corporate borrowers if the reported sales (ie turnover) as well as total assets for the consolidated group of which the firm is a part of are less than €500 million.

applies_to.note: National discretion, applied jurisdiction-wide if adopted; borrower must be a domestic consolidated group with both sales and total assets under EUR 500m.

numeric_values: €500 million sales and total assets threshold
R-CRE32.45-fixed-maturity-500m.portfolio_relevance: Where the discretion is exercised, long-dated lending to small domestic corporates escapes the maturity adjustment, making term SME lending relatively cheaper in capital than the same tenor to a larger borrower.

R-CRE32.46-maturity-floor-cap.title: Effective maturity floored at one year and capped at five years
R-CRE32.46-maturity-floor-cap.statement: Except for the short-term exposures identified in CRE32.51, effective maturity is subject to a floor of one year and a cap of five years.
R-CRE32.46-maturity-floor-cap.quote: Except as noted in CRE32.51, the effective maturity (M) is subject to a floor of one year and a cap of 5 years.

applies_to.note: Carve-outs for collateralised capital-market and repo-style transactions (CRE32.51), short-term trade finance (CRE32.52) and nationally defined short-term exposures (CRE32.53).

R-CRE32.46-maturity-floor-cap.portfolio_relevance: Bounds the maturity lever: shortening corporate facilities below one year or lengthening beyond five years produces no further change in the maturity adjustment.

R-CRE32.50-revolving-maturity.title: Maturity of revolving exposures uses maximum contractual termination date
R-CRE32.50-revolving-maturity.statement: For revolving exposures effective maturity must be determined using the maximum contractual termination date of the facility, not the repayment date of the current drawing.
R-CRE32.50-revolving-maturity.quote: For revolving exposures, effective maturity must be determined using the maximum contractual termination date of the facility. Banks must not use the repayment date of the current drawing.

applies_to.note: Relevant to corporate revolvers; retail risk-weight functions have no maturity adjustment (CRE31.13).

R-CRE32.50-revolving-maturity.portfolio_relevance: Prevents a bank from claiming a short effective maturity on a corporate revolver by pointing to the current drawing's repayment date, so committed revolving corporate lines carry full-tenor maturity capital.

R-CRE32.57-sovereign-guarantee-floor-exe.title: Risk-component floors do not apply to sovereign-guaranteed retail exposures
R-CRE32.57-sovereign-guarantee-floor-exe.statement: Where a retail exposure is guaranteed by a sovereign, the floors that apply to the risk components do not apply to the guaranteed portion; the ungaranteed portion remains subject to the relevant floors.
R-CRE32.57-sovereign-guarantee-floor-exe.quote: In the case of an exposure that is guaranteed by a sovereign, the floors that apply to the risk components do not apply to that part of the exposure covered by the sovereign guarantee

applies_to.note: Applies to the retail risk components section (CRE32.57-CRE32.67); an identically worded carve-out appears at CRE32.2 for corporate, sovereign and bank exposures.

R-CRE32.57-sovereign-guarantee-floor-exe.portfolio_relevance: Government-guaranteed retail lending (eg guaranteed student or SBA-type loans) escapes the PD and LGD floors on the guaranteed slice, making guaranteed origination a distinct capital-efficient retail segment.

R-CRE32.58-retail-pd-floors.title: Retail PD floors: 0.1% for QRRE revolvers, 0.05% for all other retail
R-CRE32.58-retail-pd-floors.statement: The PD for retail exposures is the greater of the one-year PD of the assigned internal borrower grade and a floor of 0.1% for QRRE revolvers or 0.05% for all other retail exposures.
R-CRE32.58-retail-pd-floors.quote: Additionally, the PD for retail exposures is the greater of: (i) the one-year PD associated with the internal borrower grade to which the pool of retail exposures is assigned; and (ii) 0.1% for qualifying revolving retail exposure (QRRE) revolvers (see CRE30.24 for the definition of QRRE revolvers) and 0.05% for all other exposures.

applies_to.note: Note the asymmetry: QRRE revolvers carry double the PD floor (0.1%) of QRRE transactors and all other retail (0.05%).

numeric_values: 0.05% PD floor for all other retail exposures
R-CRE32.58-retail-pd-floors.portfolio_relevance: Directly computable: the QRRE revolver PD floor is twice the transactor/other-retail floor, so shifting a card book toward transactors lowers both the modelled PD and the binding floor, compounding the RWA saving on high-quality accounts.

R-CRE32.58-retail-lgd-floors.title: Retail LGD floors: 50% QRRE, 5% mortgages, 30% other retail unsecured
R-CRE32.58-retail-lgd-floors.statement: Own-estimate retail LGDs must not fall below 50% for QRRE (both transactors and revolvers), 5% for secured residential mortgages, and 30% for unsecured other retail, with secured other retail floored at 0% for financial collateral, 10% for receivables, 10% for commercial or residential real estate and 15% for other physical collateral.
R-CRE32.58-retail-lgd-floors.quote: LGD parameter floors for retail exposures Type of exposure Unsecured Secured Mortgages Not applicable 5% QRRE (transactors and 50% Not applicable revolvers) Other retail 30% Varying by collateral type: 0% financial 10% receivables 10% commercial or residential real estate 15% other physical

applies_to.note: Introduced by the December 2017 Basel III finalisation. The QRRE floor applies to transactors and revolvers alike; QRRE is unsecured by definition (CRE30.24), so no secured QRRE floor exists.

numeric_values: 50% LGD floor for QRRE (transactors and revolvers)
5% LGD floor for secured residential mortgages
30% LGD floor for unsecured other retail
10% commercial or residential real estate floor
R-CRE32.58-retail-lgd-floors.portfolio_relevance: The 50% QRRE LGD floor is the single hardest numeric constraint on credit-card capital modelling: no matter how strong a card issuer's observed recoveries, half of every defaulted card balance is assumed lost, so RWA per dollar of card EAD has a hard lower bound.

R-CRE32.59-mortgage-lgd-floor-5pct.title: Residential mortgage LGD floor fixed at 5% irrespective of collateral level
R-CRE32.59-mortgage-lgd-floor-5pct.statement: The LGD floor for residential mortgages is fixed at 5% regardless of the level of collateral provided by the property; other retail partially secured LGD floors are computed under the CRE32.17 weighted-average formula.
R-CRE32.59-mortgage-lgd-floor-5pct.quote: The LGD floor for residential mortgages is fixed at 5%, irrespective of the level of collateral provided by the property.

applies_to.note: Unlike other retail, the mortgage floor does not vary with LTV or collateral coverage.

R-CRE32.59-mortgage-lgd-floor-5pct.portfolio_relevance: Makes mortgages by far the least LGD-constrained retail product (5% vs 50% for QRRE and 30% for unsecured other retail), so on LGD grounds alone a shift from cards to mortgages is strongly capital-favoured.

R-CRE32.60-retail-guarantee-recognition.title: Retail guarantees and credit derivatives recognised via PD or LGD adjustment
R-CRE32.60-retail-guarantee-recognition.statement: Banks may reflect the risk-reducing effects of guarantees and credit derivatives, either on an individual obligation or a pool of exposures, by adjusting either the PD or the LGD estimate, applied consistently for a given guarantee or credit derivative type.
R-CRE32.60-retail-guarantee-recognition.quote: Banks may reflect the risk-reducing effects of guarantees and credit derivatives, either in support of an individual obligation or a pool of exposures, through an adjustment of either the PD or LGD estimate, subject to the minimum requirements in CRE36.100 to CRE36.111.

applies_to.note: Conditional on CRE36.100-CRE36.111 minimum requirements; consistency of method required per guarantee type.

R-CRE32.60-retail-guarantee-recognition.portfolio_relevance: Permits pool-level credit protection on a retail portfolio to be recognised, giving a card issuer a route to reduce modelled PD or LGD by buying protection rather than shrinking balances.

R-CRE32.61-no-double-default-retail.title: No double-default recognition; adjusted risk weight floored at the protection provider's
R-CRE32.61-no-double-default-retail.statement: Banks must not include the effect of double default in guarantee or credit derivative adjustments, and the adjusted risk weight must not be less than that of a comparable direct exposure to the protection provider; banks may decline to recognise protection that would raise the capital requirement.
R-CRE32.61-no-double-default-retail.quote: banks must not include the effect of double default in such adjustments. The adjusted risk weight must not be less than that of a comparable direct exposure to the protection provider.

applies_to.note: Substitution-style floor; mirrors CRE32.22 for corporate exposures.

R-CRE32.61-no-double-default-retail.portfolio_relevance: Caps the benefit of hedging a retail portfolio: buying protection can never take the risk weight below what a direct exposure to the guarantor would attract, so protection from a weak counterparty is worthless for capital.

R-CRE32.62-retail-ead-gross.title: Retail EAD measured gross of provisions and write-offs, with a floor
R-CRE32.62-retail-ead-gross.statement: Both on- and off-balance-sheet retail exposures are measured gross of specific provisions or partial write-offs, and EAD on drawn amounts must be at least the sum of the capital reduction from a full write-off plus any specific provisions and partial write-offs; any positive difference is a discount.
R-CRE32.62-retail-ead-gross.quote: Both on- and off-balance sheet retail exposures are measured gross of specific provisions or partial write-offs. The EAD on drawn amounts should not be less than the sum of: (i) the amount by which a bank’s regulatory capital would be reduced if the exposure were written-off fully; and (ii) any specific provisions and partial write-offs.

applies_to.note: Discounts may only enter total eligible provisions under the limited CRE35.4 circumstances.

R-CRE32.62-retail-ead-gross.portfolio_relevance: Provisioning against a delinquent card book does not reduce its EAD, so a bank cannot cut card RWA simply by taking specific provisions — the relief comes through the EL-provision comparison in CRE35 instead.

R-CRE32.63-retail-own-ead-mandatory.title: Retail banks must use own EAD estimates for undrawn revolving commitments
R-CRE32.63-retail-own-ead-mandatory.statement: Banks must use their own estimates of EAD for undrawn revolving commitments to extend credit, purchase assets or issue credit substitutes, provided the exposure is not subject to a 100% CCF in the standardised approach and the CRE36.89-CRE36.99 minimum requirements are satisfied; foundation CCFs must be used for all other off-balance-sheet items and where the minimum requirements are not met.
R-CRE32.63-retail-own-ead-mandatory.quote: Banks must use their own estimates of EAD for undrawn revolving commitments to extend credit, purchase assets or issue credit substitutes provided the exposure is not subject to a CCF of 100% in the standardised approach (see CRE20.92) and the minimum requirements in CRE36.89 to CRE36.99 are satisfied.

applies_to.note: Mandatory (not optional) for retail, unlike the permissive corporate version at CRE32.36; conditional on meeting CRE36.89-CRE36.99. Exposures at 100% SA CCF are excluded.

R-CRE32.63-retail-own-ead-mandatory.portfolio_relevance: An IRB card issuer is obliged to estimate its own CCF on undrawn card lines from drawdown history, so the observed relationship between limit utilisation and default directly determines the EAD it must carry on the undrawn book.

R-CRE32.63-retail-commitment-definition.title: Retail definition of commitment identical to the standardised approach
R-CRE32.63-retail-commitment-definition.statement: For retail IRB purposes the definition of commitment is the same as in the standardised approach as set out in CRE20.94.
R-CRE32.63-retail-commitment-definition.quote: The definition of commitment is the same as in the standardised approach, as set out in CRE20.94.

applies_to.note: Definitional cross-reference to CRE20.94; identical object under both approaches, which matters for any SA/IRB comparison of a card book's undrawn lines.

R-CRE32.63-retail-commitment-definition.portfolio_relevance: Fixes what counts as a committed undrawn card line, which is the denominator of any CCF estimate and the quantity a bank shrinks when it cuts unused credit limits.

R-CRE32.64-retail-ead-floor-50pct.title: Retail EAD floor: on-balance-sheet plus 50% of off-balance-sheet at SA CCF
R-CRE32.64-retail-ead-floor-50pct.statement: Where a bank uses own EAD estimates, retail EAD used as input into the risk-weight formula and expected loss calculation is floored at the on-balance-sheet amount plus 50% of the off-balance-sheet exposure computed with the applicable standardised approach CCF.
R-CRE32.64-retail-ead-floor-50pct.quote: Regarding own estimates of EAD, the EAD for each exposure that is used as input into the risk weight formula and the calculation of expected loss is subject to a floor that is the sum of: (i) the on balance sheet amount; and (ii) 50% of the off balance sheet exposure using the applicable CCF in the standardised approach.

applies_to.note: Basel III finalisation floor applying specifically to own-estimate retail EAD.

numeric_values: 50% of off-balance-sheet exposure at the SA CCF
EAD floor = on-BS amount + 50% x SA CCF x off-BS amount
R-CRE32.64-retail-ead-floor-50pct.portfolio_relevance: The most directly computable constraint on a credit-card book's modelled EAD: however low the issuer's observed CCF, undrawn card lines must contribute at least half the standardised conversion, so a large undrawn-limit book carries irreducible capital.

R-CRE32.65-credit-card-drawdown-ccf.title: Credit cards: additional drawings before default must be captured in EAD or LGD
R-CRE32.65-credit-card-drawdown-ccf.statement: For retail exposures with uncertain future drawdown such as credit cards, banks must take account of their history and expectation of additional drawings prior to default in their overall calibration of loss estimates; if conversion factors for undrawn lines are not reflected in EAD estimates, the likelihood of additional drawings must be reflected in LGD estimates, and vice versa.
R-CRE32.65-credit-card-drawdown-ccf.quote: For retail exposures with uncertain future drawdown such as credit cards, banks must take into account their history and/or expectation of additional drawings prior to default in their overall calibration of loss estimates. In particular, where a bank does not reflect conversion factors for undrawn lines in its EAD estimates, it must reflect in its LGD estimates the likelihood of additional drawings prior to default. Conversely, if the bank does not incorporate the possibility of additional drawings in its LGD estimates, it must do so in its EAD estimates.

applies_to.note: Names credit cards explicitly. A no-double-count / no-gap requirement: the drawdown effect must appear in exactly one of EAD or LGD, and the bank must have the drawdown history to calibrate it.

R-CRE32.65-credit-card-drawdown-ccf.portfolio_relevance: The core credit-card modelling obligation: pre-default line utilisation must be capitalised somewhere. A card issuer whose delinquent customers draw down remaining limits cannot escape the capital cost by choosing which parameter to book it in.

R-CRE32.66-securitised-revolving-retail-.title: Undrawn balances remain capitalised when drawn revolving retail balances are securitised
R-CRE32.66-securitised-revolving-retail-.statement: Where only the drawn balances of revolving retail facilities have been securitised, banks must continue to hold required capital against the associated undrawn balances using the IRB approach to credit risk for commitments.
R-CRE32.66-securitised-revolving-retail-.quote: When only the drawn balances of revolving retail facilities have been securitised, banks must ensure that they continue to hold required capital against the undrawn balances associated with the securitised exposures using the IRB approach to credit risk for commitments.

applies_to.note: Retail-specific counterpart to CRE32.31; directly aimed at credit-card master trusts.

R-CRE32.66-securitised-revolving-retail-.portfolio_relevance: Closes the main credit-card securitisation arbitrage: a card issuer that sells receivables into a trust still capitalises every undrawn line behind those accounts, so securitisation shrinks on-balance-sheet assets far more than it shrinks RWA.

R-CRE32.67-retail-fx-ir-commitments.title: No internal credit-equivalent amounts for FX and interest-rate commitments in retail
R-CRE32.67-retail-fx-ir-commitments.statement: Where foreign exchange and interest rate commitments exist within a bank's retail IRB portfolio, banks are not permitted to provide internal assessments of credit equivalent amounts; the standardised approach rules apply instead.
R-CRE32.67-retail-fx-ir-commitments.quote: To the extent that foreign exchange and interest rate commitments exist within a bank’s retail portfolio for IRB purposes, banks are not permitted to provide their internal assessments of credit equivalent amounts.

applies_to.note: Carve-out from the general retail own-estimates regime; standardised rules continue to apply.

R-CRE32.67-retail-fx-ir-commitments.portfolio_relevance: Removes modelling discretion from embedded FX and rate commitments in a retail book, so products bundling such features carry standardised conversion amounts and are relatively capital-expensive.

R-CRE34.2-qrre-fallback-other-retail.title: Purchased receivables failing QRRE standards fall to other retail; hybrid pools take the worst function
R-CRE34.2-qrre-fallback-other-retail.statement: Banks that cannot comply with the QRRE standards should use the other retail risk-weight function for purchased receivables, and for hybrid pools whose exposures cannot be separated by type, the risk-weight function producing the highest capital requirement applies.
R-CRE34.2-qrre-fallback-other-retail.quote: For example, if banks cannot comply with the standards for qualifying revolving retail exposures (defined in CRE30.24), they should use the risk-weight function for other retail exposures. For hybrid pools containing mixtures of exposure types, if the purchasing bank cannot separate the exposures by type, the risk-weight function producing the highest capital requirements for the exposure types in the receivable pool applies.

applies_to.note: Explicit worst-of rule for unsegregable hybrid pools.

R-CRE34.2-qrre-fallback-other-retail.portfolio_relevance: Buying a mixed consumer receivable pool without the data to split it by product type forces the most punitive risk-weight function on the entire pool, so data quality at acquisition is worth real capital.

R-CRE34.3-purchased-retail-standalone.title: Purchased retail receivables: retail quantification standards on a stand-alone basis
R-CRE34.3-purchased-retail-standalone.statement: For purchased retail receivables a bank must meet the retail risk quantification standards but may use external and internal reference data to estimate PD and LGD, and the estimates must be calculated on a stand-alone basis without any assumption of recourse or guarantees from the seller or other parties.
R-CRE34.3-purchased-retail-standalone.quote: For purchased retail receivables, a bank must meet the risk quantification standards for retail exposures but can utilise external and internal reference data to estimate the probabilities of default (PDs) and losses-given-default (LGDs). The estimates for PD and LGD (or expected loss, EL) must be calculated for the receivables on a stand-alone basis

applies_to.note: External reference data explicitly permitted, which lowers the data barrier for a purchaser relative to an originator.

R-CRE34.3-purchased-retail-standalone.portfolio_relevance: Lets a bank acquire a card or consumer receivable pool and model it from external data, but seller recourse and guarantees cannot be assumed in the parameters, so the headline purchase protections do not reduce RWA at this stage.

R-CRE34.5-firb-purchased-lgd-40.title: 40% LGD for senior purchased corporate receivables under F-IRB top-down
R-CRE34.5-firb-purchased-lgd-40.statement: Where the purchasing bank cannot reliably decompose expected loss into PD and LGD but can demonstrate the exposures are exclusively senior claims to corporate borrowers, an LGD of 40% may be used and PD derived by dividing EL by that LGD.
R-CRE34.5-firb-purchased-lgd-40.quote: (a) If the bank can demonstrate that the exposures are exclusively senior claims to corporate borrowers: (i) An LGD of 40% can be used.

applies_to.note: Requires supervisory permission for the top-down approach (CRE34.4) plus demonstrable seniority.

R-CRE34.5-firb-purchased-lgd-40.portfolio_relevance: Demonstrating exclusive seniority in a purchased corporate receivable pool cuts assumed LGD from 100% to 40%, a 60-point capital swing on the same pool.

R-CRE34.5-revolving-purchase-facility-ea.title: 40% conversion of undrawn purchase commitments in a revolving purchase facility
R-CRE34.5-revolving-purchase-facility-ea.statement: EAD for a revolving purchase facility is the current amount of receivables purchased plus 40% of any undrawn purchase commitments, minus the dilution capital charge.
R-CRE34.5-revolving-purchase-facility-ea.quote: EAD for a revolving purchase facility is the sum of the current amount of receivables purchased plus 40% of any undrawn purchase commitments minus K.

applies_to.note: Same 40% factor applies under both the foundation (CRE34.5) and advanced (CRE34.6) top-down treatments.

numeric_values: EAD = receivables purchased + 40% x undrawn purchase commitments - K_Dilution
R-CRE34.5-revolving-purchase-facility-ea.portfolio_relevance: Fixes a computable capital cost on committed but unused capacity in a revolving receivable-purchase programme, so committing to buy more future card or trade receivables consumes capital before any asset is acquired.

R-CRE34.5-non-senior-lgd-100.title: 100% LGD where seniority of purchased corporate receivables cannot be demonstrated
R-CRE34.5-non-senior-lgd-100.statement: If the purchasing bank cannot demonstrate the exposures are exclusively senior claims to corporate borrowers, PD is set to the bank's estimate of EL and LGD is set at 100%.
R-CRE34.5-non-senior-lgd-100.quote: (b) If the bank cannot demonstrate that the exposures are exclusively senior claims to corporate borrowers: (i) PD is the bank’s estimate of EL. (ii) LGD will be 100%.

applies_to.note: Punitive default parameterisation where seniority evidence is absent.

numeric_values: PD set equal to estimated EL
R-CRE34.5-non-senior-lgd-100.portfolio_relevance: Creates a sharp cliff in purchased-receivable capital: absent documented seniority, LGD jumps from 40% to 100%, so due-diligence quality on an acquired pool is directly capital-relevant.

R-CRE34.6-airb-no-internal-ead-undrawn-p.title: A-IRB banks may not use internal EAD estimates for undrawn purchase commitments
R-CRE34.6-airb-no-internal-ead-undrawn-p.statement: Banks using the advanced IRB approach for purchased receivables are not permitted to use their internal EAD estimates for undrawn purchase commitments and must apply the prescribed 40% factor.
R-CRE34.6-airb-no-internal-ead-undrawn-p.quote: thus, banks using the advanced Dilution IRB approach will not be permitted to use their internal EAD estimates for undrawn purchase commitments

applies_to.note: Explicit carve-out from the general A-IRB own-EAD privilege; the parse interleaves the 'Dilution' subscript from the source formula.

numeric_values: prescribed 40% factor replaces internal EAD estimates
R-CRE34.6-airb-no-internal-ead-undrawn-p.portfolio_relevance: Removes modelling discretion on purchase-programme capacity, so a bank cannot argue down the capital cost of an undrawn forward-flow commitment on the basis of its own utilisation history.

R-CRE34.8-dilution-risk-pd-lgd.title: Dilution risk parameterised as PD equal to estimated EL and LGD of 100%
R-CRE34.8-dilution-risk-pd-lgd.statement: For calculating risk weights for dilution risk, the corporate risk-weight function must be used with PD set equal to the estimated one-year EL for dilution and LGD set at 100%, unless the bank can demonstrate dilution risk is immaterial.
R-CRE34.8-dilution-risk-pd-lgd.quote: (a) The PD must be set equal to the estimated EL. (b) The LGD must be set at 100%.

applies_to.note: Applies to both corporate and retail purchased receivables; can be waived only if the bank demonstrates dilution risk is immaterial. A one-year maturity may be allowed if dilution is monitored and resolved within a year.

numeric_values: PD = estimated one-year EL for dilution
R-CRE34.8-dilution-risk-pd-lgd.portfolio_relevance: Adds a separate 100%-LGD capital charge on top of default risk for any purchased receivable pool subject to returns, disputes or promotional credits — directly relevant to acquired card and merchant receivable books.

R-CRE35.2-total-el-amount.title: Total EL amount is the sum of EL x EAD across IRB exposures
R-CRE35.2-total-el-amount.statement: A bank must sum the EL amount, defined as EL multiplied by exposure at default, across all exposures to which the IRB approach is applied, excluding securitisation exposures, to obtain a total EL amount.
R-CRE35.2-total-el-amount.quote: A bank must sum the EL amount (defined as EL multiplied by exposure at default) associated with its exposures to which the IRB approach is applied (excluding the EL amount associated with securitisation exposures) to obtain a total EL amount.

applies_to.note: Securitisation exposures are excluded from the EL aggregation.

R-CRE35.2-total-el-amount.portfolio_relevance: Defines the aggregate EL figure that a bank's loan-loss allowance is compared against; a high-EL card book raises the provisioning bar the bank must clear to avoid a CET1 deduction.

R-CRE35.3-el-pd-times-lgd.title: EL calculated as PD x LGD for non-defaulted exposures
R-CRE35.3-el-pd-times-lgd.statement: Banks must calculate expected loss as PD multiplied by LGD for corporate, sovereign, bank and retail exposures not in default; for defaulted exposures the best estimate of expected loss (advanced) or supervisory LGD (foundation) is used.
R-CRE35.3-el-pd-times-lgd.quote: Banks must calculate EL as probability of default (PD) x loss-given-default (LGD) for corporate, sovereign, bank, and retail exposures not in default.

applies_to.note: Securitisation exposures do not contribute to the EL amount.

R-CRE35.3-el-pd-times-lgd.portfolio_relevance: Makes EL for a card book the product of the floored PD (0.1% for revolvers) and the floored LGD (50%), so the CRE32.58 floors set a hard minimum EL of about 5bp of EAD on even the best QRRE revolver pool.

R-CRE35.4-total-eligible-provisions.title: Definition of total eligible provisions
R-CRE35.4-total-eligible-provisions.statement: Total eligible provisions are the sum of all provisions attributed to IRB exposures, including specific provisions, partial write-offs and portfolio-specific or general provisions, plus any discounts on defaulted assets; provisions against securitisation exposures are excluded.
R-CRE35.4-total-eligible-provisions.quote: Total eligible provisions are defined as the sum of all provisions (eg specific provisions, partial write-offs, portfolio-specific general provisions such as country risk provisions or general provisions) that are attributed to exposures treated under the IRB approach.

applies_to.note: Securitisation-related general and specific provisions must be excluded.

R-CRE35.4-total-eligible-provisions.portfolio_relevance: Sets the measurable provision aggregate a bank compares against EL; under CECL, US card issuers typically hold large lifetime allowances, which can turn into Tier 2 capital under CRE35.9.

R-CRE35.6-general-provision-pro-rata.title: General provisions attributed pro rata to standardised and IRB RWA
R-CRE35.6-general-provision-pro-rata.statement: Banks should attribute total general provisions on a pro rata basis according to the proportion of credit risk-weighted assets subject to the standardised and IRB approaches, though provisions booked within an entity using exclusively one approach may be attributed to that approach.
R-CRE35.6-general-provision-pro-rata.quote: Banks should generally attribute total general provisions on a pro rata basis according to the proportion of credit risk-weighted assets subject to the standardised and IRB approaches.

applies_to.note: Relevant only to banks running both approaches; CRE35.7 permits an internal allocation method subject to prior supervisory approval and national discretion.

R-CRE35.6-general-provision-pro-rata.portfolio_relevance: Prevents a partially-IRB bank from steering all of its general allowance to the IRB side to maximise Tier 2 recognition, so the split of provisions follows the split of RWA.

R-CRE35.8-compare-provisions-el.title: IRB banks must compare total eligible provisions against total EL
R-CRE35.8-compare-provisions-el.statement: Banks using the IRB approach must compare the total amount of total eligible provisions with the total EL amount calculated under the IRB approach, with the resulting shortfall or excess treated under CAP10.19 and CAP30.13.
R-CRE35.8-compare-provisions-el.quote: banks using the IRB approach must compare the total amount of total eligible provisions (as defined in paragraph CRE35.4) with the total EL amount as calculated within the IRB approach

applies_to.note: Interacts with the capital definition standard: shortfalls are deducted from CET1 under CAP30.13.

R-CRE35.8-compare-provisions-el.portfolio_relevance: Creates a direct link from card-portfolio EL to CET1: if modelled EL on a high-PD card book exceeds the allowance, the difference is deducted from common equity, compounding the RWA cost of the same balances.

R-CRE35.9-excess-provisions-tier2.title: Excess provisions may be included in Tier 2 subject to supervisory assessment
R-CRE35.9-excess-provisions-tier2.statement: Where the calculated EL amount is lower than total eligible provisions, supervisors must consider whether EL fully reflects market conditions before allowing the difference to be included in Tier 2 capital, and the same assessment applies where specific provisions exceed EL on defaulted assets before that excess is used to offset EL on non-defaulted assets.
R-CRE35.9-excess-provisions-tier2.quote: Where the calculated EL amount is lower than the total eligible provisions of the bank, its supervisors must consider whether the EL fully reflects the conditions in the market in which it operates before allowing the difference to be included in Tier 2 capital.

applies_to.note: Supervisory-judgement gate on Tier 2 recognition of provision excess; the Basel cap of 0.6% of credit RWA sits in CAP10, outside this domain.

R-CRE35.9-excess-provisions-tier2.portfolio_relevance: Gives partial capital credit for over-provisioning a card book, but only at supervisory discretion, so a bank cannot count on converting conservative CECL allowances into Tier 2 when planning card growth.

R-CRE21.1-ecai-recognition.title: Only ratings from recognised ECAIs may be used for regulatory purposes
R-CRE21.1-ecai-recognition.statement: In jurisdictions permitting external ratings, a bank may use a credit assessment for regulatory capital only if it comes from a credit rating agency that the national supervisor has recognised as an eligible ECAI for that exposure type.
R-CRE21.1-ecai-recognition.quote: In jurisdictions that allow the use of external ratings for regulatory purposes, only credit assessments from credit rating agencies recognised as external credit assessment institutions (ECAIs) will be allowed. National supervisors are responsible for determining on a continuous basis whether an ECAI meets the criteria listed in CRE21.2 and recognition should only be provided in respect of ECAI ratings for types of exposure where all criteria and conditions are met.

applies_to.note: Gated on jurisdictional choice: the US does not permit use of external ratings for regulatory capital (Dodd-Frank s.939A), so the whole external-ratings branch of CRE20/CRE22 is inoperative for North American banks.

R-CRE21.1-ecai-recognition.portfolio_relevance: Determines whether a small North American bank can obtain lower risk weights by holding rated corporate/bank paper at all; under the US ban on external ratings this lever is closed, pushing the bank toward the unrated/Grade-A tables instead.

R-CRE21.2-ecai-eight-criteria.title: ECAI eligibility: eight criteria, with a minimum one-year rating-methodology track record
R-CRE21.2-ecai-eight-criteria.statement: An ECAI must satisfy eight criteria (objectivity, independence, international access/transparency, disclosure, resources, credibility, no abuse of unsolicited ratings, cooperation with the supervisor); the rating methodology for each market segment must have been established for at least one year and preferably three years before recognition.
R-CRE21.2-ecai-eight-criteria.quote: An ECAI must satisfy each of the following eight criteria. (1) Objectivity: The methodology for assigning external ratings must be rigorous, systematic, and subject to some form of validation based on historical experience. Moreover, external ratings must be subject to ongoing review and responsive to changes in financial condition. Before being recognised by supervisors, a rating methodology for each market segment, including rigorous backtesting, must have been established for at least one year and preferably three years.

applies_to.note: Binds supervisors rather than banks directly; relevant to a bank only through the list of recognised ECAIs it may cite.

numeric_values: at least one year methodology track record
R-CRE21.2-ecai-eight-criteria.portfolio_relevance: Constrains the set of rating sources a bank may lean on when it tries to shift its portfolio into externally rated (lower-risk-weight) assets.

R-CRE21.4-ecai-revenue-concentration-dis.title: ECAI must disclose single-client revenue concentration of 10% or more
R-CRE21.4-ecai-revenue-concentration-dis.statement: An ECAI should disclose in the relevant credit rating report or elsewhere if it receives 10% or more of its annual revenue from a single client.
R-CRE21.4-ecai-revenue-concentration-dis.quote: An ECAI should disclose in the relevant credit rating report or elsewhere, as appropriate, if it receives 10% or more of its annual revenue from a single client (eg a rated entity, obligor, originator, lead underwriter, arranger, or subscriber, or any of their affiliates).

applies_to.note: Obligation falls on the ECAI, not the bank; included because it is a hard numeric threshold in the ratings-eligibility chain.

numeric_values: 10% or more of annual revenue from a single client
R-CRE21.4-ecai-revenue-concentration-dis.portfolio_relevance: Indirect: a rating agency losing recognition on conflict-of-interest grounds would strip the risk-weight benefit from every exposure the bank had risk-weighted on that agency's ratings.

R-CRE21.5-rating-to-rw-mapping.title: Supervisors map ECAI rating categories to standardised risk weights
R-CRE21.5-rating-to-rw-mapping.statement: National supervisors, not banks, decide which ECAI rating categories correspond to which standardised risk weights; the mapping must be objective and cover the full spectrum of risk weights.
R-CRE21.5-rating-to-rw-mapping.quote: Supervisors will be responsible for assigning eligible ECAIs’ ratings to the risk weights available under the standardised risk weighting framework, ie deciding which rating categories correspond to which risk weights. The mapping process should be objective and should result in a risk weight assignment consistent with that of the level of credit risk reflected in the tables above. It should cover the full spectrum of risk weights.

applies_to.note: National-discretion gate: the rating-to-risk-weight map is jurisdiction-specific, so cross-border comparisons of the same rating are not automatic.
