R-CRE21.5-rating-to-rw-mapping.portfolio_relevance: The bank cannot choose its own rating-to-risk-weight mapping, so a portfolio shift into rated assets delivers only the RWA relief the local supervisor's published mapping allows.

R-CRE21.8-no-cherry-picking.title: ECAI ratings must be used consistently across all recognised exposure types
R-CRE21.8-no-cherry-picking.statement: A bank must apply its chosen ECAIs and their ratings consistently for all exposure types for which those ECAIs are recognised, for both risk-weighting and risk management, and may not cherry-pick ratings between ECAIs or arbitrarily change which ECAIs it uses.
R-CRE21.8-no-cherry-picking.quote: Banks must use the chosen ECAIs and their ratings consistently for all types of exposure where they have been recognised by their supervisor as an eligible ECAI, for both risk-weighting and risk management purposes. Banks are not allowed to “cherry-pick” the ratings provided by different ECAIs and to arbitrarily change the use of ECAIs.

applies_to.note: Applies wherever external ratings are permitted; inoperative in jurisdictions that ban external ratings.

R-CRE21.8-no-cherry-picking.portfolio_relevance: Blocks the cheapest RWA-reduction trick — shopping for the most favourable agency per exposure — so any RWA relief from ratings must be portfolio-wide and consistent.

R-CRE21.9-single-rating.title: Single available rating determines the risk weight
R-CRE21.9-single-rating.statement: Where there is only one rating from a bank's chosen ECAI for a particular exposure, that rating determines the risk weight.
R-CRE21.9-single-rating.quote: If there is only one rating by an ECAI chosen by a bank for a particular exposure, that rating should be used to determine the risk weight of the exposure.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.9-single-rating.portfolio_relevance: Baseline rule for computing the risk weight of any rated security a bank buys as part of a shift out of loans into securities.

R-CRE21.10-two-ratings-higher-rw.title: Two divergent ratings: the higher risk weight applies
R-CRE21.10-two-ratings-higher-rw.statement: If two chosen ECAIs' ratings map to different risk weights, the higher risk weight must be applied.
R-CRE21.10-two-ratings-higher-rw.quote: If there are two ratings by ECAIs chosen by a bank that map into different risk weights, the higher risk weight will be applied.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.10-two-ratings-higher-rw.portfolio_relevance: Makes dual-rated assets weakly worse for RWA than the best available rating suggests, so a bank optimising RWA cannot count on the more favourable agency.

R-CRE21.11-three-or-more-ratings.title: Three or more ratings: second-lowest risk weight applies
R-CRE21.11-three-or-more-ratings.statement: Where three or more ratings give different risk weights, the bank takes the two ratings corresponding to the lowest risk weights; if they agree, that risk weight applies, otherwise the higher of the two applies.
R-CRE21.11-three-or-more-ratings.quote: If there are three or more ratings with different risk weights, the two ratings that correspond to the lowest risk weights should be referred to. If these give rise to the same risk weight, that risk weight should be applied. If different, the higher risk weight should be applied.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.11-three-or-more-ratings.portfolio_relevance: Deterministic tie-break rule that makes multi-rated exposures machine-computable: effectively the second-best rating drives RWA.

R-CRE21.12-issue-specific-rating.title: Issue-specific rating governs an investment in that issue
R-CRE21.12-issue-specific-rating.statement: Where a bank invests in a particular issue that carries an issue-specific rating, the risk weight of that exposure is based on that rating.
R-CRE21.12-issue-specific-rating.quote: Where a bank invests in a particular issue that has an issue-specific rating, the risk weight of the exposure will be based on this rating.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.12-issue-specific-rating.portfolio_relevance: Anchors the risk weight of securities held in the investment portfolio; drives whether a shift from loans into rated securities lowers RWA.

R-CRE21.12-pari-passu-condition.title: A high-quality issue rating may be borrowed only by pari passu or senior exposures
R-CRE21.12-pari-passu-condition.statement: A high-quality rating on a borrower's specific debt may be applied to a different, unrated exposure to the same borrower only if that exposure ranks in all respects pari passu with or senior to the rated exposure; otherwise the exposure is treated as unrated.
R-CRE21.12-pari-passu-condition.quote: a high-quality credit rating (one which maps into a risk weight lower than that which applies to an unrated exposure) on that specific debt may only be applied to the bank’s unrated exposure if this exposure ranks in all respects pari passu or senior to the exposure with a rating. If not, the external rating cannot be used and the unassessed exposure will receive the risk weight for unrated exposures.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.12-pari-passu-condition.portfolio_relevance: Prevents a bank from re-labelling subordinated or structurally junior loans as low-risk by pointing at a rated senior bond of the same borrower.

R-CRE21.12-issuer-rating-contamination.title: Issuer ratings cover senior unsecured only; a low-quality rating contaminates junior exposures
R-CRE21.12-issuer-rating-contamination.statement: An issuer rating applies only to senior unsecured exposures; other unassessed exposures of a highly rated issuer are treated as unrated, and where either the issuer or a single issue carries a low-quality rating, unassessed exposures ranking pari passu with or subordinated to it take the low-quality risk weight.
R-CRE21.12-issuer-rating-contamination.quote: In circumstances where the borrower has an issuer rating, this rating typically applies to senior unsecured exposures to that issuer. Consequently, only senior exposures to that issuer will benefit from a high-quality issuer rating. Other unassessed exposures of a highly rated issuer will be treated as unrated. If either the issuer or a single issue has a low-quality rating (mapping into a risk weight equal to or higher than that which applies to unrated exposures), an unassessed exposure to the same counterparty that ranks pari passu or is subordinated to either the senior unsecured issuer rating or the exposure with a low-quality rating will be assigned the same risk weight as is applicable to the low-quality rating.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.12-issuer-rating-contamination.portfolio_relevance: Asymmetric rule: good ratings do not travel down the capital structure but bad ones do, so deteriorating credits raise RWA across a whole counterparty relationship at once.

R-CRE21.12-limited-class-rating.title: Ratings limited to a class of liabilities may only be used within that class
R-CRE21.12-limited-class-rating.statement: A high-quality issuer rating that applies only to a limited class of liabilities (such as a deposit rating or a counterparty risk rating) may be used only for exposures falling within that class.
R-CRE21.12-limited-class-rating.quote: In circumstances where the issuer has a specific high-quality rating (one which maps into a lower risk weight) that only applies to a limited class of liabilities (such as a deposit rating or a counterparty risk rating), this may only be used in respect of exposures that fall within that class.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.12-limited-class-rating.portfolio_relevance: Restricts the reach of favourable deposit/counterparty ratings, limiting RWA relief on correspondent-bank and interbank placements to the exact instrument class rated.

R-CRE21.13-rating-covers-full-exposure.title: The relied-upon rating must reflect the entire credit exposure including interest
R-CRE21.13-rating-covers-full-exposure.statement: Whether an issuer or issue rating is relied on, the rating must take into account and reflect the entire amount of credit risk the bank has, covering all payments owed including both principal and interest.
R-CRE21.13-rating-covers-full-exposure.quote: Whether the bank intends to rely on an issuer- or an issue-specific rating, the rating must take into account and reflect the entire amount of credit risk exposure the bank has with regard to all payments owed to it.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only; also the hook that bans principal-only ratings inside the CRM framework (CRE22.5).

R-CRE21.13-rating-covers-full-exposure.portfolio_relevance: Disqualifies principal-only ratings, which matters for interest-heavy revolving assets where the interest strip is a large share of expected cash flow.

R-CRE21.14-no-double-count-credit-enhanc.title: No CRM recognition where the credit enhancement is already in the issue rating
R-CRE21.14-no-double-count-credit-enhanc.statement: To avoid double-counting credit enhancement, no supervisory recognition of credit risk mitigation techniques may be taken into account if the credit enhancement is already reflected in the issue-specific rating.
R-CRE21.14-no-double-count-credit-enhanc.quote: In order to avoid any double-counting of credit enhancement factors, no supervisory recognition of credit risk mitigation techniques will be taken into account if the credit enhancement is already reflected in the issue specific rating

applies_to.note: Mirrors CRE22.5; binding wherever external ratings are used.

R-CRE21.14-no-double-count-credit-enhanc.portfolio_relevance: Caps the RWA relief obtainable from a guaranteed or wrapped asset: the bank gets the enhanced rating or the CRM substitution, never both.

R-CRE21.15-currency-of-rating.title: Foreign currency ratings for foreign currency exposures; domestic ratings for domestic currency
R-CRE21.15-currency-of-rating.statement: Where an exposure is risk-weighted on the rating of an equivalent exposure to the borrower, foreign currency ratings are used for foreign currency exposures and separate domestic currency ratings may only be used for exposures denominated in domestic currency.
R-CRE21.15-currency-of-rating.quote: Where exposures are risk-weighted based on the rating of an equivalent exposure to that borrower, the general rule is that foreign currency ratings would be used for exposures in foreign currency. Domestic currency ratings, if separate, would only be used to risk-weight exposures denominated in the domestic currency.

applies_to.note: Footnote allows national supervisors to accept the domestic currency rating where an MDB with preferred creditor status has guaranteed convertibility and transfer risk.

R-CRE21.15-currency-of-rating.portfolio_relevance: Penalises cross-currency lending: the same borrower attracts a higher risk weight when the exposure is in foreign currency, discouraging FX-denominated portfolio growth.

R-CRE21.16-short-term-rating-table.title: Risk weights for specific short-term ratings: 20/50/100/150%
R-CRE21.16-short-term-rating-table.statement: Exposures arising from specific short-term rated facilities receive risk weights of 20% (A-1/P-1), 50% (A-2/P-2), 100% (A-3/P-3) and 150% (others).
R-CRE21.16-short-term-rating-table.quote: The table below provides a framework for banks’ exposures to specific short-term facilities, such as a particular issuance of commercial paper: Risk weight table for specific short-term ratings Table 15 External rating A-1/P-1 A-2/P-2 A-3/P-3 Others Risk weight 20% 50% 100% 150%

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only; 'others' covers all non-prime and B or C ratings.

R-CRE21.16-short-term-rating-table.portfolio_relevance: Directly computable risk weights for short-term liquidity investments (commercial paper, interbank paper) that a small bank may hold instead of extending credit-card lines.

R-CRE21.16-short-term-rating-scope.title: Short-term ratings are issue-specific and cannot be generalised
R-CRE21.16-short-term-rating-scope.statement: Short-term ratings are deemed issue-specific, may only be used for the rated facility, can never support a risk weight for an unrated long-term exposure, and may only be used for short-term exposures to banks and corporates.
R-CRE21.16-short-term-rating-scope.quote: For risk-weighting purposes, short-term ratings are deemed to be issue-specific. They can only be used to derive risk weights for exposures arising from the rated facility. They cannot be generalised to other short-term exposures, except under the conditions of CRE21.18. In no event can a short-term rating be used to support a risk weight for an unrated long-term exposure. Short-term ratings may only be used for short-term exposures against banks and corporates.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.16-short-term-rating-scope.portfolio_relevance: Blocks the use of a cheap short-term rating to reduce the risk weight of a long-dated exposure, so lengthening asset maturity cannot borrow short-term rating benefits.

R-CRE21.17-st50-unrated-floor-100.title: A 50% short-term rated facility floors unrated short-term exposures at 100%
R-CRE21.17-st50-unrated-floor-100.statement: If a short-term rated facility of an issuer attracts a 50% risk weight, the bank's unrated short-term exposures to that issuer cannot attract a risk weight lower than 100%.
R-CRE21.17-st50-unrated-floor-100.quote: If a short-term rated facility attracts a 50% risk-weight, unrated short-term exposures cannot attract a risk weight lower than 100%.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.17-st50-unrated-floor-100.portfolio_relevance: Contagion floor: a single mid-grade short-term rating raises the capital cost of every other unrated short-term line to the same name, discouraging concentrated short-term exposure.

R-CRE21.17-st150-contagion.title: A 150% short-term rating forces 150% on all unrated exposures to that issuer
R-CRE21.17-st150-contagion.statement: If an issuer has a short-term facility rated so as to warrant a 150% risk weight, all unrated exposures to that issuer, long-term or short-term, must also receive 150% unless the bank applies recognised credit risk mitigation.
R-CRE21.17-st150-contagion.quote: If an issuer has a short- term facility with an external rating that warrants a risk weight of 150%, all unrated exposures, whether long-term or short-term, should also receive a 150% risk weight, unless the bank uses recognised credit risk mitigation techniques for such exposures.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only; explicitly names CRM as the escape route.

R-CRE21.17-st150-contagion.portfolio_relevance: Names CRM explicitly as the only way to escape a 150% contagion weight, making collateral or guarantees the sole RWA lever on a distressed counterparty short of exiting the exposure.

R-CRE21.18-3-month-preferential.title: General short-term preferential treatment applies to bank exposures up to three months original maturity
R-CRE21.18-3-month-preferential.statement: The general preferential treatment for short-term exposures applies to all exposures to banks of up to three months original maturity where there is no specific short-term exposure rating.
R-CRE21.18-3-month-preferential.quote: The general preferential treatment for short-term exposures applies to all exposures to banks of up to three months original maturity when there is no specific short-term exposure rating.

applies_to.note: Interacts with the CRE20.19 short-term bank exposure table.

R-CRE21.18-3-month-preferential.portfolio_relevance: A hard maturity threshold: rolling interbank placements at or under three months attracts a materially lower risk weight than longer placements, a cheap balance-sheet restructuring lever.

R-CRE21.18-worse-st-rating-blocks-prefer.title: An unfavourable specific short-term rating removes the interbank preferential treatment
R-CRE21.18-worse-st-rating-blocks-prefer.statement: Where a specific short-term rating for a short-term bank exposure maps into a less favourable (higher) risk weight, the general short-term preferential treatment cannot be used and all unrated short-term exposures must take the risk weight implied by that specific short-term rating.
R-CRE21.18-worse-st-rating-blocks-prefer.quote: When a specific short-term rating for a short term exposure to a bank maps into a less favourable (higher) risk weight, the general short-term preferential treatment for interbank exposures cannot be used. All unrated short-term exposures should receive the same risk weighting as that implied by the specific short-term rating.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.18-worse-st-rating-blocks-prefer.portfolio_relevance: Removes the maturity-shortening lever precisely when a counterparty deteriorates, so short-dated interbank exposure stops being a cheap substitute for credit exposure.

R-CRE21.20-no-group-rating-transfer.title: Group affiliate ratings cannot be used to risk-weight other group entities
R-CRE21.20-no-group-rating-transfer.statement: An external rating of one entity within a corporate group cannot be used to risk-weight other entities within the same group.
R-CRE21.20-no-group-rating-transfer.quote: External ratings for one entity within a corporate group cannot be used to risk- weight other entities within the same group.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictions permitting external ratings only.

R-CRE21.20-no-group-rating-transfer.portfolio_relevance: Prevents a bank lending to unrated SME or corporate subsidiaries from claiming the parent's rating, keeping such lending at the unrated risk weight.

R-CRE21.21-unsolicited-ratings.title: Solicited ratings by default; unsolicited ratings only with supervisory satisfaction
R-CRE21.21-unsolicited-ratings.statement: Banks should use solicited ratings from eligible ECAIs; national supervisors may permit the use of unsolicited ratings on the same basis only if satisfied that their quality is not inferior to solicited ratings.
R-CRE21.21-unsolicited-ratings.quote: As a general rule, banks should use solicited ratings from eligible ECAIs. National supervisors may allow banks to use unsolicited ratings in the same way as solicited ratings if they are satisfied that the credit assessments of unsolicited ratings are not inferior in quality to the general quality of solicited ratings.

applies_to.note: Explicit national-discretion gate on unsolicited ratings.

R-CRE21.21-unsolicited-ratings.portfolio_relevance: Narrows the universe of ratings a bank can use for RWA relief; unsolicited-rated paper may not deliver the expected risk weight unless the local supervisor has opened the door.

R-CRE22.2-crm-scope-banking-book-sa.title: Scope: the CRM framework applies to banking book exposures risk-weighted under the standardised approach
R-CRE22.2-crm-scope-banking-book-sa.statement: The credit risk mitigation framework in CRE22 applies to banking book exposures that are risk-weighted under the standardised approach.
R-CRE22.2-crm-scope-banking-book-sa.quote: The framework set out in this chapter is applicable to banking book exposures that are risk-weighted under the standardised approach.

applies_to.note: Small North American banks are almost universally on the standardised approach, so this chapter is the operative CRM regime for them.

R-CRE22.2-crm-scope-banking-book-sa.portfolio_relevance: Establishes that every CRM lever in this chapter is available to a small SA bank's banking-book credit portfolio, including its credit card book.

R-CRE22.3-crm-no-worse.title: CRM may never increase the capital requirement
R-CRE22.3-crm-no-worse.statement: No transaction using credit risk mitigation techniques may receive a higher capital requirement than an otherwise identical transaction without such techniques.
R-CRE22.3-crm-no-worse.quote: No transaction in which credit risk mitigation (CRM) techniques are used shall receive a higher capital requirement than an otherwise identical transaction where such techniques are not used.

applies_to.note: General principle binding on all SA banks.

R-CRE22.3-crm-no-worse.portfolio_relevance: Guarantees a one-sided payoff to taking collateral or guarantees: RWA can only fall or stay flat, so CRM is always weakly RWA-accretive for the bank.

R-CRE22.4-disclosure-precondition.title: CRM capital relief is conditional on meeting the Pillar 3 disclosure standard
R-CRE22.4-disclosure-precondition.statement: A bank must fulfil the requirements of the disclosure standard (DIS40) in order to obtain capital relief in respect of any CRM technique.
R-CRE22.4-disclosure-precondition.quote: The requirements of the disclosure standard (DIS40) must be fulfilled for banks to obtain capital relief in respect of any CRM techniques.

applies_to.note: For small banks Pillar 3 scope is often proportionate under national rules, but the conditionality of CRM relief on disclosure is unconditional in the Basel text.

R-CRE22.4-disclosure-precondition.portfolio_relevance: Makes CRM-driven RWA reduction contingent on a reporting capability, an operational cost a small bank must incur before it can bank the capital saving.

R-CRE22.5-no-double-counting.title: CRM effects must not be double-counted
R-CRE22.5-no-double-counting.statement: The effects of CRM must not be double-counted; no additional supervisory recognition of CRM is granted on exposures whose risk weight already reflects that CRM, and principal-only ratings are not allowed within the CRM framework.
R-CRE22.5-no-double-counting.quote: The effects of CRM must not be double-counted. Therefore, no additional supervisory recognition of CRM for regulatory capital purposes will be granted on exposures for which the risk weight already reflects that CRM.

applies_to.note: Paired with CRE21.14.

R-CRE22.5-no-double-counting.portfolio_relevance: Caps the total RWA benefit obtainable from a single mitigant, preventing stacked relief on wrapped or already-enhanced exposures.

R-CRE22.6-residual-risk-controls.title: Banks must control the residual risks created by CRM or face additional capital charges
R-CRE22.6-residual-risk-controls.statement: Because CRM techniques create residual legal, operational, liquidity and market risks, banks must employ robust procedures covering strategy, underlying credit, valuation, policies, systems, roll-off risk and CRM concentration risk; where these are not adequately controlled supervisors may impose additional capital charges.
R-CRE22.6-residual-risk-controls.quote: Therefore, banks must employ robust procedures and processes to control these risks, including strategy; consideration of the underlying credit; valuation; policies and procedures; systems; control of roll-off risks; and management of concentration risk arising from the bank’s use of CRM techniques and its interaction with the bank’s overall credit risk profile. Where these risks are not adequately controlled, supervisors may impose additional capital charges or take other supervisory actions as outlined in the supervisory review process standard (SRP).

applies_to.note: Pillar 2 overlay: supervisory judgement, so the penalty is not formulaic.

R-CRE22.6-residual-risk-controls.portfolio_relevance: Imposes a qualitative brake on aggressive CRM-driven RWA optimisation: heavy reliance on one collateral type or one protection provider can be clawed back through a Pillar 2 add-on.

R-CRE22.7-wrong-way-correlation.title: CRM must not be materially positively correlated with the counterparty's credit quality
R-CRE22.7-wrong-way-correlation.statement: For CRM to provide protection the counterparty's credit quality must not have a material positive correlation with the mitigant or resulting residual risks; securities issued by the counterparty or a counterparty-related entity are therefore ineligible as collateral.
R-CRE22.7-wrong-way-correlation.quote: In order for CRM techniques to provide protection, the credit quality of the counterparty must not have a material positive correlation with the employed CRM technique or with the resulting residual risks (as defined in CRE22.6). For example, securities issued by the counterparty (or by any counterparty-related entity) provide little protection as collateral and are thus ineligible.

applies_to.note: Hard eligibility test, testable from the identity of the collateral issuer.

R-CRE22.7-wrong-way-correlation.portfolio_relevance: Rules out self-referencing collateral structures, so a bank cannot manufacture RWA relief from securities of the borrower or its affiliates.

R-CRE22.8-subdivide-multiple-crm.title: Exposures covered by multiple CRM techniques or maturities must be subdivided
R-CRE22.8-subdivide-multiple-crm.statement: Where multiple CRM techniques cover a single exposure, the bank must subdivide the exposure into the portion covered by each technique and compute RWA for each portion separately; protection from a single provider with differing maturities must likewise be subdivided.
R-CRE22.8-subdivide-multiple-crm.quote: In the case where a bank has multiple CRM techniques covering a single exposure (eg a bank has both collateral and a guarantee partially covering an exposure), the bank must subdivide the exposure into portions covered by each type of CRM technique (eg portion covered by collateral, portion covered by guarantee) and the risk-weighted assets of each portion must be calculated separately.

applies_to.note: Operationally demanding for small banks with loan-level rather than tranche-level systems.

R-CRE22.8-subdivide-multiple-crm.portfolio_relevance: Forces exposure-level tranching in the RWA calculation, so the modelled benefit of layered mitigants must be computed piecewise rather than as a blended haircut.

R-CRE22.9-legal-enforceability.title: CRM documentation must be binding and legally enforceable in all relevant jurisdictions
R-CRE22.9-legal-enforceability.statement: For any capital relief from CRM, all documentation used in collateralised transactions, on-balance sheet netting agreements, guarantees and credit derivatives must be binding on all parties and legally enforceable in all relevant jurisdictions, supported by sufficient legal review.
R-CRE22.9-legal-enforceability.quote: In order for banks to obtain capital relief for any use of CRM techniques, all documentation used in collateralised transactions, on-balance sheet netting agreements, guarantees and credit derivatives must be binding on all parties and legally enforceable in all relevant jurisdictions.

applies_to.note: Requires documented legal review; a real fixed cost for a small bank contemplating a first CRM programme.

R-CRE22.9-legal-enforceability.portfolio_relevance: Gating condition on every RWA reduction in this chapter: without enforceable documentation the modelled CRM benefit is zero.

R-CRE22.10-maturity-mismatch-definition.title: Definition of a maturity mismatch
R-CRE22.10-maturity-mismatch-definition.statement: For RWA purposes a maturity mismatch occurs when the residual maturity of the credit protection arrangement is less than that of the underlying exposure.
R-CRE22.10-maturity-mismatch-definition.quote: For the purposes of calculating risk-weighted assets, a maturity mismatch occurs when the residual maturity of a credit protection arrangement (eg hedge) is less than that of the underlying exposure.

applies_to.note: Definition consumed by CRE22.12, CRE22.13, CRE22.47 and CRE22.72.

R-CRE22.10-maturity-mismatch-definition.portfolio_relevance: Defines the trigger for maturity-mismatch haircutting, which is the binding constraint when short-dated protection is bought against long-dated loan books.

R-CRE22.11-no-mismatch-simple-approach.title: Maturity mismatches are not allowed under the simple approach
R-CRE22.11-no-mismatch-simple-approach.statement: In the case of financial collateral, maturity mismatches are not permitted under the simple approach.
R-CRE22.11-no-mismatch-simple-approach.quote: In the case of financial collateral, maturity mismatches are not allowed under the simple approach

applies_to.note: Simple approach only; a small bank choosing the simple approach loses all mismatched protection entirely rather than partially.

R-CRE22.11-no-mismatch-simple-approach.portfolio_relevance: Makes the simple approach an all-or-nothing regime: collateral shorter than the loan gives zero relief, pushing banks that fund long assets with short collateral toward the comprehensive approach.

R-CRE22.12-mismatch-1y-3m-thresholds.title: Mismatched protection recognised only if original maturity at least one year and residual at least three months
R-CRE22.12-mismatch-1y-3m-thresholds.statement: Under approaches other than the simple approach, credit protection with a maturity mismatch may only be recognised if the original maturity of the arrangement is at least one year and its residual maturity is at least three months; recognition is then partial per CRE22.13.
R-CRE22.12-mismatch-1y-3m-thresholds.quote: Under the other approaches, when there is a maturity mismatch the credit protection arrangement may only be recognised if the original maturity of the arrangement is greater than or equal to one year, and its residual maturity is greater than or equal to three months.

applies_to.note: Applies under the comprehensive approach and to guarantees/credit derivatives.

R-CRE22.12-mismatch-1y-3m-thresholds.portfolio_relevance: Two hard time thresholds: protection rolling into its final quarter stops counting, so RWA jumps mechanically as hedges approach the three-month residual cliff.

R-CRE22.13-mismatch-adjustment-formula.title: Maturity mismatch adjustment with a five-year cap on exposure maturity
R-CRE22.13-mismatch-adjustment-formula.statement: Where recognised protection has a maturity mismatch, its value is scaled by a formula in which t is the lesser of T and the protection's residual maturity in years, and T is the lesser of five years and the exposure's residual maturity in years.
R-CRE22.13-mismatch-adjustment-formula.quote: P = credit protection amount (eg collateral amount, guarantee amount) adjusted for any haircuts (3) t = min {T, residual maturity of the credit protection arrangement expressed in years} (4) T = min {five years, residual maturity of the exposure expressed in years}

applies_to.note: Applies under all approaches other than the simple approach.

numeric_values: t = min{T, residual maturity of protection}
R-CRE22.13-mismatch-adjustment-formula.portfolio_relevance: Directly computable pro-rating of protection value: the five-year cap means long-dated mortgages get no worse mismatch penalty than five-year assets, favouring long-asset/short-hedge structures.

R-CRE22.14-conservative-maturity.title: Maturities of exposure and hedge must be measured conservatively
R-CRE22.14-conservative-maturity.statement: The effective maturity of the underlying must be the longest possible remaining time before the counterparty is scheduled to perform including any grace period, while for the hedge embedded options that shorten the term must be taken into account so the shortest possible effective maturity is used.
R-CRE22.14-conservative-maturity.quote: The maturity of the underlying exposure and the maturity of the hedge must both be defined conservatively. The effective maturity of the underlying must be gauged as the longest possible remaining time before the counterparty is scheduled to fulfil its obligation, taking into account any applicable grace period. For the hedge, (embedded) options that may reduce the term of the hedge must be taken into account so that the shortest possible effective maturity is used.

applies_to.note: Asymmetric conservatism baked into the maturity-mismatch calculation.

R-CRE22.14-conservative-maturity.portfolio_relevance: Deliberately widens measured mismatches, so callable or step-up-priced protection delivers less RWA relief than its stated tenor implies.

R-CRE22.15-currency-mismatch-allowed.title: Currency mismatches allowed under all approaches; simple approach relies on the 20% floor
R-CRE22.15-currency-mismatch-allowed.statement: Currency mismatches are allowed under all approaches; under the simple approach no specific adjustment is made because a minimum risk weight floor of 20% generally applies, while the comprehensive approach and guarantees/credit derivatives use explicit FX haircuts.
R-CRE22.15-currency-mismatch-allowed.quote: Currency mismatches are allowed under all approaches. Under the simple approach there is no specific treatment for currency mismatches, given that a minimum risk weight of 20% (floor) is generally applied.

applies_to.note: Simple approach carries the 20% floor in lieu of an FX haircut.

R-CRE22.15-currency-mismatch-allowed.portfolio_relevance: Explains why the simple approach's 20% floor is not merely conservative: it substitutes for FX risk, so cross-currency collateral is comparatively cheaper under the simple approach.

R-CRE22.16-collateralised-transaction-de.title: Definition of a collateralised transaction
R-CRE22.16-collateralised-transaction-de.statement: A collateralised transaction is one in which the bank has a credit or potential credit exposure that is hedged in whole or in part by collateral posted by the counterparty or by a third party on the counterparty's behalf.
R-CRE22.16-collateralised-transaction-de.quote: A collateralised transaction is one in which: (1) banks have a credit exposure or a potential credit exposure; and (2) that credit exposure or potential credit exposure is hedged in whole or in part by collateral posted by a counterparty or by a third party on behalf of the counterparty.

applies_to.note: Gateway definition for the whole collateral section.

R-CRE22.16-collateralised-transaction-de.portfolio_relevance: Establishes that third-party-posted collateral counts, widening the set of structures a bank can use to collateralise otherwise unsecured retail or SME lending.

R-CRE22.18-simple-vs-comprehensive.title: Choice between simple approach (20% floor substitution) and comprehensive approach (volatility-adjusted offset)
R-CRE22.18-simple-vs-comprehensive.statement: Banks may choose the simple approach, which substitutes the collateral's risk weight for the counterparty's on the collateralised portion subject generally to a 20% floor, or the comprehensive approach, which reduces the exposure amount by a volatility-adjusted collateral value.
R-CRE22.18-simple-vs-comprehensive.quote: Banks may opt for either: (1) The simple approach, which replaces the risk weight of the counterparty with the risk weight of the collateral for the collateralised portion of the exposure (generally subject to a 20% floor); or (2) The comprehensive approach, which allows a more precise offset of collateral against exposures, by effectively reducing the exposure amount by a volatility-adjusted value ascribed to the collateral.

applies_to.note: Bank-level election; the simple approach is materially less operationally demanding and hence common for small banks.

R-CRE22.18-simple-vs-comprehensive.portfolio_relevance: The single largest structural CRM choice a small bank makes: the simple approach caps collateral benefit at a 20% risk weight, whereas the comprehensive approach can drive the collateralised portion to near zero exposure.

R-CRE22.19-one-approach-only.title: A bank may use either the simple or the comprehensive approach in the banking book, not both
R-CRE22.19-one-approach-only.statement: Banks may operate under either the simple approach or the comprehensive approach, but not both, in the banking book.
R-CRE22.19-one-approach-only.quote: Banks may operate under either, but not both, approaches in the banking book.

applies_to.note: Banking book only; the trading book is governed separately.

R-CRE22.19-one-approach-only.portfolio_relevance: Forces a single portfolio-wide CRM regime, so the RWA benefit of collateral must be optimised globally rather than per exposure.

R-CRE22.21-on-balance-netting-availabili.title: Net credit exposures may be used where enforceable loan/deposit netting exists
R-CRE22.21-on-balance-netting-availabili.statement: Where a bank has legally enforceable netting arrangements for loans and deposits meeting the conditions in CRE22.68 and CRE22.69, it may calculate capital requirements on the basis of net credit exposures.
R-CRE22.21-on-balance-netting-availabili.quote: Where banks have legally enforceable netting arrangements for loans and deposits that meet the conditions in CRE22.68 and CRE22.69 they may calculate capital requirements on the basis of net credit exposures as set out in that paragraph.

applies_to.note: Directly available to a deposit-funded community bank whose borrowers also hold deposits with it.

R-CRE22.21-on-balance-netting-availabili.portfolio_relevance: The most accessible CRM lever for a small retail bank: netting customer deposits against their loan balances reduces EAD without shrinking the loan book.

R-CRE22.23-guarantor-substitution-princi.title: Only lower-risk-weight protection providers reduce capital; uncovered portion keeps counterparty weight
R-CRE22.23-guarantor-substitution-princi.statement: Credit protection reduces capital only when the guarantor or protection provider has a lower risk weight than the counterparty; the protected portion takes the provider's risk weight while the uncovered portion retains the counterparty's.
R-CRE22.23-guarantor-substitution-princi.quote: Only guarantees issued by or protection provided by entities with a lower risk weight than the counterparty lead to reduced capital charges for the guaranteed exposure, since the protected portion of the counterparty exposure is assigned the risk weight of the guarantor or protection provider, whereas the uncovered portion retains the risk weight of the underlying counterparty.

applies_to.note: The substitution principle that underpins guarantee-based RWA relief.

R-CRE22.23-guarantor-substitution-princi.portfolio_relevance: Quantifies the guarantee lever: RWA relief equals the covered amount times the difference between counterparty and guarantor risk weights, and is zero if the guarantor is no better.

R-CRE22.25-collateral-preconditions.title: Collateral standards in CRE22.26 to CRE22.31 must be met before any capital relief
R-CRE22.25-collateral-preconditions.statement: Before capital relief is granted for any form of collateral, the standards in CRE22.26 to CRE22.31 must be met irrespective of whether the simple or comprehensive approach is used.
R-CRE22.25-collateral-preconditions.quote: Before capital relief is granted in respect of any form of collateral, the standards set out below in CRE22.26 to CRE22.31 must be met, irrespective of whether the simple or the comprehensive approach is used.

applies_to.note: Approach-agnostic operational gate.

R-CRE22.25-collateral-preconditions.portfolio_relevance: Sets a fixed operational compliance cost that a bank must pay before collateralisation delivers any RWA benefit at all.

R-CRE22.26-collateral-legal-mechanism.title: The bank must be able to liquidate or take possession of collateral in a timely manner on default
R-CRE22.26-collateral-legal-mechanism.statement: The legal mechanism by which collateral is pledged or transferred must give the bank the right to liquidate or take legal possession in a timely manner on default, insolvency or bankruptcy of the counterparty (and where applicable the custodian), and the bank must take all steps to obtain and maintain an enforceable security interest.
R-CRE22.26-collateral-legal-mechanism.quote: The legal mechanism by which collateral is pledged or transferred must ensure that the bank has the right to liquidate or take legal possession of it, in a timely manner, in the event of the default, insolvency or bankruptcy (or one or more otherwise-defined credit events set out in the transaction documentation) of the counterparty (and, where applicable, of the custodian holding the collateral).

applies_to.note: Requires perfection of security interests (eg UCC filing in the US).

R-CRE22.26-collateral-legal-mechanism.portfolio_relevance: Perfection failures void the RWA relief, so unsecured-in-substance secured lending must be modelled at the unsecured risk weight.

R-CRE22.27-prompt-liquidation-procedures.title: Banks must have procedures for prompt liquidation of collateral
R-CRE22.27-prompt-liquidation-procedures.statement: Banks must have clear and robust procedures for the timely liquidation of collateral, ensuring the legal conditions for declaring default and liquidating are observed and that collateral can be liquidated promptly.
R-CRE22.27-prompt-liquidation-procedures.quote: Banks must have clear and robust procedures for the timely liquidation of collateral to ensure that any legal conditions required for declaring the default of the counterparty and liquidating the collateral are observed, and that collateral can be liquidated promptly.

applies_to.note: Process requirement, not directly observable from public filings.

R-CRE22.27-prompt-liquidation-procedures.portfolio_relevance: An operational precondition that limits how quickly a small bank can scale a newly collateralised portfolio and still claim the capital benefit.

R-CRE22.28-collateral-risk-management-po.title: Collateral risk management policies must cover volatility, concentration, reuse and surrendered rights
R-CRE22.28-collateral-risk-management-po.statement: Banks must devote sufficient resources to the orderly operation of margin agreements and must have collateral risk management policies to control, monitor and report margin-agreement risk, concentration risk to particular collateral types, reuse of collateral including liquidity shortfalls, and the surrender of rights on posted collateral.
R-CRE22.28-collateral-risk-management-po.quote: Banks must ensure that sufficient resources are devoted to the orderly operation of margin agreements with OTC derivative and securities-financing counterparties, as measured by the timeliness and accuracy of its outgoing margin calls and response time to incoming margin calls.

applies_to.note: Framed around OTC derivative and securities-financing counterparties; most small North American banks have negligible margined activity.

R-CRE22.28-collateral-risk-management-po.portfolio_relevance: Adds an infrastructure cost to any strategy of margined collateral-taking, which is why small banks generally rely on cash-on-deposit collateral instead.

R-CRE22.29-custodian-segregation.title: Custodian-held collateral must be segregated from the custodian's own assets
R-CRE22.29-custodian-segregation.statement: Where collateral is held by a custodian, banks must take reasonable steps to ensure the custodian segregates the collateral from its own assets.
R-CRE22.29-custodian-segregation.quote: Where the collateral is held by a custodian, banks must take reasonable steps to ensure that the custodian segregates the collateral from its own assets.

applies_to.note: Relevant wherever securities collateral is held through a third party.

R-CRE22.29-custodian-segregation.portfolio_relevance: Failure of segregation removes eligibility, so third-party-held securities collateral carries an additional operational condition versus cash on deposit at the lending bank.

R-CRE22.30-capital-on-both-sides.title: Capital requirements apply to both sides of a collateralised transaction
R-CRE22.30-capital-on-both-sides.statement: A capital requirement must be applied on both sides of a transaction: both repos and reverse repos, and both sides of securities lending and borrowing, attract explicit capital charges, as does posting securities against derivatives or other borrowings.
R-CRE22.30-capital-on-both-sides.quote: A capital requirement must be applied on both sides of a transaction. For example, both repos and reverse repos will be subject to capital requirements.

applies_to.note: Chiefly relevant to banks with repo and securities-lending books.

R-CRE22.30-capital-on-both-sides.portfolio_relevance: Removes the illusion that collateral-financing transactions are capital-free; funding the loan book through repo carries its own RWA.

R-CRE22.31-agency-repo-guarantee.title: An agent guaranteeing a repo-style transaction must hold capital as principal
R-CRE22.31-agency-repo-guarantee.statement: Where a bank acting as agent arranges a repo-style transaction between a customer and a third party and guarantees the third party's performance, it must calculate capital requirements as if it were itself the principal.
R-CRE22.31-agency-repo-guarantee.quote: Where a bank, acting as an agent, arranges a repo-style transaction (ie repurchase /reverse repurchase and securities lending/borrowing transactions) between a customer and a third party and provides a guarantee to the customer that the third party will perform on its obligations, then the risk to the bank is the same as if the bank had entered into the transaction as a principal. In such circumstances, a bank must calculate capital requirements as if it were itself the principal.

applies_to.note: Agency securities lending is rare among small North American banks.

R-CRE22.31-agency-repo-guarantee.portfolio_relevance: Closes an off-balance-sheet route to fee income without capital, so agency guarantee programmes must be capitalised as if on-balance-sheet.

R-CRE22.32-simple-approach-substitution.title: Simple approach: the collateral's risk weight replaces the counterparty's
R-CRE22.32-simple-approach-substitution.statement: Under the simple approach the risk weight of the counterparty is replaced by the risk weight of the collateral instrument collateralising or partially collateralising the exposure.
R-CRE22.32-simple-approach-substitution.quote: Under the simple approach, the risk weight of the counterparty is replaced by the risk weight of the collateral instrument collateralising or partially collateralising the exposure.

applies_to.note: Simple approach election under CRE22.18/CRE22.19.

R-CRE22.32-simple-approach-substitution.portfolio_relevance: Machine-computable substitution: RWA on the collateralised portion becomes collateral risk weight times covered amount, so pledging cash converts a 75-100% retail weight into a floored 20% (or 0% under CRE22.39).

R-CRE22.33-simple-approach-conditions.title: Simple approach: collateral pledged for life of exposure, revalued at least six-monthly, 20% risk-weight floor
R-CRE22.33-simple-approach-conditions.statement: For collateral to be recognised in the simple approach it must be pledged for at least the life of the exposure and marked to market and revalued with a minimum frequency of six months; the collateralised portion takes the collateral's risk weight subject to a 20% floor except under CRE22.36 to CRE22.39, and the remainder keeps the counterparty's risk weight.
R-CRE22.33-simple-approach-conditions.quote: For collateral to be recognised in the simple approach, it must be pledged for at least the life of the exposure and it must be marked to market and revalued with a minimum frequency of six months. Those portions of exposures collateralised by the market value of recognised collateral receive the risk weight applicable to the collateral instrument. The risk weight on the collateralised portion is subject to a floor of 20% except under the conditions specified in CRE22.36 to CRE22.39. The remainder of the exposure must be assigned the risk weight appropriate to the counterparty.

applies_to.note: Simple approach only; the six-month revaluation frequency aligns naturally with a small bank's semi-annual collateral review cycle.

numeric_values: minimum revaluation frequency of six months
pledged for at least the life of the exposure
R-CRE22.33-simple-approach-conditions.portfolio_relevance: The core simple-approach arithmetic: covered portion at max(20%, collateral RW) and uncovered portion at the counterparty weight, with a six-month revaluation cadence as the operational cost of the relief.

R-CRE22.34-eligible-collateral-rated.title: Eligible financial collateral (simple approach): cash, gold, and debt rated at least BB- (sovereign), BBB- (other) or A-3/P-3 (short-term)
R-CRE22.34-eligible-collateral-rated.statement: Eligible collateral in the simple approach includes cash and comparable instruments on deposit with the lending bank, gold, and (in jurisdictions permitting external ratings) ECAI-rated debt securities rated at least BB- when issued by sovereigns/sovereign-treated PSEs, at least BBB- when issued by other entities including banks and prudentially regulated financial institutions, or at least A-3/P-3 for short-term instruments.
R-CRE22.34-eligible-collateral-rated.quote: The following collateral instruments are eligible for recognition in the simple approach: (1) Cash (as well as certificates of deposit or comparable instruments issued by the lending bank) on deposit with the bank that is incurring the counterparty exposure. (2) Gold. (3) In jurisdictions that allow the use of external ratings for regulatory purposes: (a) Debt securities rated by a recognised external credit assessment institution (ECAI) where these are either: (i) at least BB– when issued by sovereigns or public sector entities (PSEs) that are treated as sovereigns by the national supervisor; or (ii) at least BBB– when issued by other entities (including banks and other prudentially regulated financial institutions); or (iii) at least A-3/P-3 for short-term debt instruments.

applies_to.note: The rated-debt branch is unavailable in jurisdictions banning external ratings; cash on deposit and gold remain eligible everywhere. Footnote extends cash treatment to cash-funded credit-linked notes and to third-party-held cash under an unconditional irrevocable pledge.

R-CRE22.34-eligible-collateral-rated.portfolio_relevance: Defines the whole eligible-collateral universe; for a small deposit-funded bank the operative item is customer cash on deposit, which is the only mitigant it reliably holds against retail and credit-card exposure.

R-CRE22.34-unrated-bank-debt-collateral.title: Unrated bank debt securities eligible as collateral subject to six cumulative conditions
R-CRE22.34-unrated-bank-debt-collateral.statement: Debt securities not rated by a recognised ECAI are eligible collateral only if issued by a bank, listed on a recognised exchange, classified as senior debt, where all rated issues of the same seniority by that bank are rated at least BBB- or A-3/P-3, the bank holding the collateral has no information suggesting a lower rating, and the supervisor is satisfied about market liquidity.
R-CRE22.34-unrated-bank-debt-collateral.quote: Debt securities not rated by a recognised ECAI where these are: (i) issued by a bank; and (ii) listed on a recognised exchange; and (iii) classified as senior debt; and (iv) all rated issues of the same seniority by the issuing bank are rated at least BBB– or A-3/P-3 by a recognised ECAI; and (v) the bank holding the securities as collateral has no information to suggest that the issue justifies a rating below BBB– or A-3/P-3 (as applicable); and (vi) the supervisor is sufficiently confident that the market liquidity of the security is adequate.

applies_to.note: Includes an explicit supervisory-satisfaction gate on market liquidity; unavailable where external ratings are banned.

numeric_values: at least BBB– or A-3/P-3 for same-seniority rated issues
R-CRE22.34-unrated-bank-debt-collateral.portfolio_relevance: Opens a narrow additional collateral class (senior listed bank paper), relevant to a small bank collateralising interbank or corporate exposures.

R-CRE22.34-eligible-collateral-no-rating.title: Eligible collateral where external ratings are banned: sovereign/PSE, Grade A bank, investment-grade and sub-100% securitisation securities
R-CRE22.34-eligible-collateral-no-rating.statement: In jurisdictions that do not allow external ratings, eligible collateral (subject to supervisory satisfaction on market liquidity) comprises debt securities issued by sovereigns or sovereign-treated PSEs, debt securities of banks assigned to Grade A under the SCRA, other debt securities of investment-grade entities as defined in CRE22.76, and securitisation exposures with a risk weight below 100% under the Securitisation Standardised Approach.
R-CRE22.34-eligible-collateral-no-rating.quote: In jurisdictions that do not allow the use of external ratings for regulatory purposes, the following securities will be eligible provided that the supervisor is sufficiently confident that the market liquidity of the security is adequate: (a) Debt securities issued by sovereigns or PSEs that are treated as sovereigns by the national supervisor; (b) Debt securities issued by banks assigned to Grade A under the standardised credit risk assessment approach; (c) Other debt securities issued by “investment grade” entities as defined in CRE22.76, and (d) Securitisation exposures with a risk weight of less than 100% in the Securitisation Standardised Approach set out in CRE41.

applies_to.note: This is the operative eligible-collateral list for US banks, since US law prohibits regulatory reliance on external ratings.

R-CRE22.34-eligible-collateral-no-rating.portfolio_relevance: The list a North American bank actually works from: Treasuries and agency paper plus Grade A bank debt are the realistic collateral it can pledge against exposures, and the sub-100% securitisation test is directly computable.

R-CRE22.34-equities-ucits-collateral.title: Main index equities and qualifying UCITS/mutual funds are eligible collateral
R-CRE22.34-equities-ucits-collateral.statement: Equities including convertible bonds that are included in a main index, and UCITS/mutual funds whose unit price is publicly quoted daily and whose investments are limited to the instruments listed in CRE22.34, are eligible collateral.
R-CRE22.34-equities-ucits-collateral.quote: Equities (including convertible bonds) that are included in a main index. (6) Undertakings for Collective Investments in Transferable Securities (UCITS) and mutual funds where: (a) a price for the units is publicly quoted daily; and (b) the UCITS/mutual fund is limited to investing in the instruments listed in this paragraph.

applies_to.note: Footnote permits derivative use solely to hedge listed instruments without losing eligibility.

R-CRE22.34-equities-ucits-collateral.portfolio_relevance: Allows securities-backed lending against index equities and money-market funds to receive CRM relief, an alternative to unsecured consumer credit for a wealth-oriented small bank.

R-CRE22.35-resecuritisations-ineligible.title: Resecuritisations are not eligible financial collateral
R-CRE22.35-resecuritisations-ineligible.statement: Resecuritisations as defined in the securitisation chapters are not eligible financial collateral.
R-CRE22.35-resecuritisations-ineligible.quote: Resecuritisations as defined in the securitisation chapters (CRE40 to) are CRE45 not eligible financial collateral.

applies_to.note: Absolute prohibition with no national discretion.

R-CRE22.35-resecuritisations-ineligible.portfolio_relevance: Closes the CDO-squared collateral channel outright, so re-tranched credit-card ABS cannot be recycled into RWA relief.

R-CRE22.36-floor-exemption-conditions.title: Eight conditions exempting repo-style transactions from the simple-approach risk-weight floor
R-CRE22.36-floor-exemption-conditions.statement: Repo-style transactions are exempted from the simple-approach risk-weight floor only if both exposure and collateral are cash or a 0%-risk-weighted sovereign/PSE security, are in the same currency, the transaction is overnight or subject to daily mark-to-market and daily remargining, the close-out window is no more than four business days, settlement uses a proven system, standard market documentation is used, immediate termination is contractually specified on default, and the bank has an unfettered right to seize and liquidate the collateral.
R-CRE22.36-floor-exemption-conditions.quote: Repo-style transactions that fulfil all of the following conditions are exempted from the risk-weight floor under the simple approach: (1) Both the exposure and the collateral are cash or a sovereign security or PSE security qualifying for a 0% risk weight under the standardised approach

applies_to.note: Realistically only for banks with an active repo desk; a small community bank rarely qualifies.

R-CRE22.36-floor-exemption-conditions.portfolio_relevance: Defines the only route to sub-20% risk weights on collateralised transactions under the simple approach, tying the relief to same-currency government collateral.

R-CRE22.36-four-business-day-closeout.title: Close-out after failure to remargin must be no more than four business days
R-CRE22.36-four-business-day-closeout.statement: For the floor exemption, the time required between the last mark-to-market before a failure to remargin and the liquidation of the collateral must be considered to be no more than four business days.
R-CRE22.36-four-business-day-closeout.quote: Following a counterparty’s failure to remargin, the time that is required between the last mark-to-market before the failure to remargin and the liquidation of the collateral is considered to be no more than four business days;

applies_to.note: Sub-condition of the CRE22.36 exemption.

numeric_values: no more than four business days
R-CRE22.36-four-business-day-closeout.portfolio_relevance: A hard operational time window: exceed four business days to liquidate and the 20% floor reapplies, raising RWA on the collateralised portion.

R-CRE22.37-core-market-participants.title: Definition of core market participants
R-CRE22.37-core-market-participants.statement: Core market participants may include, at national supervisory discretion, sovereigns, central banks and PSEs; banks and securities firms; other financial companies including insurers eligible for a 20% risk weight; regulated mutual funds subject to capital or leverage requirements; regulated pension funds; and qualifying central counterparties.
R-CRE22.37-core-market-participants.quote: Core market participants may include, at the discretion of the national supervisor, the following entities: (1) Sovereigns, central banks and PSEs; (2) Banks and securities firms; (3) Other financial companies (including insurance companies) eligible for a 20% risk weight in the standardised approach; (4) Regulated mutual funds that are subject to capital or leverage requirements; (5) Regulated pension funds; and (6) Qualifying central counterparties.

applies_to.note: Explicit national-discretion gate on which entity types count.

numeric_values: 20% risk weight eligibility for other financial companies
R-CRE22.37-core-market-participants.portfolio_relevance: Definition consumed by CRE22.38 and CRE22.60; determines which counterparties allow a 0% risk weight or zero haircut on collateralised transactions.

R-CRE22.38-repo-10pct-and-0pct.title: Qualifying repo transactions receive 10% risk weight, or 0% with a core market participant
R-CRE22.38-repo-10pct-and-0pct.statement: Repo transactions fulfilling CRE22.36 receive a 10% risk weight as an exemption to the CRE22.33 floor, and if the counterparty is a core market participant the bank may apply a 0% risk weight.
R-CRE22.38-repo-10pct-and-0pct.quote: Repo transactions that fulfil the requirement in CRE22.36 receive a 10% risk weight, as an exemption to the risk weight floor described in CRE22.33. If the counterparty to the transaction is a core market participant, banks may apply a risk weight of 0% to the transaction.

applies_to.note: Depends on the national supervisor's core-market-participant list; conditional on all eight CRE22.36 conditions.

numeric_values: 0% risk weight for core market participants
R-CRE22.38-repo-10pct-and-0pct.portfolio_relevance: Explicit computable risk weights that make government-collateralised repo the cheapest possible use of a bank's balance sheet, a direct alternative to holding higher-weighted loans.

R-CRE22.39-zero-rw-cash-and-discounted-s.title: 0% risk weight for same-currency cash collateral, or 0%-weighted sovereign/PSE collateral discounted by 20%
R-CRE22.39-zero-rw-cash-and-discounted-s.statement: The 20% floor does not apply and a 0% risk weight may be applied to the collateralised portion where exposure and collateral are in the same currency and either the collateral is cash on deposit under CRE22.34(1), or is 0%-risk-weight sovereign/PSE securities whose market value has been discounted by 20%.
R-CRE22.39-zero-rw-cash-and-discounted-s.quote: The 20% floor for the risk weight on a collateralised transaction does not apply and a 0% risk weight may be applied to the collateralised portion of the exposure where the exposure and the collateral are denominated in the same currency, and either: (1) the collateral is cash on deposit as defined in CRE22.34 (1); or (2) the collateral is in the form of sovereign/PSE securities eligible for a 0% risk weight, and its market value has been discounted by 20%.

applies_to.note: Highly relevant to small banks: cash-secured lending against a same-currency deposit at the lending bank gets a 0% risk weight with no repo machinery required.

numeric_values: 20% discount to market value of sovereign/PSE collateral
R-CRE22.39-zero-rw-cash-and-discounted-s.portfolio_relevance: The most powerful and most accessible RWA lever for a small retail bank: fully cash-secured consumer or SME lending drops from a 75-100% weight to 0% without shrinking the loan book at all.

R-CRE22.40-comprehensive-haircut-require.title: Comprehensive approach: supervisory haircuts must be applied to both exposure and collateral
R-CRE22.40-comprehensive-haircut-require.statement: Under the comprehensive approach banks must calculate an adjusted exposure by applying the applicable supervisory haircuts to both the exposure amount and the value of collateral received, to reflect possible future market-driven fluctuations in either.
R-CRE22.40-comprehensive-haircut-require.quote: In the comprehensive approach, when taking collateral, banks must calculate their adjusted exposure to a counterparty in order to take account of the risk mitigating effect of that collateral. Banks must use the applicable supervisory haircuts to adjust both the amount of the exposure to the counterparty and the value of any collateral received in support of that counterparty to take account of possible future fluctuations in the value of either, as occasioned by market movements.

applies_to.note: Comprehensive approach election; footnote permits the IMM for counterparty credit risk with supervisory approval.

R-CRE22.40-comprehensive-haircut-require.portfolio_relevance: Establishes the two-sided haircut mechanism: collateral value is written down and exposure written up, so over-collateralisation is required to achieve full offset.

R-CRE22.41-holding-period-definition.title: Definition of the holding period underlying supervisory haircuts
R-CRE22.41-holding-period-definition.statement: The size of haircuts depends on the prescribed holding period, defined as the period over which exposure or collateral values are assumed to move before the bank can close out the transaction; the supervisory prescribed minimum holding period is the basis for the standard supervisory haircuts.
R-CRE22.41-holding-period-definition.quote: The size of the haircuts that banks must use depends on the prescribed holding period for the transaction. For the purposes of CRE22, the holding period is the period of time over which exposure or collateral values are assumed to move before the bank can close out the transaction. The supervisory prescribed minimum holding period is used as the basis for the calculation of the standard supervisory haircuts.

applies_to.note: Definition consumed by CRE22.42, CRE22.49, CRE22.57 and CRE22.59.

R-CRE22.41-holding-period-definition.portfolio_relevance: The parameter that scales every haircut; shortening the close-out assumption is the main way to increase measured collateral value.

R-CRE22.42-5-and-20-day-holding-periods.title: Holding periods of 5 business days (remargined repo-style) and 20 business days (secured lending)
R-CRE22.42-5-and-20-day-holding-periods.statement: Haircuts depend on instrument type, transaction type, residual maturity and remargining/mark-to-market frequency: repo-style transactions with daily mark-to-market and daily remargining use a 5-business day holding period, while secured lending with daily mark-to-market but no remargining uses a 20-business day holding period; haircuts must be scaled by the square root of time formula.
R-CRE22.42-5-and-20-day-holding-periods.quote: For example, repo-style transactions subject to daily marking-to-market and to daily remargining will receive a haircut based on a 5-business day holding period and secured lending transactions with daily mark-to-market and no remargining clauses will receive a haircut based on a 20-business day holding period. Haircuts must be scaled up using the square root of time formula depending on the actual frequency of remargining or marking to market.

applies_to.note: Comprehensive approach only.

numeric_values: 20-business day holding period (secured lending, no remargining)
R-CRE22.42-5-and-20-day-holding-periods.portfolio_relevance: Secured lending, the category a small bank's collateralised loans fall into, carries a 20-day rather than 5-day holding period and hence roughly double the haircut, materially reducing the collateral benefit on term loans.

R-CRE22.43-fx-haircut-requirement.title: Additional haircut required where exposure and collateral are in different currencies
R-CRE22.43-fx-haircut-requirement.statement: Where exposure and collateral are held in different currencies, banks must apply an additional haircut to the volatility-adjusted collateral amount in accordance with CRE22.52 and CRE22.82 to CRE22.83.
R-CRE22.43-fx-haircut-requirement.quote: Additionally, where the exposure and collateral are held in different currencies, banks must apply an additional haircut to the volatility-adjusted collateral amount in accordance with CRE22.52 and CRE22.82 to CRE22.83 to take account of possible future fluctuations in exchange rates.

applies_to.note: Comprehensive approach; guarantees and credit derivatives carry the parallel adjustment in CRE22.82-83.

R-CRE22.43-fx-haircut-requirement.portfolio_relevance: Penalises cross-currency collateral arrangements, favouring domestic-currency collateral for a bank whose loan book is in a single currency.

R-CRE22.45-comprehensive-eligible-collat.title: Comprehensive approach adds non-index listed equities and funds holding them to the eligible collateral list
R-CRE22.45-comprehensive-eligible-collat.statement: Eligible collateral in the comprehensive approach comprises all instruments listed in CRE22.34, plus equities and convertible bonds not in a main index but listed on a recognised securities exchange, plus UCITS/mutual funds including those instruments.
R-CRE22.45-comprehensive-eligible-collat.quote: The following collateral instruments are eligible for recognition in the comprehensive approach: (1) CRE22.34; All of the instruments listed in (2) Equities and convertible bonds that are not included in a main index but which are listed on a recognised security exchange; (3) UCITS/mutual funds which include the instruments in point (2).

applies_to.note: Comprehensive approach only; these instruments carry the 30% haircut in CRE22.49/22.50.

R-CRE22.45-comprehensive-eligible-collat.portfolio_relevance: Widening the eligible collateral set is a direct reason to elect the comprehensive approach if the bank lends against non-index listed securities.

R-CRE22.46-adjusted-exposure-formula.title: Comprehensive approach formula for exposure after risk mitigation
R-CRE22.46-adjusted-exposure-formula.statement: For a collateralised transaction the exposure amount after risk mitigation is computed from the current exposure value E, the exposure haircut He, the current collateral value C, the collateral haircut Hc and the currency-mismatch haircut Hfx.
R-CRE22.46-adjusted-exposure-formula.quote: For a collateralised transaction, the exposure amount after risk mitigation is calculated using the formula that follows, where: (1) = the exposure value after risk mitigation E (2) E = current value of the exposure (3) H = haircut appropriate to the exposure e (4) C = the current value of the collateral received (5) H = haircut appropriate to the collateral c (6) H = haircut appropriate for currency mismatch between the collateral and

applies_to.note: Also the formula referenced for on-balance sheet loan/deposit netting in CRE22.68.

R-CRE22.46-adjusted-exposure-formula.portfolio_relevance: The central computable CRM equation: it turns collateral holdings into an EAD reduction and is the object any RWA optimiser manipulates.

R-CRE22.47-collateral-maturity-mismatch.title: Collateral value must be adjusted for maturity mismatch
R-CRE22.47-collateral-maturity-mismatch.statement: In the case of maturity mismatches the value of collateral received must be adjusted in accordance with CRE22.10 to CRE22.14 before entering the comprehensive approach formula.
R-CRE22.47-collateral-maturity-mismatch.quote: In the case of maturity mismatches, the value of the collateral received (collateral amount) must be adjusted in accordance with CRE22.10 to CRE22.14.

applies_to.note: Comprehensive approach only; the simple approach bars mismatches entirely.

R-CRE22.47-collateral-maturity-mismatch.portfolio_relevance: Chains the maturity-mismatch pro-rating into the EAD formula, so short-dated collateral against long-dated loans yields proportionally less relief.

R-CRE22.48-rwa-from-adjusted-exposure.title: Adjusted exposure is multiplied by the counterparty risk weight
R-CRE22.48-rwa-from-adjusted-exposure.statement: The exposure amount after risk mitigation must be multiplied by the risk weight of the counterparty to obtain the risk-weighted asset amount for the collateralised transaction.
R-CRE22.48-rwa-from-adjusted-exposure.quote: The exposure amount after risk mitigation (E) must be multiplied by the risk weight of the counterparty to obtain the risk-weighted asset amount for the collateralised transaction.

applies_to.note: Comprehensive approach; contrasts with the simple approach where the collateral's risk weight is substituted instead.

R-CRE22.48-rwa-from-adjusted-exposure.portfolio_relevance: Key structural difference from the simple approach: relief comes through EAD, not through a substituted (floored) risk weight, so highly weighted retail exposures benefit proportionately more.

R-CRE22.49-haircut-basis-10-day.title: Supervisory haircuts assume daily mark-to-market, daily remargining and a 10-business day holding period
R-CRE22.49-haircut-basis-10-day.statement: The supervisory haircut tables are calibrated assuming daily mark-to-market, daily remargining and a 10-business day holding period, and must be used to determine the haircuts appropriate to collateral and to exposure.
R-CRE22.49-haircut-basis-10-day.quote: In jurisdictions that allow the use of external ratings for regulatory purposes, the following supervisory haircuts (assuming daily mark-to-market, daily remargining and a 10-business day holding period), expressed as percentages, must be used to determine the haircuts appropriate to the collateral

applies_to.note: External-ratings branch; the calibration basis carries over to CRE22.59 scaling.

R-CRE22.49-haircut-basis-10-day.portfolio_relevance: Sets the baseline against which any bank with weaker revaluation practice must scale its haircuts up, directly reducing measured collateral value.

R-CRE22.49-debt-haircut-table.title: Supervisory haircut table for debt securities (external ratings permitted)
R-CRE22.49-debt-haircut-table.statement: Debt collateral haircuts range from 0.5% for AAA to AA- sovereign paper of one year or less, through 2-12% for sovereigns and 1-20% for other issuers by residual maturity band, up to 15% for BB+ to BB- sovereign paper (with BB-rated other-issuer and securitisation collateral not eligible), and securitisation exposures carry 2-24%.
R-CRE22.49-debt-haircut-table.quote: Issue rating for debt securities Residual maturity exposures Sovereigns Other issuers Securitisation ≤ 1 year 0.5 1 2 >1 year, ≤ 3 3 2 8 years >3 years, ≤ 5 4 AAA to AA–/A-1 years >5 years, ≤ 10 6 4 16 years > 10 years 12 ≤ 1 year 1 2 4 >1 year, ≤ 3 4 3 12 years A+ to BBB–/ A-2/A-3/P-3 >3 years, ≤ 5 6 and unrated years bank securities CRE22.34 (3)(b) >5 years, ≤ 10 12 6 24 years > 10 years 20 BB+ to BB– All 15 Not eligible Not eligible

applies_to.note: Only for jurisdictions that allow external ratings; not usable in the US.

numeric_values: Not eligible: BB-rated other issuers and securitisations
R-CRE22.49-debt-haircut-table.portfolio_relevance: The full computable haircut grid: it prices the RWA benefit of each collateral type by maturity and rating, and shows long-dated or low-rated collateral gives materially less EAD relief.

R-CRE22.49-equity-gold-haircut.title: 20% haircut for main index equities and gold, 30% for other listed equities
R-CRE22.49-equity-gold-haircut.statement: Main index equities including convertible bonds, and gold, carry a 20% supervisory haircut; other equities and convertible bonds listed on a recognised exchange carry a 30% haircut.
R-CRE22.49-equity-gold-haircut.quote: Main index equities (including 20 convertible bonds) and gold Other equities and convertible 30 bonds listed on a recognised exchange

applies_to.note: Same values appear in the no-external-ratings table CRE22.50, so these two haircuts are jurisdiction-invariant.

numeric_values: 30% haircut (other listed equities and convertible bonds)
R-CRE22.49-equity-gold-haircut.portfolio_relevance: Prices securities-backed lending: a bank must hold roughly 1.25x or 1.43x cover in equities to fully offset an exposure, versus 1.0x in same-currency cash.

R-CRE22.50-debt-haircut-table-no-ratings.title: Supervisory haircut table for debt securities where external ratings are banned
R-CRE22.50-debt-haircut-table-no-ratings.statement: Where external ratings may not be used, debt collateral haircuts run from 0.5% (0% risk weight issuer, one year or less) to 20% for long-dated 0%-weighted paper, with 1-6% and 15-24% bands by issuer risk weight, 15% for other investment-grade securities of one year or less, and higher haircuts for securitisation exposures.
R-CRE22.50-debt-haircut-table-no-ratings.quote: Debt securities ≤ 1 year 0.5 1 15 2 4 > 1 year, ≤ 3 4 years 2 3 12 15 > 3 years, ≤ 5 years 6 > 5 years, ≤ 12 10 years 4 6 15 24 > 10 years 20

applies_to.note: This is the operative haircut table for US banks; the table is keyed on the issuer's risk weight (0%, 20%/50%, 100%) rather than on ratings.

R-CRE22.50-debt-haircut-table-no-ratings.portfolio_relevance: The haircut grid a North American SA bank actually applies: it makes Treasury and agency collateral cheap and long-dated corporate or securitisation collateral expensive in EAD terms.

R-CRE22.50-cash-and-other-haircuts.title: Zero haircut for same-currency cash; 30% for other exposure types
R-CRE22.50-cash-and-other-haircuts.statement: Cash collateral in the same currency attracts a zero haircut, while other exposure types attract a 30% haircut.
R-CRE22.50-cash-and-other-haircuts.quote: Cash in the 0 same currency Other exposure types 30

applies_to.note: 'Cash in the same currency' is defined by CRE22.51(4) as the eligible cash collateral of CRE22.34(1).

R-CRE22.50-cash-and-other-haircuts.portfolio_relevance: The zero-haircut treatment of same-currency cash on deposit makes deposit-secured lending the only fully efficient CRM structure available to a small deposit-funded bank.

R-CRE22.51-haircut-table-definitions.title: Definitions used in the supervisory haircut tables
R-CRE22.51-haircut-table-definitions.statement: For the haircut tables, 'sovereigns' includes PSEs treated as sovereigns and 0%-risk-weighted MDBs, 'other issuers' includes PSEs not treated as sovereigns, 'securitisation exposures' takes the securitisation framework definition, and 'cash in the same currency' means the eligible cash collateral of CRE22.34(1).
R-CRE22.51-haircut-table-definitions.quote: “Sovereigns” includes: PSEs that are treated as sovereigns by the national supervisor, as well as multilateral development banks receiving a 0% risk weight. (2) “Other issuers” includes: PSEs that are not treated as sovereigns by the national supervisor.

applies_to.note: PSE classification is a national-discretion decision that changes the applicable haircut column.

numeric_values: 0% risk weight MDBs treated as sovereigns
R-CRE22.51-haircut-table-definitions.portfolio_relevance: Determines which haircut column municipal and agency paper falls into, materially changing the collateral value of a US bank's municipal securities holdings.

R-CRE22.52-fx-haircut-8pct.title: Currency mismatch haircut of 8% for collateral
R-CRE22.52-fx-haircut-8pct.statement: The haircut for currency risk where exposure and collateral are denominated in different currencies is 8%, based on a 10-business day holding period and daily mark-to-market.
R-CRE22.52-fx-haircut-8pct.quote: The haircut for currency risk (H) where exposure and collateral are denominated fx in different currencies is 8% (also based on a 10-business day holding period and daily mark-to-market).

applies_to.note: Comprehensive approach; must be scaled by the CRE22.59 square-root-of-time formula for less frequent revaluation.

R-CRE22.52-fx-haircut-8pct.portfolio_relevance: A flat 8% penalty on cross-currency collateral, meaning a bank must hold roughly 8% more foreign-currency collateral for the same EAD relief.

R-CRE22.54-non-eligible-instrument-30pct.title: 30% haircut where the bank posts non-eligible instruments; no CRM where it borrows them
R-CRE22.54-non-eligible-instrument-30pct.statement: For SFTs in which the bank lends or posts non-eligible instruments as collateral, a 30% haircut must be applied on the exposure; where the bank borrows non-eligible instruments, credit risk mitigation may not be applied at all.
R-CRE22.54-non-eligible-instrument-30pct.quote: For SFTs in which the bank lends, or posts as collateral, non-eligible instruments, the haircut to be applied on the exposure must be 30%. For transactions in which the bank borrows non-eligible instruments, credit risk mitigation may not be applied.

applies_to.note: SFT-specific; limited relevance to small banks without securities-financing books.

numeric_values: zero CRM recognition for borrowed non-eligible instruments
R-CRE22.54-non-eligible-instrument-30pct.portfolio_relevance: Removes any capital incentive to finance ineligible assets through SFTs, keeping such positions at or above their unmitigated RWA.

R-CRE22.55-basket-haircut.title: Haircut on a basket of collateral is the weighted average of component haircuts
R-CRE22.55-basket-haircut.statement: Where collateral is a basket of assets, the basket haircut is computed from the currency-weight of each asset in the basket and the haircut applicable to that asset.
