R-CRE22.55-basket-haircut.quote: Where the collateral is a basket of assets, the haircut (H) on the basket must be calculated using the formula that follows, where: (1) a is the weight of the asset (as measured by units of currency) in the basket i (2) H the haircut applicable to that asset

applies_to.note: Comprehensive approach.

numeric_values: H = sum of a_i * H_i (weighted average)
R-CRE22.55-basket-haircut.portfolio_relevance: Makes mixed collateral pools linearly computable, so a bank can optimise the composition of a pledged securities pool to minimise the blended haircut.

R-CRE22.57-minimum-holding-periods.title: Minimum holding periods: 5, 10 and 20 business days by transaction type
R-CRE22.57-minimum-holding-periods.statement: Minimum holding periods are five business days with daily remargining for repo-style transactions, 10 business days with daily remargining for other capital market transactions, and 20 business days with daily revaluation for secured lending.
R-CRE22.57-minimum-holding-periods.quote: Minimum holding periods Summary of minimum holding periods and remargining/revaluation periods Transaction type Minimum holding period Minimum remargining /revaluation period Repo-style transaction five business days daily remargining Other capital market 10 business days daily remargining transactions Secured lending 20 business days daily revaluation

applies_to.note: Secured lending is the row that binds an ordinary collateralised loan book.

R-CRE22.57-minimum-holding-periods.portfolio_relevance: A collateralised consumer or SME loan is 'secured lending' at 20 business days, so its haircuts are roughly sqrt(2) times the 10-day table values, cutting the collateral benefit substantially versus repo.

R-CRE22.58-5000-trade-netting-set.title: Netting sets exceeding 5,000 trades in a quarter must use a 20-business day holding period
R-CRE22.58-5000-trade-netting-set.statement: Where the number of trades in a netting set exceeds 5,000 at any point during a quarter, a 20 business day minimum holding period must be used for the following quarter.
R-CRE22.58-5000-trade-netting-set.quote: For all netting sets where the number of trades exceeds 5,000 at any point during a quarter, a 20 business day minimum holding period for the following quarter must be used.

applies_to.note: A size-triggered rule: only banks with very large derivative/SFT netting sets cross a 5,000-trade threshold.

R-CRE22.58-5000-trade-netting-set.portfolio_relevance: A genuine scale penalty: growing a netting set past 5,000 trades mechanically doubles the holding period and hence raises haircuts for the next quarter.

R-CRE22.58-illiquid-collateral-20-days.title: Illiquid collateral forces a 20-business day minimum holding period
R-CRE22.58-illiquid-collateral-20-days.statement: Netting sets containing one or more trades involving illiquid collateral must use a minimum holding period of 20 business days, where illiquidity is assessed under stressed conditions by the absence of continuously active markets giving multiple non-market-moving quotes within two or fewer days.
R-CRE22.58-illiquid-collateral-20-days.quote: For netting sets containing one or more trades involving illiquid collateral, a minimum holding period of 20 business days must be used.

applies_to.note: Includes trades not marked daily and trades valued by unobservable models.

numeric_values: two or fewer days quote availability test
R-CRE22.58-illiquid-collateral-20-days.portfolio_relevance: A single illiquid item contaminates the whole netting set's holding period, so collateral pool composition, not just size, drives the haircut.

R-CRE22.58-margin-dispute-doubling.title: More than two margin call disputes in two quarters doubles the minimum holding period
R-CRE22.58-margin-dispute-doubling.statement: If a bank has experienced more than two margin call disputes on a netting set over the previous two quarters that lasted longer than its estimate of the margin period of risk, it must use a minimum holding period twice the otherwise applicable level for the subsequent two quarters.
R-CRE22.58-margin-dispute-doubling.quote: If a bank has experienced more than two margin call disputes on a particular netting set over the previous two quarters that have lasted longer than the bank's estimate of the margin period of risk (as defined in CRE50.19), then for the subsequent two quarters the bank must use a minimum holding period that is twice the level that would apply excluding the application of this sub-paragraph.

applies_to.note: Operational-performance-linked capital penalty; the trigger and the penalty window are both explicitly quarterly.

numeric_values: more than two margin call disputes
R-CRE22.58-margin-dispute-doubling.portfolio_relevance: A quarterly, observable operational trigger that raises haircuts and thus RWA without any change in portfolio composition.

R-CRE22.59-haircut-scaling.title: Haircuts must be scaled from the 10-business day default by the actual remargining frequency
R-CRE22.59-haircut-scaling.statement: When the frequency of remargining or revaluation is longer than the minimum, the 10-business day default haircuts of CRE22.49 to CRE22.51 must be scaled up or down using the square-root-of-time formula based on the minimum holding period for the transaction type and the actual number of business days between remargining or revaluation.
R-CRE22.59-haircut-scaling.quote: When the frequency of remargining or revaluation is longer than the minimum, the minimum haircut numbers must be scaled up depending on the actual number of business days between remargining or revaluation. The 10-business day haircuts provided in CRE22.49 to CRE22.51 are the default haircuts and these haircuts must be scaled up or down using the formula below

applies_to.note: Applies to collateral haircuts, FX haircuts (CRE22.52/22.83) and on-balance sheet netting (CRE22.69).

R-CRE22.59-haircut-scaling.portfolio_relevance: Directly converts a bank's revaluation cadence into a haircut multiplier: investing in more frequent collateral revaluation is a pure operational lever that lowers RWA.

R-CRE22.60-zero-haircut-core-participant.title: Zero haircut permitted for qualifying repo-style transactions with core market participants
R-CRE22.60-zero-haircut-core-participant.statement: For repo-style transactions with core market participants as defined in CRE22.37 that satisfy the CRE22.36 conditions, supervisors may apply a haircut of zero.
R-CRE22.60-zero-haircut-core-participant.quote: For repo-style transactions with core market participants as defined in CRE22.37 and that satisfy the conditions in CRE22.36 supervisors may apply a haircut of zero.

applies_to.note: Explicit supervisory discretion; requires all eight CRE22.36 conditions plus core-market-participant status.

R-CRE22.60-zero-haircut-core-participant.portfolio_relevance: Comprehensive-approach counterpart to the CRE22.38 0% risk weight: qualifying government repo with core participants becomes fully capital-free.

R-CRE22.62-sft-netting-conditions.title: Conditions for recognising bilateral netting of SFTs
R-CRE22.62-sft-netting-conditions.statement: Bilateral netting agreements over SFTs may be recognised counterparty-by-counterparty only where legally enforceable in each relevant jurisdiction on default regardless of insolvency, and where they give a right to terminate and close out all transactions in a timely manner, provide for netting of gains and losses into a single net amount, and allow prompt liquidation or set-off of collateral on default.
R-CRE22.62-sft-netting-conditions.quote: The effects of bilateral netting agreements covering SFTs may be recognised on a counterparty-by-counterparty basis if the agreements are legally enforceable in each relevant jurisdiction upon the occurrence of an event of default and regardless of whether the counterparty is insolvent or bankrupt. In addition, netting agreements must: (1) provide the non-defaulting party the right to terminate and close out in a timely manner all transactions under the agreement upon an event of default, including in the event of insolvency or bankruptcy of the counterparty; (2) provide for the netting of gains and losses on transactions (including the value of any collateral) terminated and closed out under it so that a single net amount is owed by one party to the other; (3) allow for the prompt liquidation or set-off of collateral upon the event of default;

applies_to.note: SFT master netting; a bank may elect not to recognise netting, in which case each transaction is capitalised separately (CRE22.44).

R-CRE22.62-sft-netting-conditions.portfolio_relevance: Gates the ability to compute SFT capital on a net rather than gross basis, which is the difference between a large and a small measured exposure to the same counterparty.

R-CRE22.63-cross-book-netting.title: Netting across banking and trading book requires daily marking and banking-book-eligible collateral
R-CRE22.63-cross-book-netting.statement: Netting across positions in the banking and trading book may only be recognised where all transactions are marked to market daily and the collateral instruments used are recognised as eligible financial collateral in the banking book.
R-CRE22.63-cross-book-netting.quote: Netting across positions in the banking and trading book may only be recognised when the netted transactions fulfil the following conditions: (1) All transactions are marked to market daily; and (2) The collateral instruments used in the transactions are recognised as eligible financial collateral in the banking book.

applies_to.note: Only relevant to banks running a trading book; most small North American banks do not.

R-CRE22.63-cross-book-netting.portfolio_relevance: Prevents banking-book exposures from being netted against trading positions unless the collateral would independently qualify in the banking book.

R-CRE22.68-on-balance-sheet-netting-cond.title: Four conditions for netting loans against deposits for capital purposes
R-CRE22.68-on-balance-sheet-netting-cond.statement: A bank may use the net exposure of loans and deposits for capital adequacy under the CRE22.46 formula only if it has a well-founded legal basis for enforceability in each relevant jurisdiction regardless of insolvency, can at any time identify the assets and liabilities with the same counterparty subject to the agreement, and monitors and controls both its roll-off risks and the relevant exposures on a net basis.
R-CRE22.68-on-balance-sheet-netting-cond.quote: A bank may use the net exposure of loans and deposits as the basis for its capital adequacy calculation in accordance with the formula in CRE22.46, when the bank: (1) has a well-founded legal basis for concluding that the netting or offsetting agreement is enforceable in each relevant jurisdiction regardless of whether the counterparty is insolvent or bankrupt; (2) is able at any time to determine those assets and liabilities with the same counterparty that are subject to the netting agreement; (3) monitors and controls its roll-off risks; and (4) monitors and controls the relevant exposures on a net basis,

applies_to.note: The single most accessible CRM technique for a deposit-funded community bank; requires customer-level linkage of deposit and loan systems.

R-CRE22.68-on-balance-sheet-netting-cond.portfolio_relevance: Lets a small bank cut EAD on retail and SME borrowers who also hold deposits, reducing RWA without repricing, tightening underwriting or shrinking the credit-card book.

R-CRE22.69-on-balance-netting-haircuts.title: On-balance sheet netting: loans as exposure, deposits as collateral, zero haircuts except currency mismatch
R-CRE22.69-on-balance-netting-haircuts.statement: When calculating the net exposure, assets (loans) are treated as exposure and liabilities (deposits) as collateral; haircuts are zero except where a currency mismatch exists, and a 10-business day holding period applies when daily mark-to-market is conducted, with CRE22.49, CRE22.59 and the maturity-mismatch rules also applying.
R-CRE22.69-on-balance-netting-haircuts.quote: When calculating the net exposure described in the paragraph above, assets (loans) are treated as exposure and liabilities (deposits) as collateral. The haircuts are zero except when a currency mismatch exists. A 10-business day holding period applies when daily mark-to-market is conducted.

applies_to.note: Zero haircut applies only where loan and deposit are in the same currency; maturity mismatch rules of CRE22.10-22.14 still bite on term deposits shorter than the loan.

R-CRE22.69-on-balance-netting-haircuts.portfolio_relevance: Quantifies the deposit-offset lever exactly: same-currency deposits offset loan EAD dollar for dollar with no haircut, making cross-selling deposits to credit-card holders a pure RWA reduction.

R-CRE22.70-guarantor-risk-weight-substit.title: Guarantor's risk weight may be substituted for the counterparty's where conditions are met
R-CRE22.70-guarantor-risk-weight-substit.statement: If the operational conditions for guarantees and credit derivatives are met, banks can substitute the risk weight of the counterparty with the risk weight of the guarantor.
R-CRE22.70-guarantor-risk-weight-substit.quote: If conditions set below are met, banks can substitute the risk weight of the counterparty with the risk weight of the guarantor.

applies_to.note: Available to any SA bank; in North America the practical case is government guarantee programmes (SBA, FHA/VA-type).

R-CRE22.70-guarantor-risk-weight-substit.portfolio_relevance: The core guarantee lever: shifting SME or consumer lending into government-guaranteed programmes converts the guaranteed portion to the sovereign risk weight, often 0%.

R-CRE22.71-guarantee-operational-require.title: Guarantees and credit derivatives must be direct, explicit, irrevocable and unconditional
R-CRE22.71-guarantee-operational-require.statement: A guarantee or credit derivative must represent a direct claim on the protection provider, be explicitly referenced to specific exposures or a pool so the cover is clearly defined, be irrevocable other than for the purchaser's non-payment, contain no clause allowing the provider unilaterally to cancel or shorten cover or raise its cost on credit deterioration, and be unconditional with no clause outside the bank's control that could prevent timely payout.
R-CRE22.71-guarantee-operational-require.quote: A guarantee (counter-guarantee) or credit derivative must satisfy the following requirements: (1) it represents a direct claim on the protection provider; (2) it is explicitly referenced to specific exposures or a pool of exposures, so that the extent of the cover is clearly defined and incontrovertible; (3) other than non-payment by a protection purchaser of money due in respect of the credit protection contract it is irrevocable; (4) there is no clause in the contract that would allow the protection provider unilaterally to cancel the credit cover, change the maturity agreed ex post, or that would increase the effective cost of cover as a result of deteriorating credit quality in the hedged exposure; (5) it must be unconditional; there should be no clause in the protection contract outside the direct control of the bank that could prevent the protection provider from being obliged to pay out in a timely manner in the event that the underlying counterparty fails to make the payment(s) due.

applies_to.note: Five cumulative eligibility tests, all documentary and hence auditable.

R-CRE22.71-guarantee-operational-require.portfolio_relevance: Rules out conditional or cancellable credit insurance, so a portfolio shift toward guaranteed lending only earns RWA relief where the guarantee is genuinely unconditional.

R-CRE22.72-guarantee-maturity-mismatch.title: Guarantee amount must be adjusted for maturity mismatch
R-CRE22.72-guarantee-maturity-mismatch.statement: In the case of maturity mismatches, the amount of credit protection provided by a guarantee or credit derivative must be adjusted in accordance with CRE22.10 to CRE22.14.
R-CRE22.72-guarantee-maturity-mismatch.quote: In the case of maturity mismatches, the amount of credit protection that is provided must be adjusted in accordance with CRE22.10 to CRE22.14.

applies_to.note: Subject to the one-year original / three-month residual eligibility gates of CRE22.12.

R-CRE22.72-guarantee-maturity-mismatch.portfolio_relevance: Short-dated credit insurance against long-dated loans yields only pro-rated relief, so buying annual protection on a five-year book delivers far less than face value in RWA terms.

R-CRE22.73-guarantee-payment-mechanics.title: Guarantee must permit direct pursuit of the guarantor without first suing the counterparty
R-CRE22.73-guarantee-payment-mechanics.statement: For a guarantee to be recognised, on qualifying default or non-payment the bank must be able to pursue the guarantor in a timely manner for monies outstanding and receive payment without first having to take legal action against the counterparty, and the guarantee must be an explicitly documented obligation of the guarantor.
R-CRE22.73-guarantee-payment-mechanics.quote: On the qualifying default/non-payment of the counterparty, the bank may in a timely manner pursue the guarantor for any monies outstanding under the documentation governing the transaction. The guarantor may make one lump sum payment of all monies under such documentation to the bank, or the guarantor may assume the future payment obligations of the counterparty covered by the guarantee. The bank must have the right to receive any such payments from the guarantor without first having to take legal action in order to pursue the counterparty for payment. (2) The guarantee is an explicitly documented obligation assumed by the guarantor.

applies_to.note: Additional to the legal certainty requirements of CRE22.9.

R-CRE22.73-guarantee-payment-mechanics.portfolio_relevance: Excludes secondary or surety-style guarantees requiring exhaustion of remedies, narrowing which third-party support on consumer or SME loans actually reduces RWA.

R-CRE22.73-principal-only-guarantee.title: Principal-only guarantees leave interest and other payments unsecured
R-CRE22.73-principal-only-guarantee.statement: Where a guarantee covers payment of principal only, interest and other uncovered payments must be treated as an unsecured amount under the proportional cover rules of CRE22.80.
R-CRE22.73-principal-only-guarantee.quote: Where a guarantee covers payment of principal only, interests and other uncovered payments must be treated as an unsecured amount in accordance with the rules for proportional cover described in CRE22.80.

applies_to.note: Consistent with the ban on principal-only ratings in CRE21.13 and CRE22.5.

R-CRE22.73-principal-only-guarantee.portfolio_relevance: Materially reduces the value of principal-only protection on high-yield revolving assets such as credit cards, where accrued interest and fees are a large share of the exposure.

R-CRE22.74-credit-derivative-credit-even.title: Credit derivative must at minimum cover failure to pay, bankruptcy and restructuring
R-CRE22.74-credit-derivative-credit-even.statement: For a credit derivative to be recognised, the specified credit events must at minimum cover failure to pay (with a grace period closely in line with the underlying), bankruptcy/insolvency or inability to pay debts, and restructuring involving forgiveness or postponement of principal, interest or fees that results in a credit loss event such as a write-off or specific provision.
R-CRE22.74-credit-derivative-credit-even.quote: The credit events specified by the contracting parties must at a minimum cover: (a) failure to pay the amounts due under terms of the underlying obligation that are in effect at the time of such failure (with a grace period that is closely in line with the grace period in the underlying obligation); (b) bankruptcy, insolvency or inability of the obligor to pay its debts, or its failure or admission in writing of its inability generally to pay its debts as they become due, and analogous events; and (c) restructuring of the underlying obligation involving forgiveness or postponement of principal, interest or fees that results in a credit loss event (ie write-off, specific provision or other similar debit to the profit and loss account).

applies_to.note: Footnote waives the restructuring event for corporate hedges where a 100% vote is needed to amend key terms and the jurisdiction has a well-established bankruptcy code. Small banks rarely buy single-name credit protection.

numeric_values: 100% vote condition in the corporate-exposure footnote
R-CRE22.74-credit-derivative-credit-even.portfolio_relevance: Ties the definition of a covered loss to write-off or specific provision, linking CRM recognition directly to the bank's own provisioning outcomes.

R-CRE22.75-restructuring-not-covered-60p.title: Credit derivatives not covering restructuring are recognised at only 60%
R-CRE22.75-restructuring-not-covered-60p.statement: Where restructuring of the underlying obligation is not covered by the credit derivative but all other requirements are met, only partial recognition is allowed: 60% of the hedge amount if it does not exceed the underlying obligation, and the eligible hedge is capped at 60% of the underlying obligation if the hedge is larger.
R-CRE22.75-restructuring-not-covered-60p.quote: When the restructuring of the underlying obligation is not covered by the credit derivative, but the other requirements in CRE22.74 are met, partial recognition of the credit derivative will be allowed. If the amount of the credit derivative is less than or equal to the amount of the underlying obligation, 60% of the amount of the hedge can be recognised as covered. If the amount of the credit derivative is larger than that of the underlying obligation, then the amount of eligible hedge is capped at 60% of the amount of the underlying obligation.

applies_to.note: Applies only where the CRE22.74 footnote waiver does not apply.

R-CRE22.75-restructuring-not-covered-60p.portfolio_relevance: A directly computable coefficient: restructuring-excluded protection delivers only 60 cents of RWA relief per dollar of notional, which prices the cost of narrower CDS documentation.

R-CRE22.76-eligible-guarantors.title: Range of eligible guarantors and protection providers
R-CRE22.76-eligible-guarantors.statement: Credit protection is recognised only from sovereigns, PSEs, MDBs, banks, securities firms and other prudentially regulated financial institutions with a lower risk weight than the counterparty, and (where external ratings are permitted) other externally rated entities including parents, subsidiaries and affiliates with a lower risk weight than the obligor.
R-CRE22.76-eligible-guarantors.quote: Credit protection given by the following entities can be recognised when they have a lower risk weight than the counterparty: (1) Sovereign entities, PSEs, multilateral development banks (MDBs), banks, securities firms and other prudentially regulated financial institutions with a lower risk weight than the counterparty; (2) In jurisdictions that allow the use of external ratings for regulatory purposes: (a) other entities that are externally rated except when credit protection is provided to a securitisation exposure. This would include credit protection provided by a parent, subsidiary and affiliate companies when they have a lower risk weight than the obligor; (b) when credit protection is provided to a securitisation exposure, other entities that currently are externally rated BBB– or better and that were externally rated A– or better at the time the credit protection was provided. This would include credit protection provided by parent, subsidiary and affiliate companies when they have a lower risk weight than the obligor.

applies_to.note: Footnote defines prudentially regulated financial institution to include insurers, broker/dealers, thrifts, FCMs and QCCPs; sub-branch (2) is inoperative where external ratings are banned.

numeric_values: A– or better at inception (securitisation protection)
R-CRE22.76-eligible-guarantors.portfolio_relevance: Defines who can supply RWA relief; for a small US bank the practical set is government agencies, banks and regulated insurers, so private credit insurance from an unregulated provider gives no capital benefit.

R-CRE22.76-securitisation-protection-rat.title: Protection on securitisation exposures requires BBB- now and A- at inception
R-CRE22.76-securitisation-protection-rat.statement: Where credit protection is provided to a securitisation exposure, the protection provider must currently be externally rated BBB- or better and must have been rated A- or better at the time the protection was provided.
R-CRE22.76-securitisation-protection-rat.quote: when credit protection is provided to a securitisation exposure, other entities that currently are externally rated BBB– or better and that were externally rated A– or better at the time the credit protection was provided.

applies_to.note: Only in jurisdictions permitting external ratings; a two-point-in-time test.

R-CRE22.76-securitisation-protection-rat.portfolio_relevance: A dual rating test that can strip capital relief from a credit-card ABS wrap if the monoline is downgraded below BBB-, an event risk that must be modelled for banks holding wrapped securitisation exposures.

R-CRE22.76-investment-grade-guarantor.title: Definition of an investment grade guarantor where external ratings are banned
R-CRE22.76-investment-grade-guarantor.statement: Where external ratings may not be used, other eligible guarantors are entities defined as investment grade, meaning they have adequate capacity to meet financial commitments in a timely manner irrespective of the economic cycle, assessed on business model complexity, performance against industry and peers, and operating-environment risk; corporates must also have securities outstanding on a recognised exchange and must not be positively correlated with the guaranteed exposures.
R-CRE22.76-investment-grade-guarantor.quote: Other entities, defined as “investment grade” meaning they have adequate capacity to meet their financial commitments (including repayments of principal and interest) in a timely manner, irrespective of the economic cycle and business conditions. When making this determination, the bank should assess the entity against the investment grade definition taking into account the complexity of its business model, performance against industry and peers, and risks posed by the entity

applies_to.note: This is the operative guarantor-eligibility test for US banks; it requires the bank to perform and document its own investment-grade determination.

R-CRE22.76-investment-grade-guarantor.portfolio_relevance: Puts the burden of an internal investment-grade assessment on the bank, so relying on corporate guarantees for RWA relief carries a credit-analysis cost a small bank may not be able to bear.

R-CRE22.77-only-cds-and-trs.title: Only credit default swaps and total return swaps are eligible credit derivatives
R-CRE22.77-only-cds-and-trs.statement: Only credit default swaps and total return swaps that provide credit protection equivalent to guarantees are eligible for recognition; a total return swap is not recognised where the bank records net payments received as income without recording offsetting deterioration in the protected asset's value.
R-CRE22.77-only-cds-and-trs.quote: Only credit default swaps and total return swaps that provide credit protection equivalent to guarantees are eligible for recognition.

applies_to.note: Footnote treats cash-funded credit-linked notes issued by the bank as cash-collateralised, exempt from the CRE22.76 protection-provider restrictions.

R-CRE22.77-only-cds-and-trs.portfolio_relevance: The credit-linked note carve-out is the notable lever: a bank can issue a cash-funded CLN against its own credit-card book and treat it as cash collateral without any guarantor eligibility test.

R-CRE22.78-nth-to-default-ineligible.title: First-to-default and nth-to-default credit derivatives give no capital relief
R-CRE22.78-nth-to-default-ineligible.statement: First-to-default and all other nth-to-default credit derivatives are not eligible as credit risk mitigation and cannot provide any regulatory capital relief; a bank providing protection through such instruments applies the CRE20.103 treatment.
R-CRE22.78-nth-to-default-ineligible.quote: First-to-default and all other nth-to-default credit derivatives (ie by which a bank obtains credit protection for a basket of reference names and where the first- or nth–to-default among the reference names triggers the credit protection and terminates the contract) are not eligible as a credit risk mitigation technique and therefore cannot provide any regulatory capital relief.

applies_to.note: Absolute prohibition on the buy side; the sell side is capitalised under CRE20.103.

R-CRE22.78-nth-to-default-ineligible.portfolio_relevance: Closes basket-protection structures as an RWA lever, forcing name-by-name protection if a bank wants recognised hedging of a diversified book.

R-CRE22.79-protected-portion-and-1250-th.title: Protected portion takes the provider's risk weight; amounts below a materiality threshold get 1250%
R-CRE22.79-protected-portion-and-1250-th.statement: The protected portion of an exposure is assigned the protection provider's risk weight and the uncovered portion the underlying counterparty's; materiality thresholds below which the provider is exempt from payment are equivalent to retained first-loss positions and the portion of the exposure below such a threshold must be risk-weighted at 1250% by the protection-buying bank.
R-CRE22.79-protected-portion-and-1250-th.quote: The protected portion is assigned the risk weight of the protection provider. The uncovered portion of the exposure is assigned the risk weight of the underlying counterparty. (2) Materiality thresholds on payments below which the protection provider is exempt from payment in the event of loss are equivalent to retained first- loss positions. The portion of the exposure that is below a materiality threshold must be assigned a risk weight of 1250% by the bank purchasing the credit protection.

applies_to.note: 1250% is the risk weight equivalent of a full capital deduction at an 8% minimum ratio.

numeric_values: 1250% risk weight on the retained first-loss portion
protected portion at the protection provider's risk weight
R-CRE22.79-protected-portion-and-1250-th.portfolio_relevance: The most punitive number in the chapter: a deductible or first-loss retention on portfolio credit insurance is capitalised dollar-for-dollar, so structures that look like cheap protection can raise total RWA.

R-CRE22.80-proportional-cover.title: Pari passu pro rata loss sharing gives proportional capital relief
R-CRE22.80-proportional-cover.statement: Where losses are shared pari passu on a pro rata basis between the bank and the guarantor, capital relief is proportional: the protected portion receives the eligible guarantee/credit derivative treatment and the remainder is treated as unsecured.
R-CRE22.80-proportional-cover.quote: Where losses are shared pari passu on a pro rata basis between the bank and the guarantor, capital relief is afforded on a proportional basis, ie the protected portion of the exposure receives the treatment applicable to eligible guarantees /credit derivatives, with the remainder treated as unsecured.

applies_to.note: The rule that makes partially guaranteed government-programme lending computable.

R-CRE22.80-proportional-cover.portfolio_relevance: Makes partially guaranteed loan programmes linearly computable: a 75% government guarantee on an SME loan gives exactly 75% of the exposure the sovereign risk weight.

R-CRE22.81-tranched-protection-securitis.title: Tranched risk transfer is treated under the securitisation standard
R-CRE22.81-tranched-protection-securitis.statement: Where a bank transfers a portion of an exposure's risk in one or more tranches of differing seniority and retains some risk, whether it buys protection on the senior or junior tranche, the rules set out in the securitisation standard apply.
R-CRE22.81-tranched-protection-securitis.quote: Where the bank transfers a portion of the risk of an exposure in one or more tranches to a protection seller or sellers and retains some level of the risk of the loan, and the risk transferred and the risk retained are of different seniority, banks may obtain credit protection for either the senior tranches (eg the second-loss portion) or the junior tranche (eg the first-loss portion). In this case the rules as set out in the securitisation standard apply.

applies_to.note: Redirects to CRE40-CRE45; significant-risk-transfer tests and the securitisation RW floor then apply instead of simple substitution.

R-CRE22.81-tranched-protection-securitis.portfolio_relevance: Marks the boundary where a synthetic risk transfer on a credit-card book stops being simple CRM and becomes a securitisation, subject to a much stricter and less generous capital regime.

R-CRE22.82-guarantee-currency-mismatch.title: Guarantee amount reduced by an FX haircut where currencies differ
R-CRE22.82-guarantee-currency-mismatch.statement: Where credit protection is denominated in a different currency from the exposure, the amount deemed protected must be reduced by applying a currency-mismatch haircut to the nominal amount of the protection.
R-CRE22.82-guarantee-currency-mismatch.quote: Where the credit protection is denominated in a currency different from that in which the exposure is denominated – ie there is a currency mismatch – the amount of the exposure deemed to be protected must be reduced by the application of a haircut

applies_to.note: Parallel to the collateral FX haircut in CRE22.52.

R-CRE22.82-guarantee-currency-mismatch.portfolio_relevance: Reduces the recognised size of foreign-currency guarantees, favouring domestic-currency protection for a single-currency loan book.

R-CRE22.83-guarantee-fx-haircut-8pct.title: 8% currency mismatch haircut for credit protection, scaled by revaluation frequency
R-CRE22.83-guarantee-fx-haircut-8pct.statement: The currency mismatch haircut for credit protection is 8% for a 10-business day holding period assuming daily marking to market, and must be scaled up using the square root of time formula depending on the frequency of revaluation of the protection.
R-CRE22.83-guarantee-fx-haircut-8pct.quote: The currency mismatch haircut for a 10-business day holding period (assuming daily marking to market) is 8%. This haircut must be scaled up using the square root of time formula, depending on the frequency of revaluation of the credit protection as described in CRE22.59.

applies_to.note: Since guarantees are rarely revalued daily, the effective haircut is usually well above 8% after square-root-of-time scaling.

R-CRE22.83-guarantee-fx-haircut-8pct.portfolio_relevance: A cross-currency guarantee revalued only quarterly can attract a haircut several times the headline 8%, which can wipe out most of the intended RWA relief.

R-CRE22.84-sovereign-counter-guarantee.title: Sovereign guarantees and indirect sovereign counter-guarantees may receive the domestic sovereign treatment
R-CRE22.84-sovereign-counter-guarantee.statement: National supervisors may extend the preferential domestic-currency sovereign treatment to portions of exposures guaranteed by the sovereign or central bank where the guarantee is in domestic currency and the exposure funded in that currency; an exposure indirectly counter-guaranteed by a sovereign may be treated as sovereign-guaranteed if the counter-guarantee covers all credit risk elements, both guarantees meet the operational requirements except that the counter-guarantee need not be direct and explicit, and the supervisor is satisfied the cover is robust.
R-CRE22.84-sovereign-counter-guarantee.quote: National supervisors may extend this treatment to portions of exposures guaranteed by the sovereign (or central bank), where the guarantee is denominated in the domestic currency and the exposure is funded in that currency. An exposure may be covered by a guarantee that is indirectly counter-guaranteed by a sovereign. Such an exposure may be treated as covered by a sovereign guarantee provided that: (1) the sovereign counter-guarantee covers all credit risk elements of the exposure; (2) both the original guarantee and the counter-guarantee meet all operational requirements for guarantees, except that the counter-guarantee need not be direct and explicit to the original exposure; and (3) the supervisor is satisfied that the cover is robust and that no historical evidence suggests that the coverage of the counter-guarantee is less than effectively equivalent to that of a direct sovereign guarantee.

applies_to.note: Explicit national discretion plus a supervisory-satisfaction gate on the robustness of the counter-guarantee.

R-CRE22.84-sovereign-counter-guarantee.portfolio_relevance: The route by which US government-agency-guaranteed lending (SBA, guaranteed student and housing programmes) obtains a 0% risk weight, making a shift from unsecured credit cards into guaranteed lending the single largest RWA-reducing portfolio move available to a small bank.

R-LCR20.1-lcr-objective.title: Purpose of the LCR: survive a 30-calendar-day liquidity stress
R-LCR20.1-lcr-objective.statement: The LCR requires a bank to hold sufficient high-quality liquid assets to survive a significant liquidity stress scenario lasting 30 calendar days.
R-LCR20.1-lcr-objective.quote: to promote the short-term resilience of the liquidity risk profile of banks by ensuring that they have sufficient high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) to survive a significant stress scenario lasting 30 calendar days.

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR20.1-lcr-objective.portfolio_relevance: Sets the 30-day measurement window; any funding or asset repricing pushed beyond 30 days drops out of the constraint entirely, rewarding term-extension of liabilities.

R-LCR20.2-stress-undrawn-facilities.title: LCR stress scenario includes unscheduled draws on committed but unused credit and liquidity facilities
R-LCR20.2-stress-undrawn-facilities.statement: The prescribed LCR stress scenario assumes unscheduled draws on committed but unused credit and liquidity facilities the bank has provided to clients.
R-LCR20.2-stress-undrawn-facilities.quote: (6) unscheduled draws on committed but unused credit and liquidity facilities that the bank has provided to its clients;

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR20.2-stress-undrawn-facilities.portfolio_relevance: Establishes that unused credit card lines and other undrawn commitments are a modelled liquidity drain, so growing open-to-buy raises the HQLA requirement even with no balance growth.

R-LCR20.2-stress-retail-runoff.title: LCR stress scenario includes run-off of a proportion of retail deposits
R-LCR20.2-stress-retail-runoff.statement: The LCR scenario is a combined idiosyncratic and market-wide shock whose first element is the run-off of a proportion of retail deposits.
R-LCR20.2-stress-retail-runoff.quote: The scenario for this standard entails a combined idiosyncratic and market-wide shock that would result in: (1) the run-off of a proportion of retail deposits;

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR20.2-stress-retail-runoff.portfolio_relevance: Frames retail deposit funding as the primary stressed outflow, so a card-lending bank funded by retail deposits is penalised on both sides of the ratio.

R-LCR20.3-internal-stress-tests.title: LCR is a minimum; banks must run their own longer-horizon stress tests
R-LCR20.3-internal-stress-tests.statement: The LCR stress test is a minimum supervisory requirement and banks are expected to run additional internal stress tests over longer horizons to size liquidity above the minimum.
R-LCR20.3-internal-stress-tests.quote: This stress test should be viewed as a minimum supervisory requirement for banks. Banks are expected to conduct their own stress tests to assess the level of liquidity they should hold beyond this minimum

applies_to.note: Expectation applies to all banks; scale of internal programme is proportionate to the bank's business activities.

R-LCR20.3-internal-stress-tests.portfolio_relevance: Means a bank cannot optimise portfolio composition purely to a 100% LCR; concentrated card portfolios with volatile draw behaviour attract additional internally-assessed buffers.

R-LCR20.4-two-components.title: LCR has two components: stock of HQLA and total net cash outflows
R-LCR20.4-two-components.statement: The LCR is composed of the stressed value of the stock of HQLA (numerator) and total net cash outflows over 30 days (denominator).
R-LCR20.4-two-components.quote: The LCR has two components: (1) value of the stock of HQLA in stressed conditions; and (2) total net cash outflows

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR20.4-two-components.portfolio_relevance: Defines the two levers: raise HQLA or cut 30-day net outflows; shifting assets from cards into Level 1 securities moves both simultaneously.

R-LCR20.5-minimum-100pct.title: Minimum LCR of 100%
R-LCR20.5-minimum-100pct.statement: Absent financial stress, a bank's LCR must be no lower than 100%, ie the stock of HQLA must at least equal total net cash outflows over 30 days, on an ongoing basis.
R-LCR20.5-minimum-100pct.quote: The standard requires that, absent a situation of financial stress, the value of the ratio be no lower than 100% (ie the stock of HQLA should at least equal total net cash outflows) on an ongoing basis

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR20.5-minimum-100pct.portfolio_relevance: The binding ratio constraint: every additional dollar of stressed net outflow generated by growing undrawn card lines or less-stable deposits must be matched dollar-for-dollar with HQLA.

R-LCR20.5-30-day-horizon.title: Net cash outflows measured over 30 calendar days
R-LCR20.5-30-day-horizon.statement: Total net cash outflows for the LCR scenario are calculated for 30 calendar days into the future.
R-LCR20.5-30-day-horizon.quote: The total net cash outflows for the scenario are to be calculated for 30 calendar days into the future.

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR20.5-30-day-horizon.portfolio_relevance: Fixes the maturity boundary that determines which deposits, drawdowns and loan receipts enter the calculation.

R-LCR20.5-usability-in-stress.title: HQLA may be used in stress, allowing the LCR to fall below 100%
R-LCR20.5-usability-in-stress.statement: During periods of stress it is appropriate for banks to draw down the stock of HQLA and thereby fall below the 100% minimum.
R-LCR20.5-usability-in-stress.quote: During periods of stress, however, it would be entirely appropriate for banks to use their stock of HQLA, thereby falling below the minimum.

applies_to.note: Usability is a supervisory judgement; supervisors assess and give guidance according to circumstances.

R-LCR20.5-usability-in-stress.portfolio_relevance: Makes the 100% floor soft in stress, so an optimiser should treat LCR as a soft constraint with a supervisory penalty rather than a hard bound.

R-LCR20.6-proportionate-response.title: Supervisory response to a reported LCR below 100% must be proportionate
R-LCR20.6-proportionate-response.statement: Supervisors should allow differentiated responses to an LCR below 100%, proportionate to the drivers, magnitude, duration and frequency of the shortfall.
R-LCR20.6-proportionate-response.quote: (2) Supervisors should allow for differentiated responses to a reported LCR below 100%. Any potential supervisory response should be proportionate with the drivers, magnitude, duration and frequency of the reported shortfall.

applies_to.note: Explicit proportionality gate on supervisory action, not on the requirement itself.

R-LCR20.6-proportionate-response.portfolio_relevance: Implies the cost of a shortfall is graduated, which matters when sizing how close to 100% a card-heavy balance sheet should be run.

R-LCR20.7-monthly-reporting.title: LCR must be reported at least monthly with capacity for weekly or daily
R-LCR20.7-monthly-reporting.statement: Banks must report the LCR to supervisors at least monthly and have the operational capacity to report weekly or daily in stressed situations at supervisory discretion.
R-LCR20.7-monthly-reporting.quote: The LCR must be reported to supervisors at least monthly, with the operational capacity to increase the frequency to weekly or even daily in stressed situations at the discretion of the supervisors.

applies_to.note: Frequency escalation is at supervisory discretion; reporting lag ideally no more than two weeks.

numeric_values: reporting lag no more than two weeks
R-LCR20.7-monthly-reporting.portfolio_relevance: Establishes the observation frequency; quarterly published financials are a coarser proxy than the regime itself assumes.

R-LCR20.8-notify-breach.title: Immediate notification if LCR has fallen or is expected to fall below 100%
R-LCR20.8-notify-breach.statement: Banks must notify supervisors immediately if their LCR has fallen, or is expected to fall, below 100%.
R-LCR20.8-notify-breach.quote: Banks must also notify supervisors immediately if their LCR has fallen, or is expected to fall, below 100%.

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR20.8-notify-breach.portfolio_relevance: Creates a hard trigger event, so any portfolio shift that forecasts an LCR below 100% carries a supervisory notification cost.

R-LCR30.1-hqla-numerator.title: Numerator must be unencumbered HQLA covering 30-day net outflows
R-LCR30.1-hqla-numerator.statement: Banks must hold a stock of unencumbered HQLA sufficient to cover total net cash outflows over a 30-day period under the prescribed stress scenario.
R-LCR30.1-hqla-numerator.quote: banks must hold a stock of unencumbered HQLA to cover the total net cash outflows (as defined in LCR40) over a 30-day period under the stress scenario prescribed in LCR20.

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR30.1-hqla-numerator.portfolio_relevance: Requires that the offsetting asset be unencumbered and liquid, so pledged securities backing FHLB advances cannot also relieve card-line outflow pressure.

R-LCR30.15-periodic-monetisation.title: Periodic monetisation of a representative proportion of HQLA
R-LCR30.15-periodic-monetisation.statement: A bank must periodically monetise a representative proportion of its HQLA stock via repo or outright sale to test market access and monetisation processes.
R-LCR30.15-periodic-monetisation.quote: A bank must periodically monetise a representative proportion of the assets in the stock through repo or outright sale, in order to test its access to the market, the effectiveness of its processes for monetisation, the availability of the assets, and to minimise the risk of negative signalling during a period of actual stress.

applies_to.note: May be satisfied through normal-course business transactions; extent and frequency assessed case by case.

R-LCR30.15-periodic-monetisation.portfolio_relevance: Operational cost attached to holding HQLA, mildly reducing the attractiveness of very large securities buffers held purely for ratio management.

R-LCR30.16-unencumbered.title: Definition of unencumbered for HQLA eligibility
R-LCR30.16-unencumbered.statement: All assets in the HQLA stock must be unencumbered, meaning free of legal, regulatory, contractual or other restrictions on the bank's ability to liquidate, sell, transfer or assign the asset.
R-LCR30.16-unencumbered.quote: All assets in the stock must be unencumbered. “Unencumbered” means free of legal, regulatory, contractual or other restrictions on the ability of the bank to liquidate, sell, transfer or assign the asset.

applies_to.note: Assets pre-positioned or pledged to a central bank or PSE but not used to generate liquidity may still be included.

R-LCR30.16-unencumbered.portfolio_relevance: Directly penalises balance sheets that pledge securities for secured borrowings or public deposits, a common structure at small banks.

R-LCR30.18-treasury-control.title: HQLA must be under the control of the liquidity management function
R-LCR30.18-treasury-control.statement: The HQLA stock must be under the continuous authority and legal and operational control of the function managing the bank's liquidity, with demonstrated ability to monetise any asset at any point in the 30-day stress period.
R-LCR30.18-treasury-control.quote: The stock must be under the control of the function charged with managing the liquidity of the bank (eg the treasurer), meaning the function has the continuous authority, and legal and operational capability, to monetise any asset in the stock.
R-LCR30.18-treasury-control.portfolio_relevance: Securities held for hedging or ALM strategies that cannot be sold without breaching internal risk limits cannot count as HQLA.

R-LCR30.24-rehypothecation-exclusion.title: Assets received under right of rehypothecation excluded when withdrawable within 30 days
R-LCR30.24-rehypothecation-exclusion.statement: Banks must not include in HQLA any assets, or liquidity generated from assets, received under right of rehypothecation where the beneficial owner may contractually withdraw them within the 30-day stress period.
R-LCR30.24-rehypothecation-exclusion.quote: Banks must not include in the stock of HQLA any assets, or liquidity generated from assets, they have received under right of rehypothecation, if the beneficial owner has the contractual right to withdraw those assets during the 30-day stress period.

applies_to.note: Materially relevant only to banks with securities financing activity.

R-LCR30.24-rehypothecation-exclusion.portfolio_relevance: Blocks inflating HQLA with borrowed collateral, so the buffer must be genuinely owned.

R-LCR30.28-30day-cliff-grace.title: 30 calendar-day grace period when an HQLA asset becomes ineligible
R-LCR30.28-30day-cliff-grace.statement: Where an eligible liquid asset becomes ineligible (eg on rating downgrade), the bank may keep it in the HQLA stock for an additional 30 calendar days.
R-LCR30.28-30day-cliff-grace.quote: a bank is permitted to keep such assets in its stock of liquid assets for an additional 30 calendar days.
R-LCR30.28-30day-cliff-grace.portfolio_relevance: Softens cliff risk on rating migration of corporate or covered bond holdings in the buffer.

R-LCR30.29-diversification.title: HQLA stock should be diversified within asset classes
R-LCR30.29-diversification.statement: The HQLA stock should be well diversified within asset classes, other than home-jurisdiction sovereign debt, central bank reserves, central bank debt securities and cash, and banks should set concentration limits.
R-LCR30.29-diversification.quote: The stock of HQLA should be well diversified within the asset classes themselves (except for sovereign debt of the bank’s home jurisdiction or from the jurisdiction in which the bank operates; central bank reserves; central bank debt securities; and cash).
R-LCR30.29-diversification.portfolio_relevance: Rewards a buffer built on cash, reserves and domestic sovereigns, which carry no diversification obligation, over corporate bond buffers.

R-LCR30.31-level2-40pct-cap.title: Level 1 assets unlimited; Level 2 assets capped at 40% of the HQLA stock
R-LCR30.31-level2-40pct-cap.statement: Level 1 assets may be included in the HQLA stock without limit, while Level 2 assets may comprise no more than 40% of the stock.
R-LCR30.31-level2-40pct-cap.quote: There are two categories of assets that can be included in the stock. Assets to be included in each category are those that the bank is holding on the first day of the stress period, irrespective of their residual maturity. “Level 1” assets can be included without limit, while “Level 2” assets can only comprise up to 40% of the stock.

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR30.31-level2-40pct-cap.portfolio_relevance: Caps how far a bank can meet the buffer with yield-bearing Level 2 securities, forcing low-yield cash and sovereigns and raising the opportunity cost of the buffer that card growth generates.

R-LCR30.33-level2b-15pct-cap.title: Level 2B assets capped at 15% of the HQLA stock
R-LCR30.33-level2b-15pct-cap.statement: Where a supervisor permits Level 2B assets, they must not exceed 15% of the total HQLA stock and must also fit within the overall 40% Level 2 cap.
R-LCR30.33-level2b-15pct-cap.quote: If included, these assets must not comprise more than 15% of the total stock of HQLA. They must also be included within the overall 40% cap on Level 2 assets.

applies_to.note: Inclusion of Level 2B is at national discretion; the 15% cap applies only where the supervisor permits the category.

R-LCR30.33-level2b-15pct-cap.portfolio_relevance: Strictly bounds the amount of RMBS, BBB corporates and equities that can count, limiting how much a bank can self-fund the buffer out of securitised retail assets.

R-LCR30.34-caps-post-haircut.title: Level 2 and Level 2B caps determined after haircuts and after unwinding short-term SFTs
R-LCR30.34-caps-post-haircut.statement: The 40% Level 2 and 15% Level 2B caps must be computed after required haircuts and after unwinding short-term securities financing and collateral swap transactions maturing within 30 calendar days that involve an exchange of HQLA.
R-LCR30.34-caps-post-haircut.quote: The 40% cap on Level 2 assets and the 15% cap on Level 2B assets must be determined after the application of required haircuts, and after taking into account the unwind of short-term securities financing transactions and collateral swap transactions maturing within 30 calendar days that involve the exchange of HQLA.
R-LCR30.34-caps-post-haircut.portfolio_relevance: Prevents window-dressing the buffer composition through repo, making the cap bind on economic rather than reported holdings.

R-LCR30.35-level2-two-thirds.title: Adjusted Level 2 assets capped at two-thirds of adjusted Level 1 assets
R-LCR30.35-level2-two-thirds.statement: The maximum amount of adjusted Level 2 assets equals two-thirds of the adjusted amount of Level 1 assets after haircuts.
R-LCR30.35-level2-two-thirds.quote: The maximum amount of adjusted Level 2 assets is equal to two-thirds of the adjusted amount of Level 1 assets after haircuts have been applied.
R-LCR30.35-level2-two-thirds.portfolio_relevance: Restates the 40% cap as a computable ratio: every dollar of Level 2 in the buffer requires 1.5 dollars of Level 1.

R-LCR30.36-level2b-15-85-ratio.title: Adjusted Level 2B assets capped at 15/85 of Level 1 plus Level 2A, or 1/4 of Level 1
R-LCR30.36-level2b-15-85-ratio.statement: The maximum amount of adjusted Level 2B assets equals 15/85 times the sum of adjusted Level 1 and Level 2A assets, or, where the 40% cap binds, at most 1/4 times adjusted Level 1 assets, both after haircuts.
R-LCR30.36-level2b-15-85-ratio.quote: The maximum amount of adjusted Level 2B assets is equal to the ratio of 15/85 times the sum of the adjusted amounts of Level 1 and Level 2A assets, or, in cases where the 40% cap is binding, up to a maximum of 1/4 times the adjusted amount of Level 1 assets, both after haircuts have been applied.
R-LCR30.36-level2b-15-85-ratio.portfolio_relevance: Gives the exact arithmetic bound on retained RMBS and low-rated corporates in the buffer.

R-LCR30.40-level1-no-haircut.title: Level 1 assets carry no haircut and no cap
R-LCR30.40-level1-no-haircut.statement: Level 1 assets may comprise an unlimited share of the HQLA pool and are not subject to a haircut under the LCR, although national supervisors may impose haircuts on Level 1 securities.
R-LCR30.40-level1-no-haircut.quote: Level 1 assets can comprise an unlimited share of the pool and are not subject to a haircut under the LCR.

applies_to.note: National supervisors may require haircuts on Level 1 securities; Level 1 must be measured at no greater than current market value.

R-LCR30.40-level1-no-haircut.portfolio_relevance: Makes reserves and Treasuries the cheapest way to satisfy the buffer generated by retail deposit run-off and card-line draws.

R-LCR30.41-level1-cash-reserves.title: Level 1 assets include coins, banknotes and drawable central bank reserves
R-LCR30.41-level1-cash-reserves.statement: Level 1 assets are limited to a closed list beginning with coins and banknotes and central bank reserves, including required reserves, to the extent central bank policy allows them to be drawn down in stress.
R-LCR30.41-level1-cash-reserves.quote: Level 1 assets are limited to: (1) coins and banknotes; (2) central bank reserves (including required reserves), to the extent that the central bank policies allow them to be drawn down in times of stress;

applies_to.note: The extent to which required reserves count is agreed between the local supervisor and the central bank.

R-LCR30.41-level1-cash-reserves.portfolio_relevance: Interest-bearing balances at the Federal Reserve are the dominant Level 1 line for small US banks and the direct offset to stressed outflows.

R-LCR30.41-level1-0pct-rw-securities.title: Level 1 marketable securities must carry a 0% standardised risk weight
R-LCR30.41-level1-0pct-rw-securities.statement: Marketable securities claiming on or guaranteed by sovereigns, central banks, PSEs, the BIS, IMF, ECB, ESM, EFSF or MDBs qualify as Level 1 only if, among other conditions, they are assigned a 0% risk weight under the standardised approach to credit risk.
R-LCR30.41-level1-0pct-rw-securities.quote: (3) marketable securities representing claims on or guaranteed by sovereigns, central banks, PSEs, the Bank for International Settlements, the International Monetary Fund, the European Central Bank and European Community, the European Stability Mechanism, the European Financial Stability Facility or multilateral development banks, and satisfying all of the following conditions: (a) assigned a 0% risk weight under the standardised approach to credit risk;

applies_to.note: Ties HQLA eligibility to the CRE20 standardised risk weight; also requires deep repo markets, a proven stress record, and no financial-institution obligation.

R-LCR30.41-level1-0pct-rw-securities.portfolio_relevance: Directly links the credit-risk risk weight to liquidity eligibility, so buying 0% RW sovereigns improves both RWA density and the LCR.

R-LCR30.42-level2-40pct-of-stock.title: Level 2 assets no more than 40% of overall stock after haircuts
R-LCR30.42-level2-40pct-of-stock.statement: Level 2 assets, comprising Level 2A and any supervisor-permitted Level 2B assets, may be included in HQLA only up to 40% of the overall stock after haircuts.
R-LCR30.42-level2-40pct-of-stock.quote: Level 2 assets (comprising Level 2A assets and any Level 2B assets permitted by the supervisor) can be included in the stock of HQLA, subject to the requirement that they comprise no more than 40% of the overall stock after haircuts have been applied.
R-LCR30.42-level2-40pct-of-stock.portfolio_relevance: Restates the binding composition constraint on the numerator that any buffer-building strategy must satisfy.

R-LCR30.43-level2a-15pct-haircut.title: 15% haircut on Level 2A assets
R-LCR30.43-level2a-15pct-haircut.statement: A 15% haircut is applied to the current market value of each Level 2A asset held in the HQLA stock.
R-LCR30.43-level2a-15pct-haircut.quote: A 15% haircut is applied to the current market value of each Level 2A asset held in the stock of HQLA. Level 2A assets are limited to the following:
R-LCR30.43-level2a-15pct-haircut.portfolio_relevance: Makes agency and high-grade corporate holdings worth only 85 cents of buffer per dollar, a computable drag when a bank funds card growth with securities sales.

R-LCR30.43-level2a-20pct-rw.title: Level 2A sovereign, PSE and MDB securities must carry a 20% risk weight
R-LCR30.43-level2a-20pct-rw.statement: Marketable securities on or guaranteed by sovereigns, central banks, PSEs or MDBs qualify as Level 2A only if assigned a 20% risk weight under CRE20, among other market-depth and non-financial-issuer conditions.
R-LCR30.43-level2a-20pct-rw.quote: (1) Marketable securities representing claims on or guaranteed by sovereigns, central banks, PSEs or multilateral development banks that satisfy all of the following conditions: (a) assigned a 20% risk weight under CRE20;

applies_to.note: Requires maximum price decline not exceeding 10% or haircut increase not exceeding 10 percentage points over a 30-day stress period.

R-LCR30.43-level2a-20pct-rw.portfolio_relevance: Another direct SA risk-weight-to-liquidity link, guiding which government-related securities a small bank should hold.

R-LCR30.43-level2a-corporate-aa.title: Level 2A corporate debt and covered bonds require a rating of at least AA-
R-LCR30.43-level2a-corporate-aa.statement: Corporate debt securities and covered bonds qualify as Level 2A only if not issued by a financial institution (or the bank itself for covered bonds) and rated at least AA- by a recognised ECAI, or internally rated at a PD corresponding to AA-.
R-LCR30.43-level2a-corporate-aa.quote: (2) Corporate debt securities (including commercial paper) and covered bonds that satisfy all the following conditions: (a) in the case of corporate debt securities: not issued by a financial institution or any of its affiliated entities; (b) in the case of covered bonds: not issued by the bank itself or any of its affiliated entities; (c) either: (i) have a long-term credit rating from a recognised external credit assessment institution (ECAI) of at least AA- or in the absence of a long-term rating, a short-term rating equivalent in quality to the long-term rating; or (ii) do not have a credit assessment by a recognised ECAI but are internally rated as having a probability of default (PD) corresponding to a credit rating of at least AA-;

applies_to.note: Local ECAI rating scales may be recognised for local-currency liquidity needs; internal PD-based rating requires the relevant credit-risk machinery.

R-LCR30.43-level2a-corporate-aa.portfolio_relevance: Sets the credit quality floor above which a corporate bond portfolio contributes to the buffer at an 85% value.

R-LCR30.44-level2b-national-discretion.title: Level 2B inclusion is at national discretion
R-LCR30.44-level2b-national-discretion.statement: Level 2B assets may be included in Level 2 only at the discretion of national authorities, who must ensure full compliance with the qualifying criteria and adequate bank systems to monitor the risks.
R-LCR30.44-level2b-national-discretion.quote: Certain additional assets (Level 2B assets) may be included in Level 2 at the discretion of national authorities.

applies_to.note: Explicit national-discretion gate: a jurisdiction may exclude Level 2B entirely.

R-LCR30.44-level2b-national-discretion.portfolio_relevance: Whether retained RMBS from a securitised card or mortgage book can count as buffer is a jurisdictional switch, not a Basel entitlement.

R-LCR30.45-rmbs-25pct-haircut.title: Eligible RMBS included in Level 2B subject to a 25% haircut
R-LCR30.45-rmbs-25pct-haircut.statement: Residential mortgage backed securities meeting all the specified conditions may be included in Level 2B subject to a 25% haircut.
R-LCR30.45-rmbs-25pct-haircut.quote: (1) Residential mortgage backed securities (RMBS) that satisfy all of the following conditions may be included in Level 2B, subject to a 25% haircut:

applies_to.note: Subject to the national-discretion gate on Level 2B and the 15% Level 2B cap.

R-LCR30.45-rmbs-25pct-haircut.portfolio_relevance: Retained senior RMBS is worth 75 cents on the dollar of buffer and only within the 15% cap, so securitising retail assets is a weak route to liquidity relief.

R-LCR30.45-rmbs-ltv-80.title: Level 2B RMBS underlying mortgages must be full recourse with maximum 80% average LTV at issuance
R-LCR30.45-rmbs-ltv-80.statement: RMBS qualify for Level 2B only where the underlying mortgages are full recourse loans with a maximum loan-to-value ratio of 80% on average at issuance.
R-LCR30.45-rmbs-ltv-80.quote: (f) the underlying mortgages are “full recourse” loans (ie in the case of foreclosure the mortgage owner remains liable for any shortfall in sales proceeds from the property) and have a maximum loan-to-value ratio (LTV) of 80% on average at issuance;

applies_to.note: The 80% LTV test is the weighted-average LTV of the underlying pool at the time the RMBS is issued, not a per-loan limit; also requires the RMBS to be issued by a third party and subject to risk-retention rules.

R-LCR30.45-rmbs-ltv-80.portfolio_relevance: Non-recourse US residential mortgages generally fail this test, so US RMBS holdings are a poor buffer candidate and cash or Treasuries dominate.

R-LCR30.45-corporate-2b-50pct-haircut.title: Level 2B corporate debt securities subject to a 50% haircut
R-LCR30.45-corporate-2b-50pct-haircut.statement: Corporate debt securities meeting the specified conditions, including a rating of at least BBB-, may be included in Level 2B subject to a 50% haircut.
R-LCR30.45-corporate-2b-50pct-haircut.quote: (2) Corporate debt securities (including commercial paper) that satisfy all of the following conditions may be included in Level 2B, subject to a 50% haircut:

applies_to.note: Requires at least BBB- from a recognised ECAI or an equivalent internal PD, non-financial issuer, and maximum price decline not exceeding 20% over a 30-day stress period.

R-LCR30.45-corporate-2b-50pct-haircut.portfolio_relevance: Investment-grade but sub-AA corporate bonds count for only half their market value and only inside the 15% cap.

R-LCR30.45-equity-50pct-haircut.title: Level 2B common equity shares subject to a 50% haircut
R-LCR30.45-equity-50pct-haircut.statement: Common equity shares meeting the specified conditions, including index membership and exchange trading, may be included in Level 2B subject to a 50% haircut.
R-LCR30.45-equity-50pct-haircut.quote: (3) Common equity shares that satisfy all of the following conditions may be included in Level 2B, subject to a 50% haircut:

applies_to.note: Requires major-index membership decided by the supervisor and maximum price decline not exceeding 40% over a 30-day stress period; small banks rarely hold qualifying equity.

R-LCR30.45-equity-50pct-haircut.portfolio_relevance: Equities are a heavily discounted and capped buffer source, rarely material for a small deposit-funded card lender.

R-LCR30.46-rclf-75bp-fee.title: Restricted-use committed liquidity facility must carry a commitment fee of at least 75bp
R-LCR30.46-rclf-75bp-fee.statement: A central bank restricted-use committed liquidity facility counted in Level 2B must, in normal times, carry a commitment fee on the total drawn and undrawn amount of at least the greater of 75 basis points per annum, or 25 basis points per annum above the yield differential between the securing assets and a representative HQLA portfolio.
R-LCR30.46-rclf-75bp-fee.quote: (a) 75 basis points per annum; or (b) at least 25 basis points per annum above the difference in yield on the assets used to secure the RCLF and the yield on a representative portfolio of HQLA after adjusting for any material differences in credit risk.

applies_to.note: Available only where the national central bank offers RCLFs and the national authority permits their inclusion in HQLA.

numeric_values: 25 basis points per annum above yield differential
R-LCR30.46-rclf-75bp-fee.portfolio_relevance: Prices an alternative to holding securities outright; where offered, it converts a buffer requirement into an annual fee rather than a balance-sheet reallocation.

R-LCR40.1-net-cash-outflow-definition.title: Total net cash outflows defined as expected outflows minus expected inflows over 30 days
R-LCR40.1-net-cash-outflow-definition.statement: Total net cash outflows is the total expected cash outflows minus total expected cash inflows in the specified stress scenario for the subsequent 30 calendar days.
R-LCR40.1-net-cash-outflow-definition.quote: The term total net cash outflows is defined as the total expected cash outflows minus total expected cash inflows in the specified stress scenario for the subsequent 30 calendar days.

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR40.1-net-cash-outflow-definition.portfolio_relevance: Defines the denominator that portfolio composition drives: deposit mix determines outflows and loan amortisation determines inflows.

R-LCR40.1-outflow-computation.title: Expected outflows are balances multiplied by run-off and drawdown rates
R-LCR40.1-outflow-computation.statement: Total expected cash outflows are computed by multiplying the outstanding balances of each category of liability and off-balance sheet commitment by the applicable run-off or drawdown rate.
R-LCR40.1-outflow-computation.quote: Total expected cash outflows are calculated by multiplying the outstanding balances of various categories or types of liabilities and off-balance sheet commitments by the rates at which they are expected to run off or be drawn down.

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR40.1-outflow-computation.portfolio_relevance: This is the computable core: outflow = sum over buckets of balance times factor, with undrawn card lines entering as an off-balance sheet commitment balance.

R-LCR40.1-inflow-cap-75pct.title: Expected cash inflows capped at 75% of total expected cash outflows
R-LCR40.1-inflow-cap-75pct.statement: Total expected cash inflows are balances of contractual receivables multiplied by prescribed inflow rates, subject to an aggregate cap of 75% of total expected cash outflows.
R-LCR40.1-inflow-cap-75pct.quote: Total expected cash inflows are calculated by multiplying the outstanding balances of various categories of contractual receivables by the rates at which they are expected to flow in under the scenario up to an aggregate cap of 75% of total expected cash outflows.

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR40.1-inflow-cap-75pct.portfolio_relevance: Caps how much scheduled card and loan repayment can offset stressed outflows, so a high-yield amortising retail book cannot fully substitute for HQLA.

R-LCR40.2-national-parameters.title: Certain run-off parameters are set nationally and must be publicly transparent
R-LCR40.2-national-parameters.statement: While most run-off and drawdown rates are harmonised, a few parameters are set by national supervisors and must be transparent and publicly available.
R-LCR40.2-national-parameters.quote: a few parameters are to be determined by supervisory authorities at the national level. Where this is the case, the parameters should be transparent and made publicly available.

applies_to.note: Explicit national-discretion carve-out; the US assigns its own rates for less-stable deposits and revocable commitments.

R-LCR40.2-national-parameters.portfolio_relevance: Flags that the credit-card-relevant factors (revocable line run-off, less-stable deposit buckets) are jurisdiction-set, so any US evaluation must overlay 12 CFR 249 rates.

R-LCR40.4-no-double-counting.title: No double-counting of items between HQLA and inflows, and outflow capped at maximum contractual amount
R-LCR40.4-no-double-counting.statement: An asset counted in HQLA cannot also generate a counted cash inflow, and where an item could fall in multiple outflow categories the bank need assume only up to the maximum contractual outflow for that product.
R-LCR40.4-no-double-counting.quote: Banks will not be permitted to double-count items, ie if an asset is included as part of the stock of high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) (ie the numerator), the associated cash inflows cannot also be counted as cash inflows (ie part of the denominator). Where there is potential that an item could be counted in multiple outflow categories (eg committed liquidity facilities granted to cover debt maturing within the 30 calendar day period), a bank only has to assume up to the maximum contractual outflow for that product.
R-LCR40.4-no-double-counting.portfolio_relevance: Prevents a security in the buffer from also being counted as a maturing inflow, tightening the effective coverage of card-line drawdowns.

R-LCR40.5-retail-deposit-definition.title: Retail deposits defined as deposits placed by a natural person
R-LCR40.5-retail-deposit-definition.statement: Retail deposits are deposits placed with a bank by a natural person; deposits from legal entities, sole proprietorships or partnerships fall into wholesale categories.
R-LCR40.5-retail-deposit-definition.quote: Retail deposits are defined as deposits placed with a bank by a natural person. Deposits from legal entities, sole proprietorships or partnerships are captured in wholesale deposit categories.

applies_to.note: Retail deposits include demand and term deposits unless excluded under LCR40.16 and LCR40.17.

R-LCR40.5-retail-deposit-definition.portfolio_relevance: The classification gate determining whether a deposit runs at 3-10% or at 20-100%, and hence the single largest driver of a small bank's stressed outflow.

R-LCR40.6-runoff-rates-are-floors.title: Retail deposit run-off rates are minimum floors
R-LCR40.6-runoff-rates-are-floors.statement: Retail deposits are split into stable and less stable portions with prescribed minimum run-off rates, which are floors that individual jurisdictions may raise to capture local depositor behaviour in stress.
R-LCR40.6-runoff-rates-are-floors.quote: These retail deposits are divided into “stable” and “less stable” portions of funds as described below, with minimum run-off rates listed for each category. The run- off rates for retail deposits are minimum floors, with higher run-off rates established by individual jurisdictions as appropriate to capture depositor behaviour in a period of stress in each jurisdiction.

applies_to.note: Explicit national discretion to set higher rates; Basel numbers are minimums, not the applied rates.

R-LCR40.6-runoff-rates-are-floors.portfolio_relevance: Means an evaluation against real US filings must treat 3%/5%/10% as lower bounds on the deposit outflow the bank actually faces.

R-LCR40.7-stable-deposit-5pct.title: Stable retail deposits receive a 5% run-off factor
R-LCR40.7-stable-deposit-5pct.statement: Stable deposits, which usually receive a 5% run-off factor, are deposits fully insured by an effective deposit insurance scheme or equivalent public guarantee where the depositor has an established relationship or the deposit is in a transactional account.
R-LCR40.7-stable-deposit-5pct.quote: Stable deposits, which usually receive a run-off factor of 5%, are the amount of the deposits that are fully insured by an effective deposit insurance scheme or by a public guarantee that provides equivalent protection and where:

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; the US LCR (12 CFR 249) applies only to Category I-IV firms (broadly >= $100bn assets), so small North American banks are outside the binding scope and this is a shadow/benchmark metric for them.

R-LCR40.7-stable-deposit-5pct.portfolio_relevance: Rewards insured transactional deposit funding: a bank funding a card book with fully-insured checking accounts needs one half the buffer per dollar compared with less-stable funding.

R-LCR40.7-fully-insured-definition.title: Fully insured means 100% of the deposit amount up to the insurance limit
R-LCR40.7-fully-insured-definition.statement: Fully insured means 100% of the deposit amount, up to the deposit insurance limit, is covered by an effective deposit insurance scheme; balances above the limit must be treated as less stable.
R-LCR40.7-fully-insured-definition.quote: “Fully insured” means that 100% of the deposit amount, up to the deposit insurance limit, is covered by an effective deposit insurance scheme.

applies_to.note: If the scheme covers only a percentage of funds from the first currency unit, the entire deposit is less stable.

R-LCR40.7-fully-insured-definition.portfolio_relevance: Makes the insured/uninsured split (FDIC-insured versus above-limit balances) the direct computable input for the stable/less-stable allocation.

R-LCR40.8-effective-dis-definition.title: Definition of an effective deposit insurance scheme
R-LCR40.8-effective-dis-definition.statement: An effective deposit insurance scheme guarantees prompt payouts, has clearly defined coverage, high public awareness, and an insurer with formal legal powers that is operationally independent, transparent and accountable.
R-LCR40.8-effective-dis-definition.quote: an “effective deposit insurance scheme” refers to a scheme: (1) that guarantees that it has the ability to make prompt payouts; (2) for which the coverage is clearly defined; (3) of which public awareness is high; and (4) in which the deposit insurer has formal legal powers to fulfil its mandate and is operationally independent, transparent and accountable.
