R-CRE20.44-corporate-100pct-no-external-.quote: banks will assign a 100% risk weight to all corporate exposures, with the exception of: (1) exposures to corporates identified as “investment grade” in CRE20.46; and (2) exposures to corporate SMEs in CRE20.47.

applies_to.note: This is the operative corporate rule for US banks under Dodd-Frank s939A; only two carve-outs exist.

R-CRE20.44-corporate-100pct-no-external-.portfolio_relevance: Fixes the commercial loan book at 100% with no rating-based relief, so for a US small bank the only levers on corporate RWA are the 65% investment-grade and 85% SME carve-outs.

R-CRE20.46-investment-grade-corporate-65.title: 65% risk weight for investment grade corporates in no-ratings jurisdictions
R-CRE20.46-investment-grade-corporate-65.statement: Banks in jurisdictions that do not allow regulatory use of external ratings may assign a 65% risk weight to corporates assessed as investment grade, provided the corporate or its parent has securities outstanding on a recognised securities exchange.
R-CRE20.46-investment-grade-corporate-65.quote: may assign a 65% risk weight to exposures to "investment grade" corporates. An "investment grade" corporate is a corporate entity that has adequate capacity to meet its financial commitments in a timely manner and its ability to do so is assessed to be robust against adverse changes in the economic cycle and business conditions. When making this determination, the bank should assess the corporate entity against the investment grade definition taking into account the complexity of its business model, performance against industry and peers, and risks posed by the entity's operating environment. Moreover, the corporate entity (or its parent company) must have securities outstanding on a recognised securities exchange.

applies_to.note: Requires a listed-securities test, which most of a small community bank's commercial borrowers fail.

R-CRE20.46-investment-grade-corporate-65.portfolio_relevance: Offers a 35 percentage point RWA saving on large listed corporate borrowers, but the listing test makes it largely unavailable to small banks lending to private local businesses.

R-CRE20.47-corporate-sme-definition-50m.title: Definition of a corporate SME: consolidated annual sales up to EUR 50 million
R-CRE20.47-corporate-sme-definition-50m.statement: A corporate SME is a corporate exposure where reported annual sales for the consolidated group of which the counterparty is part are less than or equal to EUR 50 million for the most recent financial year.
R-CRE20.47-corporate-sme-definition-50m.quote: Corporate SMEs are defined as corporate exposures where the reported annual sales for the consolidated group of which the corporate counterparty is a part is less than or equal to €50 million for the most recent financial year.

applies_to.note: National supervisors may set a more conservative (lower) sales threshold; the euro figure requires currency conversion for North American reporting.

numeric_values: annual sales less than or equal to EUR 50 million
R-CRE20.47-corporate-sme-definition-50m.portfolio_relevance: Draws the line between the 85% SME weight and the 100% general corporate weight, so borrower sales size is a directly capital-relevant portfolio attribute.

R-CRE20.47-corporate-sme-85pct.title: 85% risk weight for corporate SME exposures
R-CRE20.47-corporate-sme-85pct.statement: An 85% risk weight applies to unrated corporate SME exposures in jurisdictions allowing external ratings and to all corporate SME exposures in jurisdictions that do not allow them.
R-CRE20.47-corporate-sme-85pct.quote: For unrated exposures to corporate SMEs in jurisdictions that allow the use of external ratings for regulatory purposes, and for all exposures to corporate SMEs in jurisdictions that do not allow the use of external ratings for regulatory purposes, an 85% risk weight will be applied.

applies_to.note: For US banks, which cannot use external ratings, this covers the whole SME book.

R-CRE20.47-corporate-sme-85pct.portfolio_relevance: Small business lending at 85% sits between regulatory retail at 75% and general corporate at 100%, so shifting commercial exposure down-market into SMEs reduces RWA by 15 points per dollar.

R-CRE20.47-regulatory-retail-sme-75pct.title: SMEs meeting regulatory retail criteria are weighted 75%
R-CRE20.47-regulatory-retail-sme-75pct.statement: Exposures to SMEs that meet the product, EUR 1 million size and 0.2% granularity criteria of CRE20.65(1) to (3) are treated as regulatory retail SME exposures and risk weighted at 75%.
R-CRE20.47-regulatory-retail-sme-75pct.quote: Exposures to SMEs that meet the criteria in CRE20.65 (1) to CRE20.65 (3) will be treated as regulatory retail SME exposures and risk weighted at 75%.

applies_to.note: Bridges the corporate and retail classes; the granularity test is measured against the whole regulatory retail portfolio.

R-CRE20.47-regulatory-retail-sme-75pct.portfolio_relevance: Gives a direct 10 point RWA saving for keeping small business facilities, including small business credit cards, below EUR 1 million and granular enough to sit in the regulatory retail pool.

R-CRE20.48-specialised-lending-definitio.title: Definition of specialised lending exposures
R-CRE20.48-specialised-lending-definitio.statement: A corporate exposure is specialised lending where it finances physical assets through an entity, often an SPV, whose primary repayment source is the income generated by the financed assets rather than the borrower's independent capacity.
R-CRE20.48-specialised-lending-definitio.quote: A corporate exposure will be treated as a specialised lending exposure if such lending possesses some or all of the following characteristics, either in legal form or economic substance: (1) The exposure is not related to real estate and is within the definitions of object finance, project finance or commodities finance under CRE20.49. If the activity is related to real estate, the treatment would be determined in accordance with CRE20.69 to; CRE20.91 (2) The exposure is typically to an entity (often a special purpose vehicle (SPV)) that was created specifically to finance and/or operate physical assets; (3) The borrowing entity has few or no other material assets or activities, and therefore little or no independent capacity to repay the obligation, apart from the income that it receives from the asset(s) being financed. The primary source of repayment of the obligation is the income generated by the asset(s), rather than the independent capacity of the borrowing entity;

applies_to.note: Real-estate-related activity is excluded and routed to CRE20.69 to CRE20.91 instead.

R-CRE20.48-specialised-lending-definitio.portfolio_relevance: Carves project, object and commodities finance out of the general 100% corporate bucket into weights that can reach 130%, penalising cash-flow-dependent asset finance.

R-CRE20.51-specialised-lending-risk-weig.title: Risk weights for unrated specialised lending: 100%, 130% and 80%
R-CRE20.51-specialised-lending-risk-weig.statement: Unrated object and commodities finance exposures are risk-weighted at 100%; project finance is 130% in the pre-operational phase and 100% in the operational phase, falling to 80% for high quality operational-phase project finance.
R-CRE20.51-specialised-lending-risk-weig.quote: (1) Object and commodities finance exposures will be risk-weighted at 100%; (2) Project finance exposures will be risk-weighted at 130% during the pre- operational phase and 100% during the operational phase. Project finance exposures in the operational phase which are deemed to be high quality, as described in CRE20.52, will be risk weighted at 80%.

applies_to.note: Applies where no issue-specific rating exists and to all such exposures in no-ratings jurisdictions such as the US.

numeric_values: 80% risk weight (high quality operational project finance)
R-CRE20.51-specialised-lending-risk-weig.portfolio_relevance: Construction-phase project finance costs 30% more RWA than general corporate lending, creating a measurable incentive to hold only operational, high-quality project exposure.

R-CRE20.57-equity-risk-weights-400-250.title: 400% and 250% risk weights for equity exposures
R-CRE20.57-equity-risk-weights-400-250.statement: Banks assign a 400% risk weight to speculative unlisted equity exposures and a 250% risk weight to all other equity holdings, other than those qualifying under CRE20.59.
R-CRE20.57-equity-risk-weights-400-250.quote: Banks will assign a risk weight of 400% to speculative unlisted equity exposures described in CRE20.58 and a risk weight of 250% to all other equity holdings, with the exception of those equity holdings referred to in CRE20.59.

applies_to.note: Applies to banking book equity not already deducted from regulatory capital.

R-CRE20.57-equity-risk-weights-400-250.portfolio_relevance: Equity holdings consume three to five times the capital of a credit card dollar, so any equity stake taken in lieu of lending is a heavy RWA choice.

R-CRE20.59-equity-100pct-10pct-total-cap.title: 100% equity weight for subsidised legislated programmes, capped at 10% of total capital
R-CRE20.59-equity-100pct-10pct-total-cap.statement: National supervisors may permit a 100% risk weight on equity holdings made under national legislated programmes providing significant subsidies and government oversight, but only up to an aggregate of 10% of the bank's total capital.
R-CRE20.59-equity-100pct-10pct-total-cap.quote: National supervisors may allow banks to assign a risk weight of 100% to equity holdings made pursuant to national legislated programmes that provide significant subsidies for the investment to the bank and involve government oversight and restrictions on the equity investments. Such treatment can only be accorded to equity holdings up to an aggregate of 10% of the bank

applies_to.note: National discretion plus a hard aggregate concentration cap expressed as a share of total capital.

numeric_values: aggregate cap of 10% of the bank's Total capital
R-CRE20.59-equity-100pct-10pct-total-cap.portfolio_relevance: Caps how much of a community bank's capital can sit in subsidised community-development equity at the concessional weight, limiting that as an alternative to lending.

R-CRE20.60-subordinated-debt-150pct.title: 150% risk weight for subordinated debt and non-equity capital instruments
R-CRE20.60-subordinated-debt-150pct.statement: Banks assign a 150% risk weight to subordinated debt and to capital instruments other than equities, including non-deducted other TLAC liabilities.
R-CRE20.60-subordinated-debt-150pct.quote: Banks will assign a risk weight of 150% to subordinated debt and capital instruments other than equities.

applies_to.note: Captures holdings of other banks' subordinated notes, which small banks do sometimes hold.

R-CRE20.60-subordinated-debt-150pct.portfolio_relevance: Doubles the capital cost of holding another institution's subordinated paper relative to regulatory retail lending, discouraging that as a yield substitute.

R-CRE20.61-commercial-entity-materiality.title: Materiality thresholds for investments in commercial entities: 15% and 60% of capital
R-CRE20.61-commercial-entity-materiality.statement: For significant minority- or majority-owned and controlled commercial entities, two materiality thresholds apply: 15% of the bank's capital for individual investments and 60% of the bank's capital in aggregate.
R-CRE20.61-commercial-entity-materiality.quote: the risk weight for investments in significant minority- or majority-owned and –controlled commercial entities depends upon the application of two materiality thresholds: (1) for individual investments, 15% of the bank’s capital; and (2) for the aggregate of such investments, 60% of the bank

applies_to.note: Thresholds are expressed relative to the bank's own capital, so they scale with bank size and are directly computable from published capital figures.

R-CRE20.61-commercial-entity-materiality.portfolio_relevance: Places a hard capital-relative ceiling on non-financial commercial holdings before punitive weights start, effectively forcing capital back into lending or securities.

R-CRE20.62-excess-commercial-investments.title: 1250% risk weight on commercial entity investments above the thresholds
R-CRE20.62-excess-commercial-investments.statement: Investments in significant minority- or majority-owned and controlled commercial entities in excess of the CRE20.61 materiality thresholds must be risk-weighted at 1250%.
R-CRE20.62-excess-commercial-investments.quote: Investments in excess of the materiality thresholds must be risk-weighted at 1250%.

applies_to.note: A 1250% weight is equivalent to a full capital deduction at an 8% minimum ratio.

R-CRE20.62-excess-commercial-investments.portfolio_relevance: Makes exceeding the commercial-investment thresholds economically equivalent to writing the excess off against capital, an absolute rather than marginal deterrent.

R-CRE20.63-retail-exposure-class-definit.title: Definition and boundary of the retail exposure class
R-CRE20.63-retail-exposure-class-definit.statement: The retail exposure class excludes real estate exposures and comprises exposures to individual persons and exposures to SMEs that meet the regulatory retail criteria in CRE20.65(1) to (3); SMEs failing those criteria are treated as corporate SMEs.
R-CRE20.63-retail-exposure-class-definit.quote: The retail exposure class excludes exposures within the real estate exposure class. The retail exposure class includes the following types of exposures: (1) exposures to an individual person or persons; and (2) exposures to SMEs (as defined in CRE20.47) that meet the “regulatory retail” criteria set out in CRE20.65 (1) to CRE20.65 (3) below. Exposures to SMEs that do not meet these criteria will be treated as corporate SMEs exposures under CRE20.47.

applies_to.note: Foundational classification rule for the credit card portfolio: it puts consumer card balances in retail and pushes mortgages out into the real estate class.

R-CRE20.63-retail-exposure-class-definit.portfolio_relevance: Determines whether a dollar of consumer or small business lending is priced at retail weights (45/75/100%) or corporate SME weights (85%), making the SME criteria test a direct portfolio-composition lever.

R-CRE20.64-retail-three-subclasses.title: The three risk-weighting subsets of the retail exposure class
R-CRE20.64-retail-three-subclasses.statement: For risk weighting, the retail exposure class splits into regulatory retail exposures not arising from transactors, regulatory retail exposures to transactors, and other retail exposures.
R-CRE20.64-retail-three-subclasses.quote: For the purpose of determining risk weighted assets, the retail exposure class consists of the follow three sets of exposures: (1) “Regulatory retail” exposures that do not arise from exposures to “transactors” (as defined in CRE20.66). (2) “Regulatory retail” exposures to “transactors”. (3) “Other retail

applies_to.note: This three-way split is the structure the 45/75/100% weights in CRE20.68 attach to.

R-CRE20.64-retail-three-subclasses.portfolio_relevance: Establishes the transactor/revolver split as a first-class regulatory partition, so measuring and shifting the transactor share of a card book directly changes RWA.

R-CRE20.65-regulatory-retail-product-cri.title: Regulatory retail product criterion, expressly including credit cards
R-CRE20.65-regulatory-retail-product-cri.statement: To be regulatory retail, an exposure must take the form of revolving credits and lines of credit including credit cards, charge cards and overdrafts, personal term loans and leases, or small business facilities and commitments; mortgages, derivatives and securities are excluded.
R-CRE20.65-regulatory-retail-product-cri.quote: Product criterion: the exposure takes the form of any of the following: revolving credits and lines of credit (including credit cards, charge cards and overdrafts), personal term loans and leases (eg instalment loans, auto loans and leases, student and educational loans, personal finance) and small business facilities and commitments. Mortgage loans, derivatives and other securities (such as bonds and equities), whether listed or not, are specifically excluded from this category.

applies_to.note: Credit cards, charge cards and overdrafts are named explicitly, so the card book is unambiguously eligible for regulatory retail treatment if the size and granularity tests are also met.

R-CRE20.65-regulatory-retail-product-cri.portfolio_relevance: Confirms that credit card receivables are the paradigm regulatory retail product, making the 75%/45% weights the reference cost of the card portfolio.

R-CRE20.65-regulatory-retail-1m-threshol.title: EUR 1 million absolute cap on aggregated exposure to one retail counterparty
R-CRE20.65-regulatory-retail-1m-threshol.statement: To qualify as regulatory retail, the maximum aggregated exposure to one counterparty cannot exceed an absolute threshold of EUR 1 million.
R-CRE20.65-regulatory-retail-1m-threshol.quote: Low value of individual exposures: the maximum aggregated exposure to one counterparty cannot exceed an absolute threshold of €1 million.

applies_to.note: Aggregated exposure is gross of credit risk mitigation, excludes residential real estate exposures, and for off-balance sheet claims is measured after applying credit conversion factors.

numeric_values: absolute threshold of EUR 1 million per counterparty
R-CRE20.65-regulatory-retail-1m-threshol.portfolio_relevance: Caps how large any single card or small business relationship can grow before it loses the 75% weight and reverts to 85-100%, so relationship sizing is itself an RWA decision.

R-CRE20.65-granularity-0.2pct.title: 0.2% granularity criterion for the regulatory retail portfolio
R-CRE20.65-granularity-0.2pct.statement: No aggregated exposure to one counterparty may exceed 0.2% of the overall regulatory retail portfolio unless the national supervisor has approved another diversification method, and defaulted retail exposures are excluded from the portfolio when assessing granularity.
R-CRE20.65-granularity-0.2pct.quote: Granularity criterion: no aggregated exposure to one counterparty can exceed 0.2% of the overall regulatory retail portfolio, unless national supervisors have determined another method to ensure satisfactory diversification of the regulatory retail portfolio. Defaulted retail exposures are to be excluded from the overall regulatory retail portfolio when assessing the granularity criterion.

applies_to.note: National supervisors may substitute another diversification method; the US implementation does not impose the 0.2% test in the same form.

numeric_values: 0.2% of the overall regulatory retail portfolio
R-CRE20.65-granularity-0.2pct.portfolio_relevance: Directly penalises concentration: a small bank with a modest retail book must keep every relationship under 0.2% of it, which for a USD 500m retail portfolio is USD 1m, so growing the pool itself relaxes the constraint.

R-CRE20.65fn-aggregated-exposure-after-c.title: Aggregated exposure is measured gross and after CCFs for off-balance sheet claims
R-CRE20.65fn-aggregated-exposure-after-c.statement: Aggregated exposure means the gross amount of all forms of retail exposures excluding residential real estate exposures, taking no credit risk mitigation into account, with off-balance sheet claims measured after applying credit conversion factors.
R-CRE20.65fn-aggregated-exposure-after-c.quote: Aggregated exposure means gross amount (ie not taking any credit risk mitigation into account) of all forms of retail exposures, excluding residential real estate exposures. In case of off-balance sheet claims, the gross amount would be calculated after applying credit conversion factors.

applies_to.note: Links the retail eligibility tests to the CCF machinery in CRE20.94 to CRE20.101.

R-CRE20.65fn-aggregated-exposure-after-c.portfolio_relevance: Means undrawn card lines count toward the EUR 1 million and 0.2% tests only at their post-CCF value, so the 10% CCF on unconditionally cancellable lines materially relaxes both eligibility tests.

R-CRE20.65fn-granularity-three-step-meth.title: Three-step method for applying the 0.2% granularity threshold
R-CRE20.65fn-granularity-three-step-meth.statement: To apply the 0.2% granularity threshold banks must first identify all retail class exposures, then the subset meeting the product and EUR 1 million criteria, and then exclude any exposure worth more than 0.2% of that subset measured before exclusions.
R-CRE20.65fn-granularity-three-step-meth.quote: To apply the 0.2% threshold of the granularity criterion, banks must: first, identify the full set of exposures in the retail exposure class (as defined by CRE20.63); second, identify the subset of exposure that meet product criterion and do not exceed the threshold for the value of aggregated exposures to one counterparty (as defined by CRE20.65 (1) and CRE20.65 (2) respectively); and third, exclude any exposures that have a value greater than 0.2% of the subset before exclusions.

applies_to.note: Prescribes the exact denominator, removing the circularity in applying the granularity test.

R-CRE20.65fn-granularity-three-step-meth.portfolio_relevance: Makes the granularity test mechanically computable from a loan tape, which is what allows it to be evaluated as a hard constraint in a portfolio optimiser.

R-CRE20.66-transactor-definition.title: Definition of a transactor: full repayment at every scheduled date for 12 months
R-CRE20.66-transactor-definition.statement: Transactors are obligors on facilities such as credit cards and charge cards whose balance has been repaid in full at each scheduled repayment date for the previous 12 months, and overdraft obligors with no drawdown over the previous 12 months.
R-CRE20.66-transactor-definition.quote: are obligors in relation to facilities such as credit cards and charge cards where the balance has been repaid in full at each scheduled repayment date for the previous 12 months. Obligors in relation to overdraft facilities would also be considered as transactors if there has been no drawdown over the previous 12 months.

applies_to.note: The single most important definition in this chapter for a credit card portfolio: it is the gate to the 45% rather than 75% weight, and requires 12 months of per-account repayment history.

numeric_values: repaid in full at each scheduled repayment date for the previous 12 months
no drawdown over the previous 12 months
R-CRE20.66-transactor-definition.portfolio_relevance: Creates a 30 percentage point RWA reward for shifting the card book toward customers who repay in full monthly, and makes the transactor share a directly optimisable portfolio parameter.

R-CRE20.67-other-retail-definition.title: Definition of other retail exposures
R-CRE20.67-other-retail-definition.statement: Other retail exposures are exposures to an individual person or persons that fail to meet all of the regulatory retail criteria in CRE20.65.
R-CRE20.67-other-retail-definition.quote: exposures are defined as exposures to an individual person or persons that do not meet all of the regulatory retail criteria in CRE20.65.

applies_to.note: Residual retail bucket; failing any single CRE20.65 criterion moves an exposure here.

R-CRE20.67-other-retail-definition.portfolio_relevance: Failing the product, EUR 1 million or 0.2% granularity test costs 25 percentage points of risk weight (75% to 100%), so eligibility maintenance has direct capital value.

R-CRE20.68-retail-rw-non-transactor-75.title: 75% risk weight for regulatory retail exposures to non-transactors
R-CRE20.68-retail-rw-non-transactor-75.statement: Regulatory retail exposures that do not arise from exposures to transactors are risk weighted at 75%.
R-CRE20.68-retail-rw-non-transactor-75.quote: (1) Regulatory retail exposures that do not arise from exposures to transactors (as defined in CRE20.66) will be risk weighted at 75%.

applies_to.note: The default weight for revolving card balances and personal loans held by a small bank on the standardised approach.

R-CRE20.68-retail-rw-non-transactor-75.portfolio_relevance: Sets the baseline capital cost of the revolver portion of a credit card book at 75% of exposure, the reference point against which the 45% transactor weight and the 100% other-retail weight are traded off.

R-CRE20.68-retail-rw-transactor-45.title: 45% risk weight for regulatory retail exposures to transactors
R-CRE20.68-retail-rw-transactor-45.statement: Regulatory retail exposures that arise from exposures to transactors, as defined in CRE20.66, are risk weighted at 45%.
R-CRE20.68-retail-rw-transactor-45.quote: (2) Regulatory retail exposures that arise from exposures to transactors (as defined in CRE20.66) will be risk weighted at 45%.

applies_to.note: Requires 12 months of full-repayment history per obligor; the transactor/revolver split is not separately reported in US call reports, so it must be proxied.

R-CRE20.68-retail-rw-transactor-45.portfolio_relevance: Rewards a card portfolio tilted toward full-payers with a 40% reduction in risk weight versus revolvers, making transactor share the highest-leverage single lever on credit card RWA.

R-CRE20.68-other-retail-rw-100.title: 100% risk weight for other retail exposures
R-CRE20.68-other-retail-rw-100.statement: Other retail exposures, being retail exposures to individuals that fail the regulatory retail criteria, are risk weighted at 100%.
R-CRE20.68-other-retail-rw-100.quote: (3) Other retail exposures will be risk weighted at 100%.

applies_to.note: Catches large individual exposures above EUR 1 million and any retail exposure breaching granularity.

R-CRE20.68-other-retail-rw-100.portfolio_relevance: Imposes a 25 point RWA penalty on retail lending that breaks the size or granularity tests, discouraging concentration in a few large personal relationships.

R-CRE20.69-real-estate-class-definition.title: Composition of the real estate exposure class
R-CRE20.69-real-estate-class-definition.statement: The real estate exposure class comprises exposures secured by real estate classified as regulatory real estate, exposures secured by real estate classified as other real estate, and land acquisition, development and construction exposures.
R-CRE20.69-real-estate-class-definition.quote: Real estate is immovable property that is land, including agricultural land and forest, or anything treated as attached to land, in particular buildings, in contrast to being treated as movable/personal property. The real estate exposure asset class consists of: (1) Exposures secured by real estate that are classified as “regulatory real estate” exposures. (2) Exposures secured by real estate that are classified as “other real estate” exposures. (3) Exposures that are classified as “land acquisition, development and construction

applies_to.note: Real estate is carved out of the retail class entirely by CRE20.63.

R-CRE20.69-real-estate-class-definition.portfolio_relevance: Separates the mortgage book from the retail book, so a bank rebalancing between mortgages and cards moves between two entirely different weight schedules.

R-CRE20.71-regulatory-real-estate-criter.title: Criteria for classification as a regulatory real estate exposure
R-CRE20.71-regulatory-real-estate-criter.statement: To be a regulatory real estate exposure a loan must meet requirements covering finished property, legal enforceability, claims over the property, borrower ability to repay, prudent property valuation and documentation, starting with security over a fully completed immovable property.
R-CRE20.71-regulatory-real-estate-criter.quote: For an exposure secured by real estate to be classified as a “regulatory real estate” exposure, the loan must meet the following requirements: (1) Finished property: the exposure must be secured by a fully completed immovable property.

applies_to.note: Subject to national discretion for loans to individuals on one-to-four family residential property under construction.

R-CRE20.71-regulatory-real-estate-criter.portfolio_relevance: Failing these criteria pushes a mortgage into other real estate at the counterparty weight or 150%, so underwriting and documentation quality has a direct RWA price.

R-CRE20.72-supervisors-may-raise-re-risk.title: Supervisors may require higher real estate risk weights
R-CRE20.72-supervisors-may-raise-re-risk.statement: Regulatory real estate risk weights presuppose structurally low real estate credit losses, and national supervisors should evaluate whether they are too low and may require banks to increase them.
R-CRE20.72-supervisors-may-raise-re-risk.quote: The risk weights for regulatory real estate exposures will apply to jurisdictions where structural factors result in sustainably low credit losses associated with the exposures to the real estate market. National supervisors should evaluate whether the risk weights in the corresponding risk weight tables are too low for these types of exposures in their jurisdictions based on default experience and other factors such as market price stability. Supervisors may require banks in their jurisdictions to increase these risk weights as appropriate.

applies_to.note: Explicit national-discretion uplift; means published Basel mortgage weights are a floor, not necessarily the applicable weight.

R-CRE20.72-supervisors-may-raise-re-risk.portfolio_relevance: Introduces jurisdiction-specific uncertainty into the mortgage weights, making a shift out of cards into mortgages less predictable in RWA terms than the fixed retail weights.

R-CRE20.73-mortgage-underwriting-repayme.title: Mortgage underwriting policies must assess ability to repay with defined metrics
R-CRE20.73-mortgage-underwriting-repayme.statement: Banks must have underwriting policies for granting mortgage loans that assess the borrower's ability to repay, defining metrics such as debt service coverage ratio and their corresponding relevant levels.
R-CRE20.73-mortgage-underwriting-repayme.quote: National supervisors should ensure that banks put in place underwriting policies with respect to the granting of mortgage loans that include the assessment of the ability of the borrower to repay.

applies_to.note: National supervisors may prescribe the definitions and levels; metrics should mirror the FSB Principles for sound residential mortgage underwriting practices.

R-CRE20.73-mortgage-underwriting-repayme.portfolio_relevance: Constrains how aggressively a bank can grow a mortgage book as an alternative to unsecured retail lending, since preferential mortgage weights depend on documented repayment-capacity underwriting.

R-CRE20.74-ltv-definition-value-at-origi.title: LTV definition: loan amortises but property value is frozen at origination
R-CRE20.74-ltv-definition-value-at-origi.statement: LTV is the loan amount divided by the property value; the loan amount reduces as the loan amortises while the property value is maintained at the value measured at origination, subject to specified downward adjustments.
R-CRE20.74-ltv-definition-value-at-origi.quote: The LTV is the amount of the loan divided by the value of the property. When calculating the LTV, the loan amount will be reduced as the loan amortises. The value of the property will be maintained at the value measured at origination

applies_to.note: No upward revaluation beyond origination value is permitted, so RWA relief comes only from amortisation.

R-CRE20.74-ltv-definition-value-at-origi.portfolio_relevance: Means a mortgage book's RWA declines mechanically with amortisation but cannot be improved by rising house prices, making mortgage RWA reduction slow relative to running off a revolving card book.

R-CRE20.75-ltv-includes-undrawn-committe.title: LTV loan amount includes undrawn committed amounts and is gross of provisions
R-CRE20.75-ltv-includes-undrawn-committe.statement: For LTV purposes the loan amount includes the outstanding balance plus any undrawn committed amount of the mortgage loan, calculated gross of provisions and risk mitigants other than qualifying pledged deposits.
R-CRE20.75-ltv-includes-undrawn-committe.quote: Amount of the loan: includes the outstanding loan amount and any undrawn committed amount of the mortgage loan. The loan amount must be calculated gross of any provisions and other risk mitigants, except for pledged deposits accounts with the lending bank that meet all requirements for on-balance sheet netting and have been unconditionally and irrevocably pledged for the sole purposes of redemption of the mortgage loan.

applies_to.note: Unlike off-balance sheet CCF treatment, undrawn mortgage commitments enter LTV at full nominal value.

R-CRE20.75-ltv-includes-undrawn-committe.portfolio_relevance: Penalises undrawn home equity lines in the LTV bucket calculation at full face value, unlike undrawn card lines which attract only a 10% CCF.

R-CRE20.75fn-junior-lien-1.25-multiplier.title: 1.25 multiplier on junior lien mortgage risk weights
R-CRE20.75fn-junior-lien-1.25-multiplier.statement: For junior liens the base risk weight from the LTV tables is adjusted by a multiplier of 1.25, except where the base weight is in the lowest LTV bucket, and the result is capped at the risk weight applicable when CRE20.71 is not met.
R-CRE20.75fn-junior-lien-1.25-multiplier.quote: risk weight by a multiplier of 1.25, for application to the loan amount of the junior lien. If the “base” risk weight corresponds to the lowest LTV bucket, the multiplier will not be applied. The resulting risk weight of multiplying the “base” risk weight by 1.25 will be capped at the risk weight applied to the exposure when the requirements in CRE20.71 are not met.

applies_to.note: Applies where junior liens held by a different bank are recognised under national frameworks.

R-CRE20.75fn-junior-lien-1.25-multiplier.portfolio_relevance: Raises the capital cost of second-lien home equity lending by 25% relative to first liens, weakening HELOCs as a substitute for card lending.

R-CRE20.80-material-dependence-50pct-inc.title: 50% income test for material dependence on property cash flows
R-CRE20.80-material-dependence-50pct-inc.statement: A loan may be considered materially dependent on property cash flows if more than 50% of the borrower income used in the bank's assessment of ability to service the loan comes from cash flows generated by the residential property.
R-CRE20.80-material-dependence-50pct-inc.quote: a loan may be considered materially dependent if more than 50% of the income from the borrower used in the bank's assessment of its ability to service the loan is from cash flows generated by the residential property.

applies_to.note: Illustrative threshold; national supervisors may set further criteria for specific exposure types.

R-CRE20.80-material-dependence-50pct-inc.portfolio_relevance: Determines whether a buy-to-let mortgage sits on the 20-70% table or the 30-105% table, a difference of up to 35 points of risk weight.

R-CRE20.82-rrre-whole-loan-ltv-table.title: Whole loan risk weights by LTV for residential real estate not cash-flow dependent
R-CRE20.82-rrre-whole-loan-ltv-table.statement: Regulatory residential real estate exposures not materially dependent on property cash flows are risk weighted by LTV band at 20%, 25%, 30%, 40%, 50% and 70%.
R-CRE20.82-rrre-whole-loan-ltv-table.quote: Whole loan approach risk weights for regulatory residential real estate exposures that are not materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property Table 11 LTV ≤ 50% < 60% < LTV 80% < LTV 90% < LTV ≤ LTV > 50% LTV ≤ ≤ 80% ≤ 90% 100% 100% 60% Risk 25% 20% 30% 40% 50% 70%

applies_to.note: Whole loan approach; jurisdictions may instead permit the loan splitting approach in CRE20.83.

R-CRE20.82-rrre-whole-loan-ltv-table.portfolio_relevance: Residential mortgages at 20-50% are roughly a third to two thirds the RWA cost of a 75% card revolver, so mortgage growth is the standard route for a small bank to cut credit RWA density.

R-CRE20.83-loan-splitting-20pct-to-55pct.title: Loan splitting approach: 20% weight up to 55% of property value
R-CRE20.83-loan-splitting-20pct-to-55pct.statement: Under the loan splitting alternative for residential real estate not materially dependent on property cash flows, a 20% risk weight applies to the part of the exposure up to 55% of the property value and the counterparty risk weight applies to the residual.
R-CRE20.83-loan-splitting-20pct-to-55pct.quote: Under the loan splitting approach, the risk weight of 20% is applied to the part of the exposure up to 55% of the property value and the risk weight of the counterparty (as prescribed in CRE20.89 (1)) is applied to the residual exposure.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictional election; not adopted in the United States, which uses an LTV-band approach under 12 CFR 217.

numeric_values: up to 55% of the property value
R-CRE20.83-loan-splitting-20pct-to-55pct.portfolio_relevance: For a mortgage to an individual, the residual above 55% LTV carries the 75% retail counterparty weight, so the marginal dollar of high-LTV mortgage costs exactly as much capital as a card revolver.

R-CRE20.84-rrre-cash-flow-dependent-ltv-.title: Risk weights by LTV for residential real estate materially dependent on property cash flows
R-CRE20.84-rrre-cash-flow-dependent-ltv-.statement: Regulatory residential real estate exposures materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property are risk weighted by LTV band at 30%, 35%, 45%, 60%, 75% and 105%.
R-CRE20.84-rrre-cash-flow-dependent-ltv-.quote: For regulatory residential real estate exposures that are materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property, the risk weight to be assigned to the total exposure amount will be determined based on the exposure’s LTV ratio in Table 12 below. Risk weights for regulatory residential real estate exposures that are materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property Table 12 LTV ≤ 50% < LTV 60% < LTV 80% < LTV 90% < LTV ≤ LTV > 50% ≤ 60% ≤ 80% ≤ 90% 100% 100% Risk 35% 30% 45% 60% 75% 105%

applies_to.note: Applies to investor and rental residential lending; primary residences are excluded by CRE20.81.

R-CRE20.84-rrre-cash-flow-dependent-ltv-.portfolio_relevance: Investor residential lending above 90% LTV costs as much or more RWA than a credit card revolver, removing the mortgage substitution benefit at high leverage.

R-CRE20.85-crre-whole-loan-60pct-cap.title: Commercial real estate whole loan weights: min(60%, counterparty RW) up to 60% LTV
R-CRE20.85-crre-whole-loan-60pct-cap.statement: Regulatory commercial real estate exposures not materially dependent on property cash flows are risk weighted at the lower of 60% and the counterparty risk weight where LTV is at or below 60%, and at the counterparty risk weight where LTV exceeds 60%.
R-CRE20.85-crre-whole-loan-60pct-cap.quote: Whole loan approach risk weights for regulatory commercial real estate exposures that are not materially dependent on cash flows generated by the Table property 13 LTV ≤ 60% LTV > 60% Risk weight Min (60%, RW of counterparty) RW of counterparty

applies_to.note: Counterparty weight is prescribed in CRE20.89(1): 75% for individuals, 85% for SMEs, otherwise the unsecured weight.

R-CRE20.85-crre-whole-loan-60pct-cap.portfolio_relevance: Low-LTV commercial real estate is capped at 60%, below the 75% retail weight and the 85% SME weight, making conservative CRE lending an RWA-efficient alternative to unsecured small business credit.

R-CRE20.86-crre-loan-splitting.title: Loan splitting approach for commercial real estate
R-CRE20.86-crre-loan-splitting.statement: Jurisdictions may permit a loan splitting approach for commercial real estate not materially dependent on property cash flows, applying the lower of 60% and the counterparty risk weight to the part of the exposure up to 55% of property value and the counterparty weight to the residual.
R-CRE20.86-crre-loan-splitting.quote: Under the loan splitting approach, the risk weight of 60% or the risk weight of the counterparty, whichever is lower, is applied to the part of the exposure up to 55% of the property value, and the risk weight of the counterparty is applied to the residual exposure.

applies_to.note: Jurisdictional election alternative to CRE20.85.

numeric_values: up to 55% of the property value
R-CRE20.86-crre-loan-splitting.portfolio_relevance: Gives a bank in an electing jurisdiction a way to secure a low weight on the collateralised core of a CRE loan while the uncollateralised remainder is priced like unsecured SME credit.

R-CRE20.87-crre-cash-flow-dependent-weig.title: Risk weights for commercial real estate materially dependent on property cash flows
R-CRE20.87-crre-cash-flow-dependent-weig.statement: Regulatory commercial real estate exposures materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property are risk weighted at 70% for LTV up to 60%, 90% for LTV between 60% and 80%, and 110% for LTV above 80%.
R-CRE20.87-crre-cash-flow-dependent-weig.quote: Whole loan approach risk weights for regulatory commercial real estate exposures that are materially dependent on cash flows generated by the Table property 14 LTV ≤ 60% 60% < LTV ≤ 80% LTV > 80% Risk weight 70% 90% 110%

applies_to.note: National supervisors may permit the CRE20.85 treatment instead if jurisdictional loss tests are met and publicly disclosed.

R-CRE20.87-crre-cash-flow-dependent-weig.portfolio_relevance: Income-producing CRE is weighted at or above the 75% card revolver weight once LTV exceeds 60%, so it is not an RWA-cheap substitute for retail lending.

R-CRE20.87fn-cre-loss-tests-0.3-0.5.title: Jurisdictional CRE loss tests of 0.3% and 0.5% of outstanding loans
R-CRE20.87fn-cre-loss-tests-0.3-0.5.statement: National supervisors may allow the lower CRE20.85 treatment for cash-flow-dependent commercial real estate only where losses on CRE lending up to 60% LTV do not exceed 0.3% of outstanding loans in any year and overall CRE losses do not exceed 0.5% of outstanding loans in any year.
R-CRE20.87fn-cre-loss-tests-0.3-0.5.quote: the losses stemming from commercial real estate lending up to 60% of LTV must not exceed 0.3% of the outstanding loans in any given year and (ii) overall losses stemming from commercial real estate lending must not exceed 0.5% of the outstanding loans in any given year.

applies_to.note: National discretion conditioned on measured loss rates, with a public disclosure obligation on the jurisdiction; eligibility ceases if either test fails.

numeric_values: 0.3% of the outstanding loans in any given year
0.5% of the outstanding loans in any given year
R-CRE20.87fn-cre-loss-tests-0.3-0.5.portfolio_relevance: Ties a jurisdiction-wide capital concession on CRE to realised loss rates, so a deteriorating CRE cycle can raise a bank's CRE weights from 60% to 70-110% without any change in its own portfolio.

R-CRE20.89-other-real-estate-counterpart.title: Other real estate weights: 75% for individuals, 85% for SMEs
R-CRE20.89-other-real-estate-counterpart.statement: Other real estate exposures not materially dependent on property cash flows take the counterparty risk weight, being 75% for exposures to individuals and 85% for exposures to SMEs.
R-CRE20.89-other-real-estate-counterpart.quote: The risk weight of the counterparty is used for other real estate exposures that are not materially dependent on the cash flows generated by the property. For exposures to individuals the risk weight applied will be 75%. For exposures to SMEs, the risk weight applied will be 85%.

applies_to.note: Catches real estate secured lending that fails the CRE20.71 regulatory real estate criteria.

R-CRE20.89-other-real-estate-counterpart.portfolio_relevance: A mortgage that fails documentation or valuation standards is weighted exactly like an unsecured card revolver at 75%, erasing the entire capital benefit of the collateral.

R-CRE20.89-other-real-estate-cash-flow-1.title: 150% risk weight for cash-flow-dependent other real estate exposures
R-CRE20.89-other-real-estate-cash-flow-1.statement: Other real estate exposures that are materially dependent on the cash flows generated by the property are risk weighted at 150%.
R-CRE20.89-other-real-estate-cash-flow-1.quote: The risk weight of 150% is used for other real estate exposures that are materially dependent on the cash flows generated by the property.

applies_to.note: Applies where the exposure fails the regulatory real estate criteria and repayment depends on property cash flows.

R-CRE20.89-other-real-estate-cash-flow-1.portfolio_relevance: Doubles the capital cost relative to a card revolver, making poorly documented investor property lending the most expensive form of secured real estate exposure.

R-CRE20.90-adc-150pct.title: 150% risk weight for land acquisition, development and construction exposures
R-CRE20.90-adc-150pct.statement: Land acquisition, development and construction exposures, being loans to companies or SPVs financing land acquisition for development and construction or the development and construction of residential or commercial property, are risk weighted at 150% unless they meet the CRE20.91 criteria.
R-CRE20.90-adc-150pct.quote: Land ADC exposures refers to loans to companies or SPVs financing any of the land acquisition for development and construction purposes, or development and construction of any residential or commercial property. ADC exposures will be risk-weighted at 150%, unless they meet the criteria in CRE20.91.

applies_to.note: Directly relevant to community banks with construction and development concentrations.

R-CRE20.90-adc-150pct.portfolio_relevance: Construction and development lending costs twice the RWA of a credit card revolver, so an ADC-heavy community bank can cut RWA density substantially by rotating into retail card lending.

R-CRE20.91-adc-residential-100pct.title: 100% risk weight for qualifying residential ADC exposures
R-CRE20.91-adc-residential-100pct.statement: ADC exposures to residential real estate may be risk weighted at 100% where prudential underwriting standards meet the CRE20.71 requirements and pre-sale or pre-lease contracts amount to a significant portion of total contracts or substantial equity is at risk.
R-CRE20.91-adc-residential-100pct.quote: ADC exposures to residential real estate may be risk weighted at 100%, provided that the following criteria are met:

applies_to.note: National supervisors give further guidance on the required level of pre-sale, pre-lease or equity at risk.

R-CRE20.91-adc-residential-100pct.portfolio_relevance: Offers a 50 point RWA saving on residential construction lending conditional on verifiable pre-sale contracts, making pre-sale coverage an actionable underwriting lever.

R-CRE20.92-currency-mismatch-1.5x-multip.title: 1.5x risk weight multiplier for unhedged currency-mismatched retail exposures
R-CRE20.92-currency-mismatch-1.5x-multip.statement: For unhedged retail and residential real estate exposures to individuals where the lending currency differs from the currency of the borrower's income, banks apply a 1.5 times multiplier to the applicable risk weight, capped at a maximum risk weight of 150%.
R-CRE20.92-currency-mismatch-1.5x-multip.quote: For unhedged retail and residential real estate exposures to individuals where the lending currency differs from the currency of the borrower’s source of income, banks will apply a 1.5 times multiplier to the applicable risk weight according to CRE20.63 to CRE20.68 and CRE20.82 to CRE20.84, subject to a maximum risk weight of 150%.

applies_to.note: Applies to the retail weights in CRE20.63 to CRE20.68 and the residential mortgage weights in CRE20.82 to CRE20.84.

R-CRE20.92-currency-mismatch-1.5x-multip.portfolio_relevance: Raises a non-transactor card exposure from 75% to 112.5% and a transactor from 45% to 67.5% where the borrower earns in a different currency, penalising cross-border card issuance.

R-CRE20.93-hedge-must-cover-90pct-instal.title: Hedges must cover at least 90% of the loan instalment to avoid the multiplier
R-CRE20.93-hedge-must-cover-90pct-instal.statement: For the currency mismatch multiplier, only natural or financial hedges covering at least 90% of the loan instalment are considered sufficient, regardless of the number of hedges.
R-CRE20.93-hedge-must-cover-90pct-instal.quote: only these natural or financial hedges are considered sufficient where they cover at least 90% of the loan instalment, regardless of the number of hedges.

applies_to.note: National supervisors may permit temporary use of models or proxy data to establish borrower income and hedge sufficiency.

numeric_values: at least 90% of the loan instalment
R-CRE20.93-hedge-must-cover-90pct-instal.portfolio_relevance: Sets a sharp 90% coverage cliff: partial hedging below that threshold delivers no capital relief at all, so hedging programmes must be designed to the threshold.

R-CRE20.93faq-revolving-facilities-in-sc.title: Credit cards and overdrafts are in scope of the currency mismatch multiplier, measured fully drawn
R-CRE20.93faq-revolving-facilities-in-sc.statement: Revolving credit facilities for individuals including overdrafts and credit cards are within scope of the currency mismatch multiplier; hedge sufficiency is assessed assuming the facility is fully drawn, and if the payment currency could differ from the income currency the full undrawn amount is treated as mismatched.
R-CRE20.93faq-revolving-facilities-in-sc.quote: Yes, revolving credit facilities for individuals are within the scope of this risk weight multiplier. For the purpose of determining a currency mismatch, the “lending currency” is the currency of the borrower’s payment obligation under the revolving credit facility. To determine whether there is a sufficient hedge, the loan instalments should be calculated assuming the facility is fully drawn. If the currency of the borrower’s payment obligation could be different from the currency of the borrower’s source of income, the full undrawn amount is to be treated as being in a currency different from that of the borrower

applies_to.note: Interpretive FAQ published with the consolidated framework; assessment on a fully drawn basis is materially more conservative than on outstanding balances.

R-CRE20.93faq-revolving-facilities-in-sc.portfolio_relevance: Forces multi-currency card lines to be assessed at full committed limit for currency mismatch, so granting large limits in foreign currency can trigger the 1.5x multiplier across the whole facility.

R-CRE20.94-ccf-conversion-of-undrawn-com.title: Off-balance sheet items convert to exposure via credit conversion factors
R-CRE20.94-ccf-conversion-of-undrawn-com.statement: Off-balance sheet items are converted into credit exposure equivalents using credit conversion factors, and for commitments the committed but undrawn amount is multiplied by the CCF.
R-CRE20.94-ccf-conversion-of-undrawn-com.quote: Off-balance sheet items will be converted into credit exposure equivalents through the use of credit conversion factors (CCF). In the case of commitments, the committed but undrawn amount of the exposure would be multiplied by the CCF.

applies_to.note: This is the mechanism that brings undrawn credit card lines onto the RWA calculation at all.

R-CRE20.94-ccf-conversion-of-undrawn-com.portfolio_relevance: Makes total committed card limits, not just drawn balances, a driver of RWA, so limit management is a capital lever independent of balance growth.

R-CRE20.94-commitment-definition.title: Definition of a commitment, expressly including unconditionally cancellable arrangements
R-CRE20.94-commitment-definition.statement: A commitment is any contractual arrangement offered by the bank and accepted by the client to extend credit, purchase assets or issue credit substitutes, and expressly includes arrangements that can be unconditionally cancelled by the bank at any time without prior notice and arrangements cancellable on borrower breach of documented conditions.
R-CRE20.94-commitment-definition.quote: commitment means any contractual arrangement that has been offered by the bank and accepted by the client to extend credit, purchase assets or issue credit substitutes. It includes any such arrangement that can be unconditionally cancelled by the bank at any time without prior notice to the obligor. It also includes any such arrangement that can be cancelled by the bank if the obligor fails to meet conditions set out in the facility documentation, including conditions that must be met by the obligor prior to any initial or subsequent drawdown under the arrangement.

applies_to.note: Critical for credit cards: unconditionally cancellable card lines are commitments and therefore attract a CCF, unlike under earlier Basel II treatment where they attracted 0%.

R-CRE20.94-commitment-definition.portfolio_relevance: Ends any zero-capital treatment of undrawn card lines: every dollar of unused credit card limit now enters RWA at its CCF, so reducing unused lines directly reduces RWA.

R-CRE20.94fn-national-discretion-commitm.title: National discretion to exempt certain arrangements from the commitment definition
R-CRE20.94fn-national-discretion-commitm.statement: At national discretion a jurisdiction may exempt an arrangement from the commitment definition where the bank receives no fees, the client must apply for each drawdown, the bank has full authority over each drawdown and decides only after assessing creditworthiness immediately prior to drawdown; such exemptions are limited to certain corporate and SME arrangements.
R-CRE20.94fn-national-discretion-commitm.quote: At national discretion, a jurisdiction may exempt certain arrangements from the definition of commitments provided that the following conditions are met: (i) the bank receives no fees or commissions to establish or maintain the arrangements; (ii) the client is required to apply to the bank for the initial and each subsequent drawdown; (iii) the bank has full authority, regardless of the fulfilment by the client of the conditions set out in the facility documentation, over the execution of each drawdown; and (iv) the bank’s decision on the execution of each drawdown is only made after assessing the creditworthiness of the client immediately prior to drawdown. Exempted arrangements that meet the above criteria are limited to certain arrangements for corporates and SMEs, where counterparties are closely monitored on an ongoing basis.

applies_to.note: National-discretion gate expressly limited to corporate and SME arrangements with closely monitored counterparties; it cannot be used for consumer credit card lines.

R-CRE20.94fn-national-discretion-commitm.portfolio_relevance: Allows uncommitted corporate advised lines to escape CCFs entirely, giving corporate lending an off-balance sheet capital advantage that consumer card lines cannot obtain.

R-CRE20.95-ccf-100pct-direct-credit-subs.title: 100% credit conversion factor for direct credit substitutes and similar items
R-CRE20.95-ccf-100pct-direct-credit-subs.statement: A 100% CCF applies to direct credit substitutes such as general guarantees of indebtedness and standby letters of credit serving as financial guarantees, acceptances, and sale and repurchase agreements and asset sales with recourse where the credit risk remains with the bank.
R-CRE20.95-ccf-100pct-direct-credit-subs.quote: A 100% CCF will be applied to the following items: (1) Direct credit substitutes, eg general guarantees of indebtedness (including standby letters of credit serving as financial guarantees for loans and securities) and acceptances (including endorsements with the character of acceptances). (2) Sale and repurchase agreements and asset sales with recourse where the credit risk remains with the bank.

applies_to.note: These items are weighted according to the type of asset, not the type of counterparty.

R-CRE20.95-ccf-100pct-direct-credit-subs.portfolio_relevance: Guarantees and standby letters of credit consume capital as if fully drawn, so replacing funded lending with guarantee business gives no RWA relief.

R-CRE20.96-ccf-50pct-nif-ruf.title: 50% CCF for note issuance and revolving underwriting facilities
R-CRE20.96-ccf-50pct-nif-ruf.statement: A 50% CCF applies to note issuance facilities and revolving underwriting facilities regardless of the maturity of the underlying facility.
R-CRE20.96-ccf-50pct-nif-ruf.quote: A 50% CCF will be applied to note issuance facilities and revolving underwriting facilities regardless of the maturity of the underlying facility.

applies_to.note: Maturity-independent; relevant to banks with capital markets underwriting activity.

R-CRE20.96-ccf-50pct-nif-ruf.portfolio_relevance: Prices underwriting backstops at half face value in RWA terms, a business line generally unavailable to small banks.

R-CRE20.97-ccf-50pct-transaction-conting.title: 50% CCF for transaction-related contingent items
R-CRE20.97-ccf-50pct-transaction-conting.statement: A 50% CCF applies to transaction-related contingent items such as performance bonds, bid bonds, warranties and standby letters of credit related to particular transactions.
R-CRE20.97-ccf-50pct-transaction-conting.quote: A 50% CCF will be applied to certain transaction-related contingent items (eg performance bonds, bid bonds, warranties and standby letters of credit related to particular transactions).

applies_to.note: Distinguished from financial standby letters of credit, which attract 100% under CRE20.95.

R-CRE20.97-ccf-50pct-transaction-conting.portfolio_relevance: Performance-type contingent business converts at half value, making it roughly half as capital intensive per dollar of notional as a direct credit substitute.

R-CRE20.98-ccf-40pct-commitments.title: 40% credit conversion factor for commitments generally
R-CRE20.98-ccf-40pct-commitments.statement: A 40% CCF applies to commitments regardless of the maturity of the underlying facility, unless they qualify for a lower CCF.
R-CRE20.98-ccf-40pct-commitments.quote: A 40% CCF will be applied to commitments, regardless of the maturity of the underlying facility, unless they qualify for a lower CCF.

applies_to.note: This is the default CCF; the maturity distinction between under and over one year in Basel II has been removed.

R-CRE20.98-ccf-40pct-commitments.portfolio_relevance: Any undrawn line that is not unconditionally cancellable costs four times the RWA of one that is, giving a strong contractual incentive to write card and line agreements as unconditionally cancellable.

R-CRE20.99-ccf-20pct-trade-lc.title: 20% CCF for short-term self-liquidating trade letters of credit
R-CRE20.99-ccf-20pct-trade-lc.statement: A 20% CCF applies to both the issuing and confirming banks of short-term self-liquidating trade letters of credit arising from the movement of goods, where short term means a maturity below one year.
R-CRE20.99-ccf-20pct-trade-lc.quote: A 20% CCF will be applied to both the issuing and confirming banks of short- term self-liquidating trade letters of credit arising from the movement of goods (eg documentary credits collateralised by the underlying shipment). Short term in this context means with a maturity below one year.

applies_to.note: Applies symmetrically to issuing and confirming banks.

R-CRE20.99-ccf-20pct-trade-lc.portfolio_relevance: Trade finance is the cheapest off-balance sheet exposure other than unconditionally cancellable commitments, making it RWA-efficient fee business for a bank shrinking its funded book.

R-CRE20.100-ccf-10pct-unconditionally-ca.title: 10% CCF for unconditionally cancellable commitments including credit card lines
R-CRE20.100-ccf-10pct-unconditionally-ca.statement: A 10% CCF applies to commitments that are unconditionally cancellable at any time by the bank without prior notice, or that effectively provide for automatic cancellation due to deterioration in the borrower's creditworthiness.
R-CRE20.100-ccf-10pct-unconditionally-ca.quote: A 10% CCF will be applied to commitments that are unconditionally cancellable at any time by the bank without prior notice, or that effectively provide for automatic cancellation due to deterioration in a borrower

applies_to.note: The single most important off-balance sheet rule for a credit card issuer: unused card lines are almost always unconditionally cancellable, and this raises their CCF from 0% under Basel II to 10%.

R-CRE20.100-ccf-10pct-unconditionally-ca.portfolio_relevance: Every dollar of unused credit card line now generates 0.10 dollars of exposure at 45% or 75% risk weight, so unused-limit management becomes a direct and measurable RWA lever alongside balance growth.

R-CRE20.100-supervisors-may-require-high.title: Supervisors may impose a higher CCF where cancellation is constrained in practice
R-CRE20.100-supervisors-may-require-high.statement: National supervisors should evaluate jurisdictional factors that may constrain a bank's ability to cancel a commitment in practice and should consider applying a higher CCF to certain commitments as appropriate.
R-CRE20.100-supervisors-may-require-high.quote: National supervisors should evaluate various factors in the jurisdiction, which may constrain banks’ ability to cancel the commitment in practice, and consider applying a higher CCF to certain commitments as appropriate.

applies_to.note: National-discretion uplift; consumer protection law limiting card line cancellation is precisely the kind of factor contemplated, so the effective CCF in a given jurisdiction may exceed 10%.

R-CRE20.100-supervisors-may-require-high.portfolio_relevance: Introduces jurisdictional uncertainty into the 10% card CCF, meaning a card-heavy strategy carries the risk that the effective conversion factor on unused lines is raised by the supervisor.

R-CRE20.101-lower-of-two-ccfs.title: Apply the lower of two applicable CCFs for a commitment on an off-balance sheet item
R-CRE20.101-lower-of-two-ccfs.statement: Where there is an undertaking to provide a commitment on an off-balance sheet item, banks apply the lower of the two applicable credit conversion factors.
R-CRE20.101-lower-of-two-ccfs.quote: Where there is an undertaking to provide a commitment on an off-balance sheet item, banks are to apply the lower of the two applicable CCFs.

applies_to.note: The footnote confirms an unconditionally cancellable commitment to issue direct credit substitutes attracts 10% rather than 100%.

R-CRE20.101-lower-of-two-ccfs.portfolio_relevance: Lets a bank structure layered facilities so the cheapest applicable CCF governs, meaning unconditional cancellability dominates the conversion factor of everything it wraps.

R-CRE20.103-nth-to-default-1250-cap.title: 1250% aggregation cap for first-to-default credit derivative protection sold
R-CRE20.103-nth-to-default-1250-cap.statement: A bank selling protection through a first-to-default credit derivative must aggregate the risk weights of the basket assets up to a maximum of 1250% and multiply by the nominal amount of protection provided to obtain risk-weighted assets.
R-CRE20.103-nth-to-default-1250-cap.quote: the risk weights of the assets included in the basket must be aggregated up to a maximum of 1250% and multiplied by the nominal amount of the protection provided by the credit derivative

applies_to.note: Banking book credit derivative protection sold; not a typical small bank position.

R-CRE20.103-nth-to-default-1250-cap.portfolio_relevance: Caps but heavily penalises synthetic credit risk acquisition, closing off basket credit derivatives as a cheap way to add credit exposure instead of originating loans.

R-CRE20.104-defaulted-exposure-90-days.title: Definition of a defaulted exposure: more than 90 days past due
R-CRE20.104-defaulted-exposure-90-days.statement: For standardised approach risk-weighting a defaulted exposure is one past due for more than 90 days or an exposure to a defaulted borrower, and a borrower is defaulted if any material credit obligation is past due for more than 90 days.
R-CRE20.104-defaulted-exposure-90-days.quote: a defaulted exposure is defined as one that is past due for more than 90 days, or is an exposure to a defaulted borrower. A defaulted borrower is a borrower in respect of whom any of the following events have occurred: (1) Any material credit obligation that is past due for more than 90 days.

applies_to.note: Overdrafts are past due once the customer breaches an advised limit or is advised of a limit smaller than current outstandings; 90-day delinquency is reported in US call report Schedule RC-N.

numeric_values: past due for more than 90 days
R-CRE20.104-defaulted-exposure-90-days.portfolio_relevance: The 90 day trigger is the point at which a card receivable jumps from 75% to 150% risk weight, so delinquency roll rates translate directly into RWA volatility.

R-CRE20.104-distressed-restructuring-tri.title: Distressed restructuring is a default event
R-CRE20.104-distressed-restructuring-tri.statement: A distressed restructuring of any credit obligation, meaning a restructuring that may result in a diminished financial obligation caused by material forgiveness or postponement of principal, interest or fees, agreed by the bank constitutes default of the borrower.
R-CRE20.104-distressed-restructuring-tri.quote: (5) A distressed restructuring of any credit obligation (ie a restructuring that may result in a diminished financial obligation caused by the material forgiveness, or postponement, of principal, interest or (where relevant) fees) is agreed by the bank;

applies_to.note: Directly constrains portfolio restructuring: forbearance programmes that materially forgive or postpone amounts push accounts into default treatment.

R-CRE20.104-distressed-restructuring-tri.portfolio_relevance: Means a bank cannot restructure a stressed card book out of high risk weights, since the act of granting material forbearance itself triggers defaulted status and the 100-150% weights.

R-CRE20.104-writeoff-provision-trigger.title: Account-specific provision or write-off is a default event
R-CRE20.104-writeoff-provision-trigger.statement: A write-off or account-specific provision made as a result of a significant perceived decline in credit quality after the bank took on the exposure constitutes default of the borrower.
R-CRE20.104-writeoff-provision-trigger.quote: (3) A write-off or account-specific provision is made as a result of a significant perceived decline in credit quality subsequent to the bank taking on any credit exposure to the borrower;

applies_to.note: Links accounting provisioning decisions directly to regulatory default classification.

R-CRE20.104-writeoff-provision-trigger.portfolio_relevance: Creates a coupling between provisioning policy and RWA: raising specific provisions on an account both marks it defaulted and, per CRE20.106, can lower its weight from 150% to 100%.

R-CRE20.105-retail-default-at-obligation.title: Retail default may be assessed per obligation rather than per borrower
R-CRE20.105-retail-default-at-obligation.statement: For retail exposures the definition of default may be applied at the level of the particular credit obligation rather than the borrower, so default on one obligation does not require treating the borrower's other obligations as defaulted.
R-CRE20.105-retail-default-at-obligation.quote: For retail exposures, the definition of default can be applied at the level of a particular credit obligation, rather than at the level of the borrower. As such, default by a borrower on one obligation does not require a bank to treat all other obligations to the banking group as defaulted.

applies_to.note: Retail-only relief from the cross-default principle applied to other exposure classes.

R-CRE20.105-retail-default-at-obligation.portfolio_relevance: Contains contagion of default status within a retail relationship, so a defaulted card does not drag a performing auto loan to the same borrower into the 150% bucket.

R-CRE20.106-defaulted-150pct-low-provisi.title: 150% risk weight on defaulted exposures with specific provisions below 20%
R-CRE20.106-defaulted-150pct-low-provisi.statement: The unsecured or unguaranteed portion of a defaulted exposure, risk-weighted net of specific provisions and partial write-offs, receives a 150% risk weight when specific provisions are less than 20% of the outstanding loan amount.
R-CRE20.106-defaulted-150pct-low-provisi.quote: (1) 150% risk weight when specific provisions are less than 20% of the outstanding amount of the loan;

applies_to.note: Excludes residential real estate exposures treated under CRE20.107.

numeric_values: specific provisions less than 20% of the outstanding amount
R-CRE20.106-defaulted-150pct-low-provisi.portfolio_relevance: Doubles the risk weight of a defaulted card receivable relative to a performing one unless the bank provisions at least 20% against it, tying reserve coverage directly to RWA.

R-CRE20.106-defaulted-100pct-high-provis.title: 100% risk weight on defaulted exposures with specific provisions of 20% or more
R-CRE20.106-defaulted-100pct-high-provis.statement: The unsecured or unguaranteed portion of a defaulted exposure receives a 100% risk weight when specific provisions are equal to or greater than 20% of the outstanding loan amount.
R-CRE20.106-defaulted-100pct-high-provis.quote: (2) 100% risk weight when specific provisions are equal or greater than 20% of the outstanding amount of the loan.

applies_to.note: The 20% provision coverage level is the exact switch point between the two weights.

numeric_values: specific provisions equal or greater than 20% of the outstanding amount
R-CRE20.106-defaulted-100pct-high-provis.portfolio_relevance: Gives a computable provisioning target: taking specific provisions to 20% of a defaulted balance cuts its risk weight by a third, so reserve policy is a direct RWA lever on a deteriorating card book.

R-CRE20.106fn-50pct-discretion-high-cove.title: National discretion to apply 50% weight where provisions reach 50% coverage
R-CRE20.106fn-50pct-discretion-high-cove.statement: National supervisors have discretion to reduce the risk weight on defaulted exposures to 50% when specific provisions are no less than 50% of the outstanding loan amount.
R-CRE20.106fn-50pct-discretion-high-cove.quote: National supervisors have discretion to reduce the risk weight to 50% when specific provisions are no less than 50% of the outstanding amount of the loan.

applies_to.note: National discretion; not adopted in every jurisdiction, so its availability must be checked against local implementation.

numeric_values: specific provisions no less than 50% of the outstanding amount
R-CRE20.106fn-50pct-discretion-high-cove.portfolio_relevance: Where adopted, provisioning a defaulted balance to 50% coverage makes it cheaper in RWA terms than a performing card revolver, strongly rewarding aggressive reserve building.

R-CRE20.107-defaulted-residential-100pct.title: 100% risk weight for defaulted residential real estate not cash-flow dependent
R-CRE20.107-defaulted-residential-100pct.statement: Defaulted residential real estate exposures where repayments do not materially depend on cash flows generated by the property are risk weighted net of specific provisions and partial write-offs at 100%, regardless of provision coverage.
R-CRE20.107-defaulted-residential-100pct.quote: Defaulted residential real estate exposures where repayments do not materially depend on cash flows generated by the property securing the loan shall be risk- weighted net of specific provisions and partial write-offs at 100%.

applies_to.note: Carve-out from the CRE20.106 provision-dependent scale; eligible guarantees and collateral may still be recognised.

R-CRE20.107-defaulted-residential-100pct.portfolio_relevance: Caps defaulted owner-occupied mortgage weight at 100% versus 150% for a defaulted card balance, so mortgage credit deterioration is less RWA-punitive than card deterioration.

R-CRE20.109-threshold-deduction-250pct.title: 250% risk weight on non-deducted threshold deduction items
R-CRE20.109-threshold-deduction-250pct.statement: A 250% risk weight applies to the amounts of significant investments in unconsolidated financial institutions' common shares, mortgage servicing rights and temporary-difference deferred tax assets that are not deducted from Common Equity Tier 1 under the CAP30.32 and CAP30.33 thresholds.
R-CRE20.109-threshold-deduction-250pct.quote: A 250% risk weight applies to the amount of the three “threshold deduction” items listed in CAP30.32

applies_to.note: Highly relevant to small US banks, which commonly carry material mortgage servicing rights and deferred tax assets.

R-CRE20.109-threshold-deduction-250pct.portfolio_relevance: Makes deferred tax assets and mortgage servicing rights among the most RWA-expensive items on a small bank's balance sheet, so reducing them is often a cheaper route to a higher capital ratio than shrinking the card book.

R-CRE20.110-other-assets-standard-weight.title: Standard risk weights for other assets: 100%, 0% for cash and gold, 20% for items in collection
R-CRE20.110-other-assets-standard-weight.statement: All other assets receive a standard 100% risk weight, except cash owned and held at the bank or in transit and qualifying gold bullion at 0%, and cash items in the process of collection at 20%.
R-CRE20.110-other-assets-standard-weight.quote: The standard risk weight for all other assets will be 100%, with the exception of the following exposures: (1) A 0% risk weight will apply to: (a) cash owned and held at the bank or in transit; and (b) gold bullion held at the bank or held in another bank on an allocated basis, to the extent the gold bullion assets are backed by gold bullion liabilities. (2) A 20% risk weight will apply to cash items in the process of collection.

applies_to.note: Residual bucket covering premises, equipment and other non-credit assets; right-of-use lease assets are risk weighted at 100% per the FAQ.

R-CRE20.110-other-assets-standard-weight.portfolio_relevance: Fixed assets and other non-earning assets consume more RWA per dollar than a transactor card balance at 45%, so balance sheet efficiency arguments cut against carrying excess premises and equipment.

R-RBC20.1-cet1-min-4.5.title: Minimum Common Equity Tier 1 ratio of 4.5% of RWA
R-RBC20.1-cet1-min-4.5.statement: A bank must hold Common Equity Tier 1 capital of at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets at all times.
R-RBC20.1-cet1-min-4.5.quote: (1) Common Equity Tier 1 must be at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets (RWA).

applies_to.note: Basel binds internationally active banks; in the US the 4.5% CET1 minimum is applied to all banking organisations under 12 CFR 217.10.

R-RBC20.1-cet1-min-4.5.portfolio_relevance: Sets the hardest denominator constraint: every incremental dollar of credit card RWA consumes at least 4.5 cents of CET1, so growth in high-risk-weight revolving retail is capped by retained earnings and equity issuance.

R-RBC20.1-tier1-min-6.title: Minimum Tier 1 capital ratio of 6% of RWA
R-RBC20.1-tier1-min-6.statement: A bank must hold Tier 1 capital of at least 6% of risk-weighted assets at all times.
R-RBC20.1-tier1-min-6.quote: (2) Tier 1 capital must be at least 6% of RWA.

applies_to.note: Applies at all times; measured net of CAP30 regulatory adjustments.

R-RBC20.1-tier1-min-6.portfolio_relevance: Allows up to 1.5 percentage points of the 6% to be filled with Additional Tier 1, giving a bank that cannot raise common equity a limited alternative route to fund credit portfolio growth.

R-RBC20.1-total-capital-min-8.title: Minimum Total capital ratio of 8.0% of RWA
R-RBC20.1-total-capital-min-8.statement: A bank must hold Total capital of at least 8.0% of risk-weighted assets at all times.
R-RBC20.1-total-capital-min-8.quote: (3) Total capital must be at least 8.0% of RWA.

applies_to.note: Total capital = CET1 + AT1 + Tier 2, net of CAP30 adjustments.

R-RBC20.1-total-capital-min-8.portfolio_relevance: The 8% total requirement is the binding constraint for banks that fund credit growth with Tier 2 subordinated debt and eligible general loan-loss reserves rather than equity.

R-RBC20.1-ccb-2.5-footnote.title: Capital conservation buffer of 2.5% of RWA sits above the minimums
R-RBC20.1-ccb-2.5-footnote.statement: In addition to the minimum ratios, a Common Equity Tier 1 capital conservation buffer of 2.5% of RWA applies to all banks.
R-RBC20.1-ccb-2.5-footnote.quote: In addition, a Common Equity Tier 1 capital conservation buffer is set at 2.5% of RWA for all banks.

applies_to.note: Stated for all banks; systemic surcharges and the countercyclical buffer sit on top and are described in RBC30 and RBC40.

R-RBC20.1-ccb-2.5-footnote.portfolio_relevance: Raises the effective CET1 hurdle on credit card RWA from 4.5% to 7.0% for any bank that wishes to keep paying dividends, which is the practically binding number for a small US card lender.

R-RBC20.2-capital-net-of-adjustments.title: Capital used in the ratios must be net of regulatory adjustments
R-RBC20.2-capital-net-of-adjustments.statement: The capital components used to test the minimum ratios are defined in CAP10 and must be used net of the regulatory adjustments in CAP30.
R-RBC20.2-capital-net-of-adjustments.quote: The components of capital referred to in RBC20.1 are defined in CAP10 and must be used net of regulatory adjustments (defined in CAP30) and subject to the transitional arrangements in CAP90.

applies_to.note: Links the ratio numerator to the CAP10 eligibility criteria and CAP30 deductions.

R-RBC20.2-capital-net-of-adjustments.portfolio_relevance: Means that reported book equity overstates the capital available to support a credit card book; deductions such as goodwill from card portfolio acquisitions and DTAs from loan-loss allowances shrink the usable numerator.

R-RBC20.4-rwa-higher-of.title: RWA for compliance is the higher of nominated-approach RWA and the output floor
R-RBC20.4-rwa-higher-of.statement: The RWA used to test the minimum ratios and the buffers must be the higher of RWA computed under the bank's nominated approaches and the output floor amount.
R-RBC20.4-rwa-higher-of.quote: The RWA that banks must use to determine compliance with the requirements set out in RBC20.1 (and the buffers in RBC30 and RBC40) is the higher of:

applies_to.note: Only bites for banks using internally modelled approaches; a small bank on the standardised approach alone has floor RWA equal to its own RWA.

R-RBC20.4-rwa-higher-of.portfolio_relevance: Ensures the same RWA denominator is used for both the minimums and the buffers, so any modelled reduction in credit card RWA also has to survive the standardised floor before it releases buffer headroom.

R-RBC20.4-output-floor-72.5.title: Output floor at 72.5% of standardised RWA
R-RBC20.4-output-floor-72.5.statement: RWA must be at least 72.5% of the RWA that would result from calculating credit, market and operational risk using only the listed standardised approaches.
R-RBC20.4-output-floor-72.5.quote: (2) 72.5% of the sum of the elements listed in point (1) above, calculated using only the standardised approaches listed in RBC20.11.

applies_to.note: Subject to transitional arrangements in RBC90; irrelevant for banks that use only standardised approaches, ie most small North American banks.

R-RBC20.4-output-floor-72.5.portfolio_relevance: Caps the RWA benefit an IRB bank can extract from modelling low PD/LGD on transactor credit card balances at 27.5% below the standardised outcome.
